title: A party, 101 princesses and an eccentric millionaire: Jon Ronson on a mysterious castle – and what it taught him about masculinity in crisis | Life and style | The Guardian
description: When my son texted me from a Connecticut fortress in the middle of the night with an alarming message, it set me on a quest to understand the bizarre lifestyle of its owner
Author: Jon Ronson
Headline: When my son texted me from a Connecticut fortress in the middle of the night with an alarming message, it set me on a quest to understand the bizarre lifestyle of its owner
Content: Chris Mark in front of his castle with two of his pet camels, which used to live in the grounds.Photograph: Marisa Balletti-LavoieView image in fullscreenChris Mark in front of his castle with two of his pet camels, which used to live in the grounds.Photograph: Marisa Balletti-LavoieLife and styleA party, 101 princesses and an eccentric millionaire: Jon Ronson on a mysterious castle – and what it taught him about masculinity in crisisWhen my son texted me from a Connecticut fortress in the middle of the night with an alarming message, it set me on a quest to understand the bizarre lifestyle of its ownerJon RonsonFri 21 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIawoke one morning in the summer of 2023 to discover that, while I’d slept, my son Joel had been texting my wife and me a series of unnerving messages about a perilous situation he had found himself in, in Connecticut.From what I could tell, as I frantically tried to piece together the night’s events, one of Joel’s friends had been invited to a party being held by a stranger she’d met that week on Tinder. So Joel and two others went along for the ride. But when they arrived, they found the man’s home so bizarre that Joel did something he’d never done before – he sent me the coordinates of his location and a photograph, just in case.The photograph was of a vast medieval castle with a drawbridge, gargoyles and many – I couldn’t shake the sense that there weretoomany – spires, towers and turrets, reaching like skeletal fingers to the looming clouds above.“I honestly have no clue what is going on,” read Joel’s second text. “This is very weird.” Then: “You drive down a road in the middle of a forest and then there’s this gate and it’s just a huge, massive castle.”It was a few days later and Joel and his friends were sitting in my office, recounting for me the disquieting events that had occurred that night. It began with an invitation to one of Joel’s female friends: “Castle party Saturday! 3:00pm to whenever. Dress code: Formal. Tell your friends. 18+ to come, 21+ to drink.”It was a three-hour drive from New York City to the pleasant town of Woodstock, Connecticut (160 miles from the more famous Woodstock, New York, of festival fame). Then their GPS took them out of town, on to a winding forest road, and finally to a set of imposing iron gates. They stared at the menacing castle that loomed beyond, urgently discussed turning around, but then the gates swung open and they found themselves entering.Standing on the drawbridge were a man, a woman and a large black dog. The man was the castle’s owner, Chris Mark. He was in his early 60s.“He had sharp blue eyes,” Joel’s friend Delaney said, “but glazed over.”“And he had a cut above one of his eyes,” said Joel.The dog was called Cerberus, named after the multi‑headed hound that guards the gates of Hades. The woman was blond and much younger.View image in fullscreenChris Mark Castle in Woodstock, Connecticut.Photograph: Tyra PachecoMark beckoned them inside. They crossed the drawbridge and entered the grand banqueting hall to discover …there was no party. The room was completely empty, all except for a small number of equally bewildered young people standing around awkwardly.“I’m sorry, but where’s the party?” someone asked.“Oh no,” Mark replied. “I’ve invited you here for a different reason.” The room fell silent.“Which is?” someone asked.“I’d like you all to take part in my reality show,” Mark replied.“What’s the name of your reality show?” Joel asked.“101 Princesses,” he replied.“What’s the core concept?” Joel asked.“I’m the lord,” Mark replied. “I’m looking for my queen and I’ve got 101 princesses to choose from.”He turned to Joel’s female friends. “Are you ready to get into your princess costumes? Come downstairs to my costume room.”Which they did.double quotation markThe filming began. Chris Mark walked in and a woman who apparently lived at the castle curtseyed and said: ‘Yes, my lord?’View image in fullscreenChris Mark in his castle.Photograph: Marisa Balletti-LavoieI found this part of their story especially melancholy, that these young people were prepared to follow him to the bowels of his castle to dress as princesses.Mark’s costume room was located near his hot tub grotto room, which doubled as his botanical gardens. Whirlpool baths nestled among subterranean plants illuminated by purple lamps. In the next room was his pole-dancing nightclub. There were mannequins and, one of Joel’s female friends said, “a whole collection of extravagant princess attire, racks of medieval gowns and a glass display case of tiaras. He told me to choose a dress and pick a tiara to match.”Mark seemed far more interested in the young women than in Joel and his male friend Cement, but he gave them tuxedos to change into all the same.After the women re-emerged,wearing princess outfits and tiaras, a videographer appeared. They were assured that while 101 Princesses hadn’t yet been set up with a network, it would end up on Netflix. Then filming began. Mark walked in and a woman who apparently lived at the castle curtseyed and said: “Yes, my lord?”Yet Mark seemed increasingly on edge, irritated that Joel and his friends were observing rather than participating in 101 Princesses.(It isn’t entirely clear what participating would have entailed. But they were told it was “a collaborative project” and the makers would be open to ideas. Joel later surmised that along with dance skits and other castle-themed vignettes, the princesses would have been encouraged to make out with each other on camera, while Joel and Cement would have appeared in scenes in which they were rejected by the princesses in favour of Mark.)Finally, seemingly exasperated by their lack of interest, Mark sent his videographer to inform them that: “Chris wants everyone to leave. Everyone has to leavenow.” And that was the end of their story. I stood up to thank them for telling it to me, then I let out a scream.In terms of them finding themselves in unsettling situations with older men, Joel and his friends were, I have to admit, somewhat out of the frying pan and into the fire. Six days earlier, I had been in surgery, having a foot of my colon removed due to diverticulitis. I was still in pain, which was causing me to let out sudden, unexpected shrieks.I’d been recuperating partly by sitting on park benches, staring out at nothing, trying to think up ideas for stories. But after about 10 minutes, I’d invariably find myself overwhelmed by a dreadful thought:I’m just a man sitting on a bench. It’s a terrible feeling, that sense of purposelessness, which is why I spent the following days not sensibly convalescing but instead learning whatever I could about Mark and his castle.The castle, although you’d never know it from the photographs, is newly built. Construction began in 2003 and was completed in 2010. Mark’s money was inherited. His great-grandfather Clayton had been a gilded age steel tycoon – the owner of the Clayton Mark & Company.Back during construction, when rumours were circulating around Woodstock that a wealthy scion was building an ostentatious castle on the edge of town, journalists managed to unearth fragments of strange stories about the place. Like how it had been claimed during Mark’s 2010 divorce hearing that one of the couple’s pet camels had starved to death due to neglect. Mark blamed his estranged wife; she blamed him – but given that camels can last for several months without food, that sounded like alotof neglect.Sixteen days after my surgery, I drove three hours to Mark’s castle. Each time my car hit a bump it tore at the still-raw scar, causing me to yell out. Still, I had no regrets. I was embarking on a story, one that had crashed into my life unannounced. It’s always nerve-racking to be driving into the unknown – and this journeydidfeel like it might be dangerous – but the sense of purpose I get from following strange stories like this is more powerful than any painkiller.Mark was waiting for me on his drawbridge. He knew I was coming. I’d texted him to say I was a nonfiction writer and that “my son and his friends were invited to take part in 101 Princesses, and they told me about the extraordinary world you’ve created for yourself at the castle. I’d love to come and write about it.”“OK,” he’d replied.double quotation markI always thought it would be amazing if I had living here six, eight girls, but the princessing only works if the girls love girlsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tyra PachecoHe beckoned me inside. I passed an Egyptian sarcophagusand a suit of armour, its helmet tilted forlornly towards the ground. Perhaps because of my proximity to these privately owned relics of war and death, I found myself brooding over my surgery; how while under anaesthetic I must have resembled, for a moment at least, a medieval drawing of a heretic being tortured, intestines spilling out – a drawing that wouldn’t have looked out of place inside this remarkable but disquieting castle.Guarding this great fortress had clearly gone to Cerberus’s head, because he repeatedly lurched at me and bit my foot – too hard to be considered playful, not hard enough to be deemed an assault.“Hey, pal,” I said tentatively. And, “Hey, buddy.” Finally, I tried to engage Mark. “Your dog does like biting my foot,” I said.“For some reason it’s not a negative thing,” he replied. “It means he likes you or something.”“Oh, OK,” I said.“How do you convince people to visit the castle and take part in 101 Princesses?” I asked him.“I go on dating apps,” he replied, “and I make some kind of relationship. Then I have them come here and I adapt them to this lifestyle.”I asked how he “adapts them”, and he explained that some of them have never had sex with other women so he has to coax them into trying it: “I always thought it would be amazing if I had living here six, eight girls, but the only way it works is if the girls love girls. That’s how the princessing works.”“Princessing?” I thought.“We go out and find more girls,” Mark continued, “because they’re looking for themselves. And I just benefit from it.”So it was fortunate, he said, that once he brings them round to the idea of sex with other women, “they actually really like it”.I noticed several young women padding silently around in the darkness. Some looked away when they saw me glancing in their direction; others eyed me with suspicion.I continued to pepper him with questions about his life inside the castle. Eventually, it evidently dawned on him that he was saying unwise things to a journalist, because he suddenly stood up, walked to a kitchen drawer and retrieved a document from a pile of identical documents. It was a non-disclosure agreement.“I need you to sign,” he said.“I don’t feel comfortable signing an NDA,” I said.He looked sharply at me. But he relented. He put the paperwork back in the drawer. But the atmosphere had changed, and soon afterwards I thanked him for allowing me to visit and left.I had many questions. For instance: who comes up with a word like “princessing”? Also, why was he trying to control me with an NDA? Moreover, why did he have a wholepileof NDAs? Who else was he asking to sign them, and why?Several weeks later, I was driving Joel from upstate New York to Manhattan when Mark began sending me a series of texts – 42 of them during the three‑hour journey. I asked Joel to read them out to me. He picked up my phone, his eyes darting, and read out an increasingly disturbing sample.“I’m meeting with my lawyers tonight,” he read. “I’ll spend whatever it takes to protect my family. I’m having the largest international investigation company learn everything about you. I want to get to know you really well.”I flinched. The car swerved.There were more pings. This time, as Joel looked at the texts, I saw his eyes widen in shock.“What?” I asked.“I’m going to be sending you some of my friends that were in prison for killing somebody,” Joel read. “Maybe you could help them write something good so they can turn their lives around … One of my good friends who got out of prison is on his way to New York today … Do not ever mention anything negative about the castle because this guy will get really upset. He thinks I’m like a god, and you don’t want to see him angry. He just got out of jail like a week ago and has been in there for, like, 15 years … To be honest, I’m even a little bit afraid of some of these people … Carlos and Brandon are on their way to New York right now.”double quotation markHe said how much he loved Playboy and that Hugh Hefner was one of his idolsJoel fell silent. “Meet them,” he said.“You want me tomeetCarlos and Brandon?” I said.“Yes,” he said. “But take security with you. Take five security guards.”“I’m not going to take five security guards to meet Carlos and Brandon,” I said. “You want me to escalate this to gang warfare?”Joel looked frustrated by my reluctance to hit back harder, but the truth was those last texts had brightened my mood. Libel courts surely don’t respond well to plaintiffs threatening journalists with visits from murderers – especially not when the threats were read out to the journalist by his own son, who was arguably emotionally harmed by them.“Yes,” I thought. “This is good.”Mark’s volley of texts continued. I was surprised by how uninhibited they were. He was saying the worst things he could think of: “Everything is a mirror. You destroy someone and someone destroys you.” But he’d intersperse these ominous messages with positive character references from friends and colleagues: “I am Shaolin kung fu grandmaster Tyrone Bullock. Chris Mark is an amazing and remarkable person with such a wonderful heart.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo be honest, I felt the threats were rendering the character references somewhat redundant, but on rereading the messages I was pleased to notice him dialling back the eeriness regarding Carlos and Brandon, even offering to cover my costs.“If you take my murder friends out,” he texted, “I’ll Venmo you the money.”The next day, I received an email out of the blue:Hi Jon,I am a friend and advisor to Chris Mark and handle a number of business matters for him. Somehow, someway, you really got under his skin and it’s driving him crazy … I’d love for some feedback so I can get a sense of what is happening. Thanks,Charles CadyEleven days later, I sat on Cady’s terrace, overlooking his woodland and stream, five miles from Mark’s castle. He was in his late 60s, and with his kindly demeanour he reminded me of a favourite grandfather from a Frank Capra film.“Chris and I were doing 15, 20 phone calls and texts a day about you,” he told me.“Oh God,” I said. “He says he has two murderers on his staff?”Cady chuckled.“I assume those people don’t exist,” I said.“Theydoexist,” he said.But he assured me Mark was “completely harmless”, and that he only had ex-convicts on his staff to give them a second chance in life.But I must have hit a nerve, because at the end of our two-hour conversation, Cady glanced out over his quiet, rolling land and suddenly said: “If I suspected in the least there was something creepy going on, I’d drop it like a hot potato. I have no desire to see a police car pull into the yard. I don’t have any room for that in my world.”Before Joel and his friends were kicked out that night, they’d swapped numbers with two other young women who’d arrived under similar pretences. Now, I was on the phone to one of them. I’ll call her Ari. She filled me in on what had happened next – how they’d all piled into Mark’s Rolls-Royce to go clubbing in Boston, and how Mark kept “asking if we’d be down to film a shower scene or a hot tub scene with a bunch of women. At that point we figured maybe this wasn’t actually a Netflix show.”“By the way,” I asked her, “did he ever happen to mention Hugh Hefner to you?”“Yes!” she exclaimed. “He said how much he loved Playboy, and that 101 Princesses was based on the whole Playboy situation. He said Hugh Hefner was one of his idols.”It struck me that Mark was trying to be Hugh Hefner during surely the worst period in human history to be Hugh Hefner. Unless you’re the creme de la creme of manosphere influencers, you can’t lord it over princesses in your castle like it’s the 1970s any more.And so, despite there being nothing immediately relatable about his story, being a tale about the complexities of luring women to your castle in the post‑#MeToo age, I could see a resonance. It was a story about men out of time, men failing to adjust to a world that was moving away from them. The world had changed shape and all kinds of men were discovering there were things they’d once done that they couldn’t do any more.Mark’s situation was, of course, bizarre and extreme. He had the resources to construct a fantasy bubble within which he could pretend his lifestyle wasn’t dated and weird and damaging, but aspirational. However, I was picturing less empowered and more sympathetic men than him – men who used to derive structure and meaning from, say, office or factory life, and were now struggling to adjust to a society that had reorganised itself without them in such a central position.Some were instead scratching a living as YouTubers, “personal brands”, content creators with no job protections, while others were withdrawing, folding in on themselves.There’s data to prove it. By 2022, one in six US men aged between 25 and 54 wasn’t working. But within that statistic was a more startling one: two‑thirds of those menweren’t even looking for jobs. That’s 6.7 million US men, and countless more around the world, who’ve just … bowed out.I was aghast. Why had those men opted out of society? What havoc was that purposelessness wreaking on their inner lives, and on the lives of their loved ones – partners, parents, children? And given that some of them would inevitably grow sick of a life in the shadows – of a life of male nothingness – what might happen next?While many traditionally male sectors, such as factory work, are dying, I’ve noticed one role for men that’s flourishing: actors who can play doofuses in television ads. Modern TV commercials, certainly, are an orgy of male buffoonery, of men who can’t do anything right and have to be constantly bailed out by their exasperated wives. I’ve watched men falling off lawnmowers, driving off cliffs (1st forWomeninsurance), accidentally abandoning their babies on restaurant conveyer belts (Philadelphia cream cheese) and being terrible at sex (Domino’s pizza).“Hey, honey,” says the man in the Domino’s ad, “the Domino’s lady just said we’ve got 30 minutes. Are you thinking what I’m thinking?”His partner looks at him. “What are we going to do with the other 28 minutes?” she says.I wondered about the actors who play the doofuses. Are there particular go-to men who invariably snag the parts? I messaged the veteran casting director Zita Zutic Konak, and she emailed back: “Hi Jon, meet Ed – a wonderful actor who we’ve cast in these types of roles previously.”Ed has played a man in a Specsavers ad who misses his plane because everything goes wrong at the airport due to his own ineptitude and the general frustrations of modernity. He can’t scan his boarding pass. The barcode won’t work. He refuses to give up his water at security so he guzzles it down, drenching his Hawaiian shirt. He loses his hand luggage on the moving walkway. He can’t find the gate. The ad ends with his wife, who’s already through security, looking long-suffering and irritated.“I did one for Scholl insoles where I had to gallop like a horse,” Ed said. “I’m a regular guy walking to work, but then I put on these really comfortable insoles and I start galloping like a horse down the street. I had to look quite doofusy for that.”“Fifty years ago,” I said, “there was the Marlboro man being stoical and masculine on a horse, whereas nowadays you have tobethe horse.”“Yeah,” said Ed. He thought about it. “But when you look at those old ads, do you relate to those men on any level?”“You’re right,” I said. “I don’t relate to the Marlboro Man at all. I relate far more to the man who can’t make it through the airport.”As the old structures collapse – across both office and factory life – men who feel cut adrift have had no shortage of advice about how to re-anchor themselves. Some men’s health influencers advocate stoicism, while others encourage the opposite: vulnerability, that “once we finally reveal what’s under our ‘manly masks’ we can start to live authentically”.Then there’s all those doofus men blundering around the culture. Clearly, all this reimagining of what it means to be “male” has been disorienting or irritating for some men, leaving them feeling tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actuallymeans.View image in fullscreenManospher influencer Dan Bilzerian.Photograph: Jerod Harris/Getty Images for Ignite International BrandsPerhaps that’s in part why yet another male archetype has emerged – the Manosphere Man.Take influencer and virulent antisemite Dan Bilzerian, whose 28.7 million Instagram followers get to watch him sit on thrones next to lions, walk through forests with assault rifles, and dine on private yachts with near-naked women and, in his pre‑incarceration days, with Andrew Tate.“I had sex nine times in one day. I was so proud of myself,” he told Joe Rogan in 2016, sounding a lot like Mark. And “I couldn’t fuck all the girls if I had five dicks … I’m not bragging.”“I salute you, sir,” Rogan said at one point. “You’re living a life that doesn’t even seem real.”Several months had passed since I’d been in contact with Mark. Finally, though, my curiosity got the better of me and I texted him: “How are things at the castle?” “Everything at the castle’s good,” he replied. He was working on new reality show proposals. He sent me one. It was called Queen to Fraud, and, per its synopsis, it would document Mark’s “battle for justice against Anya and Sasha [not their real names], two women who manipulated his wealth and engaged in deception on a massive scale. Tagline: She was supposed to be the queen. But she became the queen of fraud.”BothAnya and Sasha had, at one time or another, lived at the castle. Mark had already told me about Anya – how she’d reported him to the police for trying to throw her into his moat, “but they looked at my surveillance videos and saw she was lying”.I didn’t know Sasha, but the Queen to Fraud pitch document outlined his complaints against her – how he’d showered her with “endless luxuries”, but then she was disloyal to him in Bangkok. Episode three, “Betrayal in Thailand”, would recreate “the shocking moment Sasha disappears to buy drugs, leaving Christopher stranded and sick”. But by episode 10, “The Maximum Sentence”, he’d get his restitution. He’d collaborate “with law enforcement to ensure the harshest penalties” for the women’s treacheries.I suppose that answered my question about how things were going – evidently,notwell. In the short time I’d known Mark he’d gone from developing a reality show where he’d meet and woo his queen to one where he’d have her imprisoned – a similar arc, it struck me, as Henry VIII’s.He sent me ChatGPT’s assessment of Queen to Fraud. It called it “the most compelling entertainment project ever created”.“AI likes you a lot!” I texted him.“That’s who I talk to most of my time,” he replied.We continued to correspond and I met him in Fort Lauderdale, in the lobby of a beachfront hotel called Ocean Manor. He was in Florida, he said, because he was planning to build another castle and was scouting for locations. There, he outlined for me another new plan – to construct in his Connecticut castle’s grounds an orphanage called Ark of Light.“Is Charles helping you out with this?” I asked. Mark shook his head. “I don’t know what happened to him,” he replied, looking genuinely baffled. “We talked almost every day up until a few weeks ago.”Cady – Mark’s friend, spokesman and business adviser for 20 years – was suddenly no longer returning his calls? It had always been Cady’s job to handle Mark’s permit applications, on occasions when Mark had, for instance, tried to turn the castle into a bed and breakfast or a wedding venue. Now that the responsibility had presumably fallen to Mark, was he concerned that the town of Woodstock might not grant him a zone variance for a campus of orphaned prodigies?He shrugged it off. “They’d look bad if they go against me,” he said.This was Mark falling for ChatGPT’s sycophancy again. The chatbot had assured him that should Woodstock choose to “fight a billionaire humanitarian trying to help people, headlines would be brutal: Town of Woodstock opposes billionaire’s plan to feed millions.”double quotation markMy head exploded after I met with the feds. I feel incredibly, incredibly naiveCharles CadyMark’s devotion to ChatGPT was far from uncommon by this point. Millions were falling for its obsequiousness. It felt like a ripple from the downfall of the old structures. People fall apart, people become directionless, and the tech companies swoop in with new ways to monetise our feeling of purposelessness – our desire to be of use – by telling us we aren’t worthless. Far from it. We’re creating “the most compelling entertainment project ever”.A breakup can be good news for a journalist, and so, after I left Florida, I messaged Cady to let him know I’d just interviewed Mark again.“Lucky you, spending quality time with Chris,” he replied.There was a distinct and, I thought, intriguing change in his tone. We arranged to meet. I arrived at the restaurant early. Cady was already there, looking grave, tapping his fingers on the table. I sat down. We ordered lunch. And then Cady told me the news.Mark, he’d learned, was under investigation for a number of alleged sex-related crimes. It was at a federal level, with several agencies involved, including the Department of Homeland Security.“My head exploded after I met with the feds,” Cady said. “I am angry and upset. And I started thinking, ‘Oh my God, what was I involved in as an unsuspecting individual?’ I feel incredibly, incredibly naive.”At this time of writing, August 2026, the investigation into Mark is ongoing. Of course, an investigation is not evidence of criminal wrongdoing – and he has not been charged in the US. Maybe he never will be. I don’t know where Mark is. I’ve heard he’s abroad, perhaps in south‑east Asia. Maybe he’s anxious about returning to the US due to the police investigation, and the publication of my book, which tells the stories of many unravelling men, including him. But after I left Cady that day, I dug and dug and I finally feel I’ve learned the truth of what was really going on inside his castle.I think that, like many men, Mark was trying to create a fantasy life within which he didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on his own terms. It’s a growing phenomenon – men responding to the collapse of the old structures, and a shift in power, by becoming like separatists, succumbing to uninhibited behaviour, trying to create false utopias where they can behave however they want. But it feels like the experiment is failing. As Mark is presumably learning, sometimes when you push boundaries, reality bites back.When approached by the Guardian for comment on this article, Chris Mark said thatJon Ronsonhad “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner”. In relation to 101 Princesses, Mark denied deliberately deceiving people into coming to the castle, adding that “the gathering related to a proposed creative project … that also had a genuine charitable purpose”. He added: “I strongly dispute any characterisation suggesting that I groomed, conditioned or manipulated women into sexual activity.” He denied that the text messages referencing Carlos and Brandon in any way constituted a genuine threat: “I did not intend to instruct anyone to physically harm Jon Ronson.” In reference to the allegation from his 2010 divorce hearing about mistreatment of a pet camel, he said: “I dispute any implication that I intentionally starved or neglected an animal.”The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unravelling Men by Jon Ronson is published by Viking (£20). title: What is salmonella, how does it spread and are eggs safe to eat? | Health | The Guardian
description: UKHSA says imported eggs eaten in restaurants are source of outbreak that has infected more than 200 people
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: UKHSA says imported eggs eaten in restaurants are source of outbreak that has infected more than 200 people
Content: Experts say the public do not need to avoid eggs but should choose the ones they buy carefully.Photograph: Ezra Bailey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts say the public do not need to avoid eggs but should choose the ones they buy carefully.Photograph: Ezra Bailey/Getty ImagesHealthExplainerWhat is salmonella, how does it spread and are eggs safe to eat?UKHSA says imported eggs eaten in restaurants are source of outbreak that has infected more than 200 peopleDenis CampbellHealth policy editorFri 21 Aug 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContaminated eggs have infected 207 peoplewith salmonellaacross the UK, killing one and hospitalising 34.Eggs imported into Britain and eaten in cafes and restaurants were the source, the UKHealthSecurity Agency has said. The outbreak has prompted public concern. But what is salmonella, and are eggs safe to eat?What is salmonella?“Salmonella isn’t a single ‘bug’ but the name we give to a whole group of bacteria that can cause infection in humans. There are over 2,500 different types of salmonella bacteria,” said Dr Malick Gibani, a clinical associate professor at Imperial College London.Most disease in the UK is caused by just a few of those 2,500 types. They are usually found in contaminated animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. But chocolate, peanut butter and cucumbers have also been at the centre of previous UK outbreaks.Salmonella can be spread by contaminated drinking water, contact with animals, person-to-person spread or poor food hygiene and preparation, “particularly when cooked food comes into contact with contaminated and undercooked or raw foods”, said Gibani. Storing food poorly, which allows the bacteria to replicate, and not cooking contaminated foods thoroughly are also risks.How does salmonella affect people?Salmonella causes an infection of the gut – gastroenteritis – and that leads to food poisoning. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and a fever, though some people also feel very tired and suffer sore muscles and joints. Symptoms can appear within a few hours to a few days.Gibani said: “Salmonella can be unpleasant for a few days. In most cases, people will get better without any treatment, but in some instances antibiotics might be needed, particularly in vulnerable groups. Antibiotics are usually only needed when there’s a severe bloodstream infection, but thankfully this is pretty rare in healthy adults in the UK.”Who is most at risk?Children and older adults, people whose immune systems are suppressed, perhaps because they are taking chemotherapy drugs for cancer, and those with underlying health conditions can be more severely affected.Scientists aren’t sure why. But, Gibani said, the fact that such groups are hit more severely shows that “there’s definitely an immune component which influences severity”.“In some people, instead of just causing an infection inside the gut, salmonella bacteria can spread into the blood, which can be very dangerous. When this happens it can cause a severe sepsis-like illness,” he said.“We often consider salmonella as a disease with an ‘image problem’. It can be dismissed as ‘just food poisoning’ and a bit of diarrhoea. But severe and invasive cases kill thousands of people a year around the world.”Salmonella infections in England at highest level in a decade, figures showRead moreSevere infection is a big problem in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, which has high rates of salmonella bloodstream infections, including in children who have recently had malaria, are malnourished or have advanced or untreated HIV.Should you avoid eggs?No. But you should choose the eggs you buy carefully, experts say.Kimberly Coffin, the technical director of supply chain assurance at LRQA, a global risk management firm based in Birmingham, said: “The safest choice for consumers is to buy eggs produced in the UK which carry the red lion mark. These eggs come from hens that have been vaccinated against salmonella.”She offered other tips to avoid catching salmonella. “Cooking eggs and egg-containing dishes until both yolk and white are firm, or to a temperature of 71C, is the best way to provide consumer safety from salmonella.“It’s also important not to use any cracked or broken eggs, nor eggs that have external evidence of wet or dry residues due to the potential for ingress of potential microbiological contaminates on the surface into the egg. Washing dirty eggs before use does not reduce this risk and, in fact, increases the risk.”Should the public be alarmed?Gibani said: “It’s understandable that people might be worried about salmonella and what and where they ‘should’ eat. The public should be aware and informed but not alarmed.”He and Coffin both stressed that the UK has robust systems of protection against salmonella, brought in after previous outbreaks, such as the vaccination programme and strong food standards and controls, especially for eggs. But no regime is failsafe, as this new outbreak shows.TheUKHSA websiteis a useful source of information about salmonella.Explore more on these topicsHealthEggsFood safetyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: It’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in Blighty | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Hard to fathom exactly why Megxit is over and the self-exiled wonder generators are leaving California. Luckily, the internet sleuths are on the case, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Hard to fathom exactly why Megxit is over and the self-exiled wonder generators are leaving California. Luckily, the internet sleuths are on the case, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Waxworks of Harry and Meghan in Madame Tussauds museum, London.Photograph: Madame Tussauds London/ReutersView image in fullscreenWaxworks of Harry and Meghan in Madame Tussauds museum, London.Photograph: Madame Tussauds London/ReutersOpinionPrince HarryIt’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in BlightyMarina HydeHard to fathom exactly why Megxit is over and the self-exiled wonder generators are leaving California. Luckily, the internet sleuths are on the caseFri 21 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareWednesday night brought an absolute cloudburst of psychic rain for our parched land, as it emerged that Prince Harry and Meghan were reversing their self-styled “freedom flight” to California andreturning to live in the UK. Nature is healing! Is that … is that how the expression goes? Either way, all humans in Britain have taken the announcement brilliantly, while fatted calf prices climbed steeply at the news that the reverse Megxit is imminent, with only an adequate headline soubriquet yet to be found. Megain? Megraine?Inevitably, thoughts turned swiftly to what it all meant. One of the funniest aspects of Meghan and Harry coverage is how their decisions are always analysed as though we were parsing the 4D chess moves of 19th-century master strategists. We are forever imagining we are dealing with a couple of Bismarcks or Clausewitzes, as opposed to a resting actor and the “chief impact officer” of a firm designed to offer tech-based solutions to men crying in their cars or something.And so it is that motive is being obsessively pored over. There’s definitely some eye-catching speculation out there. Some feel that Meghan being willing to step so much as a toe on to our toxic shores can only be a way of telegraphing the unfortunate suggestion that the king’s days are numbered. Or maybe Harry just wants to spend more time withhis £9.5m legal bill.Others have spicier takes. I saw a few horrified Sussex Squad Americans on social media suggesting that the only conceivable explanation is that Prince Harry is simply a world-beating god of sex. Allow me to expand. I’m sure the squad diehards won’t mind me projecting their own psychological projections on to Meghan, but the logic seemed comparable to someone saying: “Sorry, so the suggestion is that I move back to live on top of a live volcano, in a plague-ridden failed state, run by psychopathically violent warlords. Who’s asking?” 1990s-era Keanu Reeves. “BRB just calling the removal firm.”Multiple other takes are of course available. In Hong Kong, they used to have an acronym for bankers who were too stupid to get the good jobs in London but were able to move out there and do very nicely: Filth (Failed in London, try Hong Kong). It’s not as good, acronym-wise, but I guess we could be looking at a Fimuk situation – Failed in Montecito, try UK. No doubt we’ve all forgotten the full ins and outs, but I believe Ellen DeGeneres hasbeen on a similar journey. It’s possible that the Sussexes have just failed to keep pace with the elite fruit-spread makers of California, and that Meghan believes the waters of home counties jam-making will be much less competitive. I look forward to her conveying this judgment to the local Women’s Institute at her earliest convenience.Or, look, possibly the real reason for this move is something in between all these things – but which of us wants to be wasting time on nuance right now?What we do know is that it’s definitely on, and the couple’s children are enrolled in a school for September. Early thoughts? Mainly that someone’s class WhatsApp group just got an incredible new member. Speaking as a veteran of these digital abysses of passive aggression, may I state that the absolute last thing you need on one is someone whose stated life philosophy is to “create wonder in every moment”.Seriously. You simply cannot run the risk of the following message materialising at Christmas/in high summer when you are limping towards the holidays. “Thinking about end-of-term presents, I thought it would be really magical to create a mirror where the frame is our children’s handprints. I can organise?” Really? Because I’ve been hurt before. But go on. “Literally all I would need from you ladies is a clay cast of your daughter’s hand with a pressed daisy picked by moonlight embedded in it. If anyone hasn’t pressed flowers before I would be very happy to offer a (fun!) tutorial at my place on Tuesday after drop-off.” Aaaaaaaaaaaagh. Please, I HAVE A JOB. I CAN’T DO ANY OF THIS. You know what everyone loves? John Lewis vouchers. Please. PLEASE. As for other events during the school year, might as well call the Vatican right now because I can assure you we have a nailed-on bake sale martyr on our hands right here.Still, this is all very sad news for the country of the United States of America, and its now decimated entertainment industry, as Harry and Meghan leave behind them failed deals with Spotify and Netflix, among others. Then again, have they? Recent years have seen the Sussexes hamstrung by having exhaustively told the only story of theirs that anyone is remotely interested in. I can hardly believe I’m typing this, but it turned out no one wants to watch documentaries about global justice activismor polo. But this week’s news could easily reignite the only kind of content Netflix’s degraded first-look deal with Meghan would be extremely interested in having a first look at: the one where their life is made miserable by a toxic family in a toxic country with a toxic press. And then you make TV all about it.It’s a bit like when there’s been a hugely successful movie with a crazy, high-concept situation, and the producers of the sequel just have to work out a way to get the characters back into the same crazy, high-concept situation, or at least a similar one, so they can go back to the money well for a second time. Having been on board a bus that can’t slow down, Speed 2 finds Sandra Bullock on a runaway cruise ship. Home Alone 2 sees Kevin once again left behind, this time in New York as opposed to Chicago, where the same burglars have somehow rematerialised. In Finding Freedom 2, it’ll probably work best for the Sussexes to embrace the absurdity with a cheeky one-liner. When Harry and Meghan are battling remorseless tabloid attention, poisonous family dynamics, and deranged public antipathy, let’s hope he turns to theNetflixcameras and quotes Bruce Willis in Die Hard 2: “How can the same shit happen to the same guy twice?” I don’t know, mate – but I assume you’re getting first-dollar gross on the box office.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the meantime, the shock news continues to spark an hourly carousel of #onlyinBritain questions. What’s going to happen on Remembrance Sunday? Will this mean “rival courts”? Hand on heart, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that there are, amazingly, a whole lot of people who are even more ridiculous and even more emotional than Harry and Meghan. And – also amazingly – they are not the population of the state of California.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber Publishing, £20) is released in September. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryOpinionMonarchyMeghan, the Duchess of SussexNetflixcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ditch the giant handbag, don’t overdo the botox and 16 other ways to extend your ‘hotspan’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: If ‘lifespan’ is the time you’re alive and ‘healthspan’ the years you’re disease-free, then ‘hotspan’ is the period you’re attractive and vibrant. Want to increase yours? Experts share their tips
Author: Joe Stone
Headline: If ‘lifespan’ is the time you’re alive and ‘healthspan’ the years you’re disease-free, then ‘hotspan’ is the period you’re attractive and vibrant. Want to increase yours? Experts share their tips
Content: Still hot to trot … Andie MacDowell, Pharrell Williams, Brad Pitt, and Jennifer Lopez.Composite: Reuters and Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStill hot to trot … Andie MacDowell, Pharrell Williams, Brad Pitt, and Jennifer Lopez.Composite: Reuters and Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Life and styleDitch the giant handbag, don’t overdo the botox and 16 other ways to extend your ‘hotspan’If ‘lifespan’ is the time you’re alive and ‘healthspan’ the years you’re disease-free, then ‘hotspan’ is the period you’re attractive and vibrant. Want to increase yours? Experts share their tipsJoe StoneFri 21 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWear sunscreenForget 12-step skincare routines, red light therapy and injectables – the single most important thing you can do for your skin is wear UV protection. “Not just sun protection, but UV protection, every single day, regardless of weather or season,” says Dr Jennifer Owens, resident aesthetic expert at the Reborne Longevity clinic in London. “Up to 90% of visible skin ageing is caused by UV exposure – nothing else comes close in terms of impact.”Choose your wordsBeware the misguided logo, warns Guardian fashion columnist Jess Cartner-Morley: “Never, ever wear a sweatshirt or, worse, carry a basket with a slogan that includes the words ‘dance’ or ‘love’. Be cautious of words in French. These are the style equivalent of having a ‘Live, laugh, prosecco’ poster in your kitchen. Sorry, but you cannot buy youthful insouciance at M&S.”StraightenupWant to look instantly better without spending a penny? Standing up straight makes you look younger – and thinner – says Nick Finney, personal trainer to celebrities including Jennifer Lopez: “Our posture suffers with age, due to a combination of weakness, atrophying muscles and tightness. The solution is to strengthen all the muscles in your posterior chain [the rear of your body] while making sure that the muscles at the front have enough mobility to allow them to pull your back upright – tight pectorals will pull your shoulders forward.” Strengthen your posterior chain in the gym by perfecting Romanian deadlifts and horizontal rows.Look after your smileView image in fullscreenJulia Roberts.Photograph: Getty ImagesPeople get hung up on wrinkles and middle-age spread, but dodgy teeth are far more ageing, says Sali Hughes,the Guardian Saturday magazine’s resident beauty expert: “Teeth that are discoloured, significantly crooked or even missing are very ageing and so, conversely, a well cared-for mouth can take years off.”According to Ten Dental’s Dr Jenni Rawes: “As we age, enamel naturally wears down, revealing more of  the dentine underneath, which is a darker, creamier colour. It’s also more porous than enamel, so absorbs staining from food and drink far more readily, making teeth look darker still over time. Brightening the smile has a huge effect on how youthful and well someone appears.” Rawes says that visiting the hygienist for a scale and polish, and whitening the teeth using custom-made at-home trays are the fastest, lowest-effort ways to upgrade your smile. Expect to pay about £375 for whitening.Ditch the ironView image in fullscreenBrad Pitt.Photograph: Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic/Getty ImagesStill operating on the presumption that a pressed outfit signals that you have your shi(r)t together? Keep up. “Youth culture treats ironing like a hobby from the 50s, which means creased natural fabrics have become the ultimate modern Prada-esque symbol of chicness,” says the Guardian’s fashion and lifestyle editor, Morwenna Ferrier. “Looking kempt means looking corporate.” Also: “Don’t tuck things in. Modern fashion is all about the drape.”Pay attention to your lower half“Why are so many men of a certain age walking around wearing hideous chinos, which sag at the knee and taper at the ankle?” bemoans fashion consultant Simon Chilvers. “A pair of trousers in a flattering cut and decent fabric are the linchpin of great style as we age. Equally, a pair of well-made and well-kept shoes are central to the stylishness of any male wardrobe – and, yes, that can include sneakers, as long as they’re not too desperately trendy.”Long hair? Don’t careView image in fullscreenAndie MacDowell.Photograph: ReutersThought middle age comes with a compulsory mum cut? Think again. “Longer hair is absolutely not the preserve of the young,” says Hughes. “Healthy hair of any colour (including grey and silver) that falls at the shoulder and beyond actually looks brilliant and sexy on women over 50.”Hairdresser George Northwood – whose clients include Alexa Chung, Gwyneth Paltrow and the Duchess of Sussex – agrees: “Hair condition and texture are more important than your age when thinking about your hairstyle. The important thing to consider is: ‘Does my hair look relevant?’, rather than subscribing to a particular length for your age, which feels a bit outdated.”Correct pigmentation“Everyone fixates on lines and wrinkles, but uneven skin tone is more ageing,” says Owens. “It’s also more fixable – home care, UV protection and treatments like peels or microneedling can reverse existing sun damage. There’s decades of evidence behind microneedling as a technique.” A course of three sessions can boost collagen for months afterwards, and you can repeat that course once a year. “It’s one of the few treatments that’s genuinely within most people’s reach, and paired with good home care and daily UV protection, the results are transformative.”Lose theMary PoppinsbagView image in fullscreenAnne Hathaway.Photograph: GC Images/Getty Images“Get a smaller handbag,” commands Cartner-Morley. “Look around you: young people have really small bags. You can basically do everything with a phone now, after all. You don’t need to carry around a wad of second-class stamps. Nor do you need two packs of tissues or spare tights. Live life on the edge!”… and the dad phone“Ditch the wallet-style phone case – you know, the one with the flip cover,” says the Guardian’s deputy fashion and lifestyle editor, Chloe Mac Donnell. “Instead, buy a thin screen protector and a slim case.Casetifydoes fun collaborations if you’re into prints.”Be age inappropriateView image in fullscreenPharrell Williams.Photograph: Getty Images for Tiffany & CoGood news, men – you don’t have to ditch your favourite hoodie and jorts, post 40. “I personally don’t think that men have to dress according to their age,” says fashion commentator Derek Guy, AKA the menswear guy. “I like it when people break expectations, such as an older man who adopts youthful fashions. To me, seeing people use clothes to express themselves outside the narrow boundaries set by class, sexuality, gender and age is what makes fashion so rich and interesting.”… within reason“Next season’s ‘visible boxer shorts’ look has the potential to come off as a wardrobe malfunction at a certain point in life,” cautions Chilvers.Update your makeup bagWhat worked in the 90s may not land today. “I meet so many people who are wearing the same makeup they wore 15 or 20 years ago – when their lifestyle, budget, skin and tastes were very different,” says Hughes. “Swapping out a heavy matt foundation for a sheerer, glowier skin tint is a fast way to look modern and more confident, and switching a complicated, dated eyeshadow palette for one cream or liquid shadow and a liner looks instantly carefree and chic.”Ferrier adds: “It’s not that a little flick or cat eye will age you, but it does betray you as someone born before 1990.”Don’t dismiss BotoxThere are no prizes for ageing naturally. “I don’t care whether people want Botox or not,” says Hughes. “There are many very valid reasons for not wanting to engage in ‘longevity treatments’, from the political to the financial. What I find baffling is that I’m asked every single day about other non-surgical treatments, from Juläine to Morpheus 8, by people that I know would find what they are looking for more quickly and more cheaply in Botox, but who – through some misplaced and wildly inconsistent guilt – can’t bear to be that person. Get it or don’t get it – but life is too short for such hand-wringing.”… but don’t overdo it“Overtreating with Botox is one of the most common mistakes I see,” says Owens. “As we age, brows naturally drop, and the frontalis is the only muscle doing the work of holding them up. Weaken it too much with Botox and it stops ‘exercising’ – it can atrophy, and brows drop lower, earlier than they otherwise would. That’s part of why heavily treated faces can end up looking older, not younger. Botox absolutely has a place, but restraint is what keeps it looking natural.”Get strong, not skinnyView image in fullscreenMichelle Obama.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIn an Ozempic-obsessed world, it’s easier than ever to lose weight – but looking frail is ageing. “As we get older, our skin loses its tautness at the same time that our muscle mass declines,” says Finney. “This combination exacerbates the soft and baggy appearance people dislike.” Instead of worrying about losing weight, consider getting stronger through resistance training in the gym. “As your muscles strengthen they’ll push closer to the skin, causing a shrink-wrapped, more taut appearance.”Be bold (and bald)View image in fullscreenJason Statham.Photograph: WireImage/Getty Images“If you’re going bald, just go bald,” advises Mac Donnell. “A shaved head will make you look more confident than a receding hairline. And it’s cheaper than a hair transplant.”As for greys? According to Northwood, they can also be embraced. “I think men look great with silver hair,” he says. “I might bleach my hair for a statement, but I don’t think men should be trying to cover their greys – often it can end up with a red or khaki tone, which looks strange. As we age, our skin lightens and it looks washed out when men have a pale face and dark hair. It’s different for women, who dye their hair, as chances are they will also wear makeup.”And, finally …View image in fullscreenMadonna.Photograph: Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images“Don’t bang on about ‘being old’,” says Mac Donnell. “Referring to yourself as ‘ancient’ when you’re 43 is an ick. You don’t hear Madonna doing it, and she’s a pensioner.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleAgeingHealthBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mike D: ‘After Yauch died I couldn’t make music. I’d open a computer file and just feel sadness’ | Beastie Boys | The Guardian
description: As part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his past
Author: Alastair Shuttleworth
Headline: As part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his past
Content: All joking aside … Mike D.Photograph: Dan LoweView image in fullscreenAll joking aside … Mike D.Photograph: Dan LoweBeastie BoysInterviewMike D: ‘After Yauch died I couldn’t make music. I’d open a computer file and just feel sadness’Alastair ShuttleworthAs part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his pastFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s funny how far a joke will get you,” Michael Diamond grins. This time 40 years ago, the New York rapper known as Mike D was working with schoolfriends Adam “MCA” Yauch and Adam “Ad-Rock” Horovitz on Licensed to Ill, their 1986 debut album as theBeastie Boys.The “joke” in question is that record’s cartoonish send-up of frat-bro culture, set to fusions of hard rock riffs and hip-hop beats. As for how far it got them: destinations included global stardom, a page in the history books with rap’s first US chart-topping album, and the crosshairs of British tabloids as they roused a generation to “fight for your right to party”.The Beastie Boys would evolve into one of the most musically and socially progressive acts of their generation, with a run of boundary-pushing albums touching on politics and spirituality until they disbanded in 2012 after Yauch’s death from cancer. Diamond has since focused his creative energies on producing records for Soft Play and the Hives, while his sons, Skyler and Davis, took up performing as musicians themselves with the indie pop duo Very Nice Person.double quotation markWhen you’re 19, you’re just spewing out whatever, like: ‘This is going to be hilarious’Sitting in the lounge of his London hotel, happily munching cereal between questions, the wiry, thoughtful 60-year-old seems content in this quieter chapter of his career. But after jamming with his sons reignited his passion for writing, he is returning to the mic with his dizzyingly creative debut solo album Thank You.The Beastie Boys formed in New York City in 1981; all three members hailed from artsy, middle-class backgrounds – Diamond’s father was an art dealer, and his mother an interior decorator.The group quickly decided “we had to have our own personas that were distinct and separate”, and took inspiration from teen comedies such as 1979’s Meatballs. The results were the beer-crushing, school-hating louts heard on Licensed to Ill. “When you’re 19,” Diamond says, “you’re just spewing out whatever, like: ‘This is going to be hilarious.’ You haven’t faced a majorreactionyet.”In the UK, they faced the strongest reaction of all. With an album strewn with sexist and homophobic jokes, shows featuring a giant inflatable penis and go-go dancers in cages, and tabloids circulating (instantly denied) rumours about them mocking sick children at Montreux pop festival, their 1987 UK tour stirred a Sex Pistols-style moral panic. MPs issued calls to ban them from performing.“Get Lost Beasties” ran one headline in the Mirror.Their Liverpool show was cut short after just 12 minutes and ended in a riot. “Britain was this lightbulb moment of: ‘Wait, what we say does actually impact people,’” Diamond says, calling the experience “terrifying, humbling, alienating and surreal”.They nearly split that year largely due to the fallout. The joke wasn’t funny any more; they also left their record label Def Jam after a dispute over royalties, then Horovitz moved to Los Angeles. But the group were creatively reinvigorated by Horovitz’s new west coast friends, the Dust Brothers, who were masters of digital sampling.“It was like our dream come true. We could have an old blues guitarist with a funk drumbeat and a jazz trumpet,” he says. “We could create these endless possibilities, this musical collage.” That collage was made into their second album, 1989’s Paul’s Boutique,a left turn that received a muted critical reception but has since been hailed as an experimental masterpiece.View image in fullscreenKings of the ill … Mike D (middle) with Adam Yauch and Adam Horovitz of the Beastie Boys, pictured in 1987.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/GettyEven more striking is how the trio who once delivered punchlines such as “You like men and we like beers” (Hold It Now, Hit It) became beacons of positive social messaging. As mainstream rap largely grew more toxic through the 1990s, the band went the other way and apologised for past lyrics, declaring “the disrespect to women has got to be through”, (Sure Shot); “homophobics ain’t all right” (Alive); and “love can conquer hate in every situation” (Bodhisattva Vow).“In the same way we felt shame after some of the reaction to Licensed to Ill, we felt this nice, enriched feeling,” he says of the later albums. “I don’t want to get too ambitious here, as we are just a rap group, but maybe it changed how some people thought a little bit.” But across their albums, comedy and music remained partners. “They’re both things humanity desperately needs.”Diamond’s new record is also experimental and socially conscious. There’s plenty of his old band’s fun-loving eclecticism, with nods to industrial music, psych and dream-pop, while the lyrics take in self-reflection – the need, he says, to “look under the hood, check inside”. But this time the backdrop of laughter was replaced by grief. “After Yauch died, I couldn’t make music for quite a while. I’d open a computer file, and I’d just feel sadness.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markPart of ageing is this thing of your own mortality. You can push it away or acknowledge it and feel what you’re feelingHis return to rapping emerged from free-wheeling home-studio jams with his sons, whose brand of vivid indie pop is stamped all over Thank You. “When we first started playing, everybody just picked up something we’d basically never played before,” Diamond says. He began to loosen up, scribbling ideas in notebooks as they came to him, and dipping back into them during sessions. “When I started actually being open to writing lyrics that were more genuinely working around how I was feeling, it started to feel good,” he says. “It was this liberating thing.”Reflections on mortality loom large in Thank You; in It’s Time, he raps about “all these things that I want to get done”. For Diamond, Yauch’s death stirred up unresolved feelings. “In the New York we grew up in, there was a high mortality rate. We grew up in a club scene that was filled with drugs. Aids was brand new, and gay figures we knew from clubs started to drop dead. My dad died when I was 15. There was all this emotion I’d never dealt with,” he says. “Part of ageing is this thing of your own mortality. You can push it away and ignore it, or acknowledge it and feel what you’re feeling.”Rap-rock beasts and drive-by eggings: Beastie Boys’ 20 greatest tracks – ranked!Read moreAn acquaintance of his sons, who was getting rich from cryptocurrency at 19, inspired Thank You’s most overtly political track, Crypto. “I was just taken aback to see that’s the reality of the world we’re in,” Diamond says of its reflections on greed and capitalism. “You just get sucked so quickly into this vacuum.” I ask how his own experiences around that age may have shaped his attitudes on greed, given the Beastie Boys’ financial disputes with their label. “It was a great lesson that everything comes with a price.”Rather than money, Diamond feels “time is the most valuable commodity”, and returning to making and releasing his own music is time well spent. “I’m the most whole version of myself when I’m creatively completely engulfed and engaged.” There’s another note of contentment when he reflects on hip-hop generally, which the Beasties helped propel into the mainstream. He praises two artists who released their debut albums just as the Beastie Boys ended: Death Grips (“a real influence” on much current music) and Tyler, the Creator. “When I first saw Odd Future come out, I felt kind of happy inside – it felt like a continuation of an energy we brought.”Thank You’s closing title track is an impressionistic look at his early years, filled with fleeting images of partying with his friends at 16 (“We were just kids freaking out,” he sings). It strikes me as a possible parting tribute to the Beasties, but Diamond explains it’s universal. “It’s for everyone. This combination of your social group, your passion, coming of age, and music all stirred up together.” The title of the album, meanwhile, was inspired by a visit to a Buddhist monastery (the religion practised by his old friend Yauch) which prompted him to reflect on “who I get to make music with, who I’ve made music with”. A smile spreads across his face: “I’m so grateful for all of this.”Thank You by Mike D is out on 28 August.Explore more on these topicsBeastie BoysHip-hopPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: When TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any more | Television | The Guardian
description: They were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted by
Author: Sirin Kale
Headline: They were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted by
Content: Ironically, it’s all too ugly … America’s Next Top Model.Photograph: Hyungwon Ryoo/CBS Broadcasting Inc.View image in fullscreenIronically, it’s all too ugly … America’s Next Top Model.Photograph: Hyungwon Ryoo/CBS Broadcasting Inc.TelevisionWhen TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any moreThey were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted bySirin Kale,Stuart Heritage,Alexi Duggins,Rachel Aroesti,Isabelle Aron,Chitra Ramaswamy,Phil Harrison,George Francis Lee,Michael Hogan,Leah Harper,Ann LeeandJack SealeFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerica’s Next Top ModelWhen I think of the summer holidays when I was a teenager, I think of watching America’s Next Top Model for hours on end, critiquing each contestant with my sister. The makeover episode was always my favourite: girls sobbing as their hair was cropped short, or even shaved off. At the time, Tyra Banks seemed like a big sister, giving the contestants the tough love they’d need to succeed in a ferociously competitive industry. Now I feel differently. I hadn’t watched America’s Next Top Model since I was young, but like many, I recently watched Netflix’s excellentseries, Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model. It was the strangest sensation, rewatching episodes I hadn’t seen in more than two decades. At times I felt almost teleported back. How could I not find these scenes of models collapsing with hunger utterly abhorrent? I wondered what influence watching a show that celebrated eating disorders had on my own brain. I think it had an impact. I think the residual taint of it is still there. I can’t watch America’s Next Top Model any more, nor do I want to. Ironically, it’s all too ugly.Sirin KaleThe ApprenticeView image in fullscreen‘No show has a worse legacy’ … Alan Sugar in The Apprentice.Photograph: Talkback/BBCTruly, has any show in the history of television had a worse legacy thanThe Apprentice? The main culprit is obviously the American original, for the way it legitimised Donald Trump, but the British version doesn’t exactly get away scot-free. In terms of values, it preaches the sort of idiocy that should have been torched after the financial crisis; competitive selfishness and relentless greed at all costs. It has also churned nimrod after nimrod out into the media landscape. Plus, it isn’t fun to sit through. Why are people still applying for this mess? Why are any of us still watching? I can’t believe I used to enjoy this show.Stuart HeritageGood OmensView image in fullscreen‘It used to be my happy place. Now, not so much’ … Michael Sheen and David Tennant in Good Omens.Photograph: Chris Raphael/Amazon PrimeThere are few less complicated joys for me than the writing of Terry Pratchett. In my early teens, I fell for it hard – until that point, I didn’t know books could be that silly, or surprisingly profound, while also featuring a magical orangutan. I spent years diving back into it whenever I needed something to make me smile. So when Prime Video’s adaptation of Pratchett and Neil Gaiman’sGood Omenscame out, I was overjoyed. After years of ropey TV adaptations that failed to channel the way Pratchett’s writing balanced goofiness with seismic moments of drama, they’d finally got it right. David Tennant and Michael Sheen’s sparkling chemistry! Gaiman keeping things true to the book! Special effects that didn’t suck! For years, it was TV that I treasured. Until, that is, Gaiman became embroiled in sexual assault allegations, which he denies. I haven’t even seen the finale. This used to be TV that took me to my happy place. Now, not so much.Alexi DugginsThe OfficeView image in fullscreenDeeply disconcerting … Ricky Gervais as David Brent in The Office.Photograph: BBCFirst things first: I still considerThe Officeto be a masterpiece. As a satire of reality TV, as a character study, as a gimlet-eyed portrait of turn-of-the-millennium Britain, it remains unmatched. And that’s precisely why it’s so difficult to enjoy a quarter of a century later: it recreates the relentless sexist banter of the era with the same nauseating accuracy it brings to everything else. The wink-wink misogyny might seem quaint compared to today’s manosphere, but to revisit the show in 2026 is to be reminded of a time when tedious yet still threatening jokes about women were part of the rhythm of everyday life. The Office was always uncomfortable – it’s pure cringe comedy – but now it feels deeply disconcerting. That’s not necessarily a bad thing: the best art never ages into a cosily banal comfort blanket. Even so, one rewatch should cure most cases of Y2K nostalgia.Rachel AroestiMarried at First SightView image in fullscreenHugely troubling … Brook in Married at First Sight: Australia.Photograph: Geoff Magee Photography/Nine/Seven.One StudiosLooking for some light relief during lockdown in 2020, I started watching Married atFirst Sight Australia. The premise of the reality TV show is this: couples are matched by a panel of experts and meet for the first time at the altar. After they tie the knot, they go on a honeymoon, then move in together. Throughout the “experiment”, as it’s referred to, the group meet every week for dinner and a “commitment ceremony”, where each couple talk through how it’s going with the experts and decide if they want to stay or go. From sparks flying between couples to dramatic arguments at dinner, it makes for compelling reality TV. But earlier this year, a BBC Panoramainvestigationinto Mafs UK revealed that there have been allegations of rape and sexual assault on the show, hearing hugely troubling accounts from three women. Meanwhile, female participants on Mafs Australia havespoken outabout the vetting process, asking why men with past allegations of domestic violence and abuse have been allowed to take part. It’s another example of safeguarding failures in reality TV, and knowing what’s gone on behind the scenes, there’s no way I’d watch it now.Isabelle AronThis LifeView image in fullscreen‘Never again!’ … Daniela Nardini as Anna, Amita Dhiri as Milly, Andrew Lincoln as Egg, Jack Davenport as Miles and Ramon Tikaram as Ferdy in This Life.Photograph: BBCI was 17 whenThis Lifesauntered on to our screens, all miniskirts, Marlboro Lights and wild shagging. A deeply foolish age, I should have reminded myself, when I also believed in cargo pants and New Labour. God knows why I thought Amy Jenkins’s landmark series would have aged well when the 1990s so bracingly have not. Still, I poured myself a (metaphorical) pint of Stella and geared up for a nostalgic rewatch. Would I still fancy Egg? And want to be Anna? (No, and God yes, I’m only human.) I managed about three episodes before I nearly died of casual sexism, homophobia and boredom. Never again.Chitra RamaswamyI’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!View image in fullscreenA new kettle of witchetty grubs … Nigel Farage on I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here!Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockTo be clear, it was only ever the guiltiest of pleasures. But for many years, I foundI’m a Celebritymindlessly enjoyable as a vicarious adventure holiday and a schadenfreude-laden Z-lister hazing ritual. Ant and Dec’s gentle but pointed teasing of the participants was inclusive: it felt as if we were all in on the joke. Everything changed in 2023, when Nigel Farage signed up. Suddenly, the joke was on us. Mainstream political figures were tiresomely tolerable. Farage, though, seemed a different kettle of witchetty grubs: a poisonous figure, trading on the electorate’s worst instincts and being allowed to massage his image in primetime. Clearly, I wasn’t going to watch that – and I never have again. Fortunately, The Celebrity Traitors has arrived now, offering a far more palatable version of challenge-based famous-people foolishness.Phil Harrisonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Great British Bake OffView image in fullscreenRuined like a cake left out in the rain … Sue Perkins and Mel Giedroyc on The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Des Willie/BBC/Love ProductionsBake Offwas ruined for me like a cake left out in the rain when the rights to the show were dramatically bought from the BBC by Channel 4. After seven ad-less series on the BBC, negotiations over production costs saw the baking competition jump three doors down. In an act of solidarity, the show’s presenters Mel Giedroyc and Sue Perkins – along with its resident cake expert Mary Berry – decided not to follow the hit show. Bread baron Paul Hollywood, however, stayed, and a new cast of talent have endured his stoicism and personal brand of handshakes since. Not me, though. The betrayal soured my taste for village fete chumminess. The cutthroat affair was incongruous with the show’s image of wholesome Britain. It taught me that sometimes, under the layers of zingy fruit and flaky pastry, there’s a soggy bottom waiting.George Francis LeeEntourageView image in fullscreen‘Toxic masculinity – the TV show’ … Adrian Grenier, Jerry Ferrara, Kevin Connolly, Jeremy Piven and Kevin Dillon in Entourage.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyThe male Sex and the City™ was kind of fun for a while back there in the 00s butEntouragehas aged appallingly. Based on executive producer Mark Wahlberg’s life, it followed a movie star and his posse of hangers-on as they navigated Hollywood. This mainly involved chasing women around LA while fetishising cars and money. Potty-mouthed agent Ari Gold (Jeremy Piven) was a workplace bully whose treatment of his assistant Lloyd (Rex Lee) was racist and homophobic. Over eight seasons and a flopfilmsequel, it went from insider satire to douche-bro fantasy. I saw it pithily described online as “toxic masculinity – the TV show”. Creator Doug Ellin has accused HBO of burying the show due to “righteous PC culture”. Let’s not hug it out, actually.Michael HoganEuphoriaView image in fullscreenFetish slop … Zendaya as Rue in Euphoria.Photograph: HBOI’ve felt torn over watching the final season ofEuphoria. On the one hand, I was up for Rue’s spiritual awakening and Maddy’s career as a perma-eye-rolling talent agent assistant – plus who wouldn’t want to watch Sydney Sweeney and Jacob Elordi get hitched? But I’m not the only one left disappointed by Rue’s evolution into a horny drug mule, Cassie’s cam-girl aspirations and the fact that Kat (Barbie Ferreira) was entirely MIA. It wasn’t the life I’d dreamed of for my favourite debauched TV teens – and the online discourse calling out Euphoria for its male-gaze misogyny and descent into “fetish slop” didn’t make watching any more fun. Did I enjoy Jules’s turn as a sugar baby? Sadly, no.Leah HarperCouplingView image in fullscreen‘Like watching a sitcom written by Nuts magazine’ … Gina Bellman, Kate Isitt, Richard Coyle, Ben Miles, Jack Davenport and Sarah Alexander in Coupling.Photograph: Bbc/AllstarI first watchedCouplingwhen it aired in 2000, I thought it was a riotous comedy that was bitingly honest about dating, sex and relationships. During a rewatch recently, I couldn’t get past the vacuous characterisation of many of the women – among the group of friends we have Jane, a manipulative stalker, and Sally, whose main focus in life is not getting wrinkles. What I remembered as edgy humour was in fact puerile “jokes” branding women who refuse to be dumped as “unflushables” and about how getting your mate’s porn collection when he dies is a bonus. Then there’s the episode where Patrick is revealed to have a cupboard full of sex tapes after recording his exes without their consent. It was like watching a sitcom written by Nuts magazine, and every bit as sexist and unfunny as that sounds.Ann LeeHouse of CardsView image in fullscreenUnwatchable now … Kevin Spacey in House of Cards.Photograph: Netflix/Sportsphoto/AllstarHouse of Cardsdidn’t work when it tried to continue without Kevin Spacey as scheming politician Frank Underwood. But with Spacey now cast out, the earlier seasons are unwatchable too. That we liked Frank when we really shouldn’t have, because he was honest with us in his asides to camera – and because, dammit, he was good at lying and killing, and some of his victims deserved it – was a unique thrill, a forbidden suspension of our moral codes. The allegations about Spacey’s personal conduct make it impossible to keep that self-deception going.Jack SealeExplore more on these topicsTelevisionReality TVDramaTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: MPs ‘failing to learn lesson’ over freebies after accepting £400,000 of hospitality | Politics | The Guardian
description: MPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awards
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: MPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awards
Content: Lucy Powell, then Labour’s deputy leader and now education secretary, declared tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley.Photograph: Anthony Pham/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLucy Powell, then Labour’s deputy leader and now education secretary, declared tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley.Photograph: Anthony Pham/ShutterstockPoliticsMPs ‘failing to learn lesson’ over freebies after accepting £400,000 of hospitalityMPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awardsRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 21 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMPs have been accused of failing to learn their lesson over freebies after taking almost £400,000 of hospitality to concerts, sport matches and other events this year, with Louise Haigh, Lucy Powell and Wes Streeting among those accepting tickets.Despite the outcry in 2024 over Keir Starmeraccepting football tickets and gifts of clothing, MPs appear to have been declaring hospitality since the start of the year on a greater scale than previously seen.The most recent disclosures include £858 worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group, which was accepted by Powell, the deputy leader and education secretary. And Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, accepted tickets to the Chelsea flower show from Lloyds Banking Group worth £1,839.Haigh also accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivor Novello awards, while Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip, enjoyed Brit Awards hospitality for two worth £3,432, hospitality at Cheltenham festival horse racing from the betting company Flutter worth £350, and tickets to the Grand National valued at £560. All were backbench MPs while accepting the hospitality and have now been elevated to cabinet jobs under Andy Burnham.Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted £1,480 of tickets to the men’s Wimbledon singles final while in her cabinet job, while Ellie Reeves, the attorney general, accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivors while solicitor general.View image in fullscreenJannik Sinner serves against Alexander Zverev in the men’s singles final at Wimbledon.
