Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted tickets worth £1,480 to the match.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBurnham declared hospitality worth about £6,000 this year – mostly relating to his former role as the mayor of Greater Manchester, such as £3,800 tickets to the Brit Awards in Manchester, but also £500 worth of tickets to Ladies’ Day at the Grand National in Aintree.The acceptance of free hospitality by MPs appeared to fall after mid-2024 when the spotlight fell on Starmer’s string of free tickets to watch Arsenal football games. In March 2025, Rachel Reeves, the then chancellor, said shewould not accept free concert tickets againafter she was criticised for using free tickets to take a family member to see Sabrina Carpenter at the O2 arena. She defended the decision on security grounds but said she would not do it again because she understood “how people feel about it”.At the time, another government minister, Matthew Pennycock, said he had accepted “zero” free concert tickets as he personally did not think it was appropriate. “If I want to go to a concert at the O2, I’ll pay for it. But individual MPs, individual ministers, make their own decisions,” he said.The value of free tickets being accepted by MPs was at about £300,000 a year in 2025, according to the Times last December. But this appears to have increased, with almost £400,000 of complimentary tickets, hospitality and other gifts having been declared between January and July this year – not including foreign trips.Sue Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, suggested MPs should consider whether they should accept free tickets. “Some ministers and MPs appear to have short memories of the freebie-gate scandal that engulfed the first few months of Starmer’s time in No 10,” she said.“Showering MPs and ministers with gifts and hospitality is a tried and tested lobbying tactic by big business and foreign governments. There is no good reason why elected officials should be accepting jaunts and tickets to events that have nothing to do with their parliamentary or constituency business.”View image in fullscreenOlivia Dean performing at the Brit Awards in Manchester in February. Andy Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, accepted tickets to attend worth £3,800.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesDuncan Hames, the director of policy at Transparency International UK, added: “Just because something is permitted it is not necessarily appropriate.“MPs should be clear-eyed about why these invitations are really being offered. Before accepting hospitality, they should stop to consider what the company might be hoping to gain and what the public will make of it.”The scale of the declared hospitality may have gone up partly because ministers have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on theMPs’ register, after Starmer changed the rules around transparency. Previously, some ministers declared the value of their free tickets on the MPs’ register and some only put it on the quarterly ministerial register without showing a value if they could argue it was connected to their government job.Now both registers are updated at least monthly and have to show how much the hospitality or gifts were worth. Ticket prices have also risen, with many consumers complaining about the unaffordable costs of going to events.Under theupdated ministerial code,the last government set out a “well-established and recognised rule that ministers should not accept any gifts, hospitality or service which would, or might reasonably appear to, compromise their judgment or place them under an obligation to people or organisations that might try inappropriately to influence their work in government”.View image in fullscreenKing Charles during his visit to the Chelsea flower show. The shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, took £1,839 of hospitality from Lloyds Banking Group to attend the show.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/ReutersIt points out that ministers have a responsibility to represent the government, and their duties will sometimes require them to attend events where hospitality may be offered, and adds that it is “primarily a matter of judgment for ministers who are personally responsible for deciding how to act” in relation to accepting gifts.The acceptance of free tickets is not limited to Labour. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accepted tickets to Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the AllEnglandClub, while her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, took £1,839 of hospitality from Lloyds Banking Group to visit the Chelsea flower show. The shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith, also took tickets worth £919.50 to go to the Chelsea flower show, and £1,800 of tickets to the Formula One grand prix from Silverstone.Hundreds of backbench MPs were also wined and dined by corporations, including Google and Diageo, the drinks company. Many free tickets were provided by sports hosts and concert promoters, and some of them related to constituency interests, such as Powell, the Manchester Central MP, accepting tickets to Manchester City football matches and the first hosting of the Brit Awards in Manchester.View image in fullscreenConservative party leader,  Kemi Badenoch, enjoyed tickets to Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageAfter cabinet ministers who accepted hospitality were asked why they took free tickets and whether they would do so again while in office, a Labour party spokesperson said: “After Labour entered office, the ministerial code was strengthened to include new transparency requirements and clear principles governing the acceptance of gifts and hospitality. All declarations have been made in line with ministerial and parliamentary rules.”A Conservative source said: “All hospitality was properly declared in line with the rules. Transparency matters and we would expect the same standards and scrutiny to be applied consistently to politicians of all parties.”A PRS for Music spokesperson said: “PRS for Music advocates to policymakers on behalf of our songwriter, composer and music publisher members to protect the rights of creators and promote thevital contribution of the music industry to the UK economy.“Our public affairs initiatives create opportunities for stakeholders to engage directly with creators, experience how our industry works, see first‑hand the challenges they face, such as the impact of AI and post‑Brexit EU touring barriers, and understand the real world implications of policy decisions on music creators’ livelihoods.”Explore more on these topicsPoliticsParty fundingEnglandLobbyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Girl, 6, dies three days after Shoreham sea incident that killed parents and sister | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Saja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West Sussex
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Saja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West Sussex
Content: A family lay flowers on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four members of the El-Khawas family died after getting in trouble in the sea.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenA family lay flowers on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four members of the El-Khawas family died after getting in trouble in the sea.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAWest SussexGirl, 6, dies three days after Shoreham sea incident that killed parents and sisterSaja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West SussexHarry CockburnFri 21 Aug 2026 18.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA six-year-old girl has died in hospital three days after being pulled from the sea off Shoreham inWest Sussex, in an incident that also killed her mother, father and sister.Saja El-Khawas died on Friday after the deaths of her sister Sara El-Khawas, 14, and her parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, on Tuesday.Saja had been in hospital in a critical condition since the incident.Police, paramedics, coastguard crews and a lifeboat attended the scene at Shoreham Fort early on Tuesday afternoon after a report of four people in difficulty in the water.In a statement, Sussex police said: “It is understood the family travelled down from their home in London to visit Shoreham, and entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort around 2pm on Tuesday afternoon, before getting into trouble.“The investigation into the incident remains open, but following review of CCTV footage and initial witness accounts, the current hypothesis is that this was a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement.”Her identity and death were confirmed in a legal notice from solicitors acting on behalf of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS foundation trust, as well as the Palestinian Forum in Britain. The Palestinian embassy previously confirmed her father was a British citizen of Palestinian descent.Sussex police said the family’s next of kin “are aware and continue to receive the full support of our officers during this unimaginably difficult time”.Ch Supt James Collis said: “This heartbreaking update is one we all feared in the aftermath of Tuesday’s tragic events.“I cannot imagine the devastation felt by the wider family of Hassan, Zeina, Sara and Saja after this loss. On behalf of everyone at Sussex police, I extend our thoughts and heartfelt condolences.“The impact of this tragedy has been felt across the country, and I know the Shoreham community, emergency responders and all involved will continue to be affected for a long time to come.”“I would like to thank all of the public who have shared their sympathies and kind words, and once again ask for the victims’ family and loved ones to be left to grieve in privacy.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000 | Liberal Democrats | The Guardian
description: David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam
Content: David Campanale in Cheam in 2022. He says he was told a ‘secular party’ was being built with no place for Christians.Photograph: Sutton Liberal democratsView image in fullscreenDavid Campanale in Cheam in 2022. He says he was told a ‘secular party’ was being built with no place for Christians.Photograph: Sutton Liberal democratsLiberal DemocratsDeselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and CheamAletha AduPolitical correspondentFri 21 Aug 2026 15.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow much is a career in politics worth? TheLiberal Democrats, despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000.It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against hisChristianitycost him his political career in a civil case against the party.Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023.The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court.Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”.But in a counter-schedule filed on Friday, the Lib Dems described Campanale’s claim as “grossly inflated and egregious”. Their lawyers say £14,000 should be awarded for injury to feelings, and as a volunteer political party member, Campanale could have been expected to withstand “rigorous political debate and criticism”. They put aggravated damages, past and future loss of earnings, an MP’s pension and the loss of political capital at £0.Campanale says he was mocked and abused over his Christian beliefs and faced an organised campaign to remove him, while some activists refused to campaign for him.In his claim Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022, he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. He also claims he was excluded from election leaflets and told not to campaign in certain wards because activists disagreed with his beliefs.His claim also referred to a phone call in March 2022 in which he said Luke Taylor, his replacement, told him that he had no right to a conscience based on his faith and that a “secular party” was being built with no place for Christians.After Campanale was removed, Taylor won the seat with a majority of 3,801. The seat has since become safer territory for the Lib Dems with recent polls putting them well ahead of the Conservatives.The case has prompted criticism from senior Liberal Democrat figures inside and outside the party. The former leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes have backed calls for an independent inquiry. Farron has urged the party to apologise, saying there had been “manifest discrimination” against Campanale and party figures at all levels of the party failed to intervene.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, warned the position taken by the Liberal Democrats could make it “impossible” for Christians and people with other strong religious beliefs to represent the party.Before admitting the claims, the Lib Dems said in their defence that the party could deselect candidates where the expression of religious beliefs conflicted with its policies or values. The Lib Dems defence also described as a “statement of fact” the claim that the era associated with prominent Christian Liberal Democrats such as Shirley Williams and Charles Kennedy was over.A Lib Dem spokesperson said before their submitted counter-schedule: “This is an ongoing legal case so it would not be appropriate to comment. The Liberal Democrats are home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians. Three Liberal Democrat MPs in neighbouring seats to Sutton and Cheam are practising Christians including party leader Ed Davey.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsChristianityReligionSurreyDiscrimination at worknewsShareReuse this content

title: Meghan reportedly in talks to join Guy Ritchie’s TV series The Gentlemen | Television | The Guardian
description: The Duchess of Sussex is said to be discussing a return to acting in the third season of Netflix’s hit crime series
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: The Duchess of Sussex is said to be discussing a return to acting in the third season of Netflix’s hit crime series
Content: The Duchess of Sussex in 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APView image in fullscreenThe Duchess of Sussex in 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APTelevisionMeghan reportedly in talks to join Guy Ritchie’s TV series The GentlemenThe Duchess of Sussex is said to be discussing a return to acting in the third season of Netflix’s hit crime seriesBenjamin LeeFri 21 Aug 2026 14.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duchess of Sussex is in talks to make her acting return in Netflix’s hit series The Gentlemen.According toVariety, Meghan is in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight. The Gentlemen is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy of the same name with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.Meghan as the next Bond? Five roles that almost certainly don’t lie behind UK returnRead moreMeghan’s role in the show is as-yet-unknown, with a contract reportedly still not in place and no official announcement.Reports have emerged quickly afternewsthat the Duke and Duchess of Sussex would relocate to the UK from the US, where they have lived for six years. It is believed that they will return in September, with early rumours suggesting it was related to Meghan’s return to acting.Meghan’s best-known acting role was in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons. Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.Harry and Meghan had previouslysigneda deal with Netflix in 2020 worth a reported $100m. It wasrenewedlast year.Meghan’s main release with the streamer was lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” ina one-star review.In a 2022 interview, Meghan claimed a return to acting was unlikely. “I’m done,” she said. “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”The first season of The Gentlemen proved to be a hit with both critics and audiences for Netflix. The second season will premiere in September with returning cast members Theo James and Kaya Scodelario joined by Love Island host Maya Jama.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMeghan, the Duchess of SussexGuy RitchieNetflixnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince Harry and others ordered to pay interim £9.5m to Daily Mail publisher | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Judge orders payment within seven days towards legal costs in failed case over alleged unlawful information gathering
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Judge orders payment within seven days towards legal costs in failed case over alleged unlawful information gathering
Content: Prince Harry arrives at court in January. The Duke of Sussex and his co-claimants lost their high court case against Associated Newspapers.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenPrince Harry arrives at court in January. The Duke of Sussex and his co-claimants lost their high court case against Associated Newspapers.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAPrince HarryPrince Harry and others ordered to pay interim £9.5m to Daily Mail publisherJudge orders payment within seven days towards legal costs in failed case over alleged unlawful information gatheringCaroline DaviesFri 21 Aug 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke of Sussex and six other high-profile claimants must make a £9.54m interim payment within seven days towards theDaily Mailpublisher’s legal costs after losing their high court case over allegations of unlawful information gathering, a judge has ruled.Associated Newspapers Ltd strongly denied the claims made by Prince Harry and co-claimants including Doreen Lawrence and Elton John.Mr Justice Nicklindismissed all the claimslast month after an 11-week trial in London earlier this year. The court had been told that ANL’s legal costs were £34.5m.Lawyers for the claimants, who also include John’s husband, David Furnish, the actors Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley and the former Liberal Democrat ministerSimon Hughes, had argued the interim payment should be just over £7.9m. The £9.54m must be paid by 4pm on 28 August.In the costs ruling on Friday, Nicklin also said that, aside from where orders had already been made, ANL’s costs should be determined on an indemnity basis. This means that, as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay towards ANL’s costs without the publisher needing to show these were reasonable and proportionate.An indemnity basis is more unusual than a standard basis, and there must be conduct or circumstances “outside of the norm”.Nicklin said in the ruling that it was “was not simply a case in which serious allegations were made and failed”, nor “merely a hard-fought piece of litigation in which, after a lengthy trial, the court preferred the evidence and submissions of one side over the other.“The claims, and the manner in which they were brought, pleaded, pursued, maintained and publicly advanced, involved a combination of circumstances and conduct which took the litigation outside the ordinary and reasonable conduct of civil proceedings.”View image in fullscreenA court sketch of Elton John giving evidence during the trial at the Royal Courts of Justice.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PAHe said in the 44-page ruling that he was granting costs on this stricter basis for several reasons, including “the speculative and substantially inferential character of the claims at their origin”, the “exceptional breadth” of the cases, “and the public presentation of allegations of serious criminality and impropriety which were not ultimately established”.He said the group were criticised for “the making and maintenance of very serious allegations against many individuals, the failure to reassess those allegations when the evidence required reassessment, and the continued pursuit of allegations which were unsupported or had ceased to be realistically maintainable”.“In my judgment, that conduct was unreasonable to a high degree,” he added.Nicklin refused to cap the costs.In a statement, ANL said the ruling “is a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives”.It added that despite the “collapse in evidence to support the extremely serious allegations of ‘abhorrent criminal activity, crimes and terrible and reprehensible covert acts’ by the Mail,” the allegations were “not withdrawn, and were pursued until the bitter end of the trial”.“The truth is that these outrageous claims should never have been brought. That they were pursued raises disturbing questions about the conduct of elements of the legal profession.”Hughes said he was “disappointed and surprised” the judge had declined to limit the costs.The ruling does not mean ANL is entitled to recover all the costs it incurred. Any incurred unreasonably will be disallowed and if the parties cannot agree, the costs will be assessed by a costs judge.The parties have been given until 2 October to lodge permission to appeal in respect of the trial judgment or the costs ruling.Friday’s ruling means the claimants may have to pay millions out of their own pockets to cover the costs, with the court having previously been told there was a shortfall between ANL’s total costs and the group’s insurance cover of a combined £16.2m.The judge described the £34m costs claim from ANL as “excessive”, “striking” and “largely unexplained”, but said imposing a ceiling “would risk unfairness and be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary”.The court did not make any findings that any of the claimants had acted dishonestly.David Bailey-Vella, the chair of the Association of Costs Lawyers, said: “This could not have gone much worse forPrince Harryand the other claimants. The only chink of light is the judge’s comments about the £34m costs claim appearing ‘excessive’ and his ‘real concerns’ about how much of it would meet that test before a costs judge.”The judgment comes after it was made public thatHarry and Meghan are moving back to the UKthis month. According to the Australian news websiteNews.com.au, Meghan is said to have been offered a role in an upcoming project based in the UK, though no further details have been confirmed. A source close to the duchess did not deny the report, according to the BBC. The former Suits star quit acting when she and Harry got married in 2018.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryDoreen LawrenceAssociated NewspapersDaily MailNational newspapersNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decision  | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Joint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workers
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Joint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workers
Content: A World Central Kitchen vehicle in Gaza after it was attacked by the IDF in April 2024.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersView image in fullscreenA World Central Kitchen vehicle in Gaza after it was attacked by the IDF in April 2024.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersGaza‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decisionJoint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workersJason BurkeFri 21 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into theApril 2024 airstrikesthat hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,”the countries’ joint statement said.It continued: “InGaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.One of the officers who was dismissed hadreportedlysigned an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where expertsdeclared a faminein August 2025.The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.Hind Rajab died aftera desperate three-hour phone callto the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsraelIsrael-Gaza warForeign policyCanadaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño develops | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave
Content: Network Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenNetwork Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAClimate crisisBritain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño developsExperts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwavePriya BharadiaFri 21 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRailway companies are racing to prepare for another brutal summer next year, as a developing El Niño could see 2027 break more heat-related records.Britain’s railway system has already been under stress from extreme heat this summer, with several operators reducing timetables and train speeds.Two trains derailedwithin 24 hoursduring the UK’s fifth heatwave in August, in what Network Rail said had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.“Traditionally, our railway system hasn’t been designed for hot weather. So that puts our railway system under stress but also our overhead lines as well. That can also cause trouble for the whole [railway] system, not just the ground infrastructure,” said Xueyu Geng, a professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick.The Met Office has said that theEl Niño eventdeveloping over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than 100 years, with the UK forecast to experience increased rainfall and stormy weather this autumn due to the “unprecedented” weather pattern.In 2024,Network Railincreased their projected five-year spending on climate, earthworks and drainage by five times the amount allocated from 2019.“I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate,” Geng said.She warned Britain must begin to factor in higher temperatures as part of the design standards for its railways. “We need to look at how the hot countries are managing their railway systems. For example, in Spain, their rail system is managing between 0C and 45C. Saudi Arabia is 10C to 55C. The track is pre-stressed. We need to manufacture the pre-stress level in order to cope [with extreme heat].”Geng explained that Britain’s railways can typically handle temperatures as low as -10C, and this will need to be maintained. “We might have extreme cold as well. But, in the meantime, we need to look at the upper boundary temperature, and to actually manufacture our rail to cope with both kinds of extreme temperatures.”Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, said the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented. “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, [with Pacific sea temperatures] peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records.”Rail operators need to be prepared in the coming year for both “potentially prolonged periods of hot dry weather and more intense rainfall and storminess,” said William Powrie, professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.“There will need to be a serious look at parts of the network where past decisions have compromised the infrastructure, such as the extensive singling on the Salisbury to Exeter line, and reducing the train speed to account for poor track quality as a result of soil moisture deficit destroys the timetable,” Powrie said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The immediate priority should be to use the warning time we have,” said Ioannis Koliousis, associate professor at the Cranfield School of Management. “Before a potentially wetter and stormier autumn and winter, Network Rail should intensify drainage clearance, culvert inspections, earthwork monitoring and vegetation management, particularly at locations with a known history of weather-related failures.“The most important consideration is that we should now distinguish between maintenance and adaptation. Clearing a drain prepares us for the next storm, [but] redesigning or increasing the capacity of that drainage system prepares us for the next 30 years. We need to be doing both.”A spokesperson for Network Rail said: “Our long-range forecast suggests it will be a warm, wet winter – in line with climate change predictions for Britain – and we are doing all we can to be ready for that. Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world and improving its resilience to more frequent and extreme weather is an ongoing priority.“We are continuing to invest in making the railway more resilient to extreme weather and climate change. This includes a £2.6bn programme of works in track maintenance and renewals, including drainage, earthworks, track and overhead power improvements, as well as monitoring and predictive technologies to identify risks earlier and enable proactive intervention.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisNetwork RailRail industryRail transportTransportTravel & leisureEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists | Hong Kong | The Guardian
description: Chow Hang-tung has been detained since 2021, and written about everything from clothes to Tiananmen Square and the meaning of freedom
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Chow Hang-tung has been detained since 2021, and written about everything from clothes to Tiananmen Square and the meaning of freedom
Content: Chow Hang-tung has been in custody since 2021 over her role in organising Hong Kong’s annual vigil marking the Tiananmen Square massacre.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung has been in custody since 2021 over her role in organising Hong Kong’s annual vigil marking the Tiananmen Square massacre.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Getty ImagesHong Kong‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activistsChow Hang-tung has been detained since 2021, and written about everything from clothes to Tiananmen Square and the meaning of freedomTiananmen Square vigil organisers in Hong Kong found guilty of ‘inciting subversion’Amy Hawkinsin BeijingFri 21 Aug 2026 19.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 19.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn one essay written from prison, Chow Hang-tung worries about her hairstyle before court appearances because there are no combs or mirrors in her cell.“In a place like prison, where anything that is personal is stripped away, it’s even more important to hold on to every means by which you can express yourself,” she writes. “Don’t let uniform, depersonalised rules, dress codes, schedules, and behavioural requirements grind down your edges and mould you into a ‘model citizen’”.The vignette is everyday, almost mundane. It stands in contrast to Chow’s position as one of Hong Kong’s most outspoken dissidents, one who has been detained for nearly five years awaiting trial over her role in organising an annual vigil marking the Tiananmen Square massacre.Her case represents one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles.On Friday, Chow and her co-defendant Lee Cheuk-yanwere found guiltyof “incitement to subversion” by a Hong Kong court. They face a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail when they are sentenced later in the year.View image in fullscreenAbove, Chow Hang-tung speaks to media in May 2021 after activist Joshua Wong was jailed for participating in an event to mark the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown. Right, a candlelit vigil outside the Chinese embassy in London in 2023 to demand the release of Chow Hang-tung.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesAs the years pass by, the 41-year-old barrister has written screeds from behind bars on everything from the meaning of freedom to the legacy of the 1989 massacre, some of which have been translated by Brian Kern, a writer and human rights activist. Chow’s profile has only grown since she has been detained. She has won several human rights awards, and her social media profiles, which are managed on her behalf, are regularly updated with her writings from prison.In another essay, she describes being handed a white Mickey Mouse t-shirt to wear in court because she is not allowed to wear clothing that carries the branding of her protest group, the Hong Kong Alliance.“The Mickey Mouse t-shirt may seem innocent on the surface, but isn’t it still a prison uniform provided by the correctional facility? Even before the Alliance has been convicted, its clothes have already become contraband,” she writes.While some writings are breezy and irreverent, many are deeply considered essays on defending civil rights in the face of a powerful and oppressive Chinese Communist party. As a highly regarded barrister who has been representing herself in court, she also dives into legal philosophy.“She’s not afraid of anything or anyone,” saidKevin Yam, a Hong Kong lawyer who now lives in exile. “For a lot of us who are outside Hong Kong now and sometimes feel a bit dispirited by things, her example and her inspiration is a big factor in us not losing hope and keeping our spirits up.”Wu Yangwei, Chow’s fiance, a Chinese activist better known by his pen name, Ye Du, said it was Chow’s interest in mainland Chinese struggles that first attracted him to her. “From the moment I met her… I felt that she was incredibly innocent, deeply compassionate, and deeply empathetic toward China’s democracy and human rights defense movements,” Wu said. He now lives under close police surveillance in Guangdong province.‘A society that loses freedom of speech … loses its very soul’Chow was arrested in September 2021 along with two other organisers of the now disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Democratic Movements of China.The Hong Kong Alliance’s annual Tiananmen vigil, which attracted tens of thousands of Hongkongers each year, was banned in 2020 on the grounds of pandemic control.View image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung and her fiance Ye Du.Photograph: suppliedChow, along withLee Cheuk-yanand Albert Ho, were charged with incitement to subversion under Hong Kong’s new sweeping national security law.Chow and Lee pleaded not guilty in their trial, which ended on 19 May, while Ho submitted a guilty plea, which could help him get a sentence reduction. All three have already served shorter sentences for other convictions relating to the vigil.A Hong Kong government spokesperson said Lee and Chow were prosecuted “because they have overstepped the boundaries of lawful conduct by committing a criminal act of inciting subversion.” The spokesperson said law enforcement actions paid “no regard to their political stance, background or occupation.”In an essay written this year for the 37th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre, Chow wrote: “A society that loses its freedom of speech never just loses a few articles or events – it loses its very soul”.“‘Power corrupts’ is a hackneyed phrase, but when the will to power permeates everything … the decline of society becomes inevitable. Conversely, resisting the encroachment of power, or even attempting to put it back in its cage, requires a steadfast return to fundamental human values.”From studying earthquakes to fighting for human rightsChow came late to the law. A straight-A student, she had originally gone to Cambridge University to study natural sciences, specialising in seismology. In 2008, a massive earthquake struck Sichuan province, killing 70,000 people. Chow travelled to the region to volunteer as a rescue worker. Friends of Chow said the experience had a profound impact on her. She believed that the failure of the Chinese government to adequately prepare for the natural disaster, and the handling of the aftermath, increased the death toll, said the friends.Chow dropped out of her PhD programme and returned to Hong Kong to retrain as a barrister. She threw herself into Hong Kong’s then vibrant civil society, volunteering for human rights groups alongside her studies. It was while preparing a bail application for a fellow pro-democracy activist, Gwyneth Ho, that Chow was arrested in September 2021.“She’s turned her scientific training to the Communist party, dissecting the party’s manoeuvres as clinically as she once looked at tectonic plates and seismic movements,” said Mark Clifford, the president of the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.View image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung communicates with her fiance by letter.Photograph: Lam Yik/ReutersSince Chow has been in jail, her fiance Wu has communicated with her by letter, and occasionally through letters published in the newspaper Ming Pao, which is available in prison. In January last year, their correspondence was cut off, Wu said. “It’s even worse than mainland China. In mainland prisons, political prisoners can still communicate with family, but Hong Kong prisons now block even that,” he said.Hong Kong’s correctional services department said that all prisoners, including Chow, can send and receive letters “subject to the requirements of the prison rules”. The department said Wu’s claim was “totally false and misleading”.Wu said that Chow’s letters are “full of fighting spirit”. “I am not worried about her,” he said.As far back as 2021, Chow published an essay about her refusal to plead guilty, writing: “A stubborn freak like me can only march on and fight my case till the end … Having a chance to exhaust oneself is better than living a purposeless life, isn’t it?”Explore more on these topicsHong KongChinaProtestTiananmen Square protests 1989Asia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy killed her children. Why do many women support her? – Stateside with Kai and Carter | Maternal mortality | The Guardian
description: The defense has rested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Jenna Amatulli, deputy head of news for Guardian US, about how the case has renewed attention on the shortcomings of the US healthcare system, and why Clancy's story has captivated so many people
Author: Jenna Amatulli
Headline: The defense has rested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Jenna Amatulli, deputy head of news for Guardian US, about how the case has renewed attention on the shortcomings of the US healthcare system, and why Clancy's story has captivated so many people
Content: 33:52Stateside with Kai and CarterMaternal mortalityLindsay Clancy killed her children. Why do many women support her? – Stateside with Kai and CarterThe trial of Lindsay Clancy, a former nurse accused of murdering her three children, is wrapping up its fifth week. On Friday morning, the defense rested, and the public attention to the case is at a fever-pitch — especially on social media. Clancy, 36, does not deny that she strangled her children, but has pleaded not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility, also known as an insanity defense. She argues that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis, a rare and devastating condition that can go unrecognized and untreated. HostCarter Shermanspeaks withJenna Amatulli, deputy head of news for Guardian US, about how the case has renewed attention on the fundamental shortcomings in the US's maternal healthcare system, and about why Clancy's story has captivated – and polarized – so many peopleHosted byCarter ShermanwithJenna Amatulli, produced byMonica Espitia, edited byAnabel Bacon, engineered byIvan Kuraev,Source: The GuardianFri 21 Aug 2026 16.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 16.54 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsMaternal mortalityStateside with Kai and CarterUS justice system

title: ‘I could have put a deposit on a house or do this crazy experiment’: the British musician playing 365 gigs this year | Music | The Guardian
description: Isaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music scene
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: Isaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music scene
Content: ‘No busking!’ … Isaac Neilson performing in Barnsley.Illustration: Luke BrennanView image in fullscreen‘No busking!’ … Isaac Neilson performing in Barnsley.Illustration: Luke BrennanMusic‘I could have put a deposit on a house or do this crazy experiment’: the British musician playing 365 gigs this yearIsaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music sceneDavid RenshawFri 21 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a lively pub in Oxford this week, Isaac Neilson picked up his guitar and performed live for the 231st day in a row.The singer-songwriter’s performance at the Old Bookbinders is part of a marathon effort to play a gig every day this year. The challenge has seen him put nearly 20,000 miles on the clock of his Peugeot 208 and cost him the best part of his life savings. “I was in a position where I could maybe put a deposit on a house or I could do this crazy experiment,” says Neilson, 26. “I chose to go all in on the music.”Neilson plays punchy indie rock (albeit acoustically on these dates), and describes the mission as “insanely ballsy, borderline insane” – but the kind of big play he feels he needs to break into an industry where “nepotism and other invisible barriers” shut out many independent and working-class artists.Over a drink before his show, Neilson says he is determined to make it as a solo artist while also highlighting the UK’s grassroots music scene and testing the “old industry myth that if you work really hard then you can get somewhere”.Isaac Neilson: No Affection – videoSo far, he has performed in more than 60 UK towns and cities including 28 gigs in his native Derby. He performed for more than 500 people supporting Cast in Barnsley and, unsurprisingly, completely empty rooms during the World Cup. He thinks he has gone through “two major mental breakdowns and six minor ones” but says his voice has “never been better”.Often performing more than once a day, he is on course to log more than 400 performances by the end of 2026, an undertaking that takes a daily average of three hours on the road. He is often accompanied by his girlfriend, Ashlea, who manages his social media, while a manager came on board after learning about his goal.Neilson has been booking gigs through relationships with promoters, and by scouring Facebook and Instagram for venues with stage time. He has set just two rules. He must perform every single day, and “no busking”. A promoter in Georgia in the US has promised to fly him out should he maintain his streak until September. “Christmas Day is going to be difficult but I have a plan,” he says.Neilson describes himself as “frugal” and knows what he is doing makes little financial sense. He went into the year with just over £30,000 in savings and expects to end it with about £3,000. He estimates it is costing him about £400 a week to keep going, with fuel as his biggest expense. Friends’ sofas and long drives home help save on accommodation costs.View image in fullscreen‘Virality is overrated’ … at the Old Bookbinders Ale House in Oxford this month.Photograph: Nina Sebastiane/Yin Yang MediaBreaking new artists is an increasingly difficult proposition in a music industry where executives value social media followers and streaming numbers over untapped talent at open mic nights.There was outrage last month when the longstanding BBC Introducing stage at Reading and Leeds festivals was axed. Organiser Festival Republic promised to offer a “much wider pool of emerging talent”, with performances from the children of David Beckham and Liam Gallagher.Neilson is proud of his “anti-algorithmic, anti-AI approach”, though he is also pleased that his streaming figures and follower numbers – both between 3,000 and 4,000 – have increased this year. “Virality is overrated,” he says. “People are yearning for community and looking for a connection. Numbers on a screen don’t represent the impact you can make in the world if you actually go out and meet people. My marketing budget is the time I spend in a room with you.”Neilson’s mission wouldn’t be possible without the pubs, clubs and small venues in which he has performed, sites also facing their own challenges. Recently publishedfigures by the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA)suggest British pubs are in trouble. A total of 161, or two a day, closed in the first quarter of 2026 amid spiralling costs.“Hospitality is an experience economy now,” says Bruno King of the Temple pub in Doncaster, where Neilson performed in May. “You have to offer something different and we have live music three times a week. It’s one of the most popular aspects of our venue. People really do appreciate being able to support grassroots musicians.”‘This keeps the dream alive’: the bands sleeping at venues to make touring workRead moreConversely, last year the number of grassroots music venues in the UKshowed the lowest rate of annual decline since 2018, suggesting that the sector is stabilising five years on from the pandemic. Andy Burnham’s recent announcement thatpubs, clubs and live music venues will receive a 20% cutto their business rates bills next year was further welcome news.Live Trust CEO Jon Collins says the positive figures are “testimony to the commitment and passion of the people who are running the venues” but warns that challenges are still there. “It’s more expensive than ever to put shows on. Customers are still facing cost of living challenges while promoters having a bad night can lose a couple of thousand pounds.”Collins praises Neilson’s commitment and shares his belief that new talent can still be discovered on stage. “Nobody arrives fully formed on [Glastonbury’s] Pyramid stage,” he says. “You learn your trade, you find your voice and you build your audience from those earliest gigs onwards.”In Oxford, Neilson earns big cheers from a packed room of early evening drinkers, most of whom he manages to add to his ever-growing mailing list. After he steps off stage he is relaxed about where his undertaking will take him. “Regardless of the outcome of this year, I can die knowing I threw everything at it,” he says. And with that he is off to his next gig.Neilson plays Frome (21 August), Cwmbran (22 August), Bristol (23 August) and Mexborough (24 August), among others. title: You’re Killing Me review – did an AI monkey write this terrible Brooke Shields crime caper? | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second season
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second season
Content: Lower your expectations … Brooke Shields in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVView image in fullscreenLower your expectations … Brooke Shields in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewYou’re Killing Me review – did an AI monkey write this terrible Brooke Shields crime caper?I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second seasonLucy ManganFri 21 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLook, we all want Brooke Shields to be in gainful employment. We all want her to have a fabulous third act to her career. God knows, the child model turned star of prurient fever dreams Pretty Baby and The Blue Lagoon (and the “Nothing comes between me and my Calvins” jeans ad campaign when she was 15) has earned it. Plus, she did a fine turn in Friends and a number of us remember Suddenly Susan very fondly.But she’s terrible in the terrible new thing she’s in, which is a six-part comedy drama called You’re Killing Me. Shields plays successful cosy mystery novelist Allison Chandler, who lives in the picturesque town of Founder’s Cove, Maine. It’s Murder, She Wrote vibes all right, but please lower your expectations.Allison’s publishers are beginning to make noises about the need to attract a younger demographic to her books. Allison – who is less a character than a loose assemblage of simple responses to stimulants, though things improve slightly after the pilot – is outraged. She is also incredibly rude to young true crime podcaster Andi (Amalia Williamson), who comes to her book signing, because she knows Andi has called her work “outdated and inaccurate”. But when her sleazebag pal Nash Gilbert (Matthew MacFadzean) suggests that her latest book maybe isn’t her best work, she executes her reflection-response instead. Could the times actually be a-changing and leaving her behind? If only there was a young person around to ask and maybe learn from, however antagonistic she might be.View image in fullscreenSomeone to learn from? … You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVAlas, before Nash can guide her further on this voyage of self-discovery, he has plummeted to his death from a balcony. An apparent suicide – or is it? Soon, whichever AI monkey is in charge of storyboarding has contrived to bring Andi and Allison together to investigate what they believe to be murder. Soon the police, led by new county detective Coppy McCopface – sorry, I mean Jack Kerrigan (Tom Cavanagh) – agree. Plot is added (a blackmail setup, a naive stepdaughter, impromptu gift shop closures become pivotal, people are flung into car boots when the monkey realises nothing as happened for a while). Murder suspects duly emerge, are given a grilling by Allison and/or Andi, establish their alibis and then are banished to the wings until it is time for one of them to re-emerge and drop himself in it.Repeat with one new murder a week (adulterated EpiPen at a wedding, electrocution in a hot tub, and so on) set against the background of Andi and Allison learning to live, laugh, love and write a book together. It’s not the publishing deal you get that matters, of course – it’s the intergenerational bickering you are scripted along the way.There needs to be a moratorium on boomers/gen Xers watching in horror as young ’uns give their lengthy coffee orders to baristas. And on the latter explaining basic mobile phone functions to them. And on the former reacting like Victorian dowagers when they hear a word like “chatbot” or “Zoom”. I don’t know what the average age of the writers on You’re Killing Me is, but someone needs to tell them that Allison/Shields is 61, not 106. She would know what cancelling someone means and that it is not done by an annoyed woman shouting “I cancel you!” at another. Come on.View image in fullscreenShe’s 61, not 106 … You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVThe whole thing is thin, lazy and so disappointing. It could have been fine – maybe even good. The setup has perfectly legitimate dramedy potential, with each of the two main characters having what the other lacks in terms of skills, experience and attitude. With a little effort, a little genuine wit, intergenerational stuff can be fun, funny and occasionally even illuminating. Someone somewhere should have thought to try it. Shields can do comedy, but here is thrown back on shrillness and interminably hamming it up to try to make things stick. Williamson is clearly capable of much more, too, but Andi is written mostly as an arrogant brat and there is nowhere really to take her.All that said – and I could say more – it has just enough charm (and honestly, if I could work out how, I would bottle it, sell it and retire to a picturesque cove of my own) and enough goodwill attached to Shields that I greet the news that it has been commissioned for a second series with hope rather than despair. I want it to work. I want it to improve, like it did – slightly – between pilot and subsequent episodes, and to become the Gilmore Girls-inflected, Murder, She Wrote homage it once flickeringly promised to be. But they do say that it’s the hope, at least as often as poisoned EpiPens, that kills you.You’re Killing Me aired on U&Drama and is available on U and on Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionTV crime dramaTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Are baby products the secret to better skin? 15 toiletries worth trying | Life and style | The Guardian
description: With gentler formulas and lower prices, children’s toiletries can work just as well for adults. From nappy rash cream to nourishing bath milk, these are the products that have earned a place in my routine
Author: Lisa Niven-Phillips
Headline: With gentler formulas and lower prices, children’s toiletries can work just as well for adults. From nappy rash cream to nourishing bath milk, these are the products that have earned a place in my routine
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Life and styleAre baby products the secret to better skin? 15 toiletries worth tryingWith gentler formulas and lower prices, children’s toiletries can work just as well for adults. From nappy rash cream to nourishing bath milk, these are the products that have earned a place in my routineLisa Niven-PhillipsFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere may be plenty of worrying headlines about children using adult beauty products from younger and younger ages, but what about the reverse?I’ve been a beauty editor for more than a decade, but when I had my first child in 2020, I was immediately impressed with the body washes, bath products and moisturisers designed for babies, particularly as someone with eczema and sensitive skin. The products’ gentler, often fragrance-free formulas are easier on my skin, tend to cost less, and result in a less cluttered bathroom, since we can all use the same things. These are the ones I’m still using – on the entire family – five years on.The best baby toiletries for adultsWeleda baby calendula nappy change creamView image in fullscreenUK£5.30 for 75ml at John Lewis£5.30 for 75ml at BootsUS$13.43 for 2.5fl oz at iHerb$15.06 for 2.5fl oz at AmazonGreat for:eczema flare-upsThis was the only nappy cream I ever used on my children as babies, since it seemed to clear up any hint of a rash before it got bad. But it also works miracles when dabbed on my and my son’s eczema flare-ups (calendula is anti-inflammatory). The lanolin ingredient creates a barrier to lock in moisture, and the calendula and chamomile bring down redness quickly and effectively. It leaves a white cast, though, so avoid using it on your face.Boots baby organic extra-large cotton wool padsView image in fullscreen£2.10 for 50 at BootsGreat for:removing makeupBeyond nappy changes in the first couple of weeks with a newborn, I never found much use for cotton wool when caring for a baby. I did, however, discover that these extra-large, rectangular cotton wool pads are perfect for removing makeup. You only need one for your whole face, and they’re made from 100% Gots-certified organic cotton, meaning no dodgy chemicals.L’Oréal Kids extra-gentle 2-in-1 tropical mango shampooView image in fullscreenUK£4 for 310ml at Morrisons£4.25 for 310ml at AmazonUS$8.43 for 8.45 fl oz at AmazonGreat for:washing my own hairI remember a cherry version of this shampoo, which smelled like marzipan, that my sister and I used when we were kids, so I bought this mainly for nostalgia. But it’s also a great shampoo – light, effective and delicious-smelling, leaving my hair silky and easy to comb through. (Although, as my son rightly points out, it actually smells more of peaches than mango.) I pack it for all of us when we go on holiday.This Works baby sleep pillow sprayView image in fullscreenUK£25 for 75ml at Lookfantastic£25 for 75ml at AmazonUS$33 for 75ml at This WorksGreat for:a gentle pillow sprayNo amount of lavender and chamomile would have lulled either of my children to sleep in their first years, so when I was given this pillow spray as a gift, I immediately adopted it for myself. I’m actually a pretty good sleeper (given the chance), but I find this helps me wind down when I’m feeling wired. I like that the scent–a delicate lavender with a hint of lemon balm – is subtler than most sleep sprays designed for adults.Mustela bébé no-rinse cleansing waterView image in fullscreenUK£10.50 for 300ml at Boots£9.20 for 300ml at AmazonUS$19.50 for 10.14fl oz at iHerbGreat for:removing makeupA French pharmacy favourite, the Mustela bébé range has long been available in the US but used to be difficult to find in the UK. Mercifully, it launched in Boots in 2024, when my youngest child was a year old. I quickly fell in love with the gentle avocado cleansing water, which I pump on to flannels to wipe away substances (jam and face paint) on my kids, but I also use it to remove my makeup every night.Childs Farm OatDerma bath milkView image in fullscreen£7.50 for 250ml at Boots£7.80 for 250ml at OcadoGreat for:a skin-soothing soakSince my eldest son has eczema, bubble baths tend to be drying, leaving his skin tight and irritated. I bought this oat-based bath milk, which has colloidal oatmeal and oat oil – both great for eczema – as a substitute, and it left his skin so soft that I tried it myself. I now put some in my own baths, along with a slug ofAromatherapy Associates deep relax oil, and emerge with such silky-smooth skin I don’t even need to moisturise afterwards.Nivea Sun kids SPF50+ roll-on sun lotionView image in fullscreen£6.05 for 50ml at Boots£5.95 for 50ml at AmazonGreat for:a non-greasy family sunscreenDuring summer, at least one portable sun cream can be found rattling around in the bottom of my handbag at any given time. This broad-spectrum SPF50+ offers great protection and is free from ingredientsthat can cause harm to aquatic life, such as oxybenzone. It also isn’t greasy like some of the other kids’ sunscreens, so I’m happy to use it on the children and myself.Aveeno baby soothing relief emollient creamView image in fullscreen£5.59 for 150ml at Lookfantastic£7.99 for 150ml at BootsGreat for:dry skinThe Aveeno baby range is great, especially for dry and sensitive skin, but the oat-based creams are my favourite. There’s anAveeno baby dermexarange designed for eczema-prone skin, but the classic emollient cream works best for my son and me, keeping our skin hydrated and flare-ups at bay. I apply a layer over my body every morning, then top up in the evening if my skin feels dry.La Roche-Posay baby Lipikar Syndet AP+ body washView image in fullscreen£21.50 for 400ml at Lookfantastic£21.90 for 400ml at BootsGreat for:a daily body washEven before having kids, I loved the La Roche-Posay brand for its no-nonsense skincare, sun protection and body care. But since my babies were born, we’ve all used this multipurpose body wash more or less daily. With glycerine and shea butter to protect the skin barrier, it’s hypoallergenic and gentle enough to use from birth, yet still cleans effectively. The large bottle means it can last for ages, even with four of us using it.My Little SudocremView image in fullscreen£2.99 for 22g at Holland and Barrett£3.60 for 22g at BootsGreat for:bites and scratchesIt’s not exactly news that Sudocrem’s classic antiseptic healing cream is great, but it was only when I had kids that I truly understood its brilliance, and also discovered the infinitely more convenient My Little Sudocrem. Much better than a massive tub which goes out of date (and kids are destined to get their hands on and smear everywhere), this compact pot is now my go-to for the whole family’s insect bites, spots, cuts and grazes.Neal’s Yard Remedies organic pure baby oilView image in fullscreenUK£10 for 50ml at Ocado£9.50 for 50ml at AmazonUS$16 for 1.69 fl oz at Neal’s Yard RemediesGreat for:removing sticky stuff and moisturising cuticlesI bought this oil when I did a baby massage course with my first son – it’s a fragrance-free blend of borage, sunflower and jojoba oils – and while it did the job perfectly well for that, its greatest use has been as a general sticky-stuff remover. I’ve found that nothing removes the residue left by plasters and dressings quite so well. It’s a small bottle, but a drop of oil goes a long way for our purposes. I also massage it into my nail beds between manicures, and it works just as well as expensive cuticle oils.Le Petit Marseillais crème lavante mains laitView image in fullscreen£5.99 for 300ml at the French PharmacyGreat for:dry handsWith all the nappy changes, snack preparation and medicine dispensing, I have never washed my hands more than I do now that I have kids. When we started getting my eldest to wash his hands at the sink, I quickly realised I’d need a gentler product – our usual soap gave him red, itchy skin. I picked up a bottle of this mild Le Petit Marseillais soap on a trip to France and noticed an immediate, positive difference in the skin on my own hands too. I now stock up every time we’re on holiday.Kit & Kin magic salveView image in fullscreen£9.99 for 100ml at Boots£10 for 100ml at OcadoGreat for:cracked skinDue to the aforementioned constant hand-washing, I have permanently dry skin on my knuckles and between my fingers, which sometimes cracks when the weather gets especially cold. A mum friend gave me this salve to use as a nappy cream, and while I’ve never used it for that (I love theWeledaone), it is one of the few things that soothes the dry skin on my hands.Kokoso natural konjac baby bath spongeView image in fullscreen£7.49 at KokosoGreat for:a face exfoliatorKonjac sponges – natural sponges made from fibres of the konjac plant – are traditionally used in Japan to top-and-tail wash babies, as their naturally alkaline and mineral-rich fibres cleanse without the need for any product. I used them when my kids were newborns and still buy them for exfoliating my face in the shower. A word of warning: they’re biodegradable, so will start to naturally break down after a couple of months.Bioderma Atoderm cleansing oilView image in fullscreenUK£24 for 1l at Lookfantastic£24 for 1l at SephoraUS$33.99 for 38 fl oz at Ulta$33.99 for 38 fl oz at AmazonGreat for:a hydrating full-body cleanseThis incredible cleansing oil is a fairly recent discovery, but it may well give my beloved La Roche-Posay body wash a run for its money. Designed for the whole family, even newborns, its rich oil formula leaves skin hydrated, yet without a greasy residue, and is gentle enough to be used on the face as well as the body. Those without dry skin may even find it’s hydrating enough that they can skip moisturiser afterwards.Lisa Niven-Phillips is a beauty journalist with more than a decade’s experience in covering everything from lipsticks to laser treatments, shampoo to skincare. With a good radar for snake oil, she prides herself on being able to see past fancy labelsto discover the products that really work. A love of no-nonsense formulas, surprising beauty heroes, and anything that makes parents’ lives easier made this article a delight to work onExplore more on these topicsLife and styleSkincareFamilyBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: David Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needs | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?
Content: Red Guardian – perhaps not an authority on interdimensional metaphysics?Photograph: MarvelView image in fullscreenRed Guardian – perhaps not an authority on interdimensional metaphysics?Photograph: MarvelWeek in geekMoviesDavid Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needsBen ChildThe actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 20.12 EDTShareNobody knows exactly what solemn blood oaths Marvel uses to prevent spoilers. But we do know that Andrew Garfield spent most of the run-up to 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home – in which he would eventually turn up as one of two secret Spideys –behaving as if Kevin Feige was standing behind him, holding up a giant card saying: YOU HAVE NEVER MET TOBEY MAGUIRE. So we can imagine it’s pretty full on. Why, then, has Avengers: Doomsday star David Harbour this weekapparently blurted out the biggest Marvel secretsince Ben Kingsley’s Mandarin in Iron Man 3?Invited by Variety magazine to offer up a line from Doomsday “completely out of context”, Harbour thought for a moment, adopted the Russian accent of his Red Guardian character andcame out with: “You … are Tony Stark.” Which is quite a thing to say about a film whose entire marketing campaign so far has depended on us accepting that Iron Man remains dead, and that the actor who used to play him, Robert Downey Jr, is playing Victor von Doom instead.So what’s going on? The simplest and most likely explanation is that Harbour is trolling us, that Stark is not in the movie at all, and we’re all just fools. The new trailer for Doomsday, premiered last weekend at Disney’s D23 event in Anaheim, leans heavily into the prevailing wisdom that the film’s villain will be the tyrannical, unstoppable baddie of spurious eastern European extraction that Stan Lee and Jack Kirby dreamed up in 1962.We even get to hear more of Doom’s heavily accented voice, and there is no suggestion that it belongs to anyone but Downey Jr beneath the mask. The footage talks repeatedly about “Victor”, hints at the supervillain’s tragic history and seems determined to establish him as a fully fledged character in his own right. IfMarvelis planning a rug-pull here, it is certainly doing an impressively thorough job.Not that this has stopped anyone.Some fans have already noticed that one closeup of the masked villain in the new footage appears to show a pair of blue eyes, rather than Downey Jr’s brown ones. Others noticed that the costume Marvel displayed at D23, on mannequins, was subtly different from the version shown at San Diego Comic-Con in July. From this slender collection of ocular and tailoring evidence has emerged the theory that there may actually be two incarnations of the character: Downey Jr’s version, perhaps initially presented as an ally; and a nastier variant who eventually replaces or kills him.Naturally, because Cillian Murphy has blue eyes and has spent years being fancast as Victor von Doom, the internet has decided that the second man behind the mask must therefore be Cillian Murphy. If it’s correct, this may be the first big Hollywood casting decision achieved entirely through collective wishful thinking – at least since Marvel rewarded years of online fancasting by briefly turning John Krasinski into a variant Reed Richards in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.View image in fullscreenCollective wish fulfilment … Cillian Murphy.Photograph: Mark Sagliocco/Bafta/Rex/ShutterstockThe irony is that Harbour’s line sounds plausible because Marvel has spent the past two years – ever since Downey Jr was unveiled beneath Doom’s mask at San Diego Comic-Con –slyly hinting that if you watch the next two Avengers films, you may just find out what the hell is going on. Now it has to actually make good on that promise, even though this is a universe in which umpteen superheroes (and enough filmgoers to rack up the best part of $3bn at the global box office) watched Stark save all existence by snapping his fingers and expiring in front of them in Avengers: Endgame.Avengers: Endgame review – unconquerable brilliance takes Marvel to new heightsRead morePerhaps Harbour’s line is genuine, and it is only our interpretation of it that is wrong. Red Guardian is hardly the MCU’s leading authority on interdimensional metaphysics: confronted by a man with Stark’s face, “You are Tony Stark” would be a perfectly reasonable thing for Alexei to say even if the answer is simply: “No, actually, I’m Victor von Doom.” This would allow Marvel to acknowledge the elephant in the room without turning its new villain into Iron Man gone bad, and still leave Downey Jr free to be exactly who the studio keeps insisting he is.Either way, the genuinely strange possibility now seems to be that Downey Jr’s return really does have absolutely nothing to do with Tony Stark. And yet, you do not bring back the actor who spent 11 years as the face of the MCU, put another metal mask over that same face and then expect audiences to regard the resemblance as an administrative coincidence. Harbour may have leaked the biggest secret in Doomsday, or he may simply have made up the most obvious line imaginable for a laugh.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekAvengers: DoomsdayRobert Downey JrMarvelSuperhero moviescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Taliban have built a system for enslaving women in Afghanistan | Amanda Abou Abdallah | The Guardian
description: Five years on, the regime’s chokehold has left Afghan women with almost nothing, but many are still bravely fighting for their freedom, writes Tala Elissa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Five years on, the regime’s chokehold has left Afghan women with almost nothing, but many are still bravely fighting for their freedom, writes Tala Elissa
Content: A poster at a university, which became male-only under the Taliban, ordering women to wear hijabs. Women were later forced to wear a burqa in public.Photograph:  Wakil Kohsar/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA poster at a university, which became male-only under the Taliban, ordering women to wear hijabs. Women were later forced to wear a burqa in public.Photograph:  Wakil Kohsar/AFP/GettyRights and freedomGlobal developmentThe Taliban have built a system for enslaving women in AfghanistanAmanda Abou AbdallahFive years on, the regime’s chokehold has left Afghan women with almost nothing, but many are still bravely fighting for their freedomSupported byAbout this contentFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 04.42 EDTShareTheTalibandid not just ban women from schools, impose the burqa and outlaw smartphones. The Taliban built a system that enslaves nearly half the country’s population, or according to outdated statistics: 21,701,532 women and girls.In general, the Taliban’s system runs on laws that get changed, forgotten or scrapped as needed to oppress women, such as the abolition of the minimum marriage-age law, which made the only “legitimate” criterion for a girl’s marriage that she has reached puberty or in other words, that she is “fit for consummation”.And so, the state/group encourages economically crushed families, impoverished by the Taliban, tosell their young daughters in exchangefor a dowry that lets them support the rest of the family.Or the law thatlegitimises domestic violenceunder the label of “corrective beating”, which gives a husband the right to beat his wife, as long as he does not cause fractures or serious injuries.The Taliban also made sure to restrict the right to request divorce and shut down most shelters for abused women. If a girl or woman tries to escape this tragedy, the “morality police” pursue her.This tightening chokehold has made Afghanistan one of the few countries in the world where women’s suicide rates exceed men’s (globally, they are almost twice as common among males), with 75% to 80% ofrecorded suicide casesand attempts being women and girls.Five years into Taliban rule, Afghanistan plunges into a state of collapse – visualisedRead moreAnd if a woman survives an attempt to end her life, she usually cannot find treatment, because women are forbidden from being treated by male doctors.At the same time, the number of female doctors keeps shrinking through emigration or retirement, and because girls are banned from studying.So the only option left for many women is to wait for death in silence, because of course their voices are considered shameful to be heard.
