So what could a system like this be called, other than enslavement?Despite all this, Afghan women are fighting for their freedom, opening secret schools for girls, documenting violations and publishing them online under pseudonyms, and even protesting.In June,a very rare public demonstration took place, one of the few since the Taliban’s return to power in 2021, after the Americans withdrew. Women and men took to the streets of Herat demanding education, work and freedom, in the face of violent security crackdowns, arrests and a media blackout.But despite the blackout, the problem was never that the “civilised” world does not know what is happening. It knows very well what happened and what was done inAfghanistan, but as usual, it chose to just watch.Amanda Abou Abdallah, is the founder ofKhateera, a women-led platform covering the Arab regionExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomAfghanistanTalibanSouth and central AsiaWomen's rights and gender equalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Illustration: Jason White/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jason White/The GuardianOpinionCyclingI’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not meSimon JenkinsThe essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rulesFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareIplead guilty. I have loved and used the streets ofLondonall my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic.When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders ofebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyoneto moveout of the way.I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineerHans Mondermanboldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out foreach other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials.His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable successacross northern Europe, with accidents falling. In 2023,45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school.As a lifelong cyclist I admit to finding a certain exhilaration in riding a bike. I avoid main thoroughfares but like snaking through streets crammed with traffic, finding shortcuts through alleys and mews. But the essence of cycling is to keep moving. Hence I have to admit to sometimes doing what many London cyclists do at red lights. That is, look carefully, follow Monderman and “share” any unoccupied road space ahead by riding on.Traffic lights can now be rendered sensitive to queues waiting at them, and change sooner to green to allow buses through. Earlier this year, a policy director for the bike hire company Lime said he wantedlights to give priority to cyclists“to improve rider behaviour and encourage more people to cycle”. This makes sense. For the time being, at pedestrian crossings, cyclists should probably just get off at a red light and cross on foot.Investment in London’s cycle network is enabling more people to travel by bike, with the strategic cycle networknow 352km long, up from 90km in 2016. It is impressivethat this network was created by the same London planning authority that, 50 years ago, thought the answer to traffic planning was to build a giganticMotorway Box.Certainly cycling in any city is risky. The only truly safe speed is zero. But allcyclists will have their own “risk thresholds” – and the risk is largely up to them.The Highway Code’s “rules” for cyclistsare near hilarious. They boil down to two words: take care.My argument is less true when applied toebikes, I admit. These clearly do not work in shared space, whatever Monderman might have said. Electric Santander and Lime bikes may have transformed journey times: except for the simplest train ride, they can be the fastest means of travel across town. But this comes at a price.Ebikeslitter public streets with tips of abandoned machines; convenience is the mother of shambles. It cannot go on and technology must ensure bikes are properly parked.Ebikes now come in all shapes and speeds. It is astonishing that the sleek Freesky Alaska, with its 250W engine, can be treated as if it was just another manualpedal bike. To my mind, it is blatantly a motorbike. When a delivery driver on one careers past me in Hyde Park, I wonder if I took a wrong turning. These machines must be put on the roadway where they belong.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLondon used to be unique among great cities in being an enjoyable place to drive. It is no longer that. The bicycle has replaced that pleasure with a new freedom – but like all freedoms, it is one that craves intelligent regulation.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsCyclingOpinionCity transportEbikesTransportLondonRoad safetycommentShareReuse this content

title: With ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminals | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officials
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officials
Content: ‘Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionInternational criminal courtWith ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminalsKenneth RothThe US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officialsFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTShareThe Trump administration has taken another step in its crusade against theinternational criminal courtbyimposingsanctions on two more senior ICC officials. The growing number of sanctioned jurists – now13– does not change the lawless nature of this quest.Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them.The latest victims of Trump’s vendetta are the ICC president – its chief judge, Tomoko Akane of Japan – and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior ICC trial lawyer, evidently for his role advancing the prosecution of Israeli officials. Yet the real victims are not these particular individuals, but people worldwide who look to the court as one of the few avenues of recourse against unscrupulous leaders who commit mass atrocities such as fighting wars by targeting civilians.Why does the US want to ‘dismantle’ the international criminal court? | Kenneth RothRead moreWe should never let Trump normalize these sanctions. Their main effect is to deprive the target of the ability to use the international financial system – no credit cards, no access to banks, extreme difficulty navigating a modern economy. That is a tool once reserved for corrupt or violent officials who were otherwise beyond the law. Trump is using them to attack the public officials who would bring such heinous individuals to justice.Rubio, the secretary of state, dressed up the sanctions with high-sounding rhetoric about the ICC threatening “America sovereignty”. That is true only if Americans (and Israelis) have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want. Even Rubio cannot get himself to spell out what King Trump’s campaign is really about.Rubio’s main articulated complaint is that the ICC can “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. That is true, but it is wrong only if one adopts a conveniently (for Washington and the Israeli government) narrow sense of how the court should obtain jurisdiction for a crime.On the one hand, when a country joins the ICC, it accepts the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens. That might be called jurisdiction by virtue of nationality. The US government accepts that route to jurisdiction because it never joined the court.But when a country becomes a court member, it also confers jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, even when committed by a foreigner. That is hardly controversial. A hallmark of sovereignty is the ability to enforce the law on a country’s own territory. Even theTrump administrationwould not dare object to, say, the British government prosecuting an American for a crime committed in London.But the administration claims it is somehow an outrage if a country confers that same territorial jurisdiction on the ICC for war crimes and similar atrocities committed by foreigners on its territory – a major purpose of the court. The US government objected to such territorial jurisdiction when the court’s treaty was adopted at a major diplomatic conference in Rome in 1998 – andlostoverwhelmingly, by a vote of 120 to seven.Since then, even the US government has accepted territorial jurisdiction when convenient. After the ICC used it to prosecute Vladimir Putin (Russia never joined the court) for the kidnapping of children from Ukraine (a member), Joe Biden called the prosecution “justified”. The late senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican leader on foreign policy, orchestrated aunanimousSenateresolutionin support.double quotation markDonald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let themBut for Trump, territorial jurisdiction suddenly became toxic again when it was used tochargeBenjamin Netanyahu and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant with deliberately starving and depriving Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, but Palestine, where the alleged crimes took place, is.Territorial jurisdiction can also be used to charge foreigners from non-member states withaiding and abettingcrimes in a state where the ICC has jurisdiction. For example, the court might charge United Arab Emirates officials with aiding and abettinggenocidein the Darfur region of Sudan by sendingarmsandmercenariesto the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Rwandan officials with aiding and abetting war crimes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo byarmingand supporting the M23 rebel group, or US officials (Trump’s real concern) with aiding and abetting Israel’sgenocidein Gaza by supplying arms and military aid.Indeed, territorial jurisdiction means that the sanctions themselves could lead to prosecution of Trump and Rubio.Article 70of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, codifies the crime of obstructing justice when someone retaliates “against an official of the Court on account of duties performed”. That’s exactly what the Trump-Rubio sanctions do. The court would have jurisdiction because the sanctions relate to the prosecution of Israeli officials for crimes committed on Palestinian territory.Rubio hasvowedto dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”,announcing: “We expect more countries to join our campaign by ending their funding and participation in this politicized and unaccountable court.” Yet that bombast so far has produced few results among the court’s125members.Trump says he will dismantle the ICC ‘brick by brick’. It could be his most chilling move of all | Steve BloomfieldRead moreVenezuela, which has become a US vassal state since Trump’sseizureof Nicolás Maduro, has announced its withdrawal. So has Chad, whichannouncedits departure after a call from a state department official. But Chadian officials have their own reasons to worry about the court because they allowed their territory to beusedby the UAE to arm the RSF in Sudan.(Separately from Trump’s campaign, three military juntas in the Sahel have also announced their exit from the ICC:Niger,MaliandBurkina Faso.)Yet if the response to the Trump administration’s call to leave the court so far has been tepid, the defense of the court by its supposed closest defenders has not exactly been vigorous. The European Union has what is known as a “blocking statute”, legislation designed to negate the application of US sanctions in Europe by prohibiting European banks from complying. But while the EU says it “deeply regrets” these new sanctions on the ICC, it has not invoked the blocking statute to protect court personnel.One reason appears to befearamong banks, particularly in the Netherlands, of retaliation from Trump. The ICC is located in the Hague, also the Dutch seat of government.In other words, as European officials see it, fighting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity is important. Trump’s efforts to allow Americans and Israelis to commit these crimes with impunity is disgraceful. But if defending the rule of law might put Dutch banks in Trump’s crosshairs, justice can wait.The EU can do better than that.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsInternational criminal courtOpinionTrump administrationDonald TrumpMarco RubioUS politicsInternational criminal justiceIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal sweep Coventry aside to start Premier League title defence in style | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Ødegaard were on target as Arsenal began their title defence with a 3-0 win over promoted Coventry
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Ødegaard were on target as Arsenal began their title defence with a 3-0 win over promoted Coventry
Content: Kai Havertz (centre) opens the scoring for Arsenal; Bukayo Saka (left) and Martin Ødegaard (right) later joined him on the scoresheet.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKai Havertz (centre) opens the scoring for Arsenal; Bukayo Saka (left) and Martin Ødegaard (right) later joined him on the scoresheet.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPremier LeagueArsenal sweep Coventry aside to start Premier League title defence in styleEd Aaronsat the Emirates StadiumFri 21 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat a difference a title makes. The last time Arsenal played in front of their own supporters, you could cut the nervous tension with a knife as Mikel Arteta’s side scraped to a 1-0 victory over already relegated Burnley. Ninety five days on and having ended their long wait to be crowned champions the following night when Manchester City slipped up against Bournemouth, Arsenal gave Coventry a rude awakening in their firstPremier Leaguegame for 25 years.It’s now 46 matches sinceArsenallost at home to a newly promoted side and there was never any doubt about this result as soon as Kai Havertz – who scored the only goal against Burnley that turned out to be priceless – picked up where he left off by giving Arsenal the lead in the 15th minute. A tap-in from Bukayo Saka and captain Martin Ødegaard matching his Premier League tally from last season just after half-time made it almost the perfect start for the reigning champions.Arteta predicts ‘more to come’ from established players amid Alvarez talkRead moreArteta had warned beforehand that his players were hungry for more silverware this season and as well as assembling one of the deepest squads, they now have the vital experience of having actually done it. It was telling that with 15 minutes still to play and his side cruising towards victory, the Arsenal manager had the luxury of replacing the outstanding Ødegaard and Declan Rice with two World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi.It could have been much worse for Coventry had Arsenal not taken their foot off the accelerator by then. But Frank Lampard will know that their chances of survival will not rest on this result and next week’s homecoming against Hull should provide more of a barometer of their prospects.In another show of their considerable strength, Arsenal had paraded their new signing Ezri Konsa before kick-off after the England defender completed his £51m move from Aston Villa. But they were without Bruno Guimarães after the £75m midfielder picked up an injury on his debut in Sunday’s convincing Community Shield victory over City.Quick GuideArsenal 3-0 Coventry key statsShow• Mikel Arteta recorded his150th Premier League victoryin charge of Arsenal, and is now one of only five managers to reach 150 wins in fewer than 250 games (249), after Pep Guardiola (204), José Mourinho (231), Jürgen Klopp (237), and Alex Ferguson (247).• Arsenal areunbeaten in 46 Premier League home gamesagainst promoted sides, extending the longest such run by any team in the competition’s history (W41 D5). Within this run, they have won the most recent 17 matches by an aggregate score of 47-9.• Frank Lampard (pictured) haswon only one of his last 18 gamesas a manager in the Premier League (D4 L13), while his side have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of the last 17.OptaPhotograph: Tom JenkinsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Coventry’s line-up contained five new signings including the Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi and it showed. At least they managed to avoid a repeat of their only two previous visits to this stadium when they conceded 10 goals in FA and League Cup ties at a time they were in the third tier. But while not many of the supporters who made the journey to north London will remember Micky Quinn’s hat-trick in Coventry’s win on the opening day of the 1993-94 season at the old Highbury, Lampard had urged his players to show belief that they belong at this level.Sadly for him, Arsenal were in no mood for sentimentality. Christos Tzolis was not the most eye-catching arrival of the summer but the Greece forward was a lively presence from the start and could have given them the lead twice in the first 10 minutes before Havertz eventually did. Tzolis and Riccardo Calafiori teamed up on the left flank to dispossess Milan van Ewijk and the Italian rolled a pass perfectly on to the onrushing Havertz to finish.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka after scoring Arsenal’s second goal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBefore Coventry knew what had hit them they were two behind. A flowing move started by Rice involving a clever one-two with Ødegaard saw Carl Rushworth play a cross from Tzolis straight to the grateful Saka. Yirenkyi went into the book for hauling down Myles Lewis-Skelly as Coventry struggled to keep their heads above water. It was no surprise that Lampard looked so concerned as he watched on with his arms folded firmly across his chest. Only four of his squad have previous Premier League experience that amounts to little more than 200 games in total. They will need to learn quickly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLoum Tchaouna almost caught David Raya napping with a speculative lob just before half-time but Yirenkyi was perhaps fortunate not to be shown a second yellow card after catching Tzolis with a late challenge.Coventry’s luck didn’t last long. A scuffed finish from Ødegaard after he was set up by Ben White only four minutes after the restart extinguished any hopes of mounting a comeback. Rushworth’s face said it all as the ball trickled over the line.From then on it was damage limitation. Rushworth was at full stretch to tip over a powerful drive from Lewis-Skelly before Ødegaard had a goalbound effort deflected wide. But the departures of Rice and Saka with little more than 20 minutes to play was an indication that Arteta was more than satisfied with the scoreline. The substitute Jack Rudoni came closest to grabbing a consolation for the visitors in the dying minutes but Coventry can console themselves with the realisation that it doesn’t get any harder than this.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueArsenalCoventry Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United agree deal for Carlos Baleba to continue midfield rebuild | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United have agreed a deal worth an initial £65m for Carlos Baleba and the Brighton midfielder will have his medical this weekend
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester United have agreed a deal worth an initial £65m for Carlos Baleba and the Brighton midfielder will have his medical this weekend
Content: Carlos Baleba will have a medical this weekend after Manchester United agreed a deal worth an initial £65m to sign him.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersView image in fullscreenCarlos Baleba will have a medical this weekend after Manchester United agreed a deal worth an initial £65m to sign him.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersManchester UnitedManchester United agree deal for Carlos Baleba to continue midfield rebuildBrighton midfielder will join Tielemans and SantosClub’s most expensive summer signing at initial £65mJamie JacksonFri 21 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 17.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have agreed a deal worth an initial £65m for Carlos Baleba and the Brighton midfielder will have his medical this weekend in Manchester.If the 22-year-old is signed he will be the third midfielder added to Michael Carrick’s squad in the window. Baleba, a No 6, will join Youri Tielemans, a No 8, and Andrey Santos, who is also a holding player.Manchester United’s midfield rebuild leaves Carrick with no excusesRead moreEven before a potential £5m in add-ons Baleba would be United’s most expensive buy of the summer asTielemans cost £35mandSantos an initial £48m, with a possible £2m of extras. Baleba’s signing would take United’s total spend to £148m.Privately, United are delighted with the deal after failing to land the Cameroon star last summer. Last year, Brighton were hoping for a price in the region of the £115m they received when they sold Moisés Caicedo to Chelsea in 2023 but Carrick now has his midfield enforcer in a deal which represents value on and off the pitch.Speaking before the agreement was struck, Carrick outlined the importance of a functioning midfield. “I think it gives you the foundation of the team, you know. I think the foundation of the team is important to be consistent, to be consistent through one game from start to finish, to be consistent over a period of time.“You need a solid foundation through the middle of the team and trying and putting it together and getting that balance. But certainly, I think if you look at all the top teams over the years, all the great teams over the years, the spine of the team is really strong, you know.“So we’re conscious of that, and I think we’ve got a good spine of the team right now. We can keep improving as we go in different ways and coaching and helping the boys and developing them, and I think we’re in a good place.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedBrighton & Hove AlbionTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt pipped into second by Kayla White on return from European gold rush | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Amy Hunt had to be happy with second behind the American Kayla White in the 200m at the at the Lausanne Diamond League on Friday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Britain’s Amy Hunt had to be happy with second behind the American Kayla White in the 200m at the at the Lausanne Diamond League on Friday
Content: Amy Hunt could only manage second in 22.32sec, just ahead of Nigeria’s Favour Ofili.Photograph: Laurent Gilliéron/EPAView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt could only manage second in 22.32sec, just ahead of Nigeria’s Favour Ofili.Photograph: Laurent Gilliéron/EPAAthleticsAmy Hunt pipped into second by Kayla White on return from European gold rushBriton felt ‘tired’ before Lausanne Diamond League 200mAudrey Werro triumphs in 800m in front of home crowdAgence France-PresseFri 21 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s Amy Hunt, who won a historic four golds at the recent EuropeanAthleticsChampionships, had to be happy with second behind the American Kayla White in the 200m at the Lausanne Diamond League on Friday.White won in 22.18sec, with Hunt holding off Nigeria’s Favour Ofili in a photo-finish at 22.32. Jamaica’s Shericka Jackson, the two-time former world champion in the event, pulled up with 70m of the race to run. Hunt said she had been “tired before the race and my pre-competition felt pretty stiff”.Former 1500m world champion Jenny Simpson steps away from running after cardiac arrestRead moreSwitzerland’s Audrey Werro clocked a meet best to win the 800m on home soil but fell well short of the world record.The newly crowned European champion, the third fastest ever in the women’s two-lap race, is aiming to break the 1min 53.28sec run by Jarmila Kratochvilova of Czechoslovakia in 1983. It remains the oldest world record in track and field, albeit one that is highly contested having come during a period when systemic doping of athletes was prevalent. Kratochvilova, however, never failed a doping test.Emmanuel Wanyonyi, the world and Olympic champion, claimed victory in the men’s 800m in 1:42.19 ahead of Algeria’s Djamel Sedjati, the two-time world silver medallist who won bronze at the Paris Games.Botswana’s Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo dominated the men’s 200m, winning in 19.87 in a dominant display.In the triple-jump there was no joy for Italy’s Andy Díaz Hernández, who went out to the third longest distance ever, of 18.15m, to win gold at the Euros in Birmingham. He finished third in Switzerland with a best of 17.20m, Portugal’s Pedro Pichardo winning with 17.44.There were also meeting records for the American Masai Russell in the 100m hurdles (12.27) and for his teammate Rai Benjamin, who has been focused on the 400m flat this season, in the 400m hurdles (46.67), beating Edwin Moses’ mark of 47.14 from 1981.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 1: Arsenal | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: After an underwhelming season, Arsenal have made major changes with club legends departing and top talent from all over Europe arriving
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: After an underwhelming season, Arsenal have made major changes with club legends departing and top talent from all over Europe arriving
Content: Stina Blackstenius is congratulated on scoring in a pre-season friendly against Manchester City. Photograph: David Price/David Price, Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesAfter an underwhelming season, Arsenal have made major changes with club legends departing and top talent from all over Europe arrivingBySuzanne WrackFri 21 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:2nd (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wrack’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:2ndProspectsLast season was a disappointment for Arsenal when it came to silverware, the inauguralFifa Champions Cupcoming nowhere near to sating the hunger there was to build on the Champions League success of 2025. To a certain extent, that helped paper over the cracks for a squad that needed an overhaul. That has come this summer, with 11 players departing, including the club legends Beth Mead and Katie McCabe, and seven arriving. In the Spain full-back Ona Batlle, England midfielder Georgia Stanway, Switzerland midfielder Géraldine Reuteler and German forward Selina Cerci, Arsenal have added experienced top-tier talent while also lowering the age profile of the squad.Whether Mead and McCabe, allowed to leave to Manchester City and Chelsea respectively, come back to haunt Arsenal remains to be seen, but Renée Slegers has had a full pre-season for the first time, having secured qualification for the Champions League league phase through their second-place finish in the Women’s Super League. After two slow starts to WSL campaigns, including four draws and a defeat in their opening nine matches last year, a summer without a major international tournament or Champions League qualifiers gives Arsenal no excuses going into the season.The title race will probably be tighter this year, with City also competing in the Champions League and many other sides having invested shrewdly, but Arsenal have an opportunity to end a seven-year wait for a league title. “We’re in a great place of course, but we would have liked to have won more trophies last season and that is our huge ambition coming into this year,” said the technical director, Jodie Taylor. “I’ll flat out say it: we want to win the league and want to take that next step.”Arsenal league positionsOff-field pictureArsenal’s latest accounts showed revenue was up by £6.5m, to £21.5m, for the year ending May 2025. During that year, the average attendance at the Emirates Stadium for eight games was 29,833 and Arsenal brought in matchday revenue of just under £6m. Arsenal’s filing will probably show further progress when the effect of last season’s average attendance of more than 34,000 for all 11 of their WSL home games is revealed. There have been successes in other areas too: broadcast revenue was up to more than £2m, more than double the £956,000 of 2024 (in part thanks to their Champions League success) and commercial revenue increased from £649,000 to £1.77m. Like many WSL sides though, Arsenal are still very reliant on money from the parent club, with group income increased from £9.3m to £11.85m, more than half of their overall revenue.The managerSlegers goes into her second full season in charge with expectations high. The 37-year-old has worked wonders since stepping in as interim manager after the exit of Jonas Eidevall and has a chance to show her quality. Slegers inherited an established squad and this summer’s overhaul gives her a chance to shape the team in the way she wants it to look and play.Star signingArsenal have plunged into the transfer market and come out with some big fish, with the two-time Euro-winning Stanway perhaps the pick of the bunch. Stanway brings exceptional talent and has already established relationships with several England teammates at the club. She also brings something Arsenal have been lacking: steeliness. The 27-year-old is a battling, physical midfielder, who, as she recently told the Guardian, is “ruthless and robust”. That will be a huge boost to Arsenal’s spine.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Stanway should bring steel to Arsenal’s midfield.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesStat attackArsenal led Opta’s expected points metric for the WSL in 2025-26 and lost one match all season. Why didn’t they win the league? They drew six matches to Manchester City’s one. Expected goal data suggested they comfortably deserved to win three of their drawn games with one, against Chelsea, where they probably should have lost. As they and City shared a win each in their head-to-heads, these matches proved decisive.Arsenal drawsSet for a breakthroughLast season was meant to bring breakthroughs for the 20-year-old Michelle Agyemang and 19-year-old Katie Reid after a phenomenal Euro 2025 campaign for the former and a stellar start to the domestic campaign for the latter, but anterior cruciate ligament injuries cut short such progress. After almost a year off the pitch, both are preparing to return to action. Their returns will need to be carefully managed and they will probably take time to rediscover their best form, but both will be keen to continue where they left off.What they say …“It’s like you’re cooking the most beautiful recipe and then you add the final small ingredients that make the marginal difference, that elevate, and you create something that’s beautiful and that you can relish and enjoy. That’s what we’re in the process of.” – Lotte Wubben-Moy.Where are they playing their home games?All WSL home games and European knockout games (subject to qualification) will take place at the Emirates Stadium. Domestic cup games and Champions League league-phase matches will continue to be played at Meadow Park. Arsenal have led the way in growing attendances, contributing more than 40% of WSL attendances last season, but the club are stuck when it comes to cup and European league phase games, with the Emirates too big and scheduling around men’s team fixtures too complex for such fixtures to take place there while the team have clearly outgrown Meadow Park.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Arsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Root reveals incoming England coach Fleming was in daily contact during first Test win | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Joe Root said of Stephen Fleming: ‘It’s great that he’s very invested already,’ adding that his bowling group ‘don’t understand how good they are’
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Joe Root said of Stephen Fleming: ‘It’s great that he’s very invested already,’ adding that his bowling group ‘don’t understand how good they are’
Content: Joe Root shows his delight as England seal their innings victory on day three. He later heaped praise on Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Root shows his delight as England seal their innings victory on day three. He later heaped praise on Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesEngland v Pakistan 2026Root reveals incoming England coach Fleming was in daily contact during first Test win‘It’s great that he’s very invested already,’ says captainEngland bowlers ‘don’t understand how good they are’Taha Hashimat HeadingleyFri 21 Aug 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 17.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Root celebrated a commanding start to his latest reign as England’s Test captain, his side thumping Pakistan in Leeds, and afterwards said Stephen Fleming had been in daily contact before he starts his role as head coach.Fleming does not take up his position until after the series against Pakistan but has been in touch with Root during the week. “It’s been great to have [him] on the end of the phone,” said Root. “It’s great that he’s very invested already in what we’re trying to achieve.”England’s bowlers tear through Pakistan to seal crushing innings victory in first TestRead moreThe pair have plenty to work with, as a victory margin of an innings and 103 runs attests, even if the tourists were remarkably poor across three days of play. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue took eight wickets apiece while Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence marked their returns to the XI with half-centuries.“The quality that we have within the team and our bowling group – I don’t really think they understand how good they are and how well they complement each other and in these conditions what they’re capable of doing,” said Root. “It’s really nice for them to see that and to start the series like that.“Jordan at 3 looked very calm, very composed, very comfortable within his own game in those conditions. Great to see, great to bat with. Dan as well, the way he dovetailed with [Harry Brook], played in his own way, was brilliant.”The result made it seven consecutive Test victories at Headingley for England, a run that began withan innings win against Pakistan in 2018. It will be some time before they build on it, with the ground not hosting men’s Test cricket in 2027 and 2028.“I’d love to play as many games as possible here,” said Root of his home venue. “It’s a surface that provides brilliant Test cricket and one that we’ve had quite a lot of success in recently. So it’s a shame that we don’t get to play here next year. But I’m sure we’ll see many, many more brilliant Test matches here.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPakistan’s misery was summed up by their stand-in captain’s response to whether the injured Babar Azam will return to lead for the second Test at Lord’s. “I’m more than happy to hand the captaincy to him,” said Salman Ali Agha. “Hopefully he’ll be fine. He’s our best batter so we definitely want him and to hand him the captaincy.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketPakistan cricket teamEngland cricket teamJoe RootnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wigan sink Wakefield and hit Super League summit with 12th straight win | Super League | The Guardian
description: Wigan moved to the top of Super League with a 26-12 win over Wakefield, with Bevan French leading Warriors to a 12th straight victory
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Wigan moved to the top of Super League with a 26-12 win over Wakefield, with Bevan French leading Warriors to a 12th straight victory
Content: Bevan French carries the fight to Wakefield.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBevan French carries the fight to Wakefield.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueWigan sink Wakefield and hit Super League summit with 12th straight winSuper League: Wigan 26-12 WakefieldFrench leads the way as Warriors break club recordAaron Bowerat the Brick Community StadiumFri 21 Aug 2026 17.54 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you are aWigan Warriorssupporter and a keen believer in omens, it may be wise to cancel any plans you had for the first weekend of October.The Warriors are back on top ofSuper League, albeit for potentially just 48 hours before Leeds Rhinos get the chance to return serve on Sunday in York. But this was a record-breaking night for one of rugby league’s great clubs, who have now set a club record for most consecutive league wins in the summer era after a 12th straight triumph, this time against Wakefield.The three previous time they had hit 11 consecutive wins before this season were in 1998, 2013 and 2023. The final outcome in each of those years? Wigan were ultimately crowned Super League champions – and few would back against that becoming a reality again at Old Trafford in October after another impressive display.Perhaps the biggest compliment you can pay Wigan right now is how rudimentary they are making games of this magnitude look and feel. Wakefield have been magnificent this season and while their own title charge has stuttered with back-to-back defeats of late, Trinity are no mugs these days. Yet Wigan ultimately made this look and feel straightforward.Wakefield held their own in the early exchanges and underlined why they are not to be written off come the playoffs. They showed that again with a second half effort when the game felt lost. But these crucial matches are defined by big moments and in Bevan French and Jai Field, Wigan arguably have Super League’s two most outstanding players who can decide matches.French justified that praise when he opened the scoring with a scintillating long-range break after a Wakefield attack broke down. That was the moment that swung it the way of the hosts, with French’s try the first of three in nine minutes that put Wigan in control.Liam Marshall was the beneficiary of two wonderful pieces of play to score in the corner on two occasions and with Adam Keighran converting both before adding a penalty on the half-time hooter, Wigan had rode out a difficult opening 20 minutes to lead by 20 at the interval. It was a passage of play few, if any, sides could have coped with.But as mentioned, this Wakefield side are a credible threat come the play-offs, with their place in the top six already assured in all probability. They were much-improved after half-time and Corey Hall’s try to get them on the board was the least they deserved. A period of sustained pressure from the visitors then followed and had they scored again, we could have had a grandstand finale.However, one of those crucial moments arrived with 15 minutes left. Wakefield spilled the ball while probing the Wigan line and Field collected, nonchalantly stepped around Jack Sinfield and raced the length of the field to put the result beyond doubt. It is a script we have seen so many times before, Field and French starring: but it does not get boring.There was another consolation for Wakefield with ten minutes left when Ky Rodwell crashed over, and they showed enough to suggest they will be a threat in the play-offs. But Wigan, without being on optimal form, showed right now, there is only one team really to beat.The Wigan coach, Matt Peet said: “The run is going to end at some point, but hopefully it’s not the next game. I’ve got a group I love working with. There’s a lot left in us but some of the good stuff comes through the imperfection. We can certainly be slicker but we were very hard to break down against a good team.”“It was a tough game we were in all the way through,” Wakefield’s coach, Daryl Powell, admitted. “We talked about their speed and what happens if you give them loose ball and we gave them two tries when we had the ball. Ultimately that was the difference, but we should be proud of our effort.”Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWigan WarriorsWakefield TrinityRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jannik Sinner and Jack Draper out of US Open as injuries take their toll | Jannik Sinner | The Guardian
description: The men’s world No 1, Jannik Sinner, has ⁠ruled himself out of the US Open and Jack Draper is also set to miss the event
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The men’s world No 1, Jannik Sinner, has ⁠ruled himself out of the US Open and Jack Draper is also set to miss the event
Content: Jannik Sinner has not played since the Wimbledon final.Photograph: Edgar Su/ReutersView image in fullscreenJannik Sinner has not played since the Wimbledon final.Photograph: Edgar Su/ReutersJannik SinnerJannik Sinner and Jack Draper out of US Open as injuries take their tollWorld No 1 makes ‘difficult decision’ to miss slamDraper still recovering from bone bruise in left armPA MediaFri 21 Aug 2026 12.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJannik Sinner will miss the US Open with a right knee injury. The world No 1 has not played a match since beating Alexander Zverev last month to successfully defend his Wimbledon title, missing the Masters 1000 events in Canada and Cincinnati. Great Britain’s Jack Draper is also out of the event.Can Aryna Sabalenka find a way to repair her collapsed form? | Tumaini CarayolRead moreThe news comes a day after his great rival Carlos Alcaraz, whom the Italian lost to in the final in New York 12 months ago,revealed he will make his comebackat Flushing Meadows after four months out with a wrist injury.Sinner said: “Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year. We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue.“I’m obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there.”It will be the first grand slam the 25-year-old has missed since making his debut at the US Open in 2019 and will further focus attention on the physical demands of the tennis calendar.Draper, meanwhile, is continuing to battle a bone bruise in his dominant left arm and, after two dispiriting matches in the US, PA Media understands he has concluded he needs more time to recover.Explore more on these topicsJannik SinnerUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide … the cautionary tale of the first cross-Channel swimmer | Swimming | The Guardian
description: In this content-driven age, we consume sport as fleeting entertainment – but the fate of Captain Matthew Webb suggests we always have
Author: Emma John
Headline: In this content-driven age, we consume sport as fleeting entertainment – but the fate of Captain Matthew Webb suggests we always have
Content: ‘What should have been a 21-mile distance turned into nearly 39 as tides and weather threw Matthew Webb off course.’Illustration: Robin HursthouseView image in fullscreen‘What should have been a 21-mile distance turned into nearly 39 as tides and weather threw Matthew Webb off course.’Illustration: Robin HursthouseSwimmingPull. Breathe. Kick. Glide … the cautionary tale of the first cross-Channel swimmerEmma JohnIn this content-driven age, we consume sport as fleeting entertainment – but the fate of Captain Matthew Webb suggests we always haveFri 21 Aug 2026 16.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. Three decades since my last swimming lesson, I found myself sitting in a lecture theatre chanting these words with a few dozen strangers, all of us trying not to take anyone’s eye out as we matched them to the actions.Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. I’ve been to enough Edinburgh fringe shows to inure myself to the embarrassment of audience participation. And, to be honest, this one was a pretty euphoric communal experience. It turns out you don’t need to be near water to marvel at a swimming feat, especially one that’s more than 150 years old.The comedian Adam Riches previously created a one-man show out of Jimmy Connors’ 1991 US Open run, a theatrical effort that involved a lot of leaping, smashing and two-handed backhands. The Captain, which runs through August, evokes a less explosive kind of sporting endurance. It’s named for Matthew Webb, the first man to swim the Channel unaided, although we never meet the hero himself. Instead, Riches narrates his story in the person of Fred Beckwith, the promoter who helped Webb train for his feat at Lambeth Baths.Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. Today, we probably think of breaststroke as the least flashy of all the competitive swimming disciplines. It’s hard to imagine people packing Victorian music halls to watch live demonstrations of it, but then, for the previous millennium, there hadn’t been much of a European tradition of swimming at all. Consider Leonardo da Vinci’s 16th-century notebooks, where, among his thoughts on flying machines, gunpowder, and steam-powered cannon, he mused on “how it is that all other animals which have feet with toes, know by nature how to swim, excepting man” and “in what way man ought to learn to swim”.View image in fullscreenCaptain Matthew Webb, the first man to swim the English Channel in 1875. It took him 21 hours and 45 minutes.Photograph: Getty ImagesIn Riches’ show, Beckwith tells us that “swimming, pre-Captain Webb, wasn’t an act in itself – it was merely a counterpoint to drowning”. Not entirely true, because in 1810 Lord Byron had already channelled his Main Character Energy into crossing the Hellespont – which we know today as the Dardanelles in Turkey – to prove a point. The mad, bad aristocrat managed the dangerous four-mile stretch of straits in just over an hour – with a club foot, no less – and immediately wrote a poem about his achievement. Within a couple of decades, the types of races that had been held in lakes for informal wagers were gradually being organised into something formal by the NationalSwimmingSociety, and artificial pools were being opened in London.Still, Webb’s heroics did significantly popularise the pastime, not least because his aquatic adventure had gone almost fatally wrong. What should have been a 21-mile distance turned into nearly 39 as tides and weather threw him off course. Even then, his actions inspired plenty of others to emulate him, including Agnes Beckwith, Fred’s daughter, who set her own long-distance records, swimming 20 miles of the Thames from Westminster to Richmond and back to Mortlake.Olympic swimming owes him its own debt: the races at the first modern Games in 1896 were held in the Mediterranean Sea, where athletes contended with frigid temperatures and 13ft waves. (After winning gold in the 1200m, 18-year-old Alfréd Hajós stated that “my will to live completely overcame my desire to win”.) The Channel has had a share in Webb’s glory, too. For decades that treacherous, traffic-lined stretch of water became (and in some ways remains) the ultimate marker of endurance swimming.Gertrude Ederle’s 1926 crossing – the fastest in its day and the first by a woman – became as well known as Webb’s. And it was Ederle’s memory that inspired the legendary Lynne Cox on her own record-breaking swims: the first woman to cross the Cook Strait between New Zealand’s North and South islands, then the first human to traverse the Bering Strait between the US and the Soviet Union. A cold war effort indeed, in waters that literally froze around her.View image in fullscreenGertrude Ederle’s 1926 Channel crossing became as famous as Matthew Webb’s.Photograph: APFor me, it has been impossible to contemplate Webb without following an imaginary current to a more recent legend of the breaststroke. Admittedly, Adam Ramsay-Peaty doesn’t have to swim further than 100m at a time, and it usually takes him under a minute, as opposed to the 21 hours and 45 minutes that Webb struggled between Dover and Calais. Still, there’s something in the obstinate ambition of each man that echoes down the centuries, that calls across the 30 miles between their Shropshire and Staffordshire birthplaces. Ramsay-Peaty has been, like Webb, the greatest breaststroke swimmer that ever breathed, kicked, glided. He’salso learningthat even the lushest of laurel wreaths don’t stay green for ever.Webb’s own tale was, tragically, a cautionary one: he died at 35, chasing the fame and fortune that never lasted long enough. We’re equally minded, in this content-driven age, to consume sport as any other fleeting entertainment. And perhaps that’s how it should be. It was, after all, conceived and marshalled under its new 19th-century codes as a byproduct of the burgeoning middle classes’ appetite for leisure and recreation.But there’s something in the nature of sport – its sense of a physical science, a way of measuring human progress – that will always speak to us at a deeper level. Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelchabreaking the two-hour barrierat the London Marathon. Josh Kerr running thefastest ever mile. Katie Ledecky becoming the greatest distance swimmer in history. And Captain Matthew Webb – whose ghost John Betjeman would decades later write a poem about – doing a thing that everyone but him believed humanly impossible.Explore more on these topicsSwimmingEdinburgh festivalcommentShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way | Attieh Fard | The Guardian
description: I had few resources as a candidate but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better, says lawyer and byelection candidate Attieh Fard
Author: Attieh Fard
Headline: I had few resources as a candidate but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better, says lawyer and byelection candidate Attieh Fard
Content: A Reform UK campaign bus in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, on 4 August 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenA Reform UK campaign bus in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, on 4 August 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionClacton byelection August 2026Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same wayAttieh FardI had few resources as a candidate, but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much betterFri 21 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 09.22 EDTShareIn the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. Itshowed Nigel Farageamong his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.He was referring to the33 other candidateswho had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt ofan undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whomI was one.I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime hasmassacred thousandsof innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago thathe met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassyin London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about£250,000 of taxpayers’ money.Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UKleft the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard,but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, butNigel FarageMP has some serious work to do in Clacton.Attieh Fard is a lawyer who was an independent candidate in the Clacton parliamentary byelectionExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageImmigration and asylumReform UKUK bill of rightsHuman Rights ActHuman rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: So Harry and Meghan are moving back to the UK. Who cares? | John Crace | The Guardian
description: And as Diana’s brother announces a new book, what can possibly be left to say about the princess? Plus, the joys of car rental and Reform’s Whitehall farce
Author: John Crace
Headline: And as Diana’s brother announces a new book, what can possibly be left to say about the princess? Plus, the joys of car rental and Reform’s Whitehall farce
Content: They can live where they like: Harry and Meghan near Bondi Beach during their trip to Australia in April.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThey can live where they like: Harry and Meghan near Bondi Beach during their trip to Australia in April.Photograph: Getty ImagesDigested weekMonarchyDigested week: So Harry and Meghan are moving back to the UK. Who cares?John CraceAnd as Diana’s brother announces a new book, what can possibly be left to say about the princess? Plus, the joys of car rental and Reform’s Whitehall farceFri 21 Aug 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareMondayThere are some days you never forget. It was about 6.30 in the morning the day after we had done a long drive back from hospital. Anna was five years old, Robbie just two and both were wide awake and had got me out of bed. I took them downstairs to plonk them in front of the TV to try and buy myself some time. I switched the TV on and didn’t turn it off for the rest of the day. Princess Diana had been killed in a car crash. I just stared and stared, not quite taking it in. Hard to believe that it all took place nearly 30 years ago, but Penguin has just announced that next month it will be publishing a biography of Diana written by her brother, Charles Spencer. “I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way,” he has said, adding that she was “A one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.” Yup. Well it was hardly ever going to be a hatchet job, was it.I can’t help wondering what more there can possibly be to say about Diana. Maybe we will be surprised. Maybe her brother has access to information that will completely reframe the way Diana is remembered. But somehow I doubt it. There again, I may not be the target market. I appear to be the only person who doesn’t give a toss that Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. As far as I’m concerned, they can live where they like. Even so, I am sure I will still read the Diana offering.View image in fullscreenThe king and Ethel Caterham, who turned 117 today. Charles: ‘That’s how I felt when I heard Harry was coming back.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PATuesdayPart One. After a wonderful week away with friends in France where we managed to relax, laugh and forget about cancer, there’s one thing that’s almost always guaranteed to bring you down to earth. A reminder that your holiday is well and truly over. That’s the moment when you take your car back to the car hire centre at Toulouse airport.What a difference a week makes. On the way out, the staff at the car hire desk could not have been more helpful. How lovely to see you, he said. Then the inevitable hard sell. Would you like to buy the extra insurance that you thought you had already bought when you booked the car online? I could have sworn it had said it was fully inclusive but the sales rep with the golden smile insisted I was wrong. When it had said fully inclusive on the booking form, what it meant was that it was fully inclusive with exemptions. What I needed to know was that there was fully inclusive and fullyfullyinclusive and that I needed to take out further insurance if I wanted total peace of mind. Which I did, because I have memories in the past of winging it and getting stiffed for some invisible damage when I returned the car.So I signed up, with my wife shaking her head and muttering that I had undoubtedly just been ripped off. Then the sales rep said that – because I was a valued customer or an easy mark, take your pick – he was also offering me another special deal. I could return the car without a full tank of petrol and be charged only €1.90 a litre for the missing fuel. This sounded like a deal. Unleaded is about €2.00 a litre and I know from past experience it’s a nightmare trying to find a garage near the airport on the way back. So I took that option, too, and was finally on my way.View image in fullscreenBuses near the abandoned village of Imber: ‘You wait for 10 minutes and then 30 come along at once.’Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesWednesdayPart Two. The car, to no one’s surprise, turned out to be a bit of a dud. The engine monitor light came on halfway through day two and never went off. I tried to ignore it but had this niggling worry throughout the holiday that the car was going to break down at our favourite lake where there is no network coverage to call for assistance. I also couldn’t stop thinking that the whole point of hiring a car was that you weren’t supposed to be worried about maintaining it. On day four the tyre pressure warning light also came on. A trip to the garage revealed the tyres to be at the correct pressure but the light stayed on.Given all this, I’m not entirely sad to be shot of the car, us and it in one piece, at the airport. Only it turns out there is no one to check it in and complete the paperwork. Don’t worry, says the man at the desk. Just leave the keys with us and we will sort it. An hour later, after I’ve checked in, I get an email from the car hire place. A reconciliation notice. There was €350 of damage to the car. There really wasn’t. It was spotless. Not even a scratch. But because I had full insurance, I won’t be charged. Phew. Only I will be charged €35 for someone having to estimate the damage. On top of this, I will be charged another €100 for petrol, even though the car was two-thirds full and would take €30-worth at most. Moments later, the same car hire company sends me another email asking me to fill out a customer satisfaction survey. Bad timing.ThursdayWe’re deep into the dog days of August when almost nothing is happening in Westminster. Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey have gone to ground, presumably having family holidays. Only Andy Burnham has limited himself to just a week off and that’s because he’s only been prime minister for a month. So Burnham has been doing daily 90-second pool clips for the broadcasters, but no one is really paying that much attention. Yet there is still entertainment to be had, as Reform has chosen this summer to offer its own clown show. First we have had theClacton byelection, which turned into a two-horse race between Nige and a man with a bin on his head. Rather sweetly, Richard Tice called Nige’s win “a triumph”. Nige has rather gone to ground. Dicky isn’t normally let out on his own and you can see why, as he has been enthusing about the benefits of climate change that he doesn’t believe is happening. We should all justenjoy the heathe says. Then there’s the infighting. Everyone in Reform seems to hate Zia Yusuf but isn’t allowed to say so because the only person with the authority to criticise a member of the inner circle is Nige and he rather enjoys Zia’s money. So Tim Montgomerie has been suspended for saying what everyone thinks. It’s a genuine Whitehall farce. A treat for those of us who can’t make it to the Edinburgh fringe.View image in fullscreenExam results: ‘Fantastic. We’ve just qualified for £50k of student debt.’Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAFridayConfession time. When the ultra low emission zone was introduced in London by Sadiq Khan in 2019, I had my doubts. I thought the claims about improving people’s health were probably overstated and its main purpose was as another revenue stream for the London mayor. It just felt like another area of state interference: back in 2011 we had bought a diesel car because in those days we had been told they were more environmentally friendly than petrol vehicles. Now we had to sell it at a rock bottom price, because no one in London wanted to buy a diesel, and fork out for a hybrid. I felt the same way about the 20mph signs that began to take over London. It seemed a deliberate, unnecessary attempt to annoy drivers further and to catch them out with speeding fines. I myself picked up a fine for doing 24mph in a 20 zone, just because I wasn’t paying enough attention. But time is a great healer and for the past few years I’ve rather got used to dawdling everywhere. I make my family mad by how slowly I drive. I’m rapidly turning into my dad. And now Sadiq has been completely vindicated. In what is genuinely a good news story, the first research is in and children’slung capacity has improvedsignificantly as a result of the imposition of Ulez. So huge respect to Sadiq for having the vision to stand up to the doubters like me. And what a legacy for the mayor. Not all politicians get to leave the country better than they found it.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDigested weekPrince HarryDiana, Princess of WalesReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Women’s football shouldn’t have to copy a men’s game that isn’t working – just look at Ted Lasso | Karen Dobres | The Guardian
description: The rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinct, says author Karen Dobres
Author: Karen Dobres
Headline: The rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinct, says author Karen Dobres
Content: Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in season 4 of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAView image in fullscreenBrendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in season 4 of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAOpinionWomen's footballWomen’s football shouldn’t have to copy a men’s game that isn’t working – just look at Ted LassoKaren DobresThe rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinctKaren Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club BoardFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareThe fourth season of the critically acclaimed football drama Ted Lassohas taken a surprising twist. The show’s writers have decided to have their hero coach AFC Richmond’s women’s team, testing whether Ted’s “Lasso way” can work in a very different footballing environment. We’re only three episodes in, but I’ve already found myself wondering if the series will showcase what makes the women’s game distinct, or just treat it as the same sport with different characters.The early signs are promising: we’ve already seen the issue of substandard facilities, initial disinterest from the club’s fanbase and the flak that Coach Chilton gets for exhibiting the same qualities lauded in the men’s coach, Roy Kent.Watching the show, I found myself thinking about real-life football and asking whether, in growing the women’s game, we can avoid reproducing systems and structures present in its male counterpart.The classicist Mary Beard says in her book, Women & Power, “You cannot easily fit women into a structure that is already coded as male; you have to change the structure.” She was writing about women in public life, but her words could be easily applied to football, which remains stubbornly male-dominated.The typical men’s football clubis loss-makingand more than half of fans feel thathigh ticket costs have made the game less enjoyable. Why copy that?I discovered this reality when I (then an avowed football-disliker) visited Lewes FC in 2017, as this small club in East Sussex became the first in the world to equalise resources and facilities between its men’s and women’s teams. ItsEquality FCcampaign generated headlines around the world, and predictable criticism. Detractors said that the women’s squad didn’t attract the same crowds as the men’s, so why should they get the same resources?I went to watch Lewes FC Women for the first time, because, as a feminist and local, I was drawn by its pioneering closure of football’s gender resource gap. In a safe, joyful, inclusive environment, I experienced an “a-ha moment”. Yes, this is sport, I thought, but it is also a social and political act of defiance and change.Watching these women take up space, compete and play with such physical freedom made me feel like more than just a spectator at a game: I was watching women breaking free from patriarchy.This was something I wanted to champion and I went on to manage Lewes’s Equality FC campaign. I knew that the solidarity I felt, and the festival-like culture I experienced could resonate with other women whom football had not yet made welcome.The women’s game has a markedly different history to the men’s. In 1920, there were around 150 women’s teams and theyfrequently drew bigger crowds than men’s clubs, until theFA banned them from playing for 50 years. The women’s game has developed a rich culture of community, accessibility and inclusion – preciselybecauseit had to survive outside the traditional structures of football.This culture is now colliding with the fast-track “professionalisation” of women’s football, accelerated by big Premier League clubs subsidising their women’s teams. The women’s game is being rushed into copying and pasting the same structures as the men’s. Worse still, the financial chasm opening up at the top of the game –between the big four teams of WSL1 and all other women’s teams– is causing some owners to reasonably conclude that the cost of becoming competitive in women’s football isescalating fasterthan the revenues they can generate. In turn this leads toa fragile football pyramid.View image in fullscreenForest Green Rovers have scrapped their women’s team for the 2026/7 season.Photograph: Phil Mingo/PPAUK/ShutterstockBack in June, Durham, the only independent second-tier women’s club, werejust daysfrom being wound up (though they happily secured last-minute investment). This summer, nearly all of Plymouth Argyle’s women’s squadfound out via emailthat they were going to be let go after the club decided that the venture was “unsustainable”. Forest Green Rovers have scrappedtheir women’s team for all of this seasonandSouthamptonhave alsocut their women’s team’s budget.A female-centric future for the game hinges on players and fans no longer being treated as “small men”. That means reimagining facilities, medical support, childcare, sports science, kit, training and match-day experiences around female bodies and lives, rather than retrofitting a male model. This is happening, but sporadically. Despite money at the very top, the experience of most women’s teams is characterised bychronic underfunding.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis isn’t about handouts, but a wider distribution of revenues from TV money and league sponsorships would enable development of the women’s game across a much wider base. Increased FA Cup prize money, shared more evenly to smaller clubs, would be – literally – a gamechanger.Women’s football offers distinct audiences and values that should be highly attractive to sponsors. Think match-day experiences combining sport with music, food, art and community that would attract people who don’t see football as “for them”.That is the approach I hope Ted Lasso will ultimately showcase. By switching to women’s football, the series can help raise the game’s profile more than any individual club ever could.Women’s football, sidelined and kept humble for so long, may finally get some of the respect it deserves, on, and consequently off, screen. This game can change communities, it can change people’s lives, it can change the world.But ultimately women’s football needs its own identity and ecosystem. And that requires radical thinking.Karen Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club BoardExplore more on these topicsWomen's footballOpinionTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: I put myself in the prime minister’s shoes – and learned some uncomfortable lessons | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: On the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrust, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: On the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrust, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Screenshots from the political survival game No 10: Full Confidence.Composite: Sleepy Boy StudiosView image in fullscreenScreenshots from the political survival game No 10: Full Confidence.Composite: Sleepy Boy StudiosOpinionPoliticsI put myself in the prime minister’s shoes – and learned some uncomfortable lessonsZoe WilliamsOn the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrustFri 21 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTShareNo 10: Full Confidenceis the gameall the lobby journalists and backbenchers are playing on their phones. Westminster hasn’t been so united by an app since the early 2010s, when everyone was trying to figure out whatDavid Cameron saw in Angry Birds.The game is quite engrossing: you are the prime minister, taking office, and your name is Yusuf Dunmore. Popularity starts high in all the important areas – cabinet, backbenchers, the media, the public. But from there, every decision you are called upon to make, from nominating a chancellor to your answers at PMQs, confronts you with an invidious choice between one crisis and another.I was ready to resign in my third week – still technically the honeymoon period. The bad faith was all too overwhelming: an opposition that howled blue murder over things it didn’t even disagree with; a press that misconstrued for fun; a public with the aggregated emotional stability of a three-year-old who hadn’t had a nap. Marshalling all that while maintaining your own probity, when you had only intended to be 15%honest in the first place, seemed like more than any decent person could stand. None of this is to cast any shade on the game itself, which is very fun.It’s always a useful corrective to put yourself in a prime minister’s shoes. Ten years ago, Peter Bull, a psychologist at York University, analysed the ways in which politicians avoid giving direct answers, and submitted that, at the time, Theresa May was our most evasive prime minister yet – in one interview, she answered a question straight only14% of the time.Bull was empathetic. Prime ministers have to protect their positive face (avoid making themselves look bad) at the same time as their negative face (avoid committing to anything, so they keep their freedom of action). The smart move in the immediate term is to say nothing of substance at all, but in the long term, that fosters an almost nihilistic alienation in the electorate. If you can’t trust someone to communicate something when they speak, what can you trust them with?It’s only when you consider things from the politician’s perspective that you recognise we’re in a dynamic system of mutual distrust that spores and intensifies from one prime minister to the next: they’re evasive because they don’t trust our reactions; we lose trust because we can’t believe or make sense of their words. They then become ever more evasive, or alternatively, start to commit themselves wildly – to opinions, policies, values – in a bid for electoral popularity, which they then renege on.It’s obvious, looking back, that May was simply the most evasive PMso far; you would definitely go to her for a straight answer before you’d go to Boris Johnson. Keir Starmer’s defenders always liked to point out, when his approval ratings tanked, that this wasn’t personal; this was politics – in the years since Brexit, every prime minister has faced severe unpopularity scores. We were meant to draw the conclusion that it wasn’t him, it was us, so we should just knuckle down and be governed; but the more devastating implication was that every time trust in a leader wanes, that lingers as a legacy for the next. In some recent cases, that was the prime minister’s only legacy (though, fair play to Liz Truss, mymortgage is also still incredibly high).What a depressing thought, so let’s get back to your phone.
