The first decision to make as prime minister is who your chancellor should be, and never has theBrazilian philosopher Roberto Ungerbeen more elegantly distilled: we think political ideas are realistic only to the extent that they match what we can already see, he argued. Your choice is between Reginald Forthwright, who the public loves and the markets hate, and Harriet Voss, ex-investment banker, who the markets love and the public has never heard of.Forthwright’s actual economic policy, though, is a 3% flat tax on everything, and Voss has no policies at all. This reflects a truth even harsher than the mutual-suspicion doom loop, which is that we have absolutely lost the ability to conceive of the economic governance of the state, except in terms of the bond markets. Those who kowtow to them are realistic; those who don’t are living in a dream world, and the markets themselves are simultaneously omnipotent and labile – they don’t even know what they’re going to like until they see something they don’t – yet we must all, for the purposes of being grownups, surrender to them.What pushed me over the edge as a new prime minister, though, was my “first howler” – in a press conference, I accidentally gave an answer that was the opposition’s policy, not my own. A gif had been made of my ensuing confusion before the event was over. In the 45 seconds I had to decide what to do next, I dwelt (unwisely, given the time constraints) on how the mistake would have come about. Either I was lukewarm about my policies and was only in the job because I thought I’d be good at it(Cameron-style). Or I was under so much pressure that my mouth was making noises without any input from my brain (could be May, Sunak, even Truss). Or perhaps I would literally just say anything to get out of a spot (a la Starmer).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter a few hours of playing, though, I was sure of one thing: the new normal that is reflected in this game – that was co-created by us, the unforgiving voters – is prime ministers without a communicable sense of self and purpose. Recovery will, likewise, be a group effort, but will have to start at the top.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionAppsMobile gamesTheresa MayDavid CameronGamesLiz TrusscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s buses: a blueprint for governing Britain | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be next
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be next
Content: Andy Burnham aboard a bus in Bath last month. ‘His critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.’Photograph: Toby Melville/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham aboard a bus in Bath last month. ‘His critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.’Photograph: Toby Melville/Pool Reuters/APOpinionPublic transportThe Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s buses: a blueprint for governing BritainEditorialThe prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be nextFri 21 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareBarely a month into his premiership, Andy Burnham is already taking the lessons of Manchester’s buses national. This week his governmentbackedthe West Midlands mayor Richard Parker’s move to bring the region’s main bus operation into public control. In July, he announced that he wouldreinstatea £2 national bus fare cap from January 2027. He’s also expanding free bus travel fordisabledpeople to all hours. Transport affordability is clearly part of Mr Burnham’s cost of living programme. That is to be applauded, as is the emphasis on public transport, which – importantly for Labour – reduces social exclusion, boosts local economies, and is better for the environment. Yet buses may matter to Mr Burnham for another reason: they offer a blueprint for how he wants to govern.This is because Mr Burnham seems to have a worked-out model. He told theTimesthis week that the prescription for services such as water, housing and energy isn’t yet clear, “with the exception of buses”. Public control, Mr Burnham reasons, gives government the power to make provision cheaper and more reliable – and to shape it around the public interest. For buses, that means the government determining the shape of the network even where private companies run the services. Municipal ownership this is not.Despite that, more money will be needed. Austerity slashed public transport budgets, and consequently bus journeys fell. Outside London, busesclockup about 736m miles a year, nearly a third below 2005. Getting back to a decent service would cost a paltry sum. For£300ma year, England could get buses back into its worst-served communities. For about £1bn, the Campaign for Better Transportcalculated, ministers could provide decent, frequent services in towns and rural areas. In 2021, the Campaign to Protect Rural England put the price of aSwiss-style bus network– an hourly service from 6am to midnight for every village of more than 300 people – at £2.7bn a year. Accounting for inflation, that would be £3.4bn today, just 1.5% of the NHS budget.Public transport isn’t only about moving people around. London’s extensive tube, rail and bus network gave Sir Sadiq Khan the room to introduceUlez. The scheme charged drivers of older, more polluting vehicles and brought measurable health benefits. A study has shown that children’s lungs grewbigger and strongerafter Ulez was introduced. It is worth noting that Mr BurnhamabandonedManchester’s clean-air charging zone when the post-pandemic cost of replacing dirty vehicles threatened to fall heavily on businesses. He instead pressed ahead with theBee Network, giving Manchester a more affordable public-transport alternative, while simultaneously spending public moneycleaningup the city’s bus fleet. It was a politically shrewd sequence: improve the alternative so that you could persuade people to use their cars less.BothTheresa MayandSir John Majorhave tried to diminish Mr Burnham’s mayoral experience by contrasting “running Manchester” and “dealing with buses” with being in Downing Street. Yet the prime minister appears to regard buses not as an incidental part of his record but as an exemplar for his government. The Centre for Cities thinktankarguesthat poor transport makes big English urban centres outside London effectively smaller in economic terms, by cutting workers off from opportunities. Perhaps his critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportOpinionAndy BurnhamRoad transportBus faresLaboureditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Scientific specimens are being sold to foreign museums or snapped up by the super-rich. They should have the same legal protections as works of art
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Scientific specimens are being sold to foreign museums or snapped up by the super-rich. They should have the same legal protections as works of art
Content: A palaeontologist lies next to the fossilised skeleton of an ichthyosaur found at Rutland Water in 2022.Photograph: Anglian Water/PAView image in fullscreenA palaeontologist lies next to the fossilised skeleton of an ichthyosaur found at Rutland Water in 2022.Photograph: Anglian Water/PAOpinionFossilsThe Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure statusEditorialScientific specimens are being sold to foreign museums or snapped up by the super-rich. They should have the same legal protections as works of artFri 21 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAs Sir David Attenborough hasobserved, “there’s nothing more magical than finding a shiny shell and knowing you’re the first person to have seen it for 150 million years”. Senior museum figures are campaigning for fossils to be classed as national treasures, according to theWaverley criteria, which control the export of objects considered culturally important to the nation. But the rules only cover natural treasures that are “made”, excluding fossils.Thesecallscome after a private collection from the Jurassic Coast wassoldto the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi for a reported eight-figure sum. Both the Natural History Museum in London and Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) were offered the 318 fossils, but they didn’t have the funds. Unlike countries such as Brazil and Mongolia, where fossils belong to the state, Britain relies largely on a voluntary code of conduct.The line between fossils as scientific specimens and fossils as aesthetic objects is becoming increasingly blurred – and their value is rocketing accordingly. Where once Damien Hirst’s shark made waves on the contemporary art scene, a dinosaur fossil appeared atLondon’s Frieze Masters in 2023. Last month, a 67m-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex fossil called Gusbroke recordsat a Sotheby’s auction in New York. He toppled Apex, a stegosaurusboughtby an American hedge fund manager in 2024, now on loan to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and Stan, another T rex, was alsoacquiredby the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in 2022.Big beasts of Hollywood have also got in on the act, with Nicolas Cage and Leonardo DiCapriobattling itout for a fossil. Today’s dinomania has everyone from tech giants to TikTokers in its grip. But there is nothing new about fossil collecting.Mary Anning, a cabinetmaker’s daughter born in Lyme Regis in 1799, was one the UK’s greatest palaeontologists, although, as a woman, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London. Her life story inspired Tracy Chevalier’s 2009 novelRemarkable Creaturesand the 2020 filmAmmonite.The Victorian passion for palaeontology provides the backdrop to the clandestine love stories in John Fowles’s French Lieutenant’s Woman (also set in Lyme Regis) and AS Byatt’s Possession. Fossils have provided a rich seam for writers and film‑makers from Tennyson (an enthusiastic collector on the Isle of Wight) to Noel Streatfeild’s 1936 children’s classic Ballet Shoes starring the foundling Fossil sisters, to Steven Spielberg’s Jurassic Park blockbusters. Last year’sJurassic World Rebornhas beencreditedwith contributing to the recent collecting boom.Fossils and dinosaurs are a source of childhood wonder. These long-dead specimens speak to us across millions of years. But they also hold important clues to the future, recording changing ecosystems, climate and biodiversity, providing vital evidence in the environmental emergency.Without private hunters, many of these discoveries would not be made, especially in rapidly eroding landscapes like the Jurassic Coast. These collections are better in a museum, even if it is abroad. And the UK has no shortage of fossils from other countries. But measures to protect them are overdue. Important fossils should not be allowed to disappear into the collections of the super-rich. They should be accessible for scientists to study and the public to enjoy for hundreds of years to come. They are national treasures and deserve to be treated as such.Explore more on these topicsFossilsOpinionNatural History MuseumMuseumsJurassic ParkeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The many tragedies of the Jason Arday case | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Guardian reports and commentary about the academic, who was found dead at his home last weekend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Guardian reports and commentary about the academic, who was found dead at his home last weekend
Content: Jason Arday. ‘Far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday. ‘Far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayLettersThe many tragedies of the Jason Arday caseReaders respond to Guardian reports and commentary about the academic, who was found dead at his home last weekendFri 21 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareHugh Muir is right to muse on the tragic nature of the Jason Arday case (A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism, 19 August). For it’s a tragedy in so many, many ways. It’s a tragedy that a man has died, leaving a grieving family and friends behind. And it’s a tragedy that the real and necessary objectives of diversity, equity and inclusion have been done a gross disservice by Cambridge University’s cynical tokenism.It’s a tragedy that this lamentable affair may set back the vital pursuit of equality of opportunity. And it’s a tragedy that in place of moderate voices who understand the need for better representation but with caveats, we have bad actors who see things only through the heated lens of ideology, be that from left or right.It’s a tragedy that the latter tendency would encourage some on the left, through anger in the wake of Arday’s death, to double down on circling the wagons for their side. And it’s a tragedy that in doing so, they risk becoming entrenched participants in a destructive culture war – and to hell with truth, integrity and decency.And finally, it is, as Muir points out, a tragedy that in pursuit of a noble cause, some would go as far as attacking the many honourable journalists who were simply doing their job to report this story, in what is still a free press.Colin MontgomeryEdinburghHugh Muir’s article identifies what has been too peripheral in media coverage of theJason Ardaytragedy so far: that this situation has been the product of a ruthless campaign by the extreme right.The Arday case is evidence of the extreme right’s obsession with academia as a key battleground, and the extent to which the views of a tiny number of highly marginal figures are hugely amplified by the mainstream media.Much of the coverage of Arday’s position ignored the fact that the campaign against him had been led by Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined “race realist” with racist views who was dismissed from Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He and his like represent a minority within academia, but this summer has shown how the powerful resources of the extreme-right media machine can overpower scholarly standards.This should be a wake-up call for all academics and universities to take seriously the power of these extreme groups and the need to hold their views to account.Eleanor NewbiginCambridgeI agree with your editorial (17 August) concerning the role of racism in press coverage concerning Jason Arday and that journalists seeking to act responsibly should not be subjected to an onslaught of abuse any more than he was. But there is something missing from the editorial that our institutions, including our media, need to reflect on. You refer to Arday as an autistic child. That autistic child became an autistic adult, and I am not aware of the implications of this being considered in media reporting.Carol AdamsBallarat East, Victoria, AustraliaThe Guardian’s coverage of the Jason Arday story was badly misjudged. Not so much the content as the prominence given to it. For at least two days the headline piece on the website was devoted to someone I had never heard of and concerned events I had little interest in. This at a time when the world is at war and on fire.The events leading up to the resignation of a Cambridge professor had a place in the UK news section of the website, but not as the lead story on successive days. Your self-serving editorial simply compounds this mistake. It justifies the content but makes no mention of the massive misjudgment in the prominence given to the story.Stephen TompsettWinchesterI appreciated the Guardian’s self-examination following the very sad death of Jason Arday as I have been reflecting on your coverage as well as that of other media. I would, however, urge you to expand the final sentence of your editorial, adding the words in italic here: “A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else:to achieve, to excel, to teach and to lead, but alsoto be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.”Annie GristHebden Bridge, West YorkshireA straightforward mea culpa from Cambridge University would be more appropriate than expressions of sorrow over the tragedy of Jason Arday’s death.The proper way to address the underrepresentation of black academics is to commit sustained time, effort and resources to the pipeline – from GCSE and A-level through undergraduate and graduate education to research fellowships and academic appointments.Instead, Cambridge chose to make Jason Arday’s appointment into a highly public symbol of its commitment to diversity.In doing so, the university inevitably focused exceptional attention on one individual and created circumstances in which both his record and his subsequent difficulties would receive exceptional scrutiny. Whatever the rights and wrongs of the allegations subsequently made against him, the immense pressure that followed was surely foreseeable.Universities should address structural inequalities structurally, rather than place the burden of representing institutional progress upon individuals.Prof John EllisGonville and Caius College, CambridgeI am deeply saddened to hear of the death of Jason Arday (Report, 14 August). I didn’t know him well enough to comment on the allegations he faced (which at the time of writing remain just that). But far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.He took the decision early in his career to speak out about prejudice and reduce barriers for those who come after him, and the legacy of his work will live on. Far from Black scholars receiving preferential treatment, solid and repeated quantitative and qualitative evidence show that systematic biases are baked deep into the academic system, from postgraduate research onwards.Yet it is so easy for us not to see racism, or not to acknowledge it. Over three decades in higher education, I have seen countless instances of plagiarism, lies on CVs and job applications, sexual misconduct and bullying by white academics; too often there has been little action taken, the academics in question have been promoted, and sometimes those raising these problems are victimised.What can we do to honour Jason’s memory? Recognise the organised campaign of intimidation that Black and Brown students and academics are now facing in the UK, and our complicity in this tragedy; educate about the realities of prejudice; and continue Jason’s work to dismantle the barriers to higher education.ProfRachel PainNewcastle UniversityExplore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeThe GuardianNewspapersNational newspapersNewspapers & magazinesHigher educationlettersShareReuse this content

title: Why I’m still annoyed about sharing a name with Jethro Tull’s flute-botherer | Music | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to letters from the Guardian writers Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss about being confused with each other
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to letters from the Guardian writers Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss about being confused with each other
Content: Ian Anderson of the English rock band Jethro Tull plays the flute at the Newport Jazz Festival in June 1969 in Newport, Rhode Island.Photograph: Tom Copi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIan Anderson of the English rock band Jethro Tull plays the flute at the Newport Jazz Festival in June 1969 in Newport, Rhode Island.Photograph: Tom Copi/Getty ImagesMusicLettersWhy I’m still annoyed about sharing a name with Jethro Tull’s flute-bothererReaders respond to letters from the Guardian writers Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss about being confused with each otherFri 21 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareThe two Stephen Mosses who both write for the Guardian (Letters, 14 August) and seem to have an amicable enough relationship have no idea what it was like being one of two Ian Andersons signed to Island Records in early 1969. Let’s just say it didn’t end well. I found having an extra initial to be the only long-term solution to the confusion.And then there was the matter of the Ian Anderson who was a leader of the National Front, or the Scottish footballer, who mercifully both seem to have long since faded from most people’s memories. The only thing that still rankles is that the mono-limbed flute-botherer of Jethro Tull, two weeks my junior, gets in the Guardian birthdays list and I don’t!Ian A AndersonCambridgeI sympathise with Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss. But I’m sure I’m not the only reader who remembers with great fondness the joint byline “Duncan Campbell and Duncan Campbell” on an article about a Home Office proposal (How a proposed secrecy law would recast journalism as spying, 20 July). Messrs Moss should count themselves lucky that they plough different furrows.Robin LustigLondonThere were two students with the same name studying English at Swansea University with me. They were both called Gillian Davies and neither had a middle name. The English department distinguished between them by adding their home town in brackets after their name – even on the final results list. I hope the years have been kind to you, Gillian Davies (Wrexham) and Gillian Davies (Tonyrefail).Carol O’ByrneCardiffSurely it’s time you invited the two Stephen Mosses to Dine Across the Divide?Rachel DavidSutton Coldfield, West MidlandsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Douglas Hurd didn’t say ‘prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse’ | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letter: Jon Silverman says that the often misattributed line was probably written by the civil servant David Faulker, but with one crucial difference
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Jon Silverman says that the often misattributed line was probably written by the civil servant David Faulker, but with one crucial difference
Content: Douglas Hurd, the former home secretary.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDouglas Hurd, the former home secretary.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianPrisons and probationLettersDouglas Hurd didn’t say ‘prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse’Jon Silvermansays that the often misattributed line was probably written by the civil servant David Faulker, but with one crucial differenceFri 21 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareIn his letter about ever-lengthier prison sentences (18 August), Nik Wood makes two familiar mistakes in attributing the quote “prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse” to Douglas Hurd.In fact, the line appeared in a white paper published in 1990 by Hurd’s successor, David Waddington. And there is no declaratory “is”. Instead,it warnsthat “prisoncan bean expensive way of making bad people worse” unless other rehabilitative measures are taken.Wood suggests that Hurd was “an unlikely figure” to author such a thought. Waddington, a hardliner who supported the return of capital punishment, was far unlikelier. The true originator of the much misquoted line was probably the civil servant David Faulkner, a liberal on penal matters, whose influence on crime and punishment ended with the arrival of Michael Howard as home secretary.Jon SilvermanFormerBBC home affairs correspondentHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Doug Kessler says parenting is a form of continuous grieving from the time your kids are born. Plus a letter from Mark de Brunner
Content: ‘The move away from home is a big one.’Photograph: Design Pics Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The move away from home is a big one.’Photograph: Design Pics Inc./AlamyParents and parentingLettersThe bafflingly hard pain we feel when our children leave home for universityDoug Kesslersays parenting is a form of continuous grieving from the time your kids are born. Plus a letter fromMark de BrunnerFri 21 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareAs a father who has seen both daughters fledge, I felt Zoe Williams’ pain and bafflement as her first son prepares to leave for university (My son is leaving home for university – and my severe denial has surprised me, 17 August).No one talks about it but, from the moment of birth, parenting is continuous grieving. We mourn the loss of our one-year-old when they turn two. The fun of the early teen years are only partial compensation for never again watching our toddler invent walking. The move away from home is a big one. When it happened to us, I was grateful for all the practice I’d been gifted. But it still hit hard. Bafflingly hard.Doug KesslerLondonZoe Williams has our sympathy. But sending her son off with a nest of saucepans? They all take saucepans. title: ‘It could only have been one person’: top ex-detective says system failed murdered journalist Lyra McKee | Lyra McKee | The Guardian
description: Jason Murphy believes he knows who killed McKee in Derry, but culture of silence and mistrust of police is denying her family justice
Author: Michael Segalov
Headline: Jason Murphy believes he knows who killed McKee in Derry, but culture of silence and mistrust of police is denying her family justice
Content: A mural of Lyra McKee, threatening IRA posters and police officers on Fanad Drive after the shooting.Composite: Guardian Design/AFP/Getty/Shutterstock/RexView image in fullscreenA mural of Lyra McKee, threatening IRA posters and police officers on Fanad Drive after the shooting.Composite: Guardian Design/AFP/Getty/Shutterstock/RexLyra McKee‘It could only have been one person’: top ex-detective says system failed murdered journalist Lyra McKeeJason Murphy believes he knows who killed McKee in Derry, but culture of silence and mistrust of police is denying her family justiceMichael SegalovFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareWhen Lyra McKee was shot and killed on the night of 18 April 2019, approximately 150 people were in her vicinity. The 29-year-old journalist had watched in a crowd as rioting broke out in Derry,Northern Ireland. Police footage captured the grainy outline of a man firing a handgun.“Someone’s fucking shot,” a bystander could be heard crying in mobile phone footage shown as evidence in court. “There’s a fucking kid shot in the head.”TheNew IRAhas claimed responsibility for her death.This July, more than seven years after McKee was killed, a Belfast judge delivered a verdict after a 25-month trial. Three men were foundnot guiltyof her murder among a series of mostly failed prosecutions.The judgment criticised the prosecution’s case, in particular the lack of evidence identifying the defendants as those depicted, often masked, in video footage. None of the many onlookers on the street that night came forward as a witness to the murder.Jason Murphy was head of major investigations for thePoliceService of Northern Ireland (PSNI) when McKee was killed. The former detective superintendent oversaw homicide investigations across Northern Ireland’s six counties while running his own caseload, including McKee’s murder. Next week Channel 4 will air a three-part documentary on his investigation.View image in fullscreenJason Murphy was the lead investigator in the Lyra Mckee murder trial in Northern Ireland.Photograph: Polly Garnett/The GuardianMurphy is confident that he successfully identified the shooter, who he believes “could only have been one person”. But while the suspect was arrested, they were not charged. The prosecuting barrister felt that based on the evidence they could present in court, a guilty verdict was not likely. No eyewitness would confirm their identity. Within days of the killing, the New IRA offered its “full and sincere apologies” to McKee’s family, but no individual was held responsible.Murphy believes that a culture of silence within this tight-knit community – partly owing to a severe mistrust of the police, and partly out of fear of violent repercussions from allies of those implicated – is denying the McKee family justice for Lyra.“She was an innocent bystander,” he says. “Quickly it was clear this was an attack on the police.”It was a challenging investigation. McKee, who was from a Catholic background, was shot on the Creggan estate, one of Northern Ireland’s last IRA hotbeds. During the Troubles, the mostly Catholic area was a violent battleground, and it remains hostile territory for the PSNI.People here were reluctant to help “find someone within their own community who killed one of their own”, Murphy says. After McKee’s death, threatening graffiti appeared acrossDerryand placards were tied to lamp-posts warning of repercussions for providing information to the police. “Informers will be shot. IRA,” read one, illustrated with a rat in crosshairs.View image in fullscreenLyra McKee rose to prominence in 2014 after a blog post titled ‘Letter to my 14-year-old self’, in which she spoke about growing up gay in Belfast.Photograph: Chiho Tang/Oranga Creative/PASimple tasks were resource intensive, with two public order units enlisted to support each house search. The murder weapon wasn’t initially recovered from the scene, meaning “there were firearms circulating in the community, uncontrolled”.Acquiring bystander mobile phone footage required “court warrants to do searches and seize mobile phones from teenagers”. This was out of necessity, but also to ensure that children weren’t targeted in revenge, Murphy says.Early on in the investigation, he learned that the TV presenter Reggie Yates had been filming in Derry the night McKee was shot. A group of young men were showing Yates around the Creggan area for an MTV documentary about the impact of Brexit, though in her judgment, Mrs Justice Smyth stated it appeared Yates had been “making a documentary about Saoradh”, widely understood to be the political wing of the New IRA.In the footage, Yates is told by one man, Patrick Gallagher, that there “could be a number of people gathered” outside a property being searched by police, including “those that are more than capable of carrying out acts of resistance”.One of the last moments filmed is a woman pleading with Yates: “The rioting is going on because of the camera crew … it’s all set up for youse.”The cameras are switched off before McKee is shot.Days later the BBC interviewed Gallagher for aNewsnight segment. He was asked if he was surprised nobody had been charged with McKee’s murder. “Not really,” he replied. “People have called for members of this community to inform … but the people of this community know the life of an informer. Judging by history, they know exactly what would happen.”Originally from Belfast, McKee had moved to Derry to live with her partner. Her book Angels with Blue Faces, about a Troubles-era murder, was published soon after her death.She rose to prominence in 2014 after a blog post titled “Letter to my 14-year-old self”, in which she spoke about the struggle of growing up gay in Belfast. The letter was later turned into a short film.Three men found not guilty of murdering journalist Lyra McKeeRead moreWhile McKee was not the intended target of the New IRA, which said she was “tragically killed while standing beside enemy forces”,the prosecution’s case was still “that Lyra had been killed in a coordinated attack by members of the New IRA”, Murphy says.It also argued that “connectivity between mobile phones showed a direct relationship between the riot and known New IRA leadership. Therefore, the riot and shooting of Lyra were one continuous event.”In total, 10 men were charged with 52 offences.Gallagher was one of them. Three were charged with joint enterprise murder. None were alleged to have fired the gun, but to have intentionally encouraged or assisted the shooter. Separately, Niall Sheerin was sentenced to seven years in prison for possessing the murder weapon.Of the nine men ultimately prosecuted (the 10th died last year), seven were acquitted on all counts by the judge, including the three charged with murder and Gallagher.Kieran McCool was found guilty of common assault, and Christopher Gillen of possessing and throwing petrol bombs, and riot. Due to the risk of paramilitary interference, there was no jury.Murphy and his team “fully expected” to secure the “vast majority” of prosecutions, including the murder charges.The defence called no witnesses and presented a small amount of evidence. The prosecution faced further difficulty when some of the little identification evidence presented was dismissed by the court after police errors. A firewall was constructed between Murphy’s team and other PSNI officers tasked with identifying suspects.“Unbeknown to me, one of my team had visited the office of some of [these] officers,” says Murphy. “Those conversations should never have taken place.”Had that evidence been considered, Murphy concedes case outcomes “could have been” different against some defendants, though there were “multiple strands the judge didn’t agree with”.View image in fullscreenLyra McKee’s sister Nichola Corner said she felt let down and that some people were ‘withholding evidence’.Photograph: PAHe believes McKee’s family are likely to feel let down by the police and prosecution. “I felt ashamed to be part of a system that failed this family and community,” Murphy says. “I hoped the judgment would be the start of the grieving processes for Lyra’s family.”He says the case raises uncomfortable questions for the Northern Irish authorities. “Howdowe bring terrorist cases before the courts, with a realistic chance of conviction?” he asks. “If we can’t convict on the basis of five hours of documentary footage that has almost the totality of events, what else can we do?”He believes the outcome risks reinforcing “fears from the public: ‘Why put my head above the parapet, give evidence in court, to have them found not guilty?’”Nichola Corner, Lyra’s sister, says she feels “really, really let down”. She adds: “Some people have evidence that would assist us and are choosing to withhold it.”The Murder Detective starts on 26 August at 9pm on Channel 4

title: Tesla recalls nearly 3m vehicles in China over door handle safety risks | Tesla | The Guardian
description: Recall comes after Chinese authorities said it would ban hidden car door handles commonly seen on Tesla models
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Recall comes after Chinese authorities said it would ban hidden car door handles commonly seen on Tesla models
Content: A Tesla model Y. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Tesla model Y. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersTeslaTesla recalls nearly 3m vehicles in China over door handle safety risksRecall comes after Chinese authorities said it would ban hidden car door handles commonly seen on Tesla modelsAssociated Press in Hong KongFri 21 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTesla and other carmakers are making a major recall of more than 4m vehicles inChinaover safety concerns mostly related to their door handles, according to Chinese authorities on Friday.The US carmaker is recalling about 2.98m China-made and imported EVs including Model 3, Model Y, Model X and Model S over door-handle safety risks, according to China’s state administration for market regulation.The recall, the largest this year, according to Chinese media, comes a few months after Chinese authorities said in February that starting next year, it would be banning hidden car door handles commonly seen onTeslaelectric vehicles and many Chinese EV models.China has stepped up scrutiny recently on hidden, or flush, car door handles following EV accidents in the country and elsewhere, in which cars’ hidden electronic doors failed and trapped people inside.In a notice on the Chinese regulator’s website, it cited safety risk. In extreme situations, such as a severe collision that causes an electrical system failure, the car handles could hinder car users from quickly opening the doors to escape, or prevent rescuers outside the car from gaining access, the notice said.Some experts in the industry said the automakers should value safety over design.Cui Dongshu, head of the China Passenger Car Association, called the recall “an inevitable step” in the development of the electric vehicle industry and said automakers were “being responsible” by moving toward a more reliable, “safety-first” approach.“This represents, in part, the growing pains of the industry. At the same time, however, this move signifies a policy-driven safety upgrade,” said Cui.Tesla will perform software updates on the vehicles to mitigate risks, the notice added.Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.Xiaomi, the Beijing-based Chinese technology giant, is recalling more than 390,000 vehicles. Hangzhou-based Leapmotor is recalling over 370,000 cars. Other Chinese carmakers, including Geely and XPENG are also recalling some vehicles.The reasons given in each case were similar, mostly relating to issues with their car door handles.A report published by the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist party, said the large-scale recall “serves as a unified safety upgrade” for existing vehicle models ahead of the 2027 implementation of the ban on hidden car door handles.“For the rapidly evolving NEV (new energy vehicle) industry, competition should be defined not only by the pace of technological innovation but also by the high standards set for safety,” the newspaper said.Explore more on these topicsTeslaAutomotive industryChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: From the classroom to the locker room: nine days of ‘deeply disturbing’ sexual assault allegations shake Australia | Sexual harassment | The Guardian
description: Cultures with codes of loyalty and bonding between men can heighten the risk of sexual violence, expert says
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Cultures with codes of loyalty and bonding between men can heighten the risk of sexual violence, expert says
Content: Teachers told Guardian Australia that boys can bark at female teachers and post degrading content.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenTeachers told Guardian Australia that boys can bark at female teachers and post degrading content.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPSexual harassmentFrom the classroom to the locker room: nine days of ‘deeply disturbing’ sexual assault allegations shake AustraliaSpaces where there are norms of sexism and high levels of alcohol consumption can be a risk factor for sexual violence, expert saysGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCait KellyFri 21 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the fourth time that week, youth advocate and educator Daniel Principe stood in a classroom and asked the same question: Are female teachers respected as much as male ones?“The boys unanimously said no,” Principe says.“If that is the case, why is this rewarded in some pockets of boy culture? Being callous and cruel and intimidating to women is being rewarded.”From primary schools to universities, he steps into a classroom every day to have conversations about respect and violence. When he asks the boys if they’ve seen content that says degrading things about women – that they’re gold diggers, that they should be in the kitchen, that they all cheat – 90% of them put their hands up.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Some of these social norms and gendered stereotypes have, of course, existed prior to this moment, but they’re just inflamed right now,” he says. “There is more social reward for acting this out.”Outside the classrooms, fiveSydney Swansplayers might have been in the spotlight, but they were far from alone this week. Across the nation, a series of high-profile sexual assault cases has put allegations involving teenagers, professional athletes and men in the centre of a storm.In the past nine days alone,three Scots College students were charged over the alleged sexual assault of a 14-year-old girlin Sydney’s eastern suburbs, and in another instance in Sydney,three 17-year-olds were charged over the alleged group sexual assault of a 17-year-old girl.In Melbourne, a 13-year-old boy was arrested over an alleged attempted sexual assault of two women; in Brisbane, a 32-year-old man was charged with allegedly raping a young woman walking her dog; and in Perth, two men, 30 and 25, pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl and were jailed.Victoria police are investigating an alleged sexual assault early on Monday morning at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne, where theSydneySwans were staying. None of the Swans players have been arrested or charged and there is much detail about the allegations and its links to the team that remains unknown.The culture goes beyond private schools and sporting clubs, and its prevalence is hard to track. While many people do not report sexual assault, the most up-to-date data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the number of sexual assaults recorded by police in 2024 exceeded 40,000 – over 100 a day nationwide and an increase of 10% or 3,735 victims, from the previous year.Nationally, around two in five victim-survivors were aged between 10 and 17 years old at the time of incident, and 81% were female. The majority of sexual assaults occurred in homes.Patty Kinnersly, the CEO of Our Watch, says the country has seen “some deeply disturbing, high-profile allegations of sexual violence” this week, but the increase in reporting shows more women are coming forward.“Police-recorded sexual assault increased by around 67% between 2014 and 2024, with 2024 the highest rate recorded since the national series began in 1993,” Kinnersly says.But the population-level picture is more complex, she says, with personal safety survey data showing recent sexual violence towards women has risen from 1.2% in 2012 to 1.9% in 2021/22, while the long term rate remained broadly stable.She says the number of police reports and the volume of media coverage can’t paint an accurate picture of whether sexual violence is increasing, but that it is encouraging more women to speak up about sexual violence.double quotation markGen Z are more likely than men in other generations to endorse traditional or hostile attitudes towards women.University of Melbourne reportFor Principe, there’s a clear connection between some of the attitudes he sees in schools and the violence directed toward women.“When heterosexual men are socially conditioned to see sex and relationships as a conquest, that’s where a lot of this stuff goes awry,” Principe says. “When it’s not seen as something that should be mutual, but instead something to be taken from women, that is where it gets really troubling.”Teachers and other educators who work in schools – and who could only speak on the condition of anonymity – told Guardian Australia a similar story: in class, male students will bark at female teachers, and the boys will laugh. They’ll post degrading content on Snapchat, knowing there are no repercussions because no one can trace it back to them. Covid has supercharged their views. And the government’s internet ban has all but failed.This week, a first-of-its-kind report, Misogyny, Online Radicalisation and Youth Extremism in Australia, surveyed 3,429 Australians, including more than 1,000 people 13 to 17, to compare attitudes on women and gender equality.About one in three teen boys expressed misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women, and a belief in traditional gender roles, according to the University of Melbourne research, with Gen Z more likely than men in other generations to endorse traditional or hostile attitudes towards women.Three private school students charged after alleged sexual assault of 14-year-old girl in Sydney’s eastRead moreAt the same time, Gen Z girls were twice as likely as millennial women to believe marriage entitled a husband to sex even if his wife did not want intercourse.Sociologist Michael Flood says research in the US across male-dominated spaces like the military, sporting codes and fraternities shows there are consistent indicators for sexual violence to be more prevalent.“There are risk factors in any setting that make sexual violence perpetration and victimisation more likely,” the professor at the Queensland University of Technology School of Justice says.“Where there’s strong codes of loyalty and bonding between men, where there’s strong norms of sexism and sexual objectification, high levels of alcohol and drug consumption, high levels of pornography consumption.”double quotation markWell-designed prevention efforts in a school and in a sporting code ... and other contexts can make change.Sociologist Michael FloodFlood says research across sporting codes shows there are higher rates of sexual assault among men who play team-based contact sports, such as NRL and AFL, than those who play individual non-contact sports like tennis or swimming.“But further research has found that it’s not just the nature of the sport,” he says. “It’s also the particular character of the clubs and communities associated with that sport or that setting.”He says the key problem is there has not been “enough effort to change”. Even when institutions like the AFL or NRL tried to shift the culture in the mid-2000s, it was not enough.“It takes comprehensive effort in a sporting code or in a school to really shift the cultures of sexism and objectification that feed into sexual violence,” Flood says.“And if our efforts are only piecemeal or tokenistic, then they won’t shift the problem.”Flood says there is a growing body of research that shows multi-session programs that focus on the key drivers of sexual violence can help to bring the number of assaults down.“Well-designed prevention efforts in a school and in a sporting code, in the military and other contexts, can make change,” he says. “The question is, are they being implemented? Are they being supported comprehensively?”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available from the following organisations. In Australia, support is available at Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsSexual harassmentSydney SwansSydneySexual violencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TikTok agrees to $400m settlement to resolve US children’s privacy litigation | TikTok | The Guardian
description: The DoJ sued TikTok and its former parent company in August 2024 for allegedly failing to protect children’s privacy and collecting their information
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The DoJ sued TikTok and its former parent company in August 2024 for allegedly failing to protect children’s privacy and collecting their information
Content: The settlement will make TikTok pay $300m immediately, in addition to an extra $100m upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree with the FTC.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe settlement will make TikTok pay $300m immediately, in addition to an extra $100m upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree with the FTC.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesTikTokTikTok agrees to $400m settlement to resolve US children’s privacy litigationThe DoJ sued TikTok and its former parent company in August 2024 for allegedly failing to protect children’s privacy and collecting their informationReutersFri 21 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google⁠TikTok and its Chinese former parent company ByteDance on Friday agreed to a $400m settlement to resolve the US Department of Justice’s allegations that the short-form video app ⁠violated children’s online ⁠privacy.The justice ​department sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024 for allegedly failing to protect children’s privacy and illegally collecting their information. The defendants were accused ⁠of violating a law requiring online services aimed at children to obtain parental consent to collect personal information from users under age 13.Associate attorney ⁠general Stanley Woodward said the justice department’s priority “is ensuring that children are protected online and that ​companies entrusted with their personal information meet ‌their legal obligations”.TikTok did ‌not immediately comment.Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300m immediately and an additional $100m upon ‌entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in 2019 against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly. As part of the consent agreement, the FTC said that TikTok, then known as Musical.ly, knew that young children used the app and had failed to get parental consent to collect their names, email addresses ‌and other personal information. It paid a fine of $5.7m.In January, ByteDance agreed to establish a majority American-owned joint venture to secure US data ​and avoid a ban on the app used by more than 200 million Americans. The government noted that since the complaint was filed, TikTok has undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions and privacy practices.DoJ said the settlement “ensures that American families continue to benefit ⁠from stronger protections without the delay and uncertainty of protracted litigation”. The TikTok ​US joint venture said ​in a court filing it requires ​all users to enter their date of birth to use the ​site.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTikTok said it ‌has developed sophisticated ​age-moderation systems that identify ​children under 13 who misrepresented their age. That court filing said that TikTok has hundreds of personnel trained in underage moderation and, as a result, deletes tens of thousands underage accounts.Explore more on these topicsTikTokSocial mediaPrivacyDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Biggest El Niño for a century forecast to bring UK more autumn rain and storms | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: ‘Unprecedented’ weather pattern over Pacific Ocean to be felt worldwide, with severe droughts expected in some areas
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: ‘Unprecedented’ weather pattern over Pacific Ocean to be felt worldwide, with severe droughts expected in some areas
Content: A woman battling with her umbrella on Brighton beach. The Met Office expert said there were signals for increased UK rainfall this autumn.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman battling with her umbrella on Brighton beach. The Met Office expert said there were signals for increased UK rainfall this autumn.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesEl Niño southern oscillationBiggest El Niño for a century forecast to bring UK more autumn rain and storms‘Unprecedented’ weather pattern over Pacific Ocean to be felt worldwide, with severe droughts expected in some areasMatthew WeaverandDamien GayleFri 21 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 03.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheEl Niño eventdeveloping over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than a century and make 2027 another record-breaking year for heat, the UK’s Met Office has said.Increased rainfall and storms are forecast to hit the UK this autumn as a result of the “unprecedented” weather pattern, while the pulse in heat it generates means the global temperature will temporarily exceed 1.5C above the preindustrial average, according to the national weather service.Some scientists have said temperatures could rise by as much as 1.7C during 2027. “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event,” said Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”Scaife said a typical El Niño involved Pacific sea temperatures rising by more than 1C, “with 2C being a really big event”. This year Pacific sea temperatures are expected to rise by 3C, making this El Niño “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.View image in fullscreenPatagonia in Argentina is likely to experience severe drought.Photograph: Harald von Radebrecht/imageBROKER/ShutterstockSpeaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Scaife said: “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records … It’s up 2C degrees already.”He said the effects would be felt worldwide, adding they would be “particularly strong throughout the tropics, where we expect really severe droughts in places like South America and the west Pacific”.He said: “Then there are wave-like disturbances that come out from the tropics and affect places like the UK. So we already see signals for increased rainfall and storminess in the autumn here in the UK around November time.”There is also a heightened risk of drought in southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – was likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions, the Met Office said.This graphic shows sea surface temperature variations in the eastern Pacific during the last El Niño and La Niña weather eventsThe Met Office is just the latest forecaster to highlight the magnitude of the current El Niño cycle. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last week said there was a “greater than 90% chance of a very strong event”.“The Met Office predictions are actually some of the most conservative out there,” said Liz Stephens, a professor in climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading.The UNwarnedin early August that the conditions created by El Niño could push 50 million people into acute hunger by the end of next year.Prof Hayley Fowler, the director of the Centre for Climate and Environmental Resilience at Newcastle University, said: “The super El Niño evolving in the Pacific will likely be the biggest ever recorded, reaching or exceeding the levels of the 1877-78 El Niño which caused widespread impacts, including famines and around 50 million deaths – 3-4% of the global population – mostly across Asia and South America.”El Niñois a cyclical weather phenomenon taking place every two to seven years. Under normal circumstances the Pacific’s trade winds push warm water to Asia, while colder water rises by South America. Under El Niño, the pattern weakens, or goes into reverse and the water in the eastern Pacific heats up, shifting weather patterns all around the equator.2:58Could ‘Godzilla’ El Niño bring the hottest year on record? – video explainerThe extent to which rising global temperatures as a result of carbon pollution affect the development of El Niño is unknown. But scientists say the pulse in heat El Niño brings can amplify baseline heating.Dr Nick Dunstone, a science fellow at the Met Office, said: “During large El Niño events, significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Niño.“Hence, 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record and be another year to temporarily exceed plus 1.5C above the preindustrial period.”Bill McGuire, professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL, said: “The addition of much of this heat to the atmosphere will make it extremely likely that next year will be the hottest on record globally, perhaps even reaching – even exceeding – 1.7C above preindustrial times.”A series of record heatwaves and a lack of rainfall in recent months has brought the driest July in 190 years and has pushed almost three-quarters (71.3%) of England, and all of Wales, into drought, putting severe pressure on the water system, wildlife, farmers, emergency services and infrastructure.View image in fullscreenA series of record heatwaves and a lack of rainfall led to the driest July in the UK in 190 years.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockAfter an emergency meeting to discuss the heatwave last week, Andy Burnham said: “We might be in for a wet autumn and winter straight after this, because of El Niño and some of the issues there, which was reported toCobra.”Parts of the country were hit by heavier showers on Wednesday and Thursday. The north-west of England recorded the wettest conditions in the last 24 hours, with 52.5mm of rain falling over the seaside town of Morecambe in Lancashire.Forecasters and officials have said it could take months of sustained rainfall before rivers, reservoirs and groundwaters are completely replenished, which is when a drought would be officially over.Seven reservoirs in England were currently classed as having “exceptionally low” storage levels,up from five a week ago, the Environment Agency said on Friday.Wimbleball and Clatworthy in Somerset, and Clywedog in Powys, which provides water for central and north-west England, are all less than half full; Hanningfield in Essex and Blithfield in Staffordshire are about half full. The Dove reservoir group in Derbyshire and Grafham in Cambridgeshire remain about two-thirds full.The overall level of reservoir storage in England stands at 63%, down from 66% a week ago and 16 percentage points below the long-term average for the time of year.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weatherClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: First ever Fat Marmot Week to kick off in effort to raise money for research | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Researchers hope contest – similar to Fat Bear Week – starting Monday will be latest wildlife watching craze
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Researchers hope contest – similar to Fat Bear Week – starting Monday will be latest wildlife watching craze
Content: A marmot  sits outside of her den on 6 August 2026, in Gothic, Colorado.Photograph: Brittany Peterson/APView image in fullscreenA marmot  sits outside of her den on 6 August 2026, in Gothic, Colorado.Photograph: Brittany Peterson/APWildlifeFirst ever Fat Marmot Week to kick off in effort to raise money for researchResearchers hope contest – similar to Fat Bear Week – starting Monday will be latest wildlife watching crazeAssociated PressFri 21 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonday sees the start of what researchers hope will be the latest wildlife watching craze – Fat Marmot Week.Last winter was tough for marmots living high in theColoradomountains, where researchers say two-thirds of one population died while hibernating because of insufficient snow cover.Those that survived are doing well, fattening up in time not just for fall and hibernation season but the very first Fat Marmot Week.Just likeFat Bear Week, an online contest to vote forAlaskan brown bearsplumped up for winter, Fat Marmot Week – beginning Monday – is mostly just for fun.But it also has a serious side, aimed at raising money for scientists to continue long-running research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado, into the rodents, despite federal funding cuts.A marmot is a cat-sized, furry ground squirrel that lives in burrows in North America, Europe and Asia. The 15 or so species worldwide include groundhogs, which have their own special day, obviously, as 2 February is Groundhog Day in the US and Canada.View image in fullscreenResearchers swab the cheek of a marmot on 6 August 2026, in Gothic, Colorado.Photograph: Brittany Peterson/APIn the Rocky Mountains, yellow-bellied marmots are plentiful. Hikers often spot these charismatic creatures perched on boulders or scurrying through wildflowers. Experts say they exhibit their own personalities and are “flexibly social”, meaning some like to intermingle in colonies of up to 30 animals while others prefer solitude.“We kind of understand these marmots just by looking at them sometimes, because we can kind of tell who’s who just by how they behave and how they interact with one another,” said Katie Adler, a doctoral student at the University of California, Los Angeles.Some marmots are difficult to study because they are wary of researchers’ efforts to trap them using wire boxes baited with an enticing mixture of oats and peanut butter, said Emily Renkey, a UCLA master’s student.“Others, you could trap three or four times in the same morning,” Renkey said.While hibernating bears snooze in a state called torpor, allowing them to wake up – or be woken up – every now and then, marmots slip into a far deeper form of hibernation. Their body temperature drops from about that of a human to as low as 41F (5C), not much warmer than their burrows in winter.“You pick up a hibernated marmot and it’s this fuzzy ball and it feels like a cold rock with fur. It’s completely surreal,” Blumstein said. “They breathe once a minute or two.”To prepare for winter, the animals do a tremendous amount of fattening. They double their weight to as much as 13lbs (6kgs), then lose all of that bulk during half a year or more of hibernation.“Marmots come out of the ground really skinny, relative to what they look like now, at least,” Adler said.Last winter, scant snowfall and warm temperatures due toglobal warmingdeprived many Colorado marmots of an insulating blanket of snow over their burrows. Researchers believe their hibernation quarters got too chilly, causing many to die of cold.“We had over 160 animals and we ended with 60 at the start of this season,” Blumstein said. “Most of them died because of the lack of snow cover.”This year’s snowpack was the worst on record in the Upper Colorado River Basin, which includes Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico. The human-causedclimate crisismade the snow drought about 14 times more likely, a new study confirms.View image in fullscreenA marmot sits with one of her pups on 6 August 2026, in Gothic, Colorado.Photograph: Brittany Peterson/APHundreds of researchers at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have observed changes including fewer bees and other pollinators, and sagebrush encroaching in valleys once dominated by wildflowers.The marmot researchers in Gothic affectionately call themselves “marmoteers”.The study, run by UCLA researchers at the center about 20 miles south of Aspen, has been ongoing since 1962, making it one of the world’s longest-running studies of individual mammals.Scientists who turned to OnlyFans to fund marmot research receive crypto boostRead more“It allows graduate students and other people to come in and suddenly capitalize on this knowledge and ask questions. Without doing all the grunt work,” Blumstein said.Funding cuts have caused Blumstein’s UCLA department to lose one-third of its graduate students. Fat Marmot Week is one approach to attract interest – and hopefully donations – to keep the work going. Among the rodents on display: one nicknamed Stonehenge, who chirps at mountain bikers; and another, dubbed Citroen, whose mate is a leader of this matriarchal marmot motherland. Voting opens Monday.The researchers have also beenposting marmot videosto the OnlyFans adult content platform, while one “super fan” created a meme coin.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAnimalsColoradoClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content
