Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Police investigating after two cars set alight in attack caught on CCTV
Content: Two of the supercars were set alight, reported to be a Lamborghini and a McLaren.Photograph: ITV NewsView image in fullscreenTwo of the supercars were set alight, reported to be a Lamborghini and a McLaren.Photograph: ITV NewsBirminghamFirebombs thrown at supercars outside Birmingham wedding venuePolice investigating after two cars set alight in attack caught on CCTVMatthew WeaverFri 21 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirebombs were thrown at supercars outside a wedding venue inBirmingham, setting two alight and prompting guests to sprint out of the building.West Midlands policesaidthey were investigating the incident, which happened in the Sparkbrook area of Birmingham at around 8.30pm on Wednesday.Videos circulating online appear to show people running from the Royal Shalimar on Highgate Road after three incendiary devices were thrown towards the entrance of the venue and the cars parked outside.CCTV footage shows moment supercars are hit with firebombTwo of the supercars, reported to be a Lamborghini and a McLaren, were set alight before three men dressed in black were seen getting into a white Volkswagen Golf and driving off.Footage shows the front of one of the vehicles on fire and a man kicking one of the incendiary devices away from the area.A spokesperson forWest Midlandsfire service said: “A fire engine from Highgate station attended after two vehicles were deliberately set alight. One vehicle was made safe by firefighters. No one was trapped or injured.”A statement from the Royal Shalimar said: “Our immediate priority was the safety of our guests, and we are grateful that no one was injured. Our staff responded quickly and the situation was dealt with promptly alongside the emergency services and police.”It added: “Royal Shalimar has always been a place for families, celebrations and the wider Birmingham community, and we remain committed to providing a safe and welcoming environment for our guests.”Police said officers had spoken to witnesses and reviewed CCTV footage. They asked for anyone with information to contact them through their website or by calling 101.Explore more on these topicsBirminghamWest MidlandsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Quarter of branded baby foods in UK still have too much sugar, analysis finds | Children's health | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Of 224 branded infant foods and snacks, more than half breached guidelines brought in a year ago
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Exclusive: Of 224 branded infant foods and snacks, more than half breached guidelines brought in a year ago
Content: The foods studied included purees, breakfasts, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands.Photograph: Posed by model/Jamie Grill/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe foods studied included purees, breakfasts, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands.Photograph: Posed by model/Jamie Grill/Getty ImagesChildren's healthQuarter of branded baby foods in UK still have too much sugar, analysis findsExclusive: Of 224 branded infant foods and snacks, more than half are in breach of guidelines brought in a year agoAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentFri 21 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost a quarter of popular branded baby foods sold in UK supermarkets still contain excessive amounts of sugar, analysis suggests, a year after the government introducedvoluntary industry guidelines.In August 2025 the governmentgave baby food manufacturers 18 monthsto reduce the sugar and salt content of their products, stop marketing snacks to infants under 12 months, and address misleading and inaccurate labelling that makes some infant foods appear healthier than they actually are.An analysis of 224 branded infant foods and snacks has found that, a year on, more than half (58%) breached at least one of the nineguidelinesand that a quarter of all products breached two or more.Nora Cavani, the chief executive and co-founder of Alba Health, a gut health company that conducted the analysis, said: “Parents are not failing their children – they are being misled. Products that contain more sugar than a child should consume in a day are sold under the banner of health and nature. A year on from the guidelines’ introduction, the data shows voluntary standards haven’t worked.”The foods studied included purees, breakfast, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands: Ella’s Kitchen, Heinz, Organix, HiPP, Kiddylicious, Little Freddie, Piccolo, Aptamil and Cow & Gate.Of these, 51 (23%) contained too much sugar, including 52% of Kiddylicious’s products, 28% of Piccolo’s, 27% of Heinz’s, and 24% of Little Freddie products. In the case of five products, more than 80% of the total calories were from sugar, including Organix raisins, which contained 66g of sugar per 100g (86.6% kcal from sugars) and Kiddylicious apple fruit wriggles, which contained 70g of sugar per 100g (85.6% sugars).The NHS recommends that babies under one consumeless than 1g of salt a day, but the analysis found about 6% of foods – 14 products – breached those limits, with Heinz spaghetti bolognese pouches containing 0.27g of salt, more than a quarter of an infant’s entire daily allowance in one meal. In all, 19% of Kiddylicious’s products, 18% of HiPP’s, 13% of Heinz’s and 6% of Cow & Gate’s breached the Office for Health Improvement and Disparity (OHID) salt and sodium guidelines.Labelling and marketing breaches were found in 28% of products, including 31 snacks marketed at children as young as six months old, while labels on others made misleading health claims.Experts said the data showed that the voluntary approach had failed. Prof Steve Turner, the president of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said: “Paediatricians have long raised concerns about the high levels of salt and sugar in some infant and baby foods, and the impact this can have on children’s long-term health, including obesity and poor oral health.“Ensuring baby food is nutritious, and does not encourage children to develop a preference for sugary foods later in life, is essential. We are clear that only mandatory nutritional standards and regulation of these products will provide the protection babies and children need.”Sonia Pombo, the head of research and impact at Action on Salt andSugar,said it was striking that there were problems among brands that positioned themselves as organic or healthy. “Parents should be able to trust that the name and imagery on the front of a pack accurately reflect what is inside, yet when a product is promoted using an appealing fruit or vegetable despite not being the main ingredient, it risks misleading parents,” she said.“With only six months until the February 2027 compliance deadline, voluntary action is clearly not delivering quickly enough. If the government is serious about protecting babies and young children, these guidelines should be made mandatory and properly enforced.”A spokesperson for the British Specialist Nutrition Association, which represents the infant food industry, said: “BSNA members welcomed the government’s guidance and have been fully engaged with OHID throughout its development. Significant progress has already been made, including reducing sugar and increasing vegetable content. Ultimately reformulation takes time, and the government recognised this when setting a deadline of February 2027 for compliance.“Parents can feel confident that members are on track to meet the guidance, offering convenient, nutritious choices that support the realities of modern family life.”A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “We want every child to have the best possible start in life, and that includes making sure the food available to babies and young children is as healthy as possible. We have already taken action, publishing targets to reduce sugar and salt and introducing guidelines to improve labelling in baby food and drink, with industry given until February 2027 to make these changes.“We will continue to work with industry to make sure parents can make healthy choices for their children.”Explore more on these topicsChildren's healthFood & drink industrySugarChildrenSupermarketsRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Many males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidance
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Many males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidance
Content: In the year to the end of March, 2,247 Albanians were deported from the UK – accounting for a quarter of enforced returns.Photograph: Benjamin John/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn the year to the end of March, 2,247 Albanians were deported from the UK – accounting for a quarter of enforced returns.Photograph: Benjamin John/AlamyImmigration and asylumHome Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to AlbaniaMany males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidanceUK politics live – latest updatesDiane TaylorFri 21 Aug 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHome Officecould be blocked from deporting many young male trafficking victims to Albania after a major court ruling.Thousands of Albanian males have been identified as potential trafficking victims in the UK in recent years. Many are sent back to their country even if they are potential or confirmed victims of trafficking, as the Home Office contends they will be safe there.The ruling is likely to come as a significant blow to the government, which is trying to increase the number of people it removes.Albanians have been the most common nationality forcibly removed from the UK in the last five years, with 2,247 deported in the 12 months to the end of March, accounting for a quarter of enforced returns, according toUK government figures.Data disclosed in the court case shows that while Albanian females were previously major victims of trafficking, in their case into the UK sex industry, they have been overtaken by males – mainly boys and young men – who are trafficked into the drugs trade, either to distribute illegal drugs or to work as “gardeners” in cannabis farms.In 2022, 4,107 Albanian males were referred to UK services over potential trafficking, in comparison with 502 women. In 2023, the figure was 3,463 males and 588 females.The legal challenge was brought by a 21-year-old victim of trafficking from Albania who was first exploited by an Albanian gang in Belgium when he visited the country with his father at 16. He was sold to another Albanian gang, who brought him to the UK and forced him to work cultivating cannabis plants. He later escaped and was recognised as a victim of trafficking, but was denied asylum because he was told it would be safe for him to return to Albania.A panel of three senior judges in the upper tribunal of the immigration court accepted his asylum claim and found that even though five years had passed since he was first trafficked, he remained at “real risk” from his traffickers and could not safely move back to Albania.The judges issued new country guidance to the government, which must be considered by the Home Office before deciding whether to send male trafficking victims back to Albania.The judgment found that while Albania has made progress on tackling corruption, it continues to be a widespread problem and that there are no dedicated shelters for adult male trafficking victims, while the risk of victims being retrafficked if returned to Albania is significant.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIslington Law Centre, which has particular expertise in representing Albanian trafficking victims, highlighted many concerning practices that gangs subject their victims to. These include deliberately videoing sexual abuse including rape of child trafficking victims and threatening to release the footage on social media; they also show videos of loved ones in Albania to young people to let them know they know who their families are; and the gangs also inflict physical injuries such as broken bones on children and young people.Esme Madill, a solicitor at Islington Law Centre specialising in representing young Albanian trafficking victims, welcomed the judgment: “This measured judgment has been reached by a court which had the benefit of significant and detailed evidence as to the worrying issue of trafficking of boys and young men by organised Albanian criminal networks. The profiles of trafficking survivors and the risks recognised in the judgment accord strongly with what we see in our work with deeply brutalised and traumatised young survivors every week.”Home Office sources said they were considering whether to apply for permission to appeal.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeAlbaniaDrugsDrugs tradeHuman traffickingEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK reports unexpected deficit of £1.8bn as John Healey prepares for first budget | Tax and spending | The Guardian
description: July data shows total public debt was £2.98tn, or 94% of GDP – up £96bn on a year earlier
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: July data shows total public debt was £2.98tn, or 94% of GDP – up £96bn on a year earlier
Content: John Healey will announce his first budget as the chancellor on 28 October.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Healey will announce his first budget as the chancellor on 28 October.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockTax and spendingUK reports unexpected deficit of £1.8bn as John Healey prepares for first budgetJuly data shows total public debt was £2.98tn, or 94% of GDP – up £96bn on a year earlierBusiness live – latest updatesHeather StewartEconomics editorFri 21 Aug 2026 02.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government ran a larger-than-expected £1.8bn deficit in July, underlining the challenges facing the chancellor,John Healey, as he draws up his first budget.City economists had expected a shortfall of zero for July, a month when Treasury receipts tend to be swollen by self-assessment income tax payments.At £17.1bn, the self-assessment tax paid in July was £1.7bn higher than the same month last year. But theOffice for National Statisticssaid the government still ran the £1.8bn deficit, as “spending growth outpaced receipts”.In the first four months of this financial year the cumulative deficit was £56.7bn – lower than last year but still £2.3bn ahead of the figure forecast by theOffice for Budget Responsibility.Healey will deliver his budget on 28 October. The public finances are expected to be gloomier than forecast at Rachel Reeves’s spring statement in March, when the Iran war had only just begun.At that time, Reeves had agenerous £23.6bn buffer, or headroom, against her fiscal rules, but analysts believe a significant proportion of that may be eaten away by higher inflation, slower growth and rising bond yields.Moves in global bond markets in recent days have pushed up the yield – in effect the interest rate – on government bonds, creating a fresh headache for the chancellor.Martin Beck, chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said: “Ten-year gilt yields are above 5%, reflecting energy-related inflation concerns, and these will gradually feed through into a larger debt-interest bill as existing debt is refinanced. At the same time, the government faces pressure to loosen inherited spending plans, meet unfunded defence commitments and deliver on its own ambitions for housing, infrastructure and public services.”The UK’s large debt pile means small moves in interest rates can be costly over time.The ONS said total public debt was £2.98tn in July, or 94% of GDP – up £96bn on a year earlier – in line with Labour’s plan to borrow for investment in infrastructure projects.In response to July’s public finances, Healey said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of our UK economic stability and national security, which is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules, with a buffer against global uncertainties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 economy, while giving people a bit of breathing space with cost of living pressures and focusing support to get young people into work.”Healey will have to find an additional £1.2bn a year to fund the defence investment plan, a plan that prompted him toresign as defence secretary in Junewhen he claimed the resources were not generous enough to meet the nation’s needs.There were also signs on Friday that the UK economy picked up pace in August. A poll of purchasing managers found that UK private sector output expanded at the fastest pace since April, driven by the services sector.The survey, by S&P Global, indicated the economy could grow by about 0.3% in the third quarter of this year.Explore more on these topicsTax and spendingBudget deficitGovernment borrowingEconomicsOffice for National StatisticsJohn HealeyOffice for Budget ResponsibilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Gun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports | Germany | The Guardian
description: Germany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinations
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Germany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinations
Content: Germany’s interior minister described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a ‘low-level agent’.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGermany’s interior minister described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a ‘low-level agent’.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesGermanyGun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reportsGermany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinationsDeborah Colein BerlinFri 21 Aug 2026 10.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany is seeking to extradite a suspect fromRomaniaover the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.Two weeks after German authorities found adrone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.“This case demonstrates that ‌we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.View image in fullscreenInterior minister Alexander Dobrindt, who confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation.Photograph: Katharina Kausche/AFP/Getty ImagesThe find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports byDer Spiegelmagazine and an investigative team led bySüddeutsche Zeitung.Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had ‌been detained so far this year.Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.View image in fullscreenThe headquarters of German domestic intelligence in Cologne.Photograph: Patrik Stollarz/AFP/Getty ImagesSinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.Last yearPolish security officials arrested several peopleallegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly posted from Romania.Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalledreports in 2024that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries inEuropethat have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.Explore more on these topicsGermanyRussiaEuropeRomaniaEspionagenewsShareReuse this content

title: New Mexico man killed in rare fatal bear attack, only second in state in a century | New Mexico | The Guardian
description: Police department for Navajo Nation neither identified the victim nor said what type of bear had killed him
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Police department for Navajo Nation neither identified the victim nor said what type of bear had killed him
Content: The Navajo Nation police department said officers within its Window Rock district received a call at about 1pm that a bear had attacked a man.Photograph: jjMiller11/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe Navajo Nation police department said officers within its Window Rock district received a call at about 1pm that a bear had attacked a man.Photograph: jjMiller11/Getty Images/iStockphotoNew MexicoNew Mexico man killed in rare fatal bear attack, only second in state in a centuryPolice department for Navajo Nation neither identified the victim nor said what type of bear had killed himVictoria BekiempisFri 21 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a rare kind of attack, a bear killed a man in Crystal,New Mexico, on Thursday, local police said.The police department for the Navajo Nation said officers within its Window Rock district received a call at about 1pm that a bear had attacked a man.Authorities shot the bear, and the creature fled into woods near the scene of the attack. They said they ultimately found the bear and “neutralized” the animal.“Our thoughts and prayers are with the victim’s family at this time,” the Navajo police departmentsaidin a Facebook post.The Native American reservation’s police department said its criminal investigations department as well as its fish and wildlife department also responded to the scene of the fatal attack.They neither identified the victim nor said what type of bear had killed him.The police department said it “urges the public to stay away from potentially dangerous wildlife. If a bear is spotted, please call your nearest [police] District.”Thursday’s fatal bear attack appeared to be the first such case inNew Mexicosince 2001, according to a comprehensive list with information about bear attacks. That 2001 case, meanwhile, was the first fatal New Mexico bear attack in a century, the Associated Press reported.The victim in that case was Adelia Trujillo, who was killed by a 250lb male bear that broke into her house.In 2020, a bear attacked a woman in Los Alamos, New Mexico. The 37-year-old woman and her husband were sitting on the deck at a ski lodge when it approached them.The bear came within a foot of the couple and started chasing her and then attacked in the parking lot. Her injuries included “several broken bones, a collapsed lung, bite marks and scratches”, New Mexico wildlife authoritiessaidat the time.The woman in that case survived,according to KRQE, and authorities reportedly killed the bear.North America generally has only a handful of fatal bear attacks annually. According to theNorth American Bear Center, a person’s chances of being murdered by a fellow human is 60,000 times greater than dying at the hands of a black bear.National park service statistics indicate that the chances of being injured by a bear is exceedingly rare atone in 2.1m.Explore more on these topicsNew MexicoAnimalsWildlifeShareReuse this content

title: Footage shows clash with French police on beach as dinghy tries to leave for UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Film emerges as France says it has stopped 185 small boat ‘events’ in three months since new £660m deal with UK
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Film emerges as France says it has stopped 185 small boat ‘events’ in three months since new £660m deal with UK
Content: French police slash small boat as migrants clash with officersImmigration and asylumFootage shows clash with French police on beach as dinghy tries to leave for UKFilm emerges as France says it has stopped 185 small boat ‘events’ in three months since new £660m deal with UKRajeev SyalHome affairs editorFri 21 Aug 2026 04.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFootage has captured the moment French police officers clashed with people on a beach in northernFranceas the authorities tried to intercept a dinghy attempting to reach the UK.Men wearing lifejackets appear to throw objects at the police to try to keep them away from their dinghy. The officers then use Pava spray before slashing the inflatable boat with a knife.The footage emerged as the French government said it had prevented 185 “small boat crossing events” in the three months since a new £660m deal with the UK.A small boat event is defined as stopping launches, seizing equipment including boats, engines and lifejackets, and arresting smugglers.Since the signing of the deal in April, extra police units have been active on French beaches, including a 50-person riot squad.Police action has included interceptions on beaches and at sea, the UK Home Office said.Since March, 12 “taxi boats” have been stopped from moving further up the coast and picking up more people.More resources have also been dedicated to seizing boats and engines before they can be used in the Channel.Smuggling gangs appear to have changed their tactics and have started putting more people into single boats. This month, a record 230 people made the journey in one boat.Ministers are keen to stress that the number of successful crossings is falling.Charities, however, have warned that the French police’s increasing activity is putting asylum seekers’ lives at risk.Utopia 56,which three weeks agogathered evidence of 35 CS gas canisters being fired by riot police near Dunkirk at migrants trying to reach a small boat, said at the time: “We can see police pressure on the beach is putting more people at risk. We saw it last week and we are seeing it now and we have seen it for some time. It is terrible.”A total of 15,897 migrants have crossed the Channel so far this year, down 43% on the same time last year, and an 18% drop from the same point in 2024.Reform UK has proposed using the Royal Navy to intercept and transport people to France or Belgium, describing the scheme as a humanitarian response.But France said the plan “would be a violation of French sovereignty as well as a violation of maritime law and international law”.The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “Our new UK-France deal is already having a real impact, stopping crossings before they happen and disrupting the criminal gangs behind them.“People smugglers should be in no doubt, we’re taking down their operations, seizing their equipment and breaking their business model for good.“Through our joint work with France, we have stopped over 47,000 small boat crossing attempts since the election and we will not let up.”Border Security Command’s Charlie Eastaugh said: “Our partnership with France is stronger than ever. Together, we are piling the pressure on the criminal gangs and preventing these illegal and dangerous crossings.“French officers are not shy in taking bold action to prevent these launches where it is safe and lawful to do so. They work in difficult and dangerous conditions to stop boats launching, seize equipment and disperse large migrant groups as well as saving thousands of lives at sea.“Our joint efforts are delivering results, and we will go further still to restore control of our borders and put these smugglers out of business.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceEuropeMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on trade | JD Vance | The Guardian
description: Audio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian Press
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Audio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian Press
Content: Vance, pictured, reportedly says in the audio that Carney is a ‘very sweet guy’ and that he gets along with him well.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVance, pictured, reportedly says in the audio that Carney is a ‘very sweet guy’ and that he gets along with him well.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockJD VanceJD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on tradeAudio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian PressOlivia Bowdenin TorontoFri 21 Aug 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaked audio from a private event has reportedly captured the US vice-president, JD Vance, mocking Canada for apparently capitulating in a trade deal and taunting the prime minister,Mark Carney, for trying to “out-tough” Donald Trump.The recording, which was reportedly made at a fundraiser andshared with the Canadian Press, comes in the last stretch of a difficult negotiation in which the US president has threatened to impose 50% tariffs on Canada.According to the Canadian Press, Vance is heard in the audio telling a room of supporters in Southampton, New York, that Carney is a “very sweet guy” and that he gets along with him well. But he also says Carney “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”Vance says: “It’s hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory forCanadawhen fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues.”The audio is unlikely to help relations between the two delegations at a crucial time. Canadian officials have said a deal is close that is likely to include Canada again allowing US alcohol sales across the country in exchange for avoiding the worst of Trump’s tariffs.Trump first said he would apply the tariffs from 19 August, but on Tuesday he backed down andannounced a three-day pause.The White House said in July that the 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada that included bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight out of 10 provinces and all three territories – a response in early 2025 to Trump’s first threats of tariffs against Canada.US producers of wine, beer and spirits have said the boycott has significantly affected their sales. Canadian imports of US alcohol are down about 81% year on year, according to the White House.The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves.“I wouldn’t say [Carney] was begging us, but what is a step before begging?” Kinew said on Thursday.Kinew encouraged Canadians to continue theirboycott of US productsregardless.“If we put the booze back on the shelves, don’t buy it … Buy the Canadian stuff instead,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job of sticking together in the face of Donald Trump’s tariff threats and I think we should continue to do that.”Kinew said he respected Carney for taking on Trump and believed Canada should stand firm in the negotiations.“I think Donald Trump is weak. America is weaker around the world today than it was a year ago, and he’s about to get slaughtered in the midterms,” he said.“Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person, and I think that rule applies here, so I think we should fight.”Explore more on these topicsJD VanceCanadaTrump tariffsMark CarneyAmericasTariffsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jamie and Jools Oliver pay themselves £1.5m dividend as profits almost halve | Jamie Oliver | The Guardian
description: Pre-tax earnings slump at chef’s food and media group after one-off costs including for a new cookery school
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Pre-tax earnings slump at chef’s food and media group after one-off costs including for a new cookery school
Content: Jamie Oliver has his hands full on This Morning with Alison Hammond and Dermot O’Leary  in July.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJamie Oliver has his hands full on This Morning with Alison Hammond and Dermot O’Leary  in July.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockJamie OliverJamie and Jools Oliver pay themselves £1.5m dividend as profits almost halvePre-tax earnings slump at chef’s food and media group after one-off costs including for a new cookery schoolSarah ButlerFri 21 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie andJools Oliverhave paid themselves a £1.5m dividend – more than 40% down on last year – after profits at their cookery and media empire almost halved.Sales atJamie OliverHoldings remained broadly steady at £28.4m in 2025, £160,000 less than in the previous year, as a strong performance at the group’s own restaurants, franchise business, cookery schools and TV productions offset a decline in royalties, licensing and endorsements.“We have delivered new Jamie Oliver titles in both book and TV formats during the year and there has been a continued strong performance from back catalogue book titles and our international television content distribution,” accounts filed at Companies House said.The Eat Yourself Healthy cookbook was a No 1 global bestseller, selling nearly 70,000 copies in its first week, making it one of Jamie’s fastest-selling books.However, pre-tax profits at the group, which became acertified B Corp in 2019, slumped to £1.25m, from £2.4m a year before, after £1.46m of exceptional costs related to a business restructure in which about 20 jobs were lost from the Olivers’ media team. Profits were also affected by pre-opening costs on a new cookery school in John Lewis’s Oxford Street outlet in London.Sales at owned and operated restaurants rose 17% to £4.3m and sales via the mainly overseas franchise restaurants, such as Jamie Oliver’s Deli and Jamie Oliver Kitchen, rose 6.5% to £4m. Cookery school income soared 48% to £1.6m. The group opened Jamie Oliver Catherine Street, his return to the UK restaurant scene with a menu focused on British produce, in 2023.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We don’t want to make the same mistakes’: Jamie’s Italian reopens in LondonRead moreThis March, Oliver also opened anew Jamie’s Italianin London’s Leicester Square, backed by the Prezzo owner Brava Hospitality Group, seven years after the chain collapsed. The original chaincalled in administratorsin 2019, leaving £83m of debt and causing 1,000 job losses.Brava’s backers have suggested there could be scope for up to 40 more of the new restaurants in the UK, and one more is planned this year if the right site can be secured.A spokesperson for Oliver said 10 new franchise restaurants under his name were planned to open this year around the world, including one just opened in Abu Dhabi after openings in Bahrain and India.However, royalties, licensing and endorsement income – which is by far the biggest part of the Oliver business and includes a Tefal pan range – slid by close to £2m to £15.9m. It was the second year of sliding income from this angle for Oliver, after a major deal with Tesco in 2023 ended in 2024.This year, Oliver has launched a social media “micro drama” involving short episodes of a “comedy drama” to promote the Life360 family tracking app.Explore more on these topicsJamie OliverHospitality industryJools OliverFood & drink industryRestaurantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Retail sales in Great Britain fall despite heatwave increasing food and drink demand | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Volume of goods sold in stores and online dropped 0.5% in July, ONS says
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Volume of goods sold in stores and online dropped 0.5% in July, ONS says
Content: Sales in non-food stores fell 1.3% on the back of a drop in clothes shopping.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSales in non-food stores fell 1.3% on the back of a drop in clothes shopping.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockRetail industryRetail sales in Great Britain fall despite heatwave increasing food and drink demandVolume of goods sold in stores and online dropped 0.5% in July, ONS saysBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffFri 21 Aug 2026 04.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetail sales across Great Britain weakened last month despite the men’s football World Cup and record temperatures boosting the demand for food and drink.The Office for National Statistics said the volume of goods sold in stores and online fell 0.5% in July. That is down from 0.7% rise in June – revised down frominitial estimates of 1%– and a 1.3% rise in May.Non-food stores took the biggest tumble, falling 1.3%, on the back of a drop in clothes shopping, after retailers brought forward cut-price sales into June while heatwaves in July resulted in more people staying home than hitting the high street.Sandra Prince, the head of consumer at Lloyds, said: “Hotter days could have shifted footfall and spending online or towards retail parks. For retailers, as the summer peak slows down, attention is now turning to the opportunities the autumn could bring to keep consumers engaged.”JD Sports boss is still struggling to turn up the heat on a tepid trainer marketRead moreDemand for furniture also took a dive, with fewer households looking to change decor during the extreme heat, while department stores suffered because of a drop in available stock. Some retailers had warned of lengthier delivery times during recent heatwaves.Food and drink sales were a rare bright spot, however, as hot and sunny weather and excitement around World Cup games boosted demand.However, the gains could have been higher had it not been for pubs and sports bars – which count as hospitality rather than retail in official statistics – luring punters to their screens to watch big matches.The British Beer & Pub Association said last month that late opening hours and England’s progress to the semi-finals gave a big boost to the industry, withpubs pouring an extra 30m pintsthan normal over the course of the tournament. That produced an extra £150m in added sales for its members.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJacqui Baker, a partner and the head of retail at the consultancy RSM UK, said: “Retail was not a World Cup winner, with many opting to cheer on England from the pub and prioritising their summer getaway, boosting hospitality and travel rather than retail sales.“Consumers splashed out on fans and food for barbeques due to the heatwave, with many avoiding soaring temperatures on the high street.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFood & drink industryOffice for National StatisticsExtreme heatExtreme weatherEconomicsEconomic growth (GDP)newsShareReuse this content

title: Airbus bows to remote working demands after series of strikes | Airbus | The Guardian
description: Aeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a week
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Aeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a week
Content: Workers mark the inauguration of the Airbus A320 aircraft family assembly line in Blagnac, France, in June.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWorkers mark the inauguration of the Airbus A320 aircraft family assembly line in Blagnac, France, in June.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAirbusAirbus bows to remote working demands after series of strikesAeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a weekKalyeena Makortoffand agenciesFri 21 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirbus has bowed to employee demands on remote working, after a series of strikesover its chief executive’s return-to-the office orders.The world’s largest aeroplane maker is said to have watered down plans to restrict remote working to one day a week from September. At present, staff are able to work remotely for two.It was part of a high-profile campaign by theAirbuschief executive, Guillaume Faury, to get staff back into the office, in an effort to ensure the company could meet record demand and prepare new products after hiring thousands more staff.Faury told employees in June that while home working had been a lifeline during the Covid pandemic, the opposite was now true as Airbus needed them to share their skills in person. “I count on all of you to support this,” he said in a memo, reported by Bloomberg.But disruption caused by a series of strikes, including in Spain,Franceand the UK in recent months, has forced him to backtrack, according to Reuters. Managers have now been told staff can work at home an average of two days a week, in effect curbing the chief executive’s efforts.InSpain, staff have been striking on and off since July, with approximately 40% of the company’s 14,000 local workers taking part in stoppages in recent weeks over issues including remote working, transport, paid leave and salaries.There have also been sporadic protests in France over plans to force white-collar staff into the office four days a week.However, Reuters said Airbus production – which is at the heart of the European defence industry – had not been affected by the strikes.An Airbus spokesperson said: “Our objective remains the same: we aim for increased on-site presence to ensure better collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“However, effective change requires listening to our people. Based on employee feedback, we have decided to implement this transition more gradually.”The spokesperson added: “We are empowering managers to organise hybrid working within their teams in a pragmatic and practical way that maximises collective efficiency and reflects the reality of their working environments. This will be done within the scope of Airbus’s current collective agreements for hybrid working.”Explore more on these topicsAirbusAirline industryWorking from homeWork-life balanceIndustrial actionFranceSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: As his new film Bitter Christmas is released the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himself
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As his new film Bitter Christmas is released the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himself
Content: ‘The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us’ …. Pedro Almodóvar.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us’ …. Pedro Almodóvar.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movieRyan GilbeyAs his new film Bitter Christmas is released, the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himselfFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlack sunglasses indoors and a tufty cloud of cotton-wool hair: it can only bePedro Almodóvar, bourgeois arthouse darling nonpareil and master of everything from screwball romps (Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown) to clammy thrillers (Live Flesh, The Skin I Live In) – and sumptuous melodramas such as his 24th film, Bitter Christmas, a cautionary tale about the perils of autofiction.We are sitting in the library of a London hotel and Almodóvar is dressed in a thin black windcheater, grey trousers and white trainers; add a whistle on a string and he could pass for a PE teacher. The 76-year-old director may have won more than 60 awards including two Oscars, five Baftas and six Goyas but when the shades come off today, he looks momentarily sorry for himself. He has been deaf in one ear since childhood, he tells me, and now the other one is giving up the ghost. In addition, a nasty stye has turned his left eye a gluey purple. Might he have picked it up while swimming? “I do swim almost every day because I have a pool,” he sighs. Never can those words have sounded so sorrowful.Then again, mixing contradictory flavours is part of what he does. There is the blank, blase approach to extreme material (murder, paedophilia, telekinesis) in his 1984 comedy What Have I Done to Deserve This? Or the climax of Matador, his kinky 1986 thriller, in which the race to prevent a double murder is paused while the characters gawp at a solar eclipse. A rape scene becomes comic in Kika, from 1993, and another rape is euphemised as a silent movie pastiche in 2002’s Oscar-winning Talk to Her.The peculiarities of Bitter Christmas begin but do not end with its release date: whoever heard of a film with a festive title opening during a summer heatwave? Almodóvar agrees: “It is weird.” Though we both know his ardent base would swarm to see whatever he did. Even when he was making cheap, guerrilla-style Super-8 shorts, he has always known the love of a good fan. Afterthe end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975, Almodóvar picked up thousands of underground followers in Madrid and Barcelona. They contributed more than $3,000 toward the budget of his 1980 debut, Pepi, Luci, Bom and the Other Girls on the Heap. Possibly the only thing he could do today to shrink his audience would be to ditch the eye-popping palette and make a film in black and white. “The colours are very important,” he says, as if anyone needed reminding.Part of the new movie already existed as a short story called Bitter Christmas, written in 2003 and published 20 years later inAlmodóvar’s collection The Last Dream. The story concerns a cult film director plagued, as Almodóvar really was at the time, by panic attacks and paralysing migraines. In the movie, Bárbara Lennie plays the stricken director, Elsa, who starts planning a new feature after years spent making commercials. “When I wrote Elsa’s little universe, I immediately got the idea that someone, a film-maker, was writing the story of Elsa that we were seeing,” he explains. That someone is Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia). Almodóvar, then, has directed a film about a director writing a film about a director writing a film.Keeping track of what is happening on screen becomes a case of mind over meta. Why should we care about Elsa’s story, though, when it is merely the product of Raúl’s imagination? “I hope that when the audience discovers that the film-within-a-film is going to change, that this change will surprise and excite them. But you’re right, it’s very risky. I think it is the riskiest film I’ve ever made. I took a whole bunch of risks, even knowing that some might not land. It requires you to pay complete attention, and it does seem to me that film audiences are increasingly getting lazy.”No prizes for guessing where he places the blame. Bitter Christmas sneaks in a jab at Netflix when someone suggests Raúl should take his new project there: “Don’t reduce me to making a TV movie!” he scoffs. Almodóvar made his own views plain in 2017 when he was president of the Cannes film festival jury. Two Netflix titles (Okja and The Meyerowitz Stories) were in competition that year even though they were never going to be exhibited theatrically in France; Almodóvar, who regarded the situation as a case of the US trampling all over European traditions,announced that he could not foresee awardsbeing “given to a film that is then not seen on the big screen”. So it proved.View image in fullscreenVictoria Luengo as Patricia in Bitter Christmas.Photograph: PRHis passionate defence of “the hypnosis of the large screen” was countered, however, by one of his jurors, Will Smith, who stood up for Netflix. The star’s name alone causes an almighty eye-roll today from Almodóvar, stye or no stye. “Will Smith was saying very silly things. The American press said things against me and in favour of him. And then, after years, they discovered how Will Smith is.” He mimes a slap, referring to the star’sattack on Chris Rock at the 2022 Academy Awards ceremony. Almodóvar, whose film Parallel Mothers was nominated for two Oscars that year,had a ringside view of the assault; his snowy dot of a head can clearly be seen in images of the incident. He later described the acceptance speech given by Smith after winning the best actor Oscar as resembling “that of a cult leader”.Reminded of this now, he says he thinks Smith still sounds like he is in a cult. “In our jury discussions at Cannes, everything he said sounded like that. He also showed me in all our discussions that he had very bad taste as a person. It was not a good experience being jury president. I didn’t want to do it but my brother [his producer Agustín Almodóvar] and [Cannes festival director] Thierry Frémaux insisted so much that I had to.”Back toNetflix. Have the streamers won the war? “They’re very close to winning,” he says gravely. “All the elements to do with releasing a film theatrically are disappearing. The film art, the posters, which we can then look back on and want to collect. Even the elements that seem banal, such as the fashion that the stars wear to a premiere.” He falls silent, then adds forlornly: “The excitement.”His principled stand in 2017 remains a lesson in defending home turf from bullies. “You can take this attitude to the political sphere. The European Union should be a shield for the crazy stuff Trump is coming up with in the US. He has created this lawless world, and we in the EU can demonstrate to him that if there’s something he wants to do, he needs to respect European laws. Trump is very angry at the EU and especially at Spain because our president has been brave and vocal in his opposition to his actions toward Ukraine and in his alliance with Israel.”Bitter Christmas is, however, less engaged with global issues than with the interior landscape of the artist, as so many of Almodóvar’s films have been. Insularity is to be expected from a director who admitted in The Last Dream that “writing about myself [is] pretty much the only thing I do”, and Bitter Christmas both addresses auto-fiction and represents an example of it. Raúl, whose loyal assistant, Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón), turns on him after discovering he has plundered her life in his screenplay, is, Almodóvar tells me, “a form of alter ego. At least 80% of Raúl’s dialogue is something I could say.”View image in fullscreen‘Cinema is what motivates me and moves me to live.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAn obsessive, perfectionist director himself, Almodóvar has written proxy figures before, most recently inPain and Glory from 2019, where the auteur played by Antonio Banderas admits that life without film-making is meaningless. But as long ago asThe Law of Desire, the torrid 1987 masterpiece, which he described in 1995 in the book Almodóvar on Almodóvar as “the key film in my life and career”, he was already alert to the threat posed by creative types like himself: that movie ends with the defenestration of a typewriter, which then bursts implausibly but spectacularly into flames.I ask whether he concurs with the poet Czesław Miłosz, who said: “When a writer is born into a family, the family is finished.” Almodóvar offers a minor tweak: “Not finished. But they’re going to have a lot of problems. It is pain that inspires me, not happiness. The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us. It’s not very nice but this is what it is. That’s why I painted Raúl as almost the villain of the film.” Almodóvar claims to have only ever pilfered responsibly. “When I’ve been inspired by someone from my life, I’ve changed many elements to make them unrecognisable.”That isn’t quite true. He took the facts of a friend’s traumatic encounter with Eta terrorists, made them Shias instead, and played the episode for giggles in Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown. The friend was aghast. “Oh yeah,” he says, remembering now. “She got very mad when she saw the film. At that time, I didn’t get it because I saw it as a homage: I’d turned something dark that happened in her life into comedy.”View image in fullscreenAntonio Banderas in Pain and Glory, 2019.Photograph: Manolo Pavón/APThoughts of the damage a writer can do lead to the subject of the late Alice Munro. In 2016, Almodóvar adapted three stories from Munro’s collection Runaway into his film Julieta; one of those stories, Silence, describes a woman who severs contact with her mother, as Munro’s daughter had done. It onlyemerged posthumously in 2024that Munro had stayed married to her second husband after learning he had sexually abused her daughter years earlier.“What’s overwhelming is that she wrote that story after everything that had happened,” the director says. “I try not to judge but I find that incredible. The whole family were silent, too, which is very dirty, and as dark as the position of the mother. If I knew what had happened there, my adaptation would have been completely different.” Would he still have made Julieta, then, even if the terrible facts had emerged in time? “Yes, but the story is much better with the stepfather, the mother doing nothing, the daughter escaping the family.” I don’t doubt his horror at Munro’s behaviour. There is a faint chill, though, in hearing the screenwriter within him express frustration that a vital piece of the narrative puzzle was hidden from view.When it came to writing the scene in Bitter Christmas in which Mónica accuses Raúl of “vampiring” her, Almodóvar found the experience of self-criticism liberating. “All the things she says to him, I could easily say to myself. It’s refreshing and fun to be so nasty about yourself.” That might be because his own critics have been so thin on the ground. What they lack in number, however, they make up for in rigour. In 1993, film-maker Alex Cox pointed out that Almodóvar’s actors speak “the ‘official’ Spanish with the lisped ‘s’”, indicating “a certain societal correctness … which is naturally divisive and detrimental to the culture”. When Volver, a gumbo of ghosts, murder and mother-daughter devotion, was released in 2006,critic Peter Matthews saw onlythe “smooth, velvety craftsmanship” of a “failed iconoclast”. After Parallel Mothers,Leo Robson arguedthat, far from being rebellious, the director’s work has consistently parroted “orthodox and to some degree official Spanish attitudes”.The auto-critique in Bitter Christmas is nowhere near as harsh as all that. Almodóvar may see Raúl, his alter ego, as something of a villain, but he has also described himself as a “victim” of his own passion for cinema. Whether villain or victim, what price has he paid? “Sometimes I’ve suffered during shoots for various reasons,” he recalls. “You can encounter problems that you can’t even fathom. There have been a lot of painful moments but that is the price. One must never complain because it’s part of the adventure.”Almodóvar shows no evidence of slowing down, deafness and styes be damned. This October in Spain, he will even publish his first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. Before we part, though, I remind him that he is now the same age that his hero Luis Buñuel was when he madehis swansong, That Obscure Object of Desire, a film which ends, as The Law of Desire later would, with an explosion. How does it feel to be at that point? “Unlike Buñuel at that time, I am still completely full of desire to keep making films. Cinema is what motivates me and moves me to live. Buñuel was pressured by his producer when what he really wanted was to rest in Mexico.” A flash of defiance. “And I don’t ever want to rest.”Bitter Christmas is in UK and Irish cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmPedro AlmodóvarComedy filmsDrama filmsSpainNetflixComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spa Weekend review – female answer to The Hangover spreads the slush with the massage oil | Movies | The Guardian
description: Despite stars Leslie Mann, Anna Faris and Isla Fisher and the writers behind The Hangover, this tale of friends at a luxury hotel is a dud
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Despite stars Leslie Mann, Anna Faris and Isla Fisher and the writers behind The Hangover, this tale of friends at a luxury hotel is a dud
Content: Isla Fisher, Anna Faris, Leslie Mann and Michelle Buteau in Spa Weekend.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIsla Fisher, Anna Faris, Leslie Mann and Michelle Buteau in Spa Weekend.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesReviewSpa Weekend review – female answer to The Hangover spreads the slush with the massage oilDespite stars Leslie Mann, Anna Faris and Isla Fisher and the writers behind The Hangover, this tale of friends at a luxury hotel is a dudPeter BradshawFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJon Lucas and Scott Moore are the screenwriters who struck gold nearly 20 years ago with The Hangover, a brilliant stag-weekend nightmare comedy about what happens in Vegas, which sadly spawned a terrible (though lucrative) franchise. Now, as writers and directors, they have tried turning it around and making a movie about how middle-aged women behave on a longed-for spa weekend at a luxury-porn hotel. The result is a comedy without gags, a comedy which, for all the strenuous high-jinks, is afraid to be flippant or mean or, indeed, funny in any way.Leslie Mann plays a hotshot lawyer called Jane who can’t make room in her life for romance; Anna Faris is goofy Sophie, PA to a rich asshole; Michelle Buteau is outspoken badass Coco, angry at her ex-husband dating again; andIsla Fisheris landed with the stridently unfunny role of Mel, a wild child who makes the other three nervous, but whose life-affirming no-filter honesty is going to break everyone’s emotional logjam and sort out their lives. As for Jane, it looks as if the hotel’s super-hot super-sensitive yoga teacher, Kai (Adam Demos), is going to hook up with her.The potentially funny idea of the one woman in the friend group whom no one really likes might have been the grit in the oyster that produced the comedy pearl, but, of course, it has to turn out that they really do like Mel – and in a much slushier, more sentimental way than the guys in The Hangover came round to liking Zach Galifianakis’s character. There’s something bland in this movie’s massage oil.● Spa Weekend is out on 20 August in Australia, and on 21 August in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsIsla FisherComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: H Is for Hawk to Doctor Strange: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Claire Foy finds a winged companion in an incredibly moving drama, plus Benedict Cumberbatch’s magical psychedelic spectacle from Marvel
Author: Simon Wardell
Headline: Claire Foy finds a winged companion in an incredibly moving drama, plus Benedict Cumberbatch’s magical psychedelic spectacle from Marvel
Content: Life-affirming … H is for Hawk.Photograph: Courtesy: LFFView image in fullscreenLife-affirming … H is for Hawk.Photograph: Courtesy: LFFThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevision & radioH Is for Hawk to Doctor Strange: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekClaire Foy finds a winged companion in an incredibly moving drama, plus Benedict Cumberbatch’s magical psychedelic spectacle from MarvelSimon WardellFri 21 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekH Is for HawkGetting up close and personal with animals can be a life-affirming way of feeling at one with nature. It can also be a way of avoiding the messier everyday of being human. For Helen Macdonald (a febrile Claire Foy), in Philippa Lowthorpe’sadaptationof Macdonald’s bestsellingmemoir, it is the tug between the two that brings her world crashing down. After her beloved father (Brendan Gleeson) dies, Helen decides to train a goshawk (“a perfectly evolved psychopath,” her mentor warns) in memory of their shared love of the great outdoors. But confronting avian life red in tooth and claw isn’t the same as dealing with the complex emotions of grief. An arresting, affecting drama.Sunday 23 August, NetflixWe Dive at DawnView image in fullscreenSub text … We Dive at Dawn.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyDespite dutifully fulfilling its propaganda brief, this 1943 film from Anthony Asquith works superbly in its own right as a tense wartime thriller. John Mills, that era’s go-to everyman, stars as the captain of the fictional submarine Sea Tiger. Sent on a mission to attack a new German battleship, he and his crew find themselves out on their own in the Baltic, facing mines, undersea nets and destroyers. Naturally, a can-do attitude prevails, but the tangled personal lives of the crew provide a comic distraction to the life-and-death stuff of winning the war.Saturday 22 August, 1.25pm, BBC TwoDoctor StrangeView image in fullscreenIt’s a kind of magic … Doctor Strange.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThis isthe moviethat, for better or worse, introduced the multiverse to Marvel’s superhero franchise. It also chucked magic into the otherwise muscle-based mix – as practised by Benedict Cumberbatch’s arrogant brain surgeon turned wielder of the mystic arts. This gives the film an enjoyably psychedelic feel, as Strange battles rogue sorcerer Kaecilius (Mads Mikkelsen), and is oddly reminiscent of Christopher Nolan’s Inception and Tenet (it was released between the two) in its architecture-twisting, time-reversing spectacle.Saturday 22 August, 8pm, Channel 4Howards EndView image in fullscreenClass act … Howards End.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyEM Forster’s 1910 novel about class, money, love and a house in the country was styled into a prestigeperiod dramaby Merchant Ivory, aided by Ruth Prawer Jhabvala’s Oscar-winning script. Three levels of society come into conflict in a story of chance encounters, misguided charity and patriarchal hypocrisy. Anthony Hopkins’s rigid, rich businessman Henry Wilcox is drawn to the bohemian, privileged Schlegel sisters Margaret (Emma Thompson) and Helen (Helena Bonham Carter), while they get involved in the life of poor clerk Leonard Bast (Samuel West).Monday 24 August, 1.15pm, Film4NightcrawlerView image in fullscreenYes he cam … Nightcrawler.Photograph: Entertainment One/Sportsphoto/AllstarIt may have dated somewhat in this age of people filming everything on their phones, but Dan Gilroy’s dark2014 dramais still wholly relevant in its clear-eyed critique of the public’s obsession with true crime. Jake Gyllenhaal – hollow of eye and creepy of smile – plays Louis, a sociopathic petty thief who finds a new job driving around LA shooting graphic footage of police incidents for the local TV news. If it bleeds it leads, with his ratings-chasing boss, Nina (Rene Russo), encouraging Louis’s worst tendencies.Monday 24 August, 9pm, Sky AtlanticArthur the KingView image in fullscreenLost and hound … Arthur the King.Photograph: Album/AlamyMichael (Mark Wahlberg) used to be an adventure racer, competing in team endurance events that involve epic stretches of running, trekking, cycling and kayaking – but never won a contest. Irked by his failure, he comes out of retirement for the world championship in the Dominican Republic. As his ragtag group struggle through mud, forest and mountain, Michael realises they are being followed – and at times assisted – by a stray dog. Simon Cellan Jones’s fact-based adventure is Lassie-like in its dog-friendly emotional manipulation but has plenty of rugged action for extreme sports fans.Tuesday 25 August, 10.40pm, BBC OneThe Day Shall ComeView image in fullscreenFed up … The Day Shall Come.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyChris Morris’s scathing2019 satireabout the US government’s “war on terror” and the innocents caught up in it may be the most neglected of his brilliant career but in its plausibility (“Based on a hundred true stories,” a title card notes) and bleak comedy it deserves more love. Moses Al Shabaz (an endearing Marchánt Davis) is a delusional Miami preacher who leads a radical black power movement (members: three) that is infiltrated by an FBI branch desperate for a win, despite posing no actual threat. Not as surreal as Four Lions but it still possesses a sharp bite.Wednesday 26 August, 1.25am, Film4Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Brooke Shields stars in a silly murder-mystery comedy  | Television | The Guardian
description: A novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: They’re on the case …  Andi (Amalia Williamson) and, right, Allie (Brooke Shields) in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVView image in fullscreenThey’re on the case …  Andi (Amalia Williamson) and, right, Allie (Brooke Shields) in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Brooke Shields stars in a silly murder-mystery comedyA novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellFri 21 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaAllie (Brooke Shields) is a bestselling “menopausal mystery” novelist; Andi (Amalia Williamson) is an aspiring true-crime podcaster. When they meet at a writing convention, it’s a boomer and gen Z culture clash. But then a murder takes place and the two team up to solve the case … Light, rompy crime drama fun.Hollie RichardsonMiles Davis: A Celebration at the Proms8pm, BBC FourCatch it on the radio or sit down and witness jazz trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire in action, as he joins conductor Miho Hazama and the BBC Concert Orchestra to celebrate the legacy of Miles Davis. It’s a night of music from Porgy and Bess, Sketches of Spain and more.HRBergerac9pm, BBC TwoJim Bergerac (Damien Molony) starts the tense season finale of the crime drama reboot at rock bottom, mentally dishevelled and facing the loss of his daughter at the hands of a vengeful criminal who thinks Bergerac fitted him up years ago. An at-gunpoint warehouse showdown beckons, as does a test of loyalty for Bergerac’s colleagues.Jack SealeStation Eleven9pm, Sky AtlanticIf you missed this pandemic drama the first time round, it’s well worth catching up. In these final two episodes, Jeevan (Himesh Patel) gets a crash course in obstetric medicine, there’s an emotional performance of Hamlet, and revelations abound about Miranda (Danielle Deadwyler), creator of the Station Eleven comic.Hannah J DaviesAnn Droid9.30pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenAn emotional ending … Sue (Sue Johnston) and Linda (Diane Morgan) in Ann Droid.Photograph: BBC/Boffola Pictures/Gary MoyesTissues at the ready for an emotional ending to a sitcom that has been both side-splittingly funny and deeply poignant. Sue (Sue Johnston) is saddened when her son says they no longer need carer robot Linda (Diane Morgan). But what happens to Linda when she’s sent back? Let’s just say, fingers crossed for a second season.HRGrimsburg10.45pm, Sky OneThis adult animation starring Jon Hamm as a small-town detective isn’t as sharp as the likes of BoJack Horseman, tending towards the scattergun chaos of Family Guy. Still, there are moments of brilliance in this triple bill, starting with an episode guest-starring Amy Sedaris as a troubled former child star.HJDFilm choiceLes Yeux Sans Visage(Georges Franju, 1960),12.50am, Talking Pictures TVView image in fullscreenEerie … Édith Scob (left) and Alida Valli in Les Yeux Sans Visage.Photograph: Cinetext/The Criterion Collection/AllstarGeorges Franju’s arresting 1960 horror is as interested in dreamlike images as jump-scare moments of terror – and in Édith Scob’s Christiane has a monster with the pathos of Frankenstein’s creature. Disfigured after a car accident, she sports a lifelike but eerie facial mask and drifts around her country house like a pale white ghost. Meanwhile, her surgeon father, Dr Génessier (Pierre Brasseur), and his assistant Louise (Alida Valli) abduct young women to supply full-face skin grafts for her. It’s occasionally grisly but mostly unsettling.Simon WardellLive sportPremier League football:Arsenal v Coventry6.30pm, Sky Sports Main Event. title: Anthony Hopkins: Life Is a Dream album review – easy on the ear melodies written from the heart | Classical music | The Guardian
description: There’s a cinematic flourish to many of Hopkins’ compositions, together with fine arrangements of Welsh tunes and pieces dedicated to family
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: There’s a cinematic flourish to many of Hopkins’ compositions, together with fine arrangements of Welsh tunes and pieces dedicated to family
Content: Anthony Hopkins in the recording hall with conductor Gustavo Dudamel.Photograph: Suzannah Letts/Charlie GrayView image in fullscreenAnthony Hopkins in the recording hall with conductor Gustavo Dudamel.Photograph: Suzannah Letts/Charlie GrayClassical musicReviewAnthony Hopkins: Life Is a Dream album review – easy on the ear melodies written from the heartPhilharmonia Orchestra/Dudamel(Decca)There’s a cinematic flourish to many of Hopkins’ compositions, together with fine arrangements of Welsh tunes and pieces dedicated to familyClive PagetFri 21 Aug 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Hopkins, it turns out, has been composing music all his life. Now, at the age of 88, the Welsh-born Hollywood actor makes his Decca debut, securing the services of LA Philharmonic’soutgoing music directorGustavo Dudamel to bring his music to life.View image in fullscreenCover art for Life Is a Dream: Music Composed by Anthony HopkinsSo, what does an Oscar winner sound like? Not surprisingly, there’s a significant cinematic influence, inspired by the music that caught the attention of a lad growing up in Margam, a suburb of Port Talbot. The opening Fanfare and March is a catchy, Technicolor splash, like everything here harmonious and written from the heart. Ditto the Khachaturian-flavoured Two Pieces for Orchestra. Welsh roots are honoured too: My Fatherland, featuring six traditional tunes, four sung in Welsh, would not seem out of place at the Last Night of the Proms.Reminiscences abound, including the lively 1947: Suite for Orchestra recalling one of the hottest summers on record. It takes its cue from the streets and mountains surrounding Hopkins’ childhood home, including an unforgettable visit with his father to the Plaza cinema. Then there are works dedicated to his wife (Stella Aria and the Stanley Myers-inspired Farewell My Love) and his niece (Tara).Soloists are distinguished – Argentinian pianist Sergio Tiempo and Venezuelan cellist Gregorio Nieto – with fine contributions from the Philharmonia Orchestra and the Bach Choir. The spacious recording is state-of-the-art. Those who appreciate easy-on-the-ear melody and good old-fashioned craft should find plenty to enjoy.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
