title: Add to playlist: the righteous jangle and snaking melodies of Jawdropped and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater tradition
Author: Huw Baines
Headline: The LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater tradition
Content: Sun-bleached cool … Jawdropped.Photograph: Julien SageView image in fullscreenSun-bleached cool … Jawdropped.Photograph: Julien SageAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the righteous jangle and snaking melodies of Jawdropped and the week’s best new tracksThe LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater traditionHuw BainesandLaura SnapesFri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromLos AngelesRecommended if you likethe Lemonheads, Sugar, the MuffsUp nextSecret to Spare released 18 SeptemberMaybe it’s to do with getting older, maybe it’s to do with the broad-spectrum grimness of it all, but the thrill of low-stakes creativity, of making something for the joy of making it rather than in the hope ofmaking it, feels particularly vital at the moment. And, if the sun-bleached cool of Jawdropped’s music is anything to go by, starting a powerpop project in your 30s will light up this pleasure centre like a dive bar pinball machine.The US quartet are all on their second, third or fourth go-around with this band thing, having spent years skating through LA’s DIY scenes before forming in 2024. Their chemistry and compositional smarts became immediately apparent on the following year’sJust FantasyEP, where co-vocalists Kyra Morling and Roman Zangari tumbled into slacker harmony over blown-out distortion and plaid-swaddled acoustic guitars.Leaning into the idea of small wins on your own terms, their debut album Secret to Spare offers a collection of stories about keeping your head above water, its luminous hooks casting the plate-spinning of day jobs, house shows and routine disappointments in a triumphant light. The Line has the righteous jangle of peak Lemonheads on a string, whileMonday’s snaking melodies are amped up by gnarly power chord scuzz in the Bob Mould tradition. The singleSplit Liphits bittersweet paydirt with a lilting chorus that doubles as another dose of reality: “Sign us all to a major label / It doesn’t always work out.” It doesn’t. But perhaps that’s OK.Huw BainesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenShygirl.Photograph: Jessica MadavoShygirl – AlyseHere’s a stunning new side to the south Londoner: imagine Bat for Lashes’ crystal-ball balladry dragged feet-first into a cybergoth club and blown up to the scope of Madonna’s William Orbit era. A thrill!Fontaines DC –Marianne“I can help you disappear,” Grian Chatten offers in a dangerously alluring chorus and a song full of cinematic gloom that more than fulfils the Irish heroes’ promise of absolution.Wild Pink – Still Coming DownIf, apparently like many of alt rock’s leading lights right now, you can’t hear Jason Molina’s influence enough, you won’t complain at hearing another gorgeously grizzled slab of Americana in his image.Actress – WithendingThe beautifully intricate synth refrain at the heart of this track undulates as beguilingly as kelp in the ocean deep, dragged deeper by insistent kick drum and haunted by vocal sprites.Heavens to Betsy – Ain’t Never Goin’ Back“I ain’t never goin’ back,” a teenaged Corin Tucker – future of Sleater-Kinney – sings in this unearthed Modern Lovers-ish demo fromthe newly reunited riot grrrl legends, slinging an arrow into the future.Lover1k – On My OwnSome might call it trash, but anyone addicted to the genre of club music best described as “withering woman sounds deathly unimpressed by you over crude beats” … it’s your lucky day.Teenage Fanclub – There Was YouFear not, trash-haters, we’re back on solid ground with Norman Blake and this gently baroque, beautifully wistful tribute to those people that always offer a port in a storm (much like the Fannies always do).Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alice Roberts: ‘By the time I’d finished Richard Dawkins I’d left faith behind’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and Toad
Author: Alice Roberts
Headline: The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and Toad
Content: ‘I love the way Darwin takes his readers on a journey’ … Alice Roberts.Photograph: Dave StevensView image in fullscreen‘I love the way Darwin takes his readers on a journey’ … Alice Roberts.Photograph: Dave StevensThe books of my lifeBooksAlice Roberts: ‘By the time I’d finished Richard Dawkins I’d left faith behind’The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and ToadAlice RobertsFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryThe first books I remember were from The Village with Three Cornersseries Sheila K McCullagh. I loved the – literally – colourful characters, like Johnny Yellow Hat. I was reading with my Grandma, in her garden perhaps, sitting on a small patio, surrounded by bright begonias and busy lizzies.My favourite book growing upArnold Lobel’s wonderful Frog and Toad stories. Toad would get himself tied up in knots, trying to find a button or fly a kite, but Frog was always there – a constant, caring and funny friend. I enjoyed reading these stories to my own children when they were young, and we still sometimes go back and revisit them. They’re so full of humour, heart and simple humanism.The book that changed me as a teenagerAt that time I loved Alan Garner, Susan Cooper and Rosemary Sutcliff. But the book I remember having a really profound effect on me was Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene. I was passionate about biology, and the gene’s-eye view turned it upside down and suddenly evolution made sense. I went on to voraciously read all of Stephen Jay Gould’s essays on evolutionary biology. Those two authors really inspired me.The writer who changed my mindWhen I picked up Dawkins’s The Blind Watchmaker,I was already beginning to seriously doubt the Anglican faith I’d been brought up in. By the time I finished it, I knew I’d left that faith behind. Biological diversity could be entirely explained through natural processes; there was no need for – and no evidence of – a divine creator. I became a humanist, although I didn’t know the word for it back then.The book that made me want to be a writerI never set out to be a writer. I wrote my first book as a handout to go with the first television series I wrote and presented on my own – Don’t Die Young on BBC Two. As a university academic, I wanted there to be something more to go with the programmes. I’d written papers of course, but nothing for a general readership, and I loved doing that. In my writing, whether that’s books or scripts for television and live shows, I always go back to Gould’s advice and example. He was adamant that it was possible to communicate complex ideas without “dumbing down” – you just need enough steps, and to strip away unnecessary jargon.The bookI came back toOne I keep coming back to – and this isn’t surprising for any biologist – is Darwin’s On the Origin of Species by Natural Selection. It’s so full of wonderful details and insights – and I love the way he takes his readers on a journey, from the known and familiar, to the novel and strange.The book I discovered later in lifeGeorge Eliot’s Middlemarch – I only really sat down to read it five years ago. I never got on with the Brontë sisters or Jane Austen at school, and in my head, I’d put Eliot away on the same shelf labelled “novels that were boring and banal but got away with it because they were early examples of the genre and so there wasn’t much competition”! It was Andrew Copson, chief executive of Humanists UK, who finally persuaded me to read Middlemarch and I was blown away by it – the complexity of the characters and the way it challenges your prejudices. It is a masterpiece.The book I am currently readingFor work I’m dipping into Fritz Graf’s Roman Festivals in the Greek East and Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price’s two volume series on the Religions of Rome. For pleasure, I have recently finished Val McDermid’s fabulous Queen Macbeth, and Karen Hao’s fascinating and troubling Empire of AI. I’m also listening to Otto English’s brilliant Notoriousaudiobook. And I am enjoying reading Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem to my teenage son – who still enjoys a bedtime story!My comfort readThe Little Book of Humanism– a book I helped to compile, full of wonderful, everyday humanist wisdom.The Goddess Queen by Alice Roberts is published on 1 September by Gallery UK. To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Marc Dubin obituary | Travel guides | The Guardian
description: Other lives: Travel writer specialising in Greece, Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Other lives: Travel writer specialising in Greece, Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean
Content: Marc Dubin hiking in Belogradchik, in northern Budapest. He was one of Rough Guides’ most dependable writers, producing guides to Greece, Cyprus, Turkey and the Balkans.View image in fullscreenMarc Dubin hiking in Belogradchik, in northern Budapest. He was one of Rough Guides’ most dependable writers, producing guides to Greece, Cyprus, Turkey and the Balkans.Other livesTravel guidesObituaryMarc Dubin obituaryJack HollandFri 21 Aug 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy friend Marc Dubin, who has died aged 70, was one of the leading English-language travel writers on Greece, Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean. For more than four decades he wrote and edited guidebooks for Rough Guides, Insight Guides, Berlitz, DK Eyewitness and Lonely Planet, combining meticulous scholarship with an infectious enthusiasm for the places he loved.In the late 1970s, Marc left his home in California to travel through Central America before settling in Europe. To finance his travels he worked as a photographer, producing many of the postcard images that introduced holidaymakers to the Mediterranean long before the digital age.By the early 80s he was contributing guidebooks to Lonely Planet. Soon afterwards I met him when, as co-founder of Rough Guides, I joined the team interviewing candidates for the second, much-expanded, edition of The Rough Guide to Greece. Asked how he would bargain for rooms in Athens’ Plaka district, Marc replied in what sounded to me like faultless Greek. The interview was effectively over.Marc became one of Rough Guides’ most dependable writers, producing guides to Greece, Cyprus, Turkey and the Balkans. His prose was informed, elegant and quietly funny, underpinned by an insistence on accuracy. If a hotel, taverna or archaeological site appeared in one of his books, it had earned its place.His interests extended beyond guidebooks. He could talk with equal authority about Byzantine churches, Ottoman architecture,rebetika(a form of urban, popular Greek music) and contemporary Greek politics.For all his achievements, Marc remained indifferent to worldly success. Material possessions interested him less than another journey, obscure church or a meal with friends.Born in Los Angeles, Marc grew up in Beverly Hills, and attended University high school in west LA. His father, Louis, was a clinical bioanalyst who served in military intelligence during the second world war, and his mother, Lee (nee Lieblich), qualified as a nurse later in life, after Louis’ premature death. Marc would recall delivering wine to his family’s neighbour, Groucho Marx, sharing his aunt’s swimming pool with Dustin Hoffman during the filming of The Graduate, and the shadow cast by the Sharon Tate murders. After graduating in biochemistry from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1977, he embarked on his travels.During the 90s he bought a derelict property on Samos, much of which he restored himself. This became his base on the Greek islands, while he kept a flat in Westcliff-on-Sea, Essex.As well as Rough Guides, Marc wrote numerous guidebooks, and his work was translated into French, German, Polish and Spanish. For many years he was the Daily Telegraph’s Greek islands destination expert.Diagnosed with a brain tumour 12 years ago, he refused to let illness define him. At the time of his death he had been updating Berlitz’s Greek Islands guide.Marc is survived by his wife, Zdravka Mihaylova, a Bulgarian diplomat whom he met at the Hydra rebetiko conference in 2003 and married in 2024, and his sisters, Vivian and Gail.Explore more on these topicsTravel guidesOther livesobituariesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest
Author: John Self
Headline: The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest
Content: A sense of the ridiculous and the serious … Pirkko Saisio.Photograph: Pirjo HonkasaloView image in fullscreenA sense of the ridiculous and the serious … Pirkko Saisio.Photograph: Pirjo HonkasaloTranslated fiction roundupFictionReviewThe best recent translated fiction – review roundupThe Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra KamiyaJohn SelfFri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Red Book of Farewellsby Pirkko Saisio, translated by Mia Spangenberg, PenguinClassics (£14.99)Following Lowest Common Denominator and Backlight, this book completes Finnish author Saisio’s autofictional trilogy. It covers her young adulthood in the 1970s, where she comes out as lesbian (“The electricity doesn’t go out. The Richter scale remains still”) and falls in love. One of her lovers, Havva, is a communist who’s engaged to a man; she relies on his rich parents for funding, but pees in their private pool as a protest. Later, Saisio is voted vice-president of a political drama company, as “she has the skills to bring about the revolution, specifically via theatre” – despite half-baked productions such as the “napalm opera” Vietnam-a-Go-Go. As that suggests, this is a story with a sense of both the ridiculous and the serious. Told in clear prose, it playfully shifts between third and first person as Saisio recounts her memories then analyses them. This enchanting series deserves to become a modern classic.Short Circuitby Wolf Haas, translated by Jamie Bulloch (HarperVia, £20)“We think [time] goes in one direction. But really you need to think of it as a loop”. This, well, loopy novel opens with jigsaw aficionado and “merciless hair-splitter” Franz Escher getting an electrician in to fix his power – then accidentally killing him. As Franz waits for the ambulance, he reads a novel about Elio, a man who helped put his own mafia family behind bars. Elio, who’s now on witness protection, kills time by reading a novel about … Franz Escher. The two stories pursue one another, accelerating until they collide, incorporating courtship by car alarm, rival funeral orators and multiple identities for many characters. Oh, and what if the electrician Franz killed turns out to be Elio? Short Circuit,recallingthe slipstream fiction ofChristopher Priestand the light-touch experimentations of David Mitchell, is an entertaining literary hall-of-mirrors.Cosmosby Lucia Odoom, translated by Hunter Simpson (Daunt, £10.99)“Lately my leap feels more and more like a fall,” writes Cosmos, a young Ghanaian man who has migrated to Copenhagen, where he contends with Denmark’s “worrying lack of smells” and collects recyclable bottles to earn money. Later he gets a job modelling, and lets the agency believe he’s an asylum seeker so they’ll feel sorry for him. He falls in love with Elizabeth: when she describes something as a guilty pleasure, “I asked her what a guilty pleasure was”. The past presses in: when Elizabeth takes him to the seaside, he recalls the vomit-streaked boat journey to Europe. All this is told in WhatsApp messages to Cosmos’s family back home – even the sex scenes. It’s a story of the challenges and hopes of a migrant’s life, made charming by the funny narrative voice and Cosmos’s optimism: he can see a plane and imagine being a crow, “flying high above the world, high above everything that no one owns”.The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra Kamiya, translated by Daniel Hahn (Pushkin, £12.99)In this collection of stories from a Japanese-Argentinian writer, people rarely say what they mean. The dark secret beneath a woman’s meticulous breakfast preparations is hinted at through imagery: a flower, “open like a yelling mouth”. A story where a family attempts to cope when their son leaves by not talking about him (“I learned to differentiate between many different types of silence”) reads like an epic in miniature. There is black comedy – a woman asks her maid to help her read the letters on an optician’s chart – as well as intense psychological drama, in the tale of a soldier who is told to “dig here until further orders” and keeps going, and going, and going. Kamiya’s collection is remarkable in its variety but united by its laconic, sometimes elliptical style. These are teasing, satisfying stories to be savoured slowly.Explore more on these topicsFictionTranslated fiction roundupFiction in translationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Life of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A teasing tale of the friendship between a writer and an actor explores the fallout from fame, and the blurring between pretence and reality
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: A teasing tale of the friendship between a writer and an actor explores the fallout from fame, and the blurring between pretence and reality
Content: Sharp reflections … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Carlotta Cardana/CAMERA PRESSView image in fullscreenSharp reflections … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Carlotta Cardana/CAMERA PRESSBook of the dayFictionReviewLife of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman?A teasing tale of the friendship between a writer and an actor explores the fallout from fame, and the blurring between pretence and realityClare ClarkFri 21 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 03.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMis a celebrated film actor. A star since childhood, now the face of a major fashion brand, she has been famous all her life. That her career closely resembles Natalie Portman’s has been gleefully seized upon by the press, something Rachel Cusk must surely have anticipated: in the novel, M’s first film has its sex scenes cut at her mother’s insistence, as happened with Portman’s 1994 debut Leon, while her ballerina movie is recognisably Black Swan. M is also, in the words of the nameless and genderless narrator of Life of M, “a good sport”. When the narrator suggests writing M’s autobiography, M likes the idea. “Would you just make it up?” she asks.A celebrity autobiography is seldom the work of the celebrity herself. And yet any suggestion that the narrator will serve as a kind of ghostwriter to M is dispensed with in a few pages. The pair meet for coffee at a luxury hotel and, after the narrator’s partner falls suddenly and seriously ill, for lunch in a restaurant. The lunch is unsatisfactory, an attempt at intimacy that the narrator acknowledges afterwards to have been a mistake. Though M is determined to live as normal a life as possible (“her personal task is to become real, or rather to acquire some reality”), the narrator is uncomfortably aware of their own falseness with M: “It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real. It was as if she was the only one good enough at acting to attain reality.” After that the two of them do not see one another again “for a long time”.double quotation markCusk’s power lies in the authority of her sharp, spare prose, the glittering exactness of her sentencesAnd yet a book about M, or at least partly about M, materialises. Episodes from M’s life are intercut with observations from the narrator’s own experiences. The M sections are precise, specific: an acting class led by a renowned theatre director, a difficult encounter with a controlling ex, a holiday in an immaculately curated villa in Greece. The impression is of clips from a film, an effect heightened by the meticulous descriptions of place that preface each scene like the stage directions from a script, detailing everything from furniture and layout to the specific texture of the artificial wood floor in a five-star hotel suite. In a world where everyone is acting, Cusk seems to be saying, the appearance of things is all the certainty we have.In this post-saturation era of social media exposure, the intersection of appearance and authenticity has been exhaustively picked over. Cusk’s insights are not strikingly new. Her power lies in the authority of her sharp, spare prose, the glittering exactness of her sentences. She writes with crisp acuity about the frictionless (and therefore strangely lifeless) existence of the celebrity, the corrosive effect of fame on family relationships, the blend of fervent purity and crushing cynicism that delimits a person forged in the forcefields of power and pretence. At Cusk’s startling best, and there is a good deal of that here, her ideas land like punches or uncomfortable secrets muttered in our ears: it is a shock to realise that they are our secrets too.Life of M, like Cusk’s previous novelParade, grew out of a piece published in the New Yorker, in this case a powerful short story titledProject. While the story has made its way almost whole into the opening chapters, the larger scope of the novel form gives Cusk the space to explore M more deeply. She may have famouslydeclared in 2018that “I don’t think character exists any more” but, stripped though her work is of the ordinary conventions of character and plot, her ideas land with greatest impact when they are rooted in the particular: a flaming sunset reflected on a switched-off television screen, a room in a museum meticulously curated to give the impression of a lived-in space, an “indifferent” fan approaching M for a selfie “as though M were a tourist monument”. M’s most compelling scenes, like those told to Faye in Cusk’s celebrated Outline trilogy, thrum with detail.Faye was a deliberate absence, a vessel for other people’s stories. The narrator of Life of M is more a mirrored surface, their reflection of M’s celebrity as much a part of the illusion as the celebrity itself. What begins with a first-person singular narrator quickly morphs into a plural “we” which sometimes appears to represent the narrator and their partner, sometimes a more public “we”, both the counterpoint to and the rapaciously hungry engine for fame. Perhaps Cusk intends to co-opt the reader, to make us complicit. Perhaps she means to throw us off balance. What is certain is that the prose in these sections has an epigrammatic absolutism that, while occasionally brilliant (“We do not, as we did when we were young, see the evening as a mysterious kingdom in which we might meet our destiny”), is more often puzzlingly specific. How is it that “we” visit the apartment of a psychic with “frazzled hair” or recall that “our longest relationship was with someone who now frightens us”? It is not always clear what these parts add to the whole. Jokes, a reliably dark pleasure in Cusk’s work, are in regrettably short supply. Life of M is powered by a formidable intelligence and shaped with exceptional technical skill, at its best it leaves one reeling, but the impression it leaves is one of detachment, even disdain. It is a book to admire enormously, but not one to love.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 review – once more unto the mercenary breach | Games | The Guardian
description: This second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releases
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releases
Content: Inhuman hustle … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiView image in fullscreenInhuman hustle … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiGamesReviewMetal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 review – once more unto the mercenary breachPC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5, Xbox Series X/S; KonamiThis second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releasesDiego Nicolás ArgüelloFri 21 Aug 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘War has changed,” claims Old Snake in Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. Back in 2008, the team at Kojima Productions waxed poetic about people recruited to fight in proxy wars they have no political or ideological stake in. As these mercenaries follow their orders, traders get rich out of the so-called war economy. The more disastrous the conflict in a specific area, the higher the bidding price.I expected my time with Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 to be nostalgic and, in good old MGS fashion, abundant with fictional events that sound eerily familiar to our current reality. Twenty minutes in, I was having an existential crisis.The package bundles remastered renditions of stealth games Ghost Babel and Peace Walker and the aforementioned Guns of the Patriots. It’s an intriguing selection, spanning a Game Boy Colour reimagination, a PlayStation Portable prequel, and the culmination of the mainline series respectively. Despite being substantially distinct in isolation, all three entries focus on perpetuating acts of cruelty in order to collect a paycheque.View image in fullscreenWar hasn’t changed … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiOld Snake willingly takes part in the war economy, every downed soldier dropping their weapon with a satisfyingclink. When picked up, each gun is automatically sold to a black market trader for points, which can be exchanged for bigger, deadlier materiel. An enemy squad stepping on a landmine is no different from unlocking a shiny loot box.Conflict is welcomed as long as it’s profitable. It puts food on the table for the group of mercenaries you lead in Peace Walker and the private military companies in Guns of the Patriots – it has also been the fuel of real-lifeprediction markets. The members of the fictional private military companies are IDed and monitored in real-time by an AI program, while in real lifevideo game datais used to train AI that can be used by the military, with game companiesfacing boycottsfor their alleged involvement in war and genocide.In 2026, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 is whiplash disguised as a trip down memory lane. As a collection, it’s an odd time capsule. Ghost Babel is almost a de-make, following in the footsteps of the original MSX entries while adapting modern mechanics and conventions, from sound detection to overly long cutscenes. Peace Walker, meanwhile, retains the roots of the current live service era – you can play both the main missions and side objectives with up to three other players online – without the predatory microtransactions and battle passes of today.Lastly, while all three games embody nostalgia, Guns of the Patriots is the epitome. Mentions of familiar characters prompt you to repeatedly press a button to get rapid-fire flashbacks to their previous appearances. There’s no shortage of reunions and nods to the entire series, with a fair degree of fan service mixed in. In an era ofremakes, unnecessary sequels and constant recycling of protagonists, it’s satisfying to revisit an entry that dared to put a nail in the coffin without hesitation.All three games now look better and are more easily accessible. The experiences are, for the most part, just as you remember them. As far as remasters go, you’ll feel right at home. At their core, the message is as eternal as ever: war, and its surrounding economy, hasn’t changed. The only noticeable difference is the inflation rate.Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 will be released on 27 August; £44.99Explore more on these topicsGamesMetal Gear Solid VPCPlayStation 5Nintendo SwitchNintendo Switch 2Xbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpse | Games | The Guardian
description: Free from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first game
Author: Bex April May
Headline: Free from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first game
Content: ‘The weakest of the weak’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50View image in fullscreen‘The weakest of the weak’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50Summer games previewsGamesStupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpseFree from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first gameBex April MayFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLove is blind. In Stupid Never Dies, it is also frozen solid and technically dead as Davy, the weakest zombie in monster society, discovers Julia’s body in a shopping centre and falls in love at first sight. He wants to bring her back to life and take her on a date. Unfortunately, that means defeating the King of Monsters (KOM) and accidentally saving humanity along the way.This is the gloriously ridiculous setup for this forthcoming action RPG from GPTrack50, a new studio founded by former Capcom producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi. Its world looks much like ours, except that monsters have always been part of everyday life: whereas we might find a bear in the mountains or a stray dog in the woods, residents here encounter werewolves and zombies.View image in fullscreenEveryday monsters … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50That uneasy normality ends when KOM crushes civilisation and leaves only 2% of humanity alive. Davy begins even lower down the social ladder.Zombies, says Kobayashi, are “the weakest of the weak”. But eating a mysterious egg gives this particularly unimpressive corpse the power to fight back.Because Davy is already dead, combat throws out the usual need for self-preservation. Forget defence: guarding and dodging are pushed aside in favour of “attacking, attacking, attacking”. Kobayashi describes it as a game made “by the action game lover, for the action gamer”.View image in fullscreen‘Funky zombie action’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50Its two main systems make full use of Davy’s unreliable body. He can consume defeated monsters, steal their skills and transform into creatures including a werewolf, vampire or harpy. The “body hack” mechanic goes further, allowing players to replace his head, arms and legs with equipment. Attach a sword to an arm and Davy gains sword attacks; fit a gun and he starts shooting. Being undead has never looked so practical.Kobayashi calls the result “funky zombie action”, a phrase coined to give the development team a shared idea of the game’s tone: fast, colourful and darkly funny. It also captures the freedom Kobayashi found after years working on some of the world’s most famous franchises, includingResident EvilandDevil May Cry.Large franchises bring large audiences and expectations. A new studio making a new IP had neither. As Kobayashi says, “We don’t have a fan yet.” That has allowed its team of around 30 developers, many recruited from companies including Capcom, Konami and Square Enix, to use stranger jokes and sharper humour than they ever could when working on those older series.The studio itself began almost as scrappily as Davy. In its early months, GPTrack50 had programmers and designers but no artists, so the team bought outside assets to build a rough white-box prototype. Around 20 external companies eventually joined the three-year production, drawn, Kobayashi says, by the chance to create something completely from scratch. He hopes players finish thinking: “This is the experience that I was looking for. This is a new thing.”Underneath the monster-eating and gun-limbs is a simple underdog story: Davy rises from the bottom of monster society to challenge its king, but he is not driven by glory. Saving the remaining humans is almost incidental, as Kobayashi explains: “He wants to go out for a date [with] this frozen girl.”Romance isn’t dead; it just needs defrosting.Stupid Never Dies is available onPCand PS5 from 21 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAction gamesZombiesPCPlayStation 5featuresShareReuse this content

title: Salty Brine: How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show) review – one of today’s most powerful stage voices | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description:
Summerhall, Edinburgh
Intertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brew
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Summerhall, EdinburghIntertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brew
Content: Overbrimming … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOverbrimming … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSalty Brine: How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show) review – one of today’s most powerful stage voicesSummerhall, EdinburghIntertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brewBrian LoganFri 21 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a hell of a swing to make a show paralleling your first love with Anne Frank’s – the more so for that show about her to end on an uplift. But Salty Brine is nothing if not the man for a big swing. This most overbrimming of cabaret artists is in town with hisLiving Record Collectionproject, which makes shows inspired by, and featuring, the songs from beloved rock and pop albums. This one takes Neutral Milk Hotel’s In the Aeroplane Over the Sea as the launchpad for an inquiry into religious traditions, the origins of the world, the migration of souls – and the adolescent passions of Frank and Brine.Is it in poor taste, I wondered, to co-opt the horrifying story of this murdered teenager for aesthetic effect? In Brine’s defence, the album in question itself riffs dreamlike on Frank’s story, fashioning from it something deeply moving – and the same could be said, for my money, of How Strange It Is.View image in fullscreenDeeply moving … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show)Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianCombining extracts from his diary and from Frank’s, Brine vividly evokes the headlong nature of youthful passion, impossible to restrain even in the most constrained circumstances. Where does all that energy go when a life – not just Frank’s but that of her sweetheart, Peter – stops? With paper aeroplanes, a PowerPoint about reincarnation and one of the most powerful voices on the stage today, Brine hurls Jeff Mangum’s lyrics at the problem to see what sticks.Badgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarnRead moreNot everything does. Brine has a tougher job here than withthe Smiths’andAnnie Lennox’swork (to cite two recent examples) making the lyrics serve the beats of his story or the points he is trying to make. That’s sometimes frustrating – and elsewhere, not all of his connection-making resonates. But the material with which he is conjuring (life and death, what love and life add up to, and what we leave behind) is so emotionally potent, and the force of will applied to the undertaking so irresistible, that he makes the synthesis soar. Rhapsodic source material, passionate performance, cosmic sense-making: it’s a heady brew late night on the fringe, and an intoxicating one.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 7-19 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreCabaretAnne FrankreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A History of Paper review – Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming sing a fragile romance | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Oliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receipts
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Oliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receipts
Content: Airy and joyful … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenAiry and joyful … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewA History of Paper review – Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming sing a fragile romancePitlochry Festival theatreOliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receiptsMark FisherFri 21 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started as a BBC radio drama in 2016, and was reworked asa small-scale musicaltwo years ago. Now, A History of Paper gets the mainstage treatment with two bona fide stars in the leads. The good news is that little is overblown about the production. Stars or not, Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming only bring a greater degree of subtlety to this fragile work.Written by the late playwrightOliver Emanueland composer Gareth Williams, it recounts an everyday romance through the medium of paper: the postcard messages, the origami gifts, the Pizza Express receipts, the shopping lists and the confetti. A cardboard box full of such detritus is a neat way to encapsulate both the grand emotions and the ephemera that sustain a love affair. Henderson and Cumming carry it with due lightness.View image in fullscreenA touch overbearing … A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanDirected by Dundee Rep’s Andrew Panton, they are the tenement neighbours who go from ratty and rattled to curious and flirtatious. Where Cumming has a puppyish enthusiasm – bounding out of a morose heartbreak soundtracked by Radiohead – Henderson is variously obstinate, contrary and funny.Hers is a fascinatingly unpredictable performance, not least when bending the rhythms of Williams’s songs: talk-singing one minute, soaring to melodic heights the next. Her duets with Cumming under Gavin Whitworth’s musical direction are things of beauty. Dressed down in jeans, cardigans and unbuttoned sleeves, the actors’ presence is airy and joyful. They pace around as if yet to decide where they will go next.On a set by Ana Inés Jabares-Pita, half rugged Fife coast, half Ground Zero and a touch overbearing, this is also a 9/11 play. Emanuel took its theme from the paper that cascaded like snow from the twin towers after they were struck. For all the narrative neatness, the play piggybacks on that event in a way that feels manipulative. No love story, however tender or calamitous, could equal the tragedy of that day.Otherwise, though, the emotions are true and, as Panton uses the bigger scale to his advantage, with Henderson stalking the auditorium and papery interventions from above, it makes for a short, sweet and touching chamber piece.AtPitlochry Festival theatreuntil 12 September. Then atDundee Rep, 16–19 September.Explore more on these topicsTheatreAlan CummingDundee RepPitlochry Festival theatreShirley HendersonMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Who Killed Marilyn? review – dismal attempt to solve mystery of Monroe with Pixie Lott | Theatre | The Guardian
description: An account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond cliche
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: An account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond cliche
Content: Tragic icon … Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at the Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenTragic icon … Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at the Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewWho Killed Marilyn? review – dismal attempt to solve mystery of Monroe with Pixie LottEmerald theatre, LondonAn account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond clicheArifa AkbarFri 21 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been 600 books written aboutMarilyn Monroesince she died in 1962. So we are told by Monroe (Pixie Lott) herself in Sharleen Cooper Cohen’s play. The star’s body was discovered by her housekeeper, and her death at the age of 36 has spawned as many conspiracy theories as Elvis Presley’s. Was it an overdose, or a contract killing by the Kennedy family because she had kompromat on them? Did the mafia have something to do with it? Was an enema administered on the night she died? These are some of the questions that have been asked by Monroe obsessives.You imagine this drama is setting itself up for something beyond the slew of familiar theories. But there is little to gain from this trot through Monroe’s life, narrated in cliches.Lott has the signature blond hair, red lipstick and white pedal-pushers (she almost but not quite resembles the Marilyn of The Seven Year Itch scenes in a halter-neck dress). Monroe tells us that her husbands only ever saw the famed icon rather than the woman beneath. Ironically, this is what she remains here, due to a thuddingly on-the-nose script that spells out Monroe’s woes and pathologies. There are brief glimpses into her marriages with baseball player Joe DiMaggio (Henry Proffit) and playwright Arthur Miller (Ben Dilloway), and encounters with JFK (Mars Sams) and Bobby Kennedy (Paul Kane). There is no exploration of her first and potentially more illuminating marriage.View image in fullscreenBasic ‘tortured starlet’ psychology … Ryan Ellsworth (left) and Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithUnder the direction of Philip Wm McKinley, Lott struts on to a stage with a bed at its centre – both her place of death and an overused motif for the life of a sex symbol. She keeps strutting on and off, striking Marilyn-esque poses, without giving any true sense of the woman beneath the iconic exterior. The other performances are also underwhelming, with the men in her life played with a wooden uniformity and no uncanny resemblances. A sex scene with JFK ends with his backache and appears like accidental farce. The whiff of drama school end-of-year show persists.Abigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a CinzanoRead moreIt pays little attention to Norma Jeane – the person she was before she created Marilyn. There are fleeting references to her family history of mental instability, her early life in an orphanage, her experience in a psychiatric unit. These are drive-by glances in a play that prefers to centre Monroe’s sex life, in the most hackneyed of ways.Her unravelling at the end conveniently takes place with her psychiatrist (Ryan Ellsworth) in situ so she can expound on her pain and her breakthrough when she realises she has been trying to fill a “bottomless pit” within her. It is basic tortured-starlet psychology, which does little to develop the complexities of her inner world.There is an answer to the titular question at the end but the bigger mystery of who Monroe was remains entirely untouched.AtEmerald theatre, London, until 29 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMarilyn MonroePixie LottreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Badgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarn | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Playwright and performer Malaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Playwright and performer Malaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer
Content: A message about the allure of storytelling … Malaika Kegode in Badgers.Photograph: Paul BlakemoreView image in fullscreenA message about the allure of storytelling … Malaika Kegode in Badgers.Photograph: Paul BlakemoreEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBadgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarnTraverse theatre, EdinburghMalaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singerMark FisherFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlaywright and performerMalaika Kegodetops and tails this show for Theatre Royal Plymouth with a message about the allure of storytelling. In a festival city bursting at the seams with stories, it is an unnecessary observation. A more important question is about which stories we choose to tell, which resonate and which pass us by. Why, for example, did Kegode want to write a story – and it is a story rather than a play – about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer?She focuses on the subsequent investigation by Meles Costas, an under-qualified true-crime podcaster, living in the shadow of a high-achieving and terminally ill mother. And she laces her story with gothic fairytale imagery: folk songs with dark-magic properties, human-to-animal transmutation and a hint of witchcraft.Four Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrésRead moreAll intriguing stuff, but if Badgers has a greater purpose than telling a story for its own sake, Kegode does not make it evident. Fortunately, she tells it well. Casting the audience in the role of Meles (whose name is the Latin for badger), she describes a podcast interview with Bridget Brock, the missing man’s landlady, and juxtaposes it with the supernatural: did singer Ben vanish in 2015 because he had turned into a badger and was it because he had been cursed after stealing Bridget’s song?With a badger stripe hair-do, Kegode leads us with charm and precision into the haunting corners of Jenny Davies’s production, with texture added by her longtime collaborators,Jakabol, whose excellent score is played live by Beth Roberts and Joe Williams, tucked away in a sound booth. All good stuff for a dark and stormy night, but unless you are concerned about the ethics of true crime, not particularly urgent.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 August;Theatre Royal Plymouth, 2–5 September;Bristol Old Vic, 8–12 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTrue crime (Podcasts)FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kapoor’s blockbusting blobs, terrible Tudors and Emin’s proteges – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Lose yourself in Anish Kapoor’s black holes while Horrible Histories’ illustrator visits Preston and Margate hosts Tracey Emin’s students’ graduation show – all in your weekly dispatch
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Lose yourself in Anish Kapoor’s black holes while Horrible Histories’ illustrator visits Preston and Margate hosts Tracey Emin’s students’ graduation show – all in your weekly dispatch
Content: ‘Exhilarating’ … Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Exhilarating’ … Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockArt Weekly newsletterArt and designKapoor’s blockbusting blobs, terrible Tudors and Emin’s proteges – the week in artLose yourself in Anish Kapoor’s black holes while Horrible Histories’ illustrator visits Preston and Margate hosts Tracey Emin’s students’ graduation show –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 21 Aug 2026 07.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekAnish KapoorIf you are looking for a summer blockbuster, here’s your show – Kapoor’s exhilarating spectacular boasts black holes and a mountain over your head.Hayward Gallery, London, until 18 OctoberAlso showingFrance-Lise McGurnSemi-figurative, semi-abstract and ironically pop art-style paintings that add up to an all-over installation.Dundee Contemporary Arts, 22 August to 15 NovemberTears Final ShowYou can still catch this graduation show by the latest batch of Tracey Emin’s art students, curated by Emin – and see the seaside too.TKE Studios, Margate, until 31 AugustCaroline WalkerPaintings of mothers and children in a social realist style slightly reminiscent of 1970s Ladybird books.Newlyn Art Gallery, Newlyn, until 31st OctoberMartin BrownDrawings of glorious Georgians, terrible Tudors and other historical favourites by the Horrible Histories illustrator.The Harris, Preston, until 31 AugustImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Carabinieri/ReutersCheese! These cheerful Carabinieri stand in Parma’s Ducal Palace with three recovered paintings that werestolen earlier this yearfrom the nearby Magnani Rocca Foundation. Escorting the paintings, the authorities returned art worth millions of pounds to the private museum: Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, valued around £5.2m, Renoir’s Fish, £2.6m, and Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace, valued at £17,000. And the beautiful work behind them? That’s a 1573 fresco by Bertoia: priceless.Watch the footage of the theft here.What we learnedDavid Shrigley is finding the funny side of some Dutch old mastersThe controversial insides-outside Lloyd’s building is opening to the publicRenaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina have been stolen from a Sicilian museumItalian police have recovered paintings by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse after a heistKaty Perry kissing the Earth after returning from ‘space’ inspired painter France-Lise McGurnA new Douglas Gordon doc captures the artist smearing himself with silver paintskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMasterpiece of the weekMountain Landscape with Lightning by Francisque Millet, c1675View image in fullscreenPhotograph: AlamyYour mind can go on a long, solitary hike simply by looking at this Romantic painting of a wild and untamed landscape. Yet this place is not so remote – it’s in the Auvergne region of France, picturesque enough, yet part of a sophisticated modern state. Just as his contemporary JMW Turner found savage windswept scenes in Scotland or braved storms in the Channel, so Rousseau sees the sublime on a trip to this characterful region of his own country. Low, ethereal, stormy light casts the hills in the distance in purple shadow, making them appear huge and terrifying. The valley that leads towards them is green, yet dark and cavernous, a veritable slough of despond. It might be a scene from an adventurous epic set in a fantastic land. But it’s a real, peopled place, and Rousseau reveals the marvellous in his own land.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get intouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Odyssey becomes highest grossing R-rated film of all time | Movies | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine
Content: The Odyssey has been R-rated – meaning anyone under 17 must be accompanied by an adult – for ‘violence and some language’.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Odyssey has been R-rated – meaning anyone under 17 must be accompanied by an adult – for ‘violence and some language’.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesThe Odyssey becomes highest grossing R-rated film of all timeChristopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & WolverineAndrew PulverFri 21 Aug 2026 06.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has overtaken Deadpool & Wolverine to become the highest grossing R-rated film of all time.According to figures compiled by the Numbers, Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s epic poem has achieved $1.35bn (£990m) at the worldwide box office, compared withthe Ryan Reynolds/Hugh Jackman superhero movie, which stands at $1.34bn (£980m) since its release in 2024.A R-rating as designated by the Motion Picture Association requires anyone under 17 to be accompanied by an adult, and is normally seen as a brake on box office expectations. In its citation, the MPA said The Odyssey was given an R-rating “for violence and some language”.In the UK, The Odyssey has beenrated 15for “strong violence”, while in Australia it has anM-ratingfor “mature themes, violence and coarse language”.Other R-rated features to do well include Nolan’s previous film Oppenheimer, which benefited from the “Barbenheimer” craze to amass $983m worldwide, the Joaquin Phoenix-starring Joker ($1.1bn), and the two standalone Deadpool movies ($782m and $786m respectively).View image in fullscreenHugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, which stands at $1.34bn at the worldwide box office.Photograph: Jay MaidmentAt the North American box office alone, Deadpool & Wolverine remains ahead, having taken $637m against The Odyssey’s $516m. Interest in Nolan’s film, however, is high in other areas of the world: the UK and Ireland’s total of $92.7m is the second highest, followed by France on $69.3m and Italy on $55.6m. China has also contributed a significant amount to The Odyssey’s coffers, with a reported $36.3m.Starring Matt Damon as Odysseus, Tom Holland as Telemachus and Anne Hathaway as Penelope,the film is already the most successful of Nolan’s career, having surpassed his previous highest grossing film, 2012’s The Dark Knight Rises, which has earned $1.082bn (£805.7m) globally.However, The Odyssey’s figures could well rise significantly as it is currently in the middle of a box office battle with Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has alreadytaken more than $2bn worldwide, becoming the second fastest film to do so (after Avengers: Endgame in 2019).Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyFilm industryDeadpool & WolverineChristopher NolannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She had this divine calling’: the incredible and transporting art of Minnie Evans | Art | The Guardian
description: Just over 50 years after she was one of the first Black artists to have a solo show at the Whitney, the museum gathers some of her most remarkable paintings for a new exhibition
Author: Veronica Esposito
Headline: Just over 50 years after she was one of the first Black artists to have a solo show at the Whitney, the museum gathers some of her most remarkable paintings for a new exhibition
Content: Minnie Evans, Untitled (Four Figures Collage), 1961–1967.Photograph: Collection of John Jerit. © The Estate of Minnie EvansView image in fullscreenMinnie Evans, Untitled (Four Figures Collage), 1961–1967.Photograph: Collection of John Jerit. © The Estate of Minnie EvansArt‘She had this divine calling’: the incredible and transporting art of Minnie EvansJust over 50 years after she was one of the first Black artists to have a solo show at the Whitney, the museum gathers some of her most remarkable paintings for a new exhibitionVeronica EspositoFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSurprisingly, the term “outsider art” was coined fairly recently – in 1972, when the art historian Roger Cardinal made it the title of the book with which he introduced the idea to the English-speaking world. Since then, debates have raged as to whether it’s really justified to use such a term to describe art made beyond the confines of the art world, and if any of the other competing terms – among them naive art, folk art and raw art – are really any better.How architect Paul Revere Williams fought racism and changed the face of Los AngelesRead moreThe Whitney Museum of American Art’s new show, The Lost World: The Art of Minnie Evans, offers audiences an opportunity to contemplate just how its subject may – or may not – have been an outsider to the art world, and to also revel in Evans’s increasing insiderness in the decades since her death in 1987. A comprehensive retrospective with nearly 100 pieces covering the entirety of Evans’s artistic output, the show occurs almost exactly 50 years after the Whitney first introduced the artist’s genius to New York’s art elite.Born in 1892, Evans created her first artwork in 1935, just a few days after the death of her grandmother, when she drew two claustrophobic pen and ink pieces that she fittingly titled My Very First and My Second. Made on scraps of paper, they are obsessive and maze-like, composed mainly of seemingly abstract jags and spirals, with closer inspection revealing what appear to be a few recognizable forms: a rainbow and sun, a field of crosses that may be a graveyard, and a canoe-like vessel containing three passengers.View image in fullscreenMinnie Evans in the Gatehouse of Airlie Gardens, Holding One of Her Crayon Drawings, 1970.Photograph: Estate of Nina Howell Starr. Courtesy of March galleryAccording to the Whitney curator Barbara Haskell, after dutifully signing and dating these pieces, Evans did not create so much as a single piece for another five years, until she had a chance encounter with these artworks as a sign that she should continue. “She painted all the time as a child, but then when she got married, she stopped making art,” said Haskell. “And then, in 1940, she took it up again.”From there, Evans would create with an inspired fervor, largely fitting art-making into quiet moments during her employment as a housekeeper at the estate of the financier Pembroke Jones, and then later as a gatekeeper at the estate’s Airlie Gardens. What propelled her forward was tantamount to a religious calling.“She felt that she saw God speaking to her from behind a wreath, three times, like this three-part conversion, and the third time she heard Him tell her to paint or die. So she had this divine calling that she felt she was answering,” Haskell said.Evans’s art is dense and inspired: forms repeat in dazzling arrays, beings are decorated with a level of detail almost too tiny to believe, and mandala-like faces sport endless curves and crevices that become spaces for Evans’s exacting use of color and shading. Biblical imagery is frequently found, as well as lush, almost tropical-feeling depictions of greenery and flowers.Evans’s pieces tend toward playful, 2D melanges bound up in symmetries radiating out from a central axis, although every now and then a more naturalistic piece will stop you cold, such as 1955’s haunting Temple by the Sea or Evans’s imposing 1954 depiction of the famed Airlie oak.View image in fullscreenMinnie Evans – Temple by the Sea, 1955.Photograph: Mike Jensen/The Estate of Minnie Evans.“They’re very dense, and there’s this kind of mixture of ecstasy and containment that’s very mesmerizing,” said Haskell. “You look at the pieces and you feel like you’re drawn into this forest of images that surround you.”As she created, Evans staged makeshift shows of her works by hanging finished pieces on Airlie Garden’s front gates, and, although reluctant to formally exhibit her work, she had her first show in 1961 in the Little Gallery in Wilmington, North Carolina. With her reputation growing, she was sought out by the photographer and art historian Nina Howell Starr in 1962. Attracted by word of Evans’s renown, Starr was drawn to meet in person – she soon became Evans’s friend, and her de facto publicist, an arrangement that would last for a quarter century.Starr helped Evans make her entry to the New York City art world and arranged for her first exhibition in the Big Apple in 1966 titled The Lost World, opening the way to a series of shows that culminated in a major exhibition at the Whitney in 1975. The show’s title was very much to the point, as Evans saw herself as depicting exactly that, a vision of a long past, glorious realm.View image in fullscreenMinnie Evans – Untitled (Day to Night with Beasts and Angels), 1966.Photograph: Collection of Christian Daniel. © The Estate of Minnie Evans“Evans would talk about how she was creating this vision of a lost world, a paradise that had been destroyed by the great flood,” said Haskell. “She was recreating images of that world and allowing us to have access to it. It was also, in a sense, a world that would come into being.”Given that Evans had been born in the south during the Jim Crow era and lived most of her life before Black Americans won any measure of civil rights, it is tempting to read her work through the lens of racial oppression, which, according to Haskell, many interpreters of her work have done. But Haskell argues for an interpretation that is instead grounded not in race but religion.“There are a lot of images of eyes that are nestled in the foliage in her work, and many commentators see those eyes as references to the surveillance that she must have felt as a Black woman in the south,” said Haskell. “But I see them more as the eyes of God – she was definitely influenced by the Bible, and she had it right there with her when she took admissions at the gate. The amazing thing about her work is that it offers the ability for both interpretations to be true.”View image in fullscreenMinnie Evans – Untitled (Face with Crown and Angels), 1968.Photograph: Christopher Burke/Collection of Wendy Williams, New York. The Estate of Minnie Evans.According to Haskell, in the years since Evans’s death, she has grown more and more beloved by the art world – just the past year has seen substantial shows at the High Museum in Atlanta and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. “The trajectory of her public acceptance has just grown,” said Haskell. “Her reputation has exploded.”The Whitney’s exhaustive retrospective offers visitors a rare chance to enter fully into Evans’s world, one that is largely a place of amazingly good feelings, grandiose luminosity and rare moments of tranquillity. It is an important reminder of the visionary force that art holds. As Haskell puts it, “she’s this remarkable artist who created an entire world of harmony and transcendency, even amid disquiet and unease. I hope people find solace in this show and hold the light in her wonder.”The Lost World: The Art of Minnie Evans is on display at the Whitney Museum of American Art from 22 August to 10 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArtExhibitionsPaintingMuseumsNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If you’re just interested in answers, you are missing out’: philosopher Lani Watson on the power of asking questions | Philosophy | The Guardian
description: The author and academic explains how an open, questioning mindset can bring people with opposing views closer together – and even change history
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The author and academic explains how an open, questioning mindset can bring people with opposing views closer together – and even change history
Content: Watson says there are four stages of questioning: proto, private, social and spoken.Photograph: Katherine Rose/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWatson says there are four stages of questioning: proto, private, social and spoken.Photograph: Katherine Rose/The GuardianThe ideas interviewPhilosophy‘If you’re just interested in answers, you are missing out’: philosopher Lani Watson on the power of asking questionsThe author and academic explains how an open, questioning mindset can bring people with opposing views closer together – and even change historyZoe WilliamsFri 21 Aug 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsking a question can change your mood, and having a questioning mindset can change your life – or, as the philosopher Lani Watson, an honorary fellow at the University of Edinburgh, is more likely to put it, “create change in your life”. When you live in an answer-oriented world, your phrasing tends towards the glib certainty, which is one of the things Watson – speaking to me from her home in Edinburgh – seems quite naturally to avoid.Questioning fosters exploration and curiosity, she says. It changes your relationship to yourself and to others: it can make you fall in love; it can stop you going to war. Watson’s challenging book,Q: The Hidden Power of Questions in a World that Wants Answers, is written with a deceptive simplicity and an almost kindly encouragement, so you’re knee-deep into her proposition before you have even considered that it might turn out to be quite hard work.The book is unusually interactive, asking the reader to read a sentence out loud, count the number of questions in a conversation between Watson and her wife, ask basic questions of themselves and stop to think about whether they can be answered. There’s an appendix at the end that promises to get you into a questioning frame of mind, which it turns out you have to write yourself (to be fair, there’s no trickery here; she does say that it’s empty – but in my reflexive quest for answers, I didn’t notice).Here are some brass tacks, what you might coarsely call proof. From the world of neuroscience and evolutionary biology, we can see that asking questions stimulates dopamine, she explains, and “all that reward circuitry activates regardless of whether you get the answer, because the brain is trying to encourage you to continue exploring your environment”.View image in fullscreenThere is a deep-seated desire for ‘cognitive closure’, says Watson.Photograph: Katherine Rose/The GuardianWatson divides questioning into four stages. First is proto-questioning, common to all organisms, which is “exploratory information-seeking, tiny little nematodes seeking nutrition”. Then there’s private questioning, which connotes some intentionality, such as asking for information from your environment in a directed and deliberated way – in Watson’s example, you might see it in a penguin leaving its enclosure in Edinburgh zoo just because it’s figured out it can.Then there’s social questioning, asking a question of another, which creates layers of joint attention and joint intentionality, and which, as far as we know, only humans do. “What’s over that horizon?” would be a classic example of social questioning sparking migration and changing human history. Finally, there is spoken questioning, which builds whole new layers of complexity and abstraction, since now we can jointly approach matters that aren’t right in front of us, that we may only have imagined.If it sounds intuitive that questioning would be so pleasurable and generative, Watson’s book wonders, how did we end up in such an answer-oriented world? Education is measured in what we know, not what we ask. Our social norms guide us away from direct questioning, in case we look dumb, or intrusive. The overriding drive of our technological experimentation is towards directing all our questions to a machine and none to one another. And so-called “why-chaining” – repeatedly asking “why?” to whatever answer you get – is universally agreed to be the most annoying thing about a three-year-old.double quotation markYour reward circuitry activates regardless of whether you get the answer to a questionThere is a deep-seated desire for “cognitive closure”, Watson says, or, put more simply, knowing. Aporia, the state of bafflement or confusion, is uncomfortable, though some people tolerate it a lot better than others. Watson is an epistemologist by training, “so I’m invested in questions about knowledge. And I do regard myself to be a pretty extreme sceptic with respect to that tradition. I really don’t think we actually do come to know anything, truly, and I’m OK with that. It’s a really interesting conversation to have in a classroom with undergraduates; you have a huge range of levels of comfort with that conclusion, and its implications.”I’m personally in the cognitive closure camp: I hate an ambiguous ending; I hate agreeing to differ. Someone’s four-year-old on social media the other day had a tantrum when he discovered infinity – he just wanted numbers to end – and I could hard-relate. But you can learn to live with aporia and be richer for it, Watson says. “It’s all about exposure – spending a lot of time confronting big unknowns. A theoretical physicist would be in a similar position.”She grew up in Southampton, her father a geologist, her mother a researcher in social housing policy, and studied philosophy for her bachelor’s degree at the University of York, before becoming a research fellow at Oxford. “This questioning mindset that I look at is so fundamental to philosophical thinking that when I advocate for it, maybe I’m trying to introduce philosophy through a back door.”View image in fullscreen‘Questioning itself creates intimacy, symmetrical questioning is more intimate still.’Photograph: Westend61/Getty Images; posed by modelsWhile Watson’s academic discipline came to her so naturally, she’s not blind to its faults. “Philosophy has an identity crisis,” she says, “that’s been formed by 2,500 years of it being done by people who want to make it seem really difficult – abstract, complicated and not for you. When, in fact, it really is something we’re all doing all the time.” It’s sometimes called the “genius only” discipline, but it isn’t only that intimidating intellectual granite face that puts people off, Watson says; it’s also the idea of utility. “We have an aversion to abstraction that is ultimately driven, to some extent, by that problem of: what good is it to me? Why do I need to worry about that?”Early in Watson’s consideration of what a question was, she stopped using question marks. This made her consider the history of this punctuation mark (it’s more recent than you would think: the court of Charlemagne), and its variations in other languages (there is one that just puts a circle above the salient word, which is cute), but she never went back to using question marks, and it never made any difference. “The only place where I feel an impulse to add a question mark is if I’m indicating that what looks like a statement is, in fact, a rhetorical question, which told me a lot about what the question mark was doing: it’s signalling something, rather than being a part of what a question is.”But the other thing punctuation is good for, the reason you would have to prise it from my dead hands, is that it speeds up the eye, surely? “Yes, the lack of a question mark helps people to slow down, around this key moment of a question, which is exactly how you develop this questioning mindset.”double quotation markI really don't think we come to know anything, truly, and I’m OK with thatYou’ll need that patience for the process Watson calls “assumption mining”, questioning yourself more deeply about what you think you already know. She describes this as a habitual intellectual exercise, almost deliberately casting yourself back into aporia. “I always think, when I do it myself, that when I get to space and time as my grounding assumptions, then I’ve reached the bottom. If we go beyond that, we’re back into theoretical physics.” Funny how we keep ending up there.The spouse-psychologists Arthur and Elaine Aron came up with the36 questionstwo people could ask one another that could make them fall in love – anyone, even strangers. Some questions are closed but searching (“Before making a telephone call, do you ever rehearse what you’re going to say? Why?”), while others are open (“What do you most value in a friendship?”). That was back in 1997, and three decades of speed dating have cast some doubt on the inevitability of love as the outcome of the process (which, to be fair, the Arons never claimed), but the idea has endured that questioning itself creates intimacy, symmetrical questioning is more intimate still, and open-ended questions flip you into a more vulnerable, receptive frame.The philosopher Peter Worley devised the question X manoeuvre, a closed question followed by an open one. “The first is the easier to answer,” Watson explains, “and once you’ve committed yourself to that, you’re happier and more comfortable exploring the area around it.”It sounds so simple as to be self-evident, but try it for yourself, and try the counterfactual. If someone bowled up with the question: “Do you enjoy what you do?” there’s something simultaneously condescending about it (“Little man, have you found satisfaction in your pursuits?”) and faux naive (“What is this thing called adulthood? Is it enjoyable?”). Try the X technique – “What do you do? Do you enjoy it?” – and not only does the second question follow more naturally from the first, but it gives you the impression that your first answer was interesting enough to have spurred the second.View image in fullscreen‘Only someone else can ask a question that you weren’t expecting, push you into a different space and make you feel cared for,’ says Watson.Photograph: Katherine Rose/The GuardianQuestion Y is the “divergent” sequence, starting with something easy, closed (“Did you vote in the referendum?”), then following up with something more open, likely to provoke difference but in a precinct you have already established as friendly – “Do you think referendums are a good idea?” Question Z is a line of inquiry that will change direction or the tightness of its focus over its course (think of the shape of a Z). I’m not wild about Watson’s example (“Do you like chocolate?”; “Given that coffee also comes from a bean, doesn’t it follow that you also like coffee?”), but you can see the potential: for unpredictability, as well as a certain inviting quality – part of what puts people off being questioned is the thought that they will be wrong or humiliated. A set of questions that slaloms all over the place is unlikely to have right answers.Unavoidably, questioning feels as if it drives towards politics of a certain kind. If, as Watson writes, cognitive closure is heightened by stress and drives in-group identification and, with it, suspicion of others, then breaking out of it with a questioning disposition would send you in the other direction, towards (broadly) philosophies of unity and hope. “I really take seriously the project of trying to write for a very broad audience,” Watson says, “so I want to be in a politically neutral space, which is not where I am myself, personally.”Right, I say. You literally have blue hair. Kemi Badenoch would probably write a speech about you. Unavoidably, she says, “a questioning mindset will bring us a lot closer together, wherever we are, because essentially you’re just opening up space to explore the possibility that you’re wrong about something. That you might not know what you thought you knew.”‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyRead moreIt’s a mistake, though, to think curiosity and certainty are utterly at odds, let alone that the first has a monopoly on harmony and the second drives division. “You build curiosity by coming to be an expert and pushing yourself to the edge of your knowledge. So certainty and curiosity can’t be diametrically opposed in that way, because you build curiosity on a foundation of certainties. But there is also a dynamic where you can close down curiosity by being certain.” Nor is she saying that there’s no value in knowledge: “Answers are good; we do need answers. That’s just not my job.”One of the first examples Watson writes about, almost the definitive question whose purpose doesn’t lie in an answer, is from a therapist: “What is the one thing now that you want to be able to do in the future?” It has elements of a few of those 36 questions to make you fall in love – inviting what might be a painful reckoning with reality, softened by the branching possibilities of the future, and the knowledge of your own agency (the more parlour-game version of this is, “What would you do if you had 12 months to live? Why aren’t you doing it now?”).“You find a new understanding as an exclusive result of that question,” Watson says, “but not because you’re secretly answering it in your head. That’s a big part of the reason why therapy is such an effective form of healing, because you could ask yourself a bunch of questions and try to solve your own issues, but only someone else can ask a question that you weren’t expecting, push you into a different space and make you feel cared for.”If interpersonal instances land the most convincingly or recognisably, the credit Watson pays to the question reaches back into decisions we could only guess at, and out into realms we can’t know. “I started to think about what encouraged human migration out of Africa,” she says. “Could it have been that questioning: ‘What’s around the corner? What’s over the horizon?’ The combination of curiosity and exploration, but also the capacity to form those into questions, is integral to moving out and moving forward.” It sounds likely, but we cannot know it for certain. “If you’re just interested in the answers, you are missing out on a form of power,” she says, which is as certain as you’ll find Watson about anything.Q: The Hidden Power of Questions in a World That Wants Answers by Lani Watson is published on 27 August (Bodley Head, £22).
