title: Can’t beat them? Eat them! Ten of the tastiest garden weeds  | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Edible weeds grow in abundance in our gardens, streets and parks. With a little know-how, you can harvest delicious, nutritious, free greens
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Edible weeds grow in abundance in our gardens, streets and parks. With a little know-how, you can harvest delicious, nutritious, free greens
Content: Spring salad with wild chickweed, nut lettuce and pomegranate.Photograph: Madeleine_Steinbach/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpring salad with wild chickweed, nut lettuce and pomegranate.Photograph: Madeleine_Steinbach/Getty ImagesGardening adviceCan’t beat them? Eat them! Ten of the tastiest garden weedsEdible weeds grow in abundance in our gardens, streets and parks. With a little know-how, you can harvest delicious, nutritious, free greensJack WallingtonFri 21 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDid you know that free food grows in our gardens, streets and parks without being planted by us? Not only does this food hide in plain sight, we’re encouraged to remove it from our gardens and throw it away. I’m talking about edible weeds, otherwise known as wildflowers. You may not be able to eat weeds into submission, but using them in the kitchen is a good excuse to welcome them into the garden.We walk past edible weeds without a second thought, yet they’re nutritious and available for much of the year. They return of their own accord every year, either perennially or by seed, making it easy to familiarise yourself with them and learn how to cook.A number of plants on this list are leafy greens that can be eaten in salad or cooked like spinach. This may feel repetitive (not another spinach substitute!) but is useful when gathering food in or around your garden because you can combine them. This helps if there is a limited quantity of one type, and increases the variety of flavour and nutrients in your diet.As with any foraging, only pick and eat plants if you are 100% sure of their identity. Avoid those that have been sprayed with pesticides (don’t pick from busy streets – delve deeper into verges, woodland and from gardens you trust) or close to busy roads, where they can absorb pollution.Plantain (Plantago lanceolata and P. major)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Avalon Studio/Getty ImagesThese common grassland perennials can be found in lawns, mini-meadows and verges – all over in fact.P. lanceolata, with long narrow leaves, has edible flowerheads best picked while still in bud that taste remarkably like mushrooms. Add them raw to salads or cook in stir-fries for the mushroom flavour.P. majorhas wide leaves and it’s the young tender leaves that are eaten as a salad or cooked.Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: R Biedermann/Getty ImagesA biennial, garlic mustard, or Jack-by-the-hedge, grows a rosette of kidney-shaped leaves with serrated edges in the first year. In the second, it fires up a vertical stem with heart-shaped leaves and four-petalled white flowers. All of the plant is edible and young leaves make an excellent salad leaf that really does taste of garlic and mustard. Older leaves are best cooked, as they can be tougher.Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Avalon Studio/Getty ImagesDandelion leaves fried lightly make an excellent and nutritious side dish. If you find them too bitter, try boiling them for a few minutes beforehand. As is the case with so many forage plants, it helps if you pick the youngest leaves. Flowerheads can be eaten – I enjoy snipping them on to a salad as a colourful garnish. They can also be fried in a light batter for a sweet starter, but snip off most of the bitter green flower base first.Ground elder (Aegopodium podagraria)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Henrik L/Getty Images/iStockphotoOne of the more vigorous perennial weeds, ground elder is thought to have been introduced to the UK by the Romans for its nutritional value. The leaves and shoots are edible and I particularly like the mild celery flavour of young leaves as a salad base. Older leaves can be boiled or fried like spinach. It’s not a plant I would intentionally add to a garden as it spreads vigorously and is notoriously hard to eradicate, but many gardens have a patch, or you may find one nearby. A variety of wildflowers in the same family look similar and some are poisonous, including the deadly hemlock, so correct identification is essential (their flowers are almost identical, so check the leaves carefully). Ground elder has pure green stems and grows in a short, spreading carpet.Fat hen (Chenopodium album)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Emilio 100/Getty ImagesAnother great leafy green that can be used in salads when the leaves are young and succulent or cooked as a side dish or addition to main courses. Fat hen, or lamb’s quarters, is an annual plant that will return each year by self-sowing. As with most plants on this list, once established your garden will have some for ever more. Its leaves are a dusty olive green and triangular in shape with toothed edges.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCleavers (Galium aparine)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Abadonian/Getty ImagesSticky weed is an easily identified annual, best picked early in the season when tender, before it turns stringy and forms bristly fruits that stick to clothes. Boil the young stems and leaves for 5-10 minutes as you would spinach. This softens the Velcro-like bristles for a pleasant dish that tastes a little like peas. You can also add a small handful of raw leaves to a jug of water kept in the fridge for a few hours or overnight. The water will have a light cucumber flavour – refreshing on a hot, sunny day.Sorrel (Rumex acetosa)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Diana Taliun/Getty ImagesA common grassland species, sorrel is a perennial wildflower with delicate inconspicuous flowers on vertical spikes that turn red as they produce seeds while glowing in sunlight. Its small oval-to-arrowhead-shaped leaves have a fresh lemony tang from the presence of oxalic acid, which can cause sore throats if eaten raw. Offset this by chopping with other salad leaves to dilute them or by cooking for a short time as you would spinach. Sorrel makes a lovely fresh pesto and, surprisingly, a delicious sorrel sorbet. Due to the oxalic acid content sorrel should only be eaten in moderation.Stinging nettle (Urtica dioica)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mik 122/Getty ImagesStinging nettles are tricky in a garden because they spread vigorously and cause painful stings, especially on summer-bare ankles. Yet they are an incredible food source for many insect larvae and useful in the kitchen too. Wearing thick protective gloves, pick the fresh young shoots and leaves in spring. Steam, fry or boil for a few minutes to wilt and deactivate the stings for a highly nutritious side. Nettles are famously good as a soup base with some extra flavours from stocks and herbs.Bramble(Rubus fruticosus)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Voren1/Getty ImagesBrambles are thorny, rambling perennials that crop up in hedgerows and woodland, spreading by seed and stem tips that root when they touch the ground. These tough, almost indestructible plants produce delicious blackberries from late-summer into autumn. Blackberries are easy to recognise and at optimal ripeness are exceptionally sweet, perfect for dessert. To contain their spread, either grow and clip as part of a mixed edible hedge (with the likes of hazelnut, guelder rose and elderflower), or remove old stems at the base when they finish fruiting, retaining a few new stems to fruit next year.Chickweed (Stellaria media)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Henrik L/Getty ImagesA tiny weed of sunny spots, chickweed is an annual that returns by dropping seeds. Treat it like a cut-and-come-again salad crop, snipping clumps off. It makes an excellent raw salad base that is rich in vitamin C. You can use it in sandwiches as you would cress, make a pesto or add it to cooked dishes as a spinach substitute. Chickweed has oval leaves, flowers with five split petals, is sprawling and has a line of hair down its stem that switches sides between leaf nodes.Grower Gatherer: Edible perennials to grow and gather in your garden by Jack Wallington is published by Bloomsbury on 3 September (£20). title: Cocktail of the week: Cafe Cùil’s Buckfast bloody Maìri – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: The favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punch
Content: Cafe Cùil's Buckfast bloody Maìri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenCafe Cùil's Buckfast bloody Maìri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Cafe Cùil’s Buckfast bloody Maìri – recipeThe favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punchClare CoghillFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is our take on the ultimate brunch cocktail, though of course we had to give it a Gaelic stamp of some kind, so have added a shot of Buckfast and renamed it Maìri. If you’re not familiar,Buckfastis a sweet tonic wine, apparently known for its “healing” properties, made in Devon by Benedictine monks, but that has been adopted by the Scots as our own.Buckfast bloody MaìriServes11 tsp capers, drained and very finely chopped1pickled gherkin, drained and very finely chopped1 tsp celery salt, or sea salt1 tbsp sriracha1 tbsp soy sauce1 tsp wholegrain mustard75ml tomato juice1 tsp sea salt1 tsp paprika50mlgin– we useRaasay25ml Buckfast tonic wineTo garnish1 lemon slice2 green olives1 slice pickleFirst, make the spicy tomato mix. Put the capers, gherkins, celery salt, sriracha, soy sauce and mustard in a small bowl, stir thoroughly, then add the tomato juice.Mix the sea salt and paprika on a small plate. Wet the rim of a tall glass, then roll it around in the salt and paprika mix, to coat.Fill the glass with ice, pour in the gin and Buckfast, then top with the tomato mix. Stir well with a long spoon, top with the lemon slice, olives and pickle, and serve.Clare Coghill, chef-owner,Café Cùil, Isle of SkyeExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodBritish food and drinkTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Blondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetness
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Blondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetness
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotIce-cream and sorbetBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwichesBlondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetnessBenjamina EbuehiFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIce-cream sandwiches have really grown on me. I used to find them a bit tricky to eat; far too many of them had outer shells so hard they would crack a tooth, while the rest would turn to mush after a few minutes out of the freezer. Finding the balance between something that has enough structural integrity to hold a good wedge of ice-cream but still soft enough to bite once frozen isn’t all that easy, but blondies make a very good option.Rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwichesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appI love infusing blondies with fresh herbs to cut through some of the sweetness and add more depth. These would be great with tarragon or thyme, but today I’ve gone with rosemary for a piney, aromatic twist.Prep5 minCook1 hrChill/freeze12 hr+Makes8150g salted butter,plus extra for greasing2 fresh rosemary sprigs180g light brown sugar1 large egg1½ tbspwhole milk130g plain flour¼ tsp salt¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda1 litre vanilla ice-creamFor the cherries150gcherries30g caster sugarSqueeze of lemon juiceHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line a 23cm x 33cm baking tin.Put the butter and rosemary in a small pan and heat gently to melt. Continue cooking until the butter gets foamy and fragrant, and the milk solids turn brown. Pour everything into a bowl, remove and discard the rosemary, and cool to room temperature.Put the sugar in a large bowl and stir in the melted butter. Whisk in the egg until smooth, followed by the milk. Sift in the flour, salt and bicarb, and stir until smooth.Pour the batter into the prepared tin, spreading out evenly; it will be quite thin. Bake for 16-22 minutes, until the blondie looks set with crisp edges but is still a little soft in the middle. Let it cool completely in the tin, then chill in the fridge to firm up – at least six hours, but ideally overnight.Stone and slice the cherries in half, then add to a pan with the sugar and lemon juice and bring to the boil. Cook for a few minutes until the cherries are softened and syrupy; set aside to cool completely.Scoop the ice-cream into a large bowl, let it soften a little, then loosely fold in the cherries – try not to overmix. Cut the blondie in half widthways and scoop the ice-cream on to one half, taking it all the way to the edges. Carefully place the second blondie half on top, then wrap in clingfilm and freeze overnight, until firm.Unwrap and trim the edges to get neat sides, then slice into bars. Serve straight away or wrap individually in baking paper and pop back in the freezer.Explore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe sweet spotFoodDessertHerbs and spicesBiscuitsBakingrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Such adept cover stars’: why dogs are taking over fashion in the ‘AI face’ era | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Cute, egoless canines offer a break from a world that feels dominated by ‘nepo babies’ and ‘Maga lady aesthetic’
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Cute, egoless canines offer a break from a world that feels dominated by ‘nepo babies’ and ‘Maga lady aesthetic’
Content: The celebrity beagle Sansa Martínez Berlingeri is becoming almost as famous as her owner, Bad Bunny.Photograph: Paul Hempstead/DogueView image in fullscreenThe celebrity beagle Sansa Martínez Berlingeri is becoming almost as famous as her owner, Bad Bunny.Photograph: Paul Hempstead/DogueFashion‘Such adept cover stars’: why dogs are taking over fashion in the ‘AI face’ eraCute, egoless canines offer a break from a world that feels dominated by ‘nepo babies’ and ‘Maga lady aesthetic’Ellie Violet BramleyFri 21 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat doNicole Kidman, a pair of “nepo babies” and a beagle called Sansa Martínez Berlingeri have in common? They all appear on the covers of the all-important September issues of Vogue and Dogue. But the winner of the unofficial battle of the covers? The one with the keenest sense of smell and a penchant for playing with socks.The September covers of BritishVogueand Vogue US have come under intense scrutiny after their recent release, while their canine counterpoint, Dogue, has been almost unanimously celebrated.Dogue this year features Bad Bunny’s beagle, Lena Dunham’s Mexican hairless Ingrid and her Chinese crested Cornichon, and Millie Bobby Brown’s miniature poodle. The Bad Bunny cover, shot by Eric Rojas in the nostalgia-tinged style of Lady and the Tramp, features four-year-old Sansa. She stares winsomely at the camera, one paw held tenderly by her owner, her tongue wonky and a bowl of spaghetti in front of her.View image in fullscreenMillie Bobby Brown and her poodle Winnie will grace the cover of next month’s Dogue.Photograph: Paul Hempstead/DogueThis contrasts with the reception for British Vogue’s Kidman cover, shot by Venetia Scott, in which the appearance of the Australian-American actor led to discussions online over what some argued was excessive airbrushing. Others questioned whether it was an AI version of the Practical Magic star.Marian Kwei, a celebrity stylist and Vogue contributor, says she “knew immediately that this was going to stir mixed reactions”. Many held it up as a win for the representation of older women in an industry and a world that is often unkind to older women: Kidman is 59. Others argued it wasn’t cause for celebration, given it presented her so agelessly.View image in fullscreenNicole Kidman, seen here at a film premiere in New York last month, appears on the latest cover of British Vogue.Photograph: Kristina Bumphrey/Paramount+/ShutterstockKwei ties the cover to the wider current phenomenon “where everyone is kind of looking like each other”. In 2019, the New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino wrote aboutwhat she saw as the emergence of “a single, cyborgian face”, otherwise known as “Instagram face”, and seven years later it’s only become more extreme. Smooth, poreless, youthful faces are now becoming so mainstream that in some quarterswrinkles are being rewritten as the new status symbols.The September issue of Vogue US – the first from itsnew editor, Chloe Malle– features the actors Kaia Gerber (24) and Homer Gere (26), stars of the new Ryan Murphy series The Shards. Photographed by Steven Meisel, a huge name in fashion, and styled by Spencer Singer, the shots have been critiqued as being bland, withJacob Gallagher in the New York Times sayingthat the cover “has about as much electricity as a JC Penney back-to-school catalog”.The photographerMisan Harriman posted on Instagramhis 2020 Black Lives Matter-inspired cover, which also featured a duo, the model Adwoa Aboah and footballer Marcus Rashford, and which made him the first Black male photographer to shoot a cover for British Vogue in its 104-year history, alongside this current one. He wrote underneath it: “An interesting observation about socio-cultural change could be made here.”View image in fullscreenHomer Gere and Kaia Gerber star in FX’s The Shards.Photograph: Tommaso Boddi/Variety/Getty ImagesKwei says: “I think the reason why that has sparked criticism is … those engaging with these covers are looking for deeper context … We are tired of thenepo babies.” The cover, she says, “feels a little soulless”.The choice of cover star has also been criticised. Gerber, a model and an actor, is the daughter of the 90s supermodel Cindy Crawford, and Gere is the son ofRichard Gere. The fact of their lineage – and their parents previously being married – gives them star power and intrigue, but they are stars yet to fully prove their chops. According to the fashion journalist Lauren Sherman: “It comes down to this: covers matter more than ever because they get passed around online, but it’s also harder than ever to get a celebrity popular enough across generations and subcultures to make an impact.”The fact of who Gerber and Gere are brought the cover into comparison with the1992 one, shot by Herb Ritts, featuring their then-married parents. Where Crawford and Gere were on a beach – Wintour was famous, from her first cover onwards, for taking models out of the bland studios that had dominated Vogue covers until then and on to the streets – their progeny are in a grey studio. For Kwei, the 1992 cover had “some context – it helps it build a story”, while “with the Kaia cover there isn’t enough context, there isn’t enough of storytelling”.The September issues of fashion magazines are the most significant of the year – and what’s on the cover is supposed to say something. “People have come to expect something very special,” says Kwei. Perhaps improbably, this has come in the shape of Sansa the beagle. “I think it was brilliant. It’s very internet-first,” Kwei says, adding that it would be easy to “turn it into a meme”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the world of AI-face, the dogs become almost more real, certainly more characterful. Oli Port is the founder and editor of the canine fashion publication Dogue magazine. Launched in 2019, it was, says Port, “the world’s first dog fashion magazine”. She is in a legal dispute withCondé Nast, who launched their take on Dogue in 2024. Port thinks dogs make perfect cover stars because “they are just so authentic”and “it’s fun to see dogs as the stars instead of humans because humans have so much ego … Dogs don’t really care, they just want a good snack.”View image in fullscreenLena Dunham’s dogs also feature on a Dogue cover.Photograph: Paul Hempstead/DogueJen Golbeck, an expert in social media and co-author of The Purest Bond: Understanding the Human-Canine Connection, locates the cover “in this space of so much AI-generated content [and] images of people that are AI-generated or AI-modified in a way that a lot of us find horrifying; like we no longer know what’s real.” As she points out: “Now we’re seeing models that don’t actually exist. They’re entirely AI.” This dog, on the other hand, is definitely not.World’s Ugliest Dog contest 2026 – in picturesRead moreShe continues: “We’re [also] seeing this veer back towards early 2000s skinny culture and there’s a lot of politics with that aesthetic – it aligns with the Trump, Maga lady aesthetic and these patriarchal views on what women are supposed to look like.”Dogs, by contrast, don’t have those kinds of politics attached to them.“Dogs are always one of those things that exist outside all of those factors that are making us stressed about life and our bodies and fashion and how we’re supposed to look; there’s something beautiful and comforting in that, that everybody wants some of right now.”So what makes a good dog a good cover girl or boy? According to Amina, whose dog Sir Spudwon this year’s second annual civilian Dogue cover contest: “Each one has a special, lovable personality, which is exactly what makes them man’s best friend and such adept cover stars.”Sir Spud has his own take over email: “We dogs exude love,l’élégance, and class from our paws to our snouts. We are natural stars and belong on the front page; seriously, have you seen me?”Explore more on these topicsFashionVogueCondé NastMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesDogsPetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything’ – the backlash to the three figure trainer | Fashion | The Guardian
description: ​W​e had years of trainerflation​ but now value ​and versatility are back in fashion
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ​W​e had years of trainerflation​ but now value ​and versatility are back in fashion
Content: It was acceptable in the 90s … Kylie Minogue loved her pricey 110s.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIt was acceptable in the 90s … Kylie Minogue loved her pricey 110s.Photograph: ShutterstockFashion Statement newsletterFashion‘If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything’ – the backlash to the three figure trainerFrom Nike’s infamous 110s to £250 and back again, sneakerheads are rediscovering why cheaper shoes can be worth just as much hype as much more expensive onesDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAdam CheungFri 21 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 03.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Nike’s Air Max 95 trainers first landed in Britain back in the mid-1990s, they looked unlike anything else. Created by footwear designer Sergio Lozano, the shoe had wavy layers running down its sides, neon yellow accents, and visible ‘Air’ bubbles underfoot. But in the UK, one detail quickly became as famous as the shoe itself: its £110 price tag.The Air Max 95 immediately picked up the nickname “110” because spending £110 on trainers seemed outrageous at the time. Owning a pair quickly became a status symbolamong young men across Britain, while in celebrity circles they were worn by everyone from Jay-Z to Kylie Minogue.Over 30 years later, £110 looks relatively modest next to the upper end of the market catering to trainer enthusiasts. In a pretty neat example of trainerflation, flagship running shoes from Nike, New Balance, and Adidas easily retail for between £200 and £250.For Dom Jacob, founder of sneaker discovery platformSneak in Peace, the story begins during the 2020 pandemic. “During Covid, the low end of the sneaker market went up massively in price,” he says. “Nike and Adidas and the rest worked out they were missing the profit on their own product, because resale websites like StockX and GOAT were taking it.”The resale boom changed what trainers meant. Limited releases weren’t simply shoes any more. They became assets to flip, and brands watched a growing slice of the money end up in somebody else’s pocket. In 2020, for example, the average Nike SB Dunk Low was reselling for more than £400, several times what many pairs originally cost at retail.“There was a lot of greed during that period,” Jacob says. “[Trainer brands] cut the quality down while they raised the prices. The price of a sneaker became disconnected from what it was actually worth to the person buying it.”View image in fullscreenCheap at half the price … New Balance’s £70 740 lifestyle trainers.Photograph: New BalanceNow, though, there are signs trainer enthusiasts are quietly pushing back. They’re buying fewer pairs, keeping old ones for longer, and getting excited about trainers that don’t cost £250 in the first place.Nike’s V5 RNR costs £80. The New Balance 740 can be picked up for £70, the Asics Gel-1130 retails for about £90, and Adidas has plenty of trainers below the £90 mark. These aren’t being hidden away as entry-level options either. They’re front and centre in campaigns and on shop floors. And sneakerheads are actually buying into them. Jacob points to the success of Nike’s slide £79.99 Mind 001, which he saysremained sold out for seven months, as proof that lower-priced trainers can generate just as much excitement as considerably more expensive releases.Mikey Clarke, an app developer, has been collecting trainers for over a decade and remembers the days of the Nike “110”. “That felt expensive at the time, but it was attainable if you saved up,” he says. “Now I think harder before buying anything because prices have gone up so much. If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything rather than just being a nice addition to the collection.”View image in fullscreenMost wanted … Phoebe Philo in her Stan Smith trainers.Photograph: Michel Dufour/WireImageFashion falling for relatively affordable trainers isn’t new. In 2010, designer Phoebe Philo helped turn the Adidas Stan Smith – then a simple £70-ish tennis shoe – into one of fashion’s most wanted trainers when she wore them to take her catwalk bow. Soon, seemingly everyone had a pair. More recently, the £95 Samba went from a humble indoor football shoe to one of the biggest trainers in fashionbefore the former PM Rishi Sunak killed them.What’s different now is the reason we’re reaching for cheaper shoes. In 2026, value itself is becoming part of the appeal. Household budgets have tightened, and the resale bubble has burst. Suddenly, shoppers are asking a question sneaker brands haven’t really had to answer for years: is thisactuallyworth the money?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCrucially, it isn’t people who have always bought cheaper trainers driving the shift, it’s enthusiasts who previously thought nothing of spending £250 on a pair. For them, getting excited about an £80 Nike represents a pretty significant change.Jacob believes trainers are returning to what they were always meant to be. “We have come back to the daily runner,” he says. “You can do your morning jog in it if you really need to, and go straight to the supermarket afterwards.” That crossover matters: one pair that can handle a light run and everything else you do that day suddenly starts looking like better value.There are thriftier ways to deal with trainerflation too. Vinnie Tao, founder of Manchester-based shoe care boutique Sneaker Pharm, has noticed more customers choosing to repair worn-out pairs rather than replace them. “I think that’s being driven by a combination of economics and sustainability,” he says.The £200 trainer isn’t going anywhere. But after years of convincing trainer enthusiasts to spend more, sportswear brands are remembering something they knew all along: affordable doesn’t necessarily have to mean undesirable.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterNikeKylie MinoguenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tuscany may be beautiful, but do they sell sticks of rock?’: readers’ favourite UK holidays | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: Your best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secret
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: Your best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secret
Content: The beach at Hengistbury Head in Dorset.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe beach at Hengistbury Head in Dorset.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty Images/iStockphotoReaders' travel tipsUnited Kingdom holidays‘Tuscany may be beautiful, but do they sell sticks of rock?’: readers’ favourite UK holidaysYour best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secretTell us about your favouriteunder-the-radar European city– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 21 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDorset’s take on the MediterraneanMudeford feels like one of England’s best-kept secrets, the sort of place visitors from abroad might never imagine exists here. Golden sand and sparkling water give it an almost Mediterranean feel, while Hengistbury Head adds beautiful coastal walks and wide-open views. Our perfect day is simple: arrive early, wander along the headland, let the children play on the beach, then stop at one of the relaxed cafes for lunch or an ice-cream. My tip is to take thelittle ferryacross the harbour – it turns an already lovely day out into a proper seaside adventure.Priti SingerLancashire’s Forest of BowlandView image in fullscreenThe Forest of Bowland has miles of moorland and valleys to explore.Photograph: Jon Sparks/AlamyThe Forest of Bowland covers a staggering 312 square miles of moorland, forests and valleys, dotted with the occasional village. It may be one of the best places for peace and quiet in England, and is also aDark Skiesarea. It’s perfect for walkers and cyclists. I visitedGisburn forest(where I only met two other people during a five-hour hike); Barley village, which attracts lots of walkers who climb Pendle Hill; and, for spectacular scenery, a trip through the Trough of Bowland is a must. For town life, I’d recommend Skipton, a 35-minute drive away, which has it all with a castle, canal and plentiful shops and restaurants. It’s also the southern gateway to the Yorkshire Dales.CatProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Crabbing and clean beaches in SuffolkView image in fullscreenWalberswick’s rowing-boat ferry.Photograph: Terry Mathews/AlamyWalberswick is popular with walkers and birders, and young families who come here to relax and go swimming on the clean beach or crabbing in the creek. A brilliant way to arrive at the town is on therowing-boat ferry(March to November) across the River Blyth from Southwold. It’s been in the same family for five generations. We had great seafood at heritage pubs like theAnchorand theBell. Across the water, there’s a lot of wonderful fish shops and the famousHarbour Inn.David Innes-WilkinIn search of the Lundy Bunny, DevonView image in fullscreenLundy offers a treasure trail of 27 letterboxes suitable for all ages.Photograph: Philip Bishop/AlamyLundy, off the north Devon coast, offers a hidden adventure for all ages by following the treasure trail of27 Lundy letterboxesspread over the island. Some are wooden boxes, some metal, but they are all hidden. There’s a set of clues to follow, and stamps collected including the elusive Lundy Bunny. My two preteen boys and I loved our exploration of this remote granite island, binoculars and compass in hand, identifying letterboxes, birds and wildlife during our magical trip there.Carol GodsmarkA spectacular rail trip in County AntrimView image in fullscreenWest Strand, Portrush.Photograph: Wirestock/Getty ImagesNo trip I’ve made as an adult has matched the buzz of my annual childhood day trip from Derry to Portrush. The Troubles were at their peak but Portrush was still largely unscathed and had a totally different atmosphere to Derry. The journey was completed by train from Coleraine, and what a train journey it is. The train hogs the coast the whole way and we would be beside ourselves when the big dipper of Barry’s Amusements came into view. We would spend the morning on the beach, fish and chips for lunch and a few hours in Barry’s before heading home. Tuscany may be beautiful but do they sell sticks of rock?Eve KearneyAn arty town in ShropshireView image in fullscreenThe House on Crutches museum in Bishop’s Castle.Photograph: Mike Hayward/AlamyFoxholes campsitesits on a hill above the arty west Shropshire town of Bishop’s Castle. The views across the Shropshire hills are splendid, and a 10-minute walk through fields leads you past a stone Buddha into the town stretched along a medieval high street. Visit theHouse on Crutches museumto get a feel for Shropshire rural life history, and be sure to check out its two brilliant pubs: theThree Tunsis probably Britain’s oldest licensed brewery, having started in 1642, while theSix Bellsprovides an unpretentious family-friendly welcome. For us, though, the highlight was theChai Shopand its charismatic owner Tahira. She serves delicious Indian snacks like bhajis and dal as well as traditional Indian sweets.Matt Luntskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCamping in south WalesView image in fullscreenView of Pen y Fan.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyWe’re by no means an experienced camping family, but we pitched up onRhydywernen Farmnear Brecon after the last August bank holiday and were able to feed goats that were as happy and hoppy as it gets. Before falling asleep to the whisper of a nearby stream and mini-waterfalls, we spent time stargazing as there was no light pollution – it felt we were somehow closer to the stars. A cool stream helped soothe us after a day of hiking on Pen y Fan, the tallest peak in Britain south of Cadair Idris in Eryri (Snowdonia). We had only just bought a tent that summer and then we fell in love with Wales, so we keep coming back for more.IzabelaNorthumberland’s atmospheric border townView image in fullscreenThe trio of bridges in Berwick-upon-Tweed.Photograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyBerwick-upon-Tweedis one of those places that feels more dramatic than its size suggests. I have visited twice, and I loved simply walking around, camera in hand. Its slightly strange sense of being a border town seems to permeate everything. Stand beside the River Tweed and you can see three bridges together: the old Berwick Bridge, the elegant Royal Tweed Bridge and the great Victorian railway viaduct of the Royal Border Bridge. Add theElizabethan walls, the North Sea and castle ruins, and Berwick feels perpetually poised between countries, centuries and land and sea. It makes a wonderfully atmospheric short break.Susanna CallaghanThe natural wonders of the WirralView image in fullscreenThe Roman Boathouse at Birkenhead Park.Photograph: Alan Novelli/AlamyThe Wirral and its country park, south-west of Liverpool, is a brilliant under-the-radar place for a UK summer holiday, full of walks and beaches.Birkenhead Parkis 57 hectares (140 acres) of meadows, fields, gardens, woodland, lakes and structures – we had picnics and family treasure hunts last summer. Opened in 1847, it inspired the 19th-century US landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted in his design of New York’s Central Park, so close your eyes and imagine you are in the Big Apple! Since 1995, it has been listed as a Grade I landscape by English Heritage. With its paths, fossil-hunting areas, bike trails and dramatic sunsets,Wirral country parkhelped us entertain our teenagers. Thurstaston beach and Port Sunlight village are great options too.NicolettaWinning tip: Caribbean vibes on the Isle of Mull, Inner HebridesView image in fullscreenDavid Balfour’s Bay.Photograph: Lynne Sutherland/AlamyDavid Balfour’s Bayis a remote and breathtaking sandy bay with clear turquoise waters and pristine white sands in a stunning setting – the tidal island of Erraid, just off south-west Mull. The play of bright sunshine on crystal clear water and waves is dazzling – it’s a literally brilliant place to visit. Throw in a few palm trees and, on a clear day, you could imagine you were in Barbados – and the sea temperature can reach a pleasant 18C in August and September. To reach the bay, walk from lovely Knockvologan beach at low tide. This scenic walk can be extended to explore the north side of Erraid, where there are magnificent views of the Sound of Iona. Just be careful of tides so you don’t get caught there – a swim back is invigorating – as I found out after an overlong afternoon snooze when some lapping waves woke me up.PeterView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysReaders' travel tipsFamily holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I fell 12 metres and smashed my pelvis into pieces | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It was clear it was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as the paramedics strapped me to a gurney
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It was clear it was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as the paramedics strapped me to a gurney
Content: ‘I didn’t have time to scream’: Emily Brough, climbing in Utah.Photograph: Josh Hawkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t have time to scream’: Emily Brough, climbing in Utah.Photograph: Josh Hawkins/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I fell 12 metres and smashed my pelvis into piecesIt was clear it was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as the paramedics strapped me to a gurneyEmily BroughFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrowing up in Utah, I was so active that my parents nicknamed me “The Blur”. My older siblings introduced me to rock climbing while I was still at primary school. By the time I was 15, I was hauling myself up cliff faces.One summer’s day in 2014, when I was 17, my friends and I went paddleboarding on a lake. My friend Trevor and I decided to climb one of the rocky boulders overlooking the water, and jump in.The rock was about 12 metres tall. I had climbed and jumped from higher. What we hadn’t counted on was a layer of moss that made the boulder slippery. Neither of us had our grippy climbing shoes with us. When I nearly fell, I thought about turning back, but I convinced myself that it was safer to keep going.From the top, we discovered the water didn’t come right up to the boulder. Instead, there was a swathe of black volcanic rock we would have to clear first. I watched as Trevor took a run-up and hurled himself over the edge. The splash told me he’d safely made it down and into the water.Normally I’d be excited, but the earlier slip had rattled me. Jumping still felt safer than climbing down, though. I backed up and started to run. As I reached the edge, I hesitated. It was the tiniest pause, but enough to slow my momentum. Instead of leaping outwards, I twisted sideways and started plummeting straight down.I didn’t have time to scream, but I registered that I was about to die. I closed my eyes, slamming so hard into the rock that a friend heard my bones break. During the fall, I’d curled my arm up to protect my head, landing on my left side.double quotation markI’d been warned I might have permanent paralysis in my legs, but I was determined to get my life backView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Josh Hawkins/The GuardianAdrenaline and shock blurred those first moments after impact. I was about to try to move when a man appeared. He was an emergency medical technician who had been fishing nearby and had seen me fall. Suspecting a broken pelvis and spinal injuries, he held my head and neck still.It took 30 minutes for the paramedics to reach me. It was clear my pelvis was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as they strapped me to a gurney.At the hospital, X-rays showed my spine was intact, but my pelvis was in pieces. I was flown by air ambulance to a better equipped hospital. Doctors there found my left arm and heel were broken too. Most dangerously, my shattered pelvic bones had cut into my organs. I was bleeding internally.I underwent 13 hours of surgery to rebuild my pelvis with pins and metal plates. I was in hospital for two weeks before going home for six months of bed rest.My family were amazing and gave me round-the-clock care. As an active person, it was a huge adjustment, but I just felt grateful to be alive. I also had a rota of friends who would play music and watch movies with me, which stopped me feeling sorry for myself. I’d been warned I might have permanent paralysis in my legs, but I was determined to get my life back. The fact that I was young and fit helped with my recovery. When the spinal cord swelling went down after four months, I was relieved to regain some movement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI climbed Mount Kilimanjaro on my handsRead moreAfter six months, I figured out how to pull myself out of bed and into a wheelchair. I returned to school for my senior year with some heavy-duty painkillers and a friend to push me between classes.Ten months after the fall, I was allowed to put pressure on my feet. I had been doing hospital physical therapy, but I wasn’t convinced it was right for me. Most people with hip and pelvic injuries are elderly, whereas I was an otherwise healthy teenager. I replaced it with yoga. It was gruelling – my muscles were weak and it was a year before I could walk on my own.I returned to the outdoors with gentle hikes, then cautiously returned to climbing – I didn’t want the accident to stop me doing something I loved. It took a couple of years to get my confidence back, but my fall made me a better climber and a stickler for safety.I’m 29 now and a yoga teacher. People ask if I wish the accident had never happened, but the honest answer is no. It led me to this fulfilling life.As told to Jacqui PatersonDo you have an experience to share? title: Country diary: Ten tonnes of solid muscle, basking sharks are booming here once again | Environment | The Guardian
description: Port Erin Bay, Isle of Man: A few years ago they disappeared from these shores, but with food stocks on the up, they’ve made a magnificent return
Author: Tim Earl
Headline: Port Erin Bay, Isle of Man: A few years ago they disappeared from these shores, but with food stocks on the up, they’ve made a magnificent return
Content: Basking shark feeding on plankton just below the surface of the water.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenBasking shark feeding on plankton just below the surface of the water.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: Ten tonnes of solid muscle, basking sharks are booming here once againPort Erin Bay, Isle of Man:A few years ago they disappeared from these shores, but with food stocks on the up, they’ve made a magnificent returnTim EarlFri 21 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot long ago, my encounters with basking sharks were pretty close up. When a scientist researching them off the Isle of Man needed help, with my experience of driving inflatable ribs, I was tasked with steering his small boat up to a 10-tonne shark, closely and carefully enough for him to jab a small tracking device into its dorsal fin.It was hair-raising work – they are solid muscle, capable of smashing our hull. Nevertheless, I guided the boat gently alongside, and the device was placed. Like many others before it, the shark swam off unconcerned.Now I observe them from further away: either I respond to alerts on social media or visit likely headlands – a good number of recorded sightings are from people on land.Basking sharks have an interesting recent history here. They migrate north through island waters from May to August and may even breed here, then are rarely seen in autumn. Their migration routesare astonishing, with tagged sharks recorded off Morocco to the south and Newfoundland to the west.But the research was stopped in 2022 as numbers dropped from 885 sightings in 2009 to just a single individual. Lack of food, warmer seas or more likely underwater electricity cables were blamed. It was suggested that electromagnetic fields emitted by the cables repulsed migrating sharks.View image in fullscreenA basking shark’s dorsal fin breaks the water’s surface.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThat theory has been turned on its head this summer, withmore than 100 sightingsso far. The south-west corner of the island is a hotspot. My second this year was from Bradda Head, where a particularly large shark was seen with two smaller ones at the entrance to Port Erin Bay. The larger shark was well across the bay by the time I arrived, but its huge rounded dorsal fin was glinting in bright sunlight – a magnificent sight.Experts in our fisheries department say that this year there has been a good bloom of microscopic crustaceans called copepods, the primary food of these sharks. Wildlife sightings in Britain do not get much bigger than basking sharks, and local spotters – including me – are thrilled.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on trade | JD Vance | The Guardian
description: Audio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian Press
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Audio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian Press
Content: Vance, pictured, reportedly says in the audio that Carney is a ‘very sweet guy’ and that he gets along with him well.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVance, pictured, reportedly says in the audio that Carney is a ‘very sweet guy’ and that he gets along with him well.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockJD VanceJD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on tradeAudio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian PressOlivia Bowdenin TorontoFri 21 Aug 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaked audio from a private event has reportedly captured the US vice-president, JD Vance, mocking Canada for apparently capitulating in a trade deal and taunting the prime minister,Mark Carney, for trying to “out-tough” Donald Trump.The recording, which was reportedly made at a fundraiser andshared with the Canadian Press, comes in the last stretch of a difficult negotiation in which the US president has threatened to impose 50% tariffs on Canada.According to the Canadian Press, Vance is heard in the audio telling a room of supporters in Southampton, New York, that Carney is a “very sweet guy” and that he gets along with him well. But he also says Carney “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”Vance says: “It’s hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory forCanadawhen fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues.”The audio is unlikely to help relations between the two delegations at a crucial time. Canadian officials have said a deal is close that is likely to include Canada again allowing US alcohol sales across the country in exchange for avoiding the worst of Trump’s tariffs.Trump first said he would apply the tariffs from 19 August, but on Tuesday he backed down andannounced a three-day pause.The White House said in July that the 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada that included bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight out of 10 provinces and all three territories – a response in early 2025 to Trump’s first threats of tariffs against Canada.US producers of wine, beer and spirits have said the boycott has significantly affected their sales. Canadian imports of US alcohol are down about 81% year on year, according to the White House.The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves.“I wouldn’t say [Carney] was begging us, but what is a step before begging?” Kinew said on Thursday.Kinew encouraged Canadians to continue theirboycott of US productsregardless.“If we put the booze back on the shelves, don’t buy it … Buy the Canadian stuff instead,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job of sticking together in the face of Donald Trump’s tariff threats and I think we should continue to do that.”Kinew said he respected Carney for taking on Trump and believed Canada should stand firm in the negotiations.“I think Donald Trump is weak. America is weaker around the world today than it was a year ago, and he’s about to get slaughtered in the midterms,” he said.“Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person, and I think that rule applies here, so I think we should fight.”Explore more on these topicsJD VanceCanadaTrump tariffsMark CarneyAmericasTariffsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Strangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’ | Mexico | The Guardian
description: With plentiful jobs and community support, one Mexico City neighbourhood has become a haven for those who have lived much of their lives in the US
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: With plentiful jobs and community support, one Mexico City neighbourhood has become a haven for those who have lived much of their lives in the US
Content: A street in the Tabacalera neighborhood of Mexico City.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA street in the Tabacalera neighborhood of Mexico City.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The GuardianMexicoStrangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’With plentiful jobs and community support, one Mexico City neighbourhood has become a haven for those who have lived much of their lives in the USOscar Lopezin Mexico CityFri 21 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith its wide avenues lined with tall palm trees, its quaint cafes and old-school cantinas, as well as the mix of English and Spanish spoken on the street, the Tabacalera neighborhood in downtown Mexico City has a certain US feel – so much so that it is has become knownas Little LA.The nickname is about more than appearances, however. In recent years, this corner of the metropolis has become a haven for many Mexicans deported from the US, particularly those who spent years or decades living across the border and for whomMexicofeels like a foreign country. In Little LA, they have found a more familiar place to belong.With theTrump administrationembarking on a massive anti-immigrant crackdown, deportations to Mexico are expected to surge. Since taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump has deported roughly 145,500 Mexican nationals.Christopher Gil Ortíz was one of them. He was on his way to work in Los Angeles in June this year when Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents stopped him, handcuffed him and threw him in detention.View image in fullscreenAnti-Trump graffiti in the Tabacalera neighborhood.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The GuardianAfter months of living in constant fear as an undocumented immigrant in Trump’s US, Ortíz said that when the detention finally happened he felt relieved. “At this point I was like, OK, that’s it, I’m going back,” he recalled. “It’s like they took a weight off my shoulders.”More than 30 years since he had left as a child, Ortíz was sent back to Mexico, leaving behind his wife and two young children. Dumped in the resort town of Tulum, he made his way to Cancún, only to have all his belongings stolen from his hotel room. Eventually, he ended up in Mexico City, where he had family.“I was nervous,” he said. “Even though I was born here, I have very vague memories of the city itself.”He was also facing the many challenges of being a deportee: getting his birth certificate, ID and finding a job. His sister sent him a TikTok post from an organization calledNew Comienzos(New Beginnings). Based in Little LA, it was set up to help returnees reintegrate. When he saw the post, Ortiz decided to check out Little LA for himself.View image in fullscreenChristopher Gil Ortíz, who was sent back to Mexico more than 30 years after he left as a child.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The Guardian“Seeing the palm trees, it kind of does make you feel like you’re in LA,” he said, adding that he was grateful to New Comienzos. “There’s a lot of people that are going through what I’m going through and I’m pretty sure there’s going to be more.”The New Comienzos founder and executive director, Israel Concha, said he was preparing for exactly that. “The atmosphere [in the US] right now is one of humanitarian crisis and panic. People no longer even want to take their children to school,” Concha said. “You’ll probably start seeing mass deportations in a few months.”Concha founded New Comienzos when he witnessed first-hand how little support the Mexican government was offering recent arrivals. In 2012, he was living in Texas with his pregnant wife and had started a successful private transport business. He had lived in the US for 30 years. “I wanted to try to achieve that American dream, and I think I succeeded,” he said.View image in fullscreenIn Little LA, many of those sent back from the US have found a more familiar place to belong.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The GuardianThen one day he was caught speeding on his way to pick up a client. While in detention, he fought his case for two years but was deported in 2014. On his first day in Mexico, he was kidnapped by a criminal gang working with local police.“That was my welcome to my native country,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ‘self-deportee’ hounded out of the US to Mexico: ‘There are days when I feel literally insane’Read moreAfter being severely beaten, Concha escaped to Mexico City, where he found a job at a bilingual call centre – one of several starting to pop up in the Tabacalera neighborhood, attracting young returnees who spoke fluent English. Less than a year later, he started New Comienzos to address the challenges faced by people like himself.“People didn’t just need a job; many of them needed emotional support because they had just lost everything following a deportation,” he said. The organisation offers legal support and free English certification and classes, as well as mentorship for recent arrivals. Little LA remains the organization’s center of operations.“A community reintegration lab,” said Concha, “that’s what we’ve created there in Little Los Angeles.”Sergio Aaron Pérez, 36, said the area felt like home. Wearing a Los Angeles Lakers jersey and baseball cap, his face and arms covered in tattoos, Pérez looked as though he had just stepped off the plane from the US. In fact, having lived in the US for more than 30 years, the former California resident was deported in 2011 for doing what he calls “bad things”.View image in fullscreenSergio Aaron Pérez in Little LA.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/The GuardianIn Little LA, he found work at call centers. “If you speak English there’s a lot of money,” said Pérez. “I love my city. There’s a lot of community.”Ortíz, for his part, had little interest in a call center job. He has applied for a job at a glass-making factory – work he used to do in the US. Next on his agenda: bringing his wife and children to Mexico.“My kids are OK with it,” he said. Referencing a local Mexican custom, he added: “My daughter told me that she was already practising drinking soda out of a plastic bag.”Explore more on these topicsMexicoICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Donald TrumpTrump administrationUS immigrationMigrationUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers in Hong Kong found guilty of ‘inciting subversion’ | Hong Kong | The Guardian
description: UK Foreign Office condemns use of national security law to convict activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: UK Foreign Office condemns use of national security law to convict activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung
Content: Chow Hang-tung in 2021. The trial began in January and took place over 24 days.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChow Hang-tung in 2021. The trial began in January and took place over 24 days.Photograph: Anthony Kwan/Getty ImagesHong KongTiananmen Square vigil organisers in Hong Kong found guilty of ‘inciting subversion’UK Foreign Office condemns use of national security law to convict activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tungDanny Vincent in Hong KongFri 21 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 22.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwoHong Kongactivists who organised annual vigils marking China’s deadly Tiananmen crackdown in 1989 have been found guilty of “incitement to subversion” in one of the most high-profile cases in Hong Kong since Beijing imposed its national security law in 2020.Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”, a press summary handed out to reporters said. The defendants each face a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail, with sentencing expected at a later date.Lee and Chow’strial began in Januaryand took place over 24 days. A third defendant, the 74-year-old former lawmaker Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January.Chow, who represented herself, told the court in May that the law itself was on trial.France and Germany said on Friday they “deeply regret” Chow’s conviction. “Peaceful advocacy for human rights does not constitute a crime,” the countries’ foreign ministries said of the activist, who was awarded the Franco-German prizefor human rights in 2023.Lee and Chow were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, which organised the city’s annual vigil in memory of those killed in the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989.In court, Lee and Chow waved to supporters from the dock, where they were surrounded by correctional officers. Lee appeared solemn as the judge handed down the verdict. He made a heart-shaped gesture with his hands and waved to supporters before being led out of the court.View image in fullscreenPolice officers stand near the media area outside court ahead of the verdict.Photograph: Leung Man Hei/AFP/Getty ImagesHong Kong and Macau were formerly the only places on Chinese soil that permitted public vigils to mourn those killed on 4 June 1989, whenChinasent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform in and around the capital’s Tiananmen Square.However, public commemoration has in effect been banned since Beijingimposed a national security lawon Hong Kong in 2020, after huge and sometimes violent pro-democracy protests the year before.The Alliance’s leaders were charged in 2021 andhave been imprisoned since. Ahead of the verdict, Chow wrote a message from prison, seen by the Guardian, addressed to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham: “They are trying to rewrite Hong Kong history … they certainly want to erase some memories, or memories of some chapters in our history.”The Cambridge-educated barrister added in the letter: “Britain has a non-delegable duty to adopt a more robust stance in the face of the growing threat from a totalitarian and aggressive China.”The case centred on the Alliance’s slogan demanding an “end to one-party rule”. The court found that the defendants “intended to cause others to lose confidence in the Chinese Communist party by stirring up hostility and causing division”.The defence argued that the Alliance was exercising its freedom of speech. The rights group Amnesty International has said the case against Lee and Chow “relies on vague, overly broad and arbitrary definitions of ‘subversion’”.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, wife of Lee Cheuk-yan, outside court on Friday.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersThe UK Foreign Office’s Indo-Pacific minister, Rosie Winterton, said: “This verdict is a further demonstration that even peaceful acts of remembrance in Hong Kong are now treated by the authorities as threats to national security. The extensive use of Beijing’s national security law to punish and restrict peaceful expression undermines the commitments China made to Hong Kong under the 1984 Sino-British joint declaration. We reiterate our call for the national security law to be repealed, and for rights and freedoms to be respected in the Hong Kong special administrative region.”Dozens of police officers gathered outside the courthouse and ushered reporters away as they stopped to film audience members queueing outside before the hearing began on Friday.Members of the public had queued for days to secure a seat in the Hong Kong court. “To me, this case illustrates the absolute power of Beijing in reshaping Hong Kong’s civil society through the national security law,” one supporter told the Guardian.Another supporter said: “This outcome highlights the central government’s total control regarding national security enforcement in the region.”Hong Kong was promised certain political freedoms not granted in the rest of the country when it was returned to China in 1997. Critics say the national security law has decimated civil society. Most of the city’s opposition leaders have been detained or have fled.Authorities say the law was needed to restore order after a year of protests rocked the international financial hub in 2019.Explore more on these topicsHong KongChinaFreedom of speechAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: Extreme rain deluges Japan and South Korea | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Downpours break records and cause transport chaos, evacuations and deaths, as people get trapped inside vehicles
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Downpours break records and cause transport chaos, evacuations and deaths, as people get trapped inside vehicles
Content: A car stranded in a flooded underpass in Kamagaya, Chiba prefecture, Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAView image in fullscreenA car stranded in a flooded underpass in Kamagaya, Chiba prefecture, Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAWeather trackerExtreme weatherAnalysisWeather tracker: Extreme rain deluges Japan and South KoreaMorgan Thomas for MetDeskDownpours break records and cause transport chaos, evacuations and deaths, as people get trapped inside vehiclesFri 21 Aug 2026 04.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareSouth Korea and Japan were hit byextreme rainlate last week and into this week. On 13 August in the city of Chiba near Tokyo there was a record-breaking 115mm of rainfall in just one hour, while the nearby city of Sakura broke its own record with 97mm in one hour. Local authorities issued a level 5 emergency warning for heavy rain, the highest alert level and the first time one has been issued since the system was implemented in May.More than 100,000 households were asked to evacuate, with more than 20,000 in the Chiba prefecture left without power, while thousands of people were stranded at Tokyo’s Narita airport. Thirteen people have been confirmed dead, at least three of whom were found trapped inside their vehicles. One person is still missing.Japan is no stranger to heavy rainfall, thanks to the conditions created when warm and moist air from the north Pacific meets cooler air. This latest event has been especially severe, however, with the Japan Meteorological Agency describing it as an “unprecedented level” of heavy rain. There was also record-breaking rain in nearbySouth Korea, where in the city of Geoje 124.5mm fell within one hour early on 17 August. In total more than 400mm fell through the night.View image in fullscreenA police officer standing in a flooded road in Geoje, South Korea.Photograph: Yonhap News Agency/ReutersMeanwhile, across the north Pacific,Hurricane Lalaachieved category 1 hurricane status on 15 August, travelling westwards towards Hawaii with wind speeds of about 80mph (130km/h). Lala passed just to the south of the island chain the following day, with the eyewall grazing the southern part of the main island, causing it to weaken back down to a tropical storm. Kona international airport on the island recorded its lowest ever pressure as Lala passed. After passing Hawaii, the storm restrengthened into a category 4 hurricane and gradually shifted to a more northerly trajectory. It is not expected to affect any other Pacific Islands before degrading.Another system in the north Pacific developed close to Micronesia last week and was named Saudel as it reached tropical storm status. Saudel is forecast to intensify through the weekend, becoming a very strong or potentially violent typhoon. Travelling north-west, it will pass very close to or even make landfall on the Northern Mariana Islands, where a warning is already in place. Next week, Saudel is expected to track towards Okinawa prefecture, the chain of islands to the south of mainlandJapan.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherWeather trackerHurricanesJapanSouth KoreaHawaiiAsia PacificUS weatheranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Russia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger Japan | Japan | The Guardian
description: Pacific fleet launched missile drills near what Moscow calls the Kuril Islands but Japan regards as its Northern Territories
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Pacific fleet launched missile drills near what Moscow calls the Kuril Islands but Japan regards as its Northern Territories
Content: Vladimir Putin watches a missile launch from the Varyag during the Russian Pacific fleet exercises.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin watches a missile launch from the Varyag during the Russian Pacific fleet exercises.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersJapanRussia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger JapanPacific fleet launched missile drills near what Moscow calls the Kuril Islands but Japan regards as its Northern TerritoriesGavin Blairin TokyoFri 21 Aug 2026 00.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 01.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan has criticised missile tests carried out by Russia’s navy around the disputed islands visited by Vladimir Putin last week amid continuing tensions between the two countries.Russia’s Pacific fleet said on Thursday that it had fired Bastion surface-to-ship missiles from Etorofu, the largest island in the disputed archipelago, simulating an attack on enemy vessels, hitting all of its targets approximately 300km away.Officials said the drills included a nuclear-powered submarine and a guided-missile cruiser, according to reports.Putin sparked a tit-for-tat summoning of ambassadors in Tokyo and Moscow with his first visit last week to Etorofu, the largest of the group of four islands. They are referred to as the Northern Territories or Four Northern Islands inJapan, and as part of the Kuril Islands in Russia.Toshimitsu Motegi, Japan’s foreign minister, said on Thursday during a trip to Oman: “We cannot tolerate moves to strengthen military power on the Four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].”The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and RussiaRead moreTerritorial rows over the islandsgo back to the 19th century. The Soviet Union seized them from Japan at the end of the second world war.Exercises by the Russian fleet began on 4 August and Japan was informed in advance that they would include live-fire drills. Japan lodged a protest against the large-scale manoeuvres on 5 August.According to the Russian news agency Tass, the drills involved “approximately 60 surface ships, submarines, and support vessels, about 30 aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial systems of the Pacific fleet’s naval aviation, as well as over 13,000 service members”.Putin observed some of the exercises from the Varyag on 12 August as part of his trip to the disputed islands and to Sakhalin, the large undisputedly Russian island north of Hokkaido.“The region is unfortunately becoming increasingly prone to conflict, with Nato seeking to gain a foothold here and the emergence of new military and political blocs,” said Putin, speaking aboard the flagship. “There are efforts and plans to deploy new weapons systems here, which creates threats for our country.”The Russian drills are scheduled to continue through 29 August.Explore more on these topicsJapanRussiaAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Victorian Labor promises free dental care if re-elected in Australia-first move | Victorian politics | The Guardian
description: Premier Ben Carroll says $230m would be earmarked for 10 public dental clinics to operate on a walk-in basis
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: Premier Ben Carroll says $230m would be earmarked for 10 public dental clinics to operate on a walk-in basis
Content: Ben Carroll says Labor’s proposal for free dental checkups is ‘structural cost-of-living support’ and a national-first intervention by a state government.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAPView image in fullscreenBen Carroll says Labor’s proposal for free dental checkups is ‘structural cost-of-living support’ and a national-first intervention by a state government.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAPVictorian politicsVictorian Labor promises free dental care if re-elected in Australia-first movePremier Ben Carroll says $230m would be earmarked for 10 public dental clinics to operate on a walk-in basisGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentFri 21 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictorians would be able to walk into a dental clinic and receive free checkups and treatment under an Australian-first proposal the Labor government will take to the November state election.The premier,Ben Carroll, will announce the plan – Labor’s first major election commitment – at a rally on Saturday to mark fewer than 100 days until Victorians go to the polls.Carroll will say a re-elected Labor government would spend $230m to open 10 public dental clinics across the state, where oral care clinicians would be able to provide free checkups and treatments, including fillings, root canals and extractions.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCarroll described the plan as “structural cost-of-living support” and a national-first intervention by a state government.“Only Labor will deliver free dental care for all Victorians,” he said in a statement.The health minister, Ingrid Stitt, described the plan as the dental equivalent of the state’s urgent care clinics, where people can “turn up and get the care you need”.“Getting dental care shouldn’t be determined by your bank balance or where you live,” Stitt said.Walk-in basisUnder the proposal, seven of the public dental clinics would be located in Melbourne and three in regional Victoria, in areas where there are gaps in services.The clinics would be open from 9am to 9pm on weekdays and 9am to 5pm on weekends and would operate on a walk-in basis, with priority given to people with the most urgent needs, including those experiencing dental pain or swelling or who have had an accident.Once fully operational, the government said they would treat more than 100,000 Victorians a year.The state’s urgent care clinics were similarly unveiled just three months before the 2022 Victorian election as part of ajoint announcementwith New South Wales.The federal government also began contributing funding to the clinics and expanded the rollout. It is unclear whether the Victorian government will seek federal funding or involvement in the proposed dental clinics.Dental costing Australians bigAcross most of Australia, free or low-cost dental care is currently only available to specific eligible groups such as children and young people, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and those with concession cards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Victoria, $239m was allocated in the 2026-27 budget to dental, including the Smile Squad program in public schools.But Medicare does not cover dental care for most adults, leaving millions of Australians to choose between dipping into their wallets or skipping treatment.‘There was grift, there was thuggery’: Victorian premier says ‘nothing is off limits’ at construction royal commissionRead moreAccording toAustralian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) data, Australia spends more than $12bn on dental services. About 61% of that cost falls to the individual, health insurance funds cover 19%, and the federal government 11% and state governments 8%. There has also been a sharp rise in applications to access superannuation early to fund dental treatment.Guardian Australiareported in 2025that people struggling to afford dental bills were delaying or skipping treatment, while untreated tooth decay was increasing and record numbers of Australians were presenting to hospitals for dental procedures.Later that year, during the federal election, the Greenscampaigned heavilyon their plan to expand Medicare to cover dental services for adults, which was costed at $195bn over 10 years. The party went backwards at the election but continues to pursue the policy.Federal Labor backbenchers have alsopreviously expressed supportfor putting dental treatment into Medicare and it remains in the party platform.In Victoria, Labor sources are hopeful Carroll’s announcement will shift the party into campaign mode after weeks spent seeking to differentiate himself from his predecessors, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, including by calling aroyal commission into the construction sectorand pausing thepassage of work from home legislation.However, sources have said the dental policy was developed under Allan and her team.Explore more on these topicsVictorian politicsBen CarrollLabor partyHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decision  | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Joint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workers
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Joint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workers
Content: A World Central Kitchen vehicle in Gaza after it was attacked by the IDF in April 2024.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersView image in fullscreenA World Central Kitchen vehicle in Gaza after it was attacked by the IDF in April 2024.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersGaza‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decisionJoint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workersJason BurkeFri 21 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into theApril 2024 airstrikesthat hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”.
