The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,”the countries’ joint statement said.It continued: “InGaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.One of the officers who was dismissed hadreportedlysigned an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where expertsdeclared a faminein August 2025.The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.Hind Rajab died aftera desperate three-hour phone callto the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsraelIsrael-Gaza warForeign policyCanadaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW ‘seeking urgent advice’ on controversial court ruling that found anti-Israel vandalism was not antisemitic | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Attorney general considering appeal after justice Desmond Fagan knocks back terror order request for Mohommed Farhat who wrote ‘Fuk Israel’ on cars
Author: Jordyn Beazley
Headline: Exclusive: Attorney general considering appeal after justice Desmond Fagan knocks back terror order request for Mohommed Farhat who wrote ‘Fuk Israel’ on cars
Content: CCTV screenshot supplied by the NSW supreme court of Mohommed Farhat and another man spray-painting a car in Sydney in November 2024.Photograph: Supplied by NSW supreme courtView image in fullscreenCCTV screenshot supplied by the NSW supreme court of Mohommed Farhat and another man spray-painting a car in Sydney in November 2024.Photograph: Supplied by NSW supreme courtNew South WalesNSW ‘seeking urgent advice’ on controversial court ruling that found anti-Israel vandalism was not antisemiticExclusive:Attorney general considering appeal after justice Desmond Fagan knocks back terror order request for Mohommed Farhat who wrote ‘Fuk Israel’ on carsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJordyn BeazleyFri 21 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNew South Walesgovernment could appeal a supreme court judge’s controversial decision to refuse its request for a terror order over a Sydney man convicted of writing “Fuk Israel” on cars and setting another vehicle alight in late 2024.Justice Desmond Fagan this week found disparaging Israel was “political comment” not antisemitism. He rejected the state’s application that Mohommed Farhat be subjected to a one-year extended supervision order under the Terrorism Act when released from prison.Australia’s peak Jewish group has labelled Fagan’s ruling dangerous judicial “activism” that should be reviewed. The Executive Council of Australian Jewry argued the ruling avoided “the community impact”.Fagan’s damning finding in relation to the handling of Farhat’s casewas published on Tuesday. The judge said on Wednesday it appeared to be “a serious miscarriage of justice”.Farhat remains behind bars despite initially being due to be released on parole from early December 2025.View image in fullscreenOne of the cars vandalised in Woollahra.Photograph: The GuardianFagan found lower courts and various state agencies had incorrectly labelled Farhat’s actions antisemitic – meaning he was treated more harshly after he pleaded guilty to 15 offences in connection with property damage in Woollahra.The supreme court was provided with intelligence which showed counter-terrorism police had accepted, three weeks after Farhat’s arrest in November 2024, that he was not ideologically motivated but rather had beenrecruited and paidto write the slogans.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailPolice had not shared that information with the prosecution or the magistrate who sentenced Farhat, Fagan found this week. It also wasn’t shared before the state sought to cast Farhat, who has a Hezbollah tattoo on his neck, as a terror threat.Fagan found there was an “insignificant” risk the now 22-year-old, who was of “limited intellect”, would commit a serious terrorism offence.A government spokesperson said on Thursday the attorney general, Michael Daley, was “seeking urgent advice about the prospects of an appeal” over Fagan’s decision to knock back the state’s request for an extended supervision order.Guardian Australia asked Daley, the police minister, Yasmin Catley, and the corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, about Fagan’s findings in relation to how the police and other agencies handled the case.NSW judge says anti-Israel graffiti case went ‘haywire’ when vandalism was labelled antisemiticRead moreA government spokesperson said that the “judiciary operates independently of government and this independence is crucial to protect the administration of justice in NSW”.“Our government has taken strong action against antisemitism and hatred,” the spokesperson said.Given the matter remained before the courts and the attorney general was seeking advice regarding an appeal, they declined to comment further.Call for investigation into police conductThe Greens MP Sue Higginson on Thursday wrote to the NSW police watchdog, the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc), requesting an urgent investigation into the police’s handling of the case.She said she was “gravely concerned systemic or deliberate maladministration has resulted in a severe miscarriage of justice”.“The material failure of police to provide critical evidence to the court has resulted in Mr Farhat’s prolonged and quite possibly wrongful incarceration, as well as serious errors of fact and law,” Higginson wrote in her letter.The watchdog’s chief executive, Peter Johnson SC, said in budget estimates on Thursday the Lecc was considering the request.NSW police said in a statement on Friday: “This matter is currently under internal police investigation and as such no further information can be released to the media at this time to protect the integrity of the investigation.”View image in fullscreenNSW supreme court justice Desmond Fagan.Photograph: NSW supreme courtFagan dedicated a significant portion of his written judgment to distinguishing anti-Israel speech from antisemitic speech.He was highly critical of thecontroversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definitionof antisemitism referred to in the crown’s evidence, and which is being adopted by Australian institutions after a push by the special envoy to combat antisemitism, Jillian Segal.Herplan to combat antisemitismstates: “The envoy will work with state and federal governments to require the IHRA working definition of antisemitism to be used across all levels of government and public institutions to inform their practical understanding of antisemitism.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn his ruling, Fagan said “the IHRA proposal is detached from the reality of the common usage and understanding of antisemitism in this country”. He said he was “not the first to have criticised the inept drafting of the IHRA formulation”.The judge ruled that disparaging Israel was not antisemitic and stated that “for decades Jewish people have been amongst the most forceful critics of Israel’s conduct towards the Palestinians”.The definition has been formally endorsed by the Australian government and is the accepted definition of the royal commission into antisemitism established afterDecember’s Bondi beach terror attackthat killed 15 people during a Hanukah festival.Segal declined to comment on Fagan’s criticism.Jewish groups respond to IHRA definition findingsThe co-chair of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Alex Ryvchin, criticised the findings and what he termed Fagan’s judicial “activism”.“It’s quite extraordinary [given] where we are as a society, as a country, globally with antisemitism, that we’re still being dragged back into these foundational discussions about what is and what isn’t antisemitism,” he told Sky News on Wednesday night.Ryvchin said the IHRA definition had been accepted “certainly by the Jewish world” and both major political parties, universities and sporting associations in Australia.“But whenever someone wants to muddy the waters and prevent us from actually looking at curing antisemitism, they drag us back to this discussion about the IHRA definition.”Ryvchin said Fagan’s focus on the definition “seems like the work of activism rather than a judicial member”.“It’s deeply troubling, and I think that influenced the overall decision the judge made and his whole thinking on the case.”Ryvchin said Farhat’s vandalism in a “Jewish neighbourhood” was antisemitic, not simply political protest. He said Fagan’s ruling “totally avoids the facts of the case but also the community impact”.Bondi library removes book How to Sell a Genocide from shelves after complaintRead more“We knew without equivocation that it was an attack on us,” Ryvchin said, adding he thought the decision should be appealed. “There’s a great danger in this judgment standing … I think it should be reviewed.”Fagan noted the state claimed that because the slogans were spray-painted in an area with a concentration of Jewish residents and there was criminal damage, the words “Fuk Israel” took on an antisemitic meaning “in context”.“I do not accept that,” he said in his decision. “The political nature of the curse was not changed by the circumstances.”Fagan’s “categorical rejection of the IHRA definition” was welcomed by the progressive Jewish Council of Australia. Executive member Bart Shteinman agreed with Fagan’s finding that “Jewish Australians are not a monolith”.“[IHRA] distorts the fight between real antisemitism while shielding Israel from legitimate scrutiny,” Shteinman said.“At a time when governments and institutions are under growing pressure to adopt IHRA, this judgment should give them time for serious pause.”Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cults, setups and rumours: years after their downfalls, former NSW Liberal MPs are exacting revenge | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: David Elliott and Eleni Petinos believe they were brought down by their own party. The Icac hearing has given them a chance to set the record straight
Author: Anne Davies
Headline: David Elliott and Eleni Petinos believe they were brought down by their own party. The Icac hearing has given them a chance to set the record straight
Content: Former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott after giving evidence at Icac. He claimed at the inquiry he was followed in public by a private investigator.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenFormer NSW Liberal minister David Elliott after giving evidence at Icac. He claimed at the inquiry he was followed in public by a private investigator.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPIndependent Commission Against CorruptionCults, setups and rumours: years after their downfalls, former NSW Liberal MPs are exacting revengeDavid Elliott and Eleni Petinos believe they were brought down by their own party. The Icac hearing has given them a chance to set the record straightGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAnne DaviesFri 21 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 22.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRevenge, they say, is a dish best served cold.It’s been almost four years since the former New South Wales MP, David Elliott, announced that hewould not seek preselectionfor a seat in the Hills in greater Sydney after his own seat was abolished. He had realised that, thanks to branch stacking in his area, he stoodno chance of securing another.Despite being a senior minister for eight years in the Baird, Berejiklian and Perrottet Liberal governments, Elliott’s political career was over.Sure, he’d been a somewhat colourful character – he’d attracted his fair share of publicity, good and bad.But, as one former colleague put it: “It was hard not to like him.”Since his departure at the 2023 election, Elliott has discovered the full scale of bastardry that was directed against him to end his career.TheIndependent Commission Against Corruptionis investigating allegations of illegal secret donations from property developers and others that were used to fund branch-stacking operations in breach of the NSW Electoral Funding Act.Elliott’s appearance at Icac on Fridaywas a chance to air many matters that had clearly rankled.He is not a person of interest in the investigation, and appeared only as a witness.The fight with a fugitive developerElliott finally got to speak about what he had suspected for years: his belief that developer Jean Nassif, who is now a fugitive in Lebanon, was responsible for planting news stories that damaged his career, having him followed by private investigators, for death threats and for starting rumours that he was having an affair while his wife was undergoing cancer treatment.Elliott told Icac the disagreements with Nassif stemmed from Elliot’s view that development needed to be slowed in the Hills because the area lacked the infrastructure to support huge housing developments.Former NSW Liberal minister tells Icac ‘cult took over the party’Read moreNassif’s company, Toplace, was behind two large developments at Castle Hill – Skyline and Atmosphere – and was seeking approval for another at Cherrybrook, where he had bought land at very high prices.Several Toplace buildings have been slapped with rectification orders by the NSW building commissioner, David Chandler (more on him later).Elliott told Icac that at first, Nassif had tried to woo him and meet him. There were attempts to make donations which were not permitted from developers under NSW laws, as Elliott pointed out.“On two occasions he followed me in public places,” Elliott told the inquiry.One occurred in a bar in Parramatta when he was meeting then-local councillor Martin Zaiter.Elliott claimed it started off pleasantly, with Nassif introducing his daughter, but soon “he did the finger in the chest”.“I told him: ‘Listen mate, I don’t meet with property developers.’ It felt like an eternity but I reckon it was three to four minutes.”His chief of staff, Tanya Raffoul, received threats through the Maronite church she attended, he told Icac.At one stage she went to a meeting organised by property development figure, Amanda Ghalloub, and found Nassif there. According to Elliott, Nassif told her: “we have pictures of your boss, we need you to spill the beans on your boss or it would not end well.”‘Shame is the punishment’: as Icac delves into the shadowy Reformers, ‘whales’ are coming to the surfaceRead moreElliot also believed that private investigators followed he and his wife.“The first time I realised it was happening was that I’d seen a vehicle at the top western end of my street on the park side of the road,” Elliott said.He didn’t speak to the private investigators, he said. “I took a photo of him taking a photo of me because, as I’ve said to the media, he was certainly the Maxwell Smart of the PI world,” he said, referring to the 1960s television show about a bumbling cold war secret agent.This was not paranoia. Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, read from a dossier of observations of the then police minister.After Elliott started to raise concerns about defective buildings, he told the inquiry Nassif went “nuts”.Negative stories were leaked to the media about Elliott, including that he hadfired an illegal gun.During the Icac inquiry, he became aware of a“shit sheet”produced by a shadowy group of young Liberal operatives known as the Reformers that alleged he had an affair – which he says is baseless.A former Liberal staffer and associate of the Reformers, Dylan Whitelaw, gave evidence to the inquiry in July andaccepted under cross-examinationfrom Elliott’s lawyer that no affair had taken place.Nassif is a person of interest in the Icac inquiry and has an arrest warrant out relating to alleged fraud involving multimillion dollar loans to Toplace. He has not returned to Australia.‘Cults’ and ‘setups’Asked about the right faction of theLiberal party– the faction behind his political demise – Elliott did not mince words.“Some call it the hard right, some call it the right, some call it the religious right, some call it the cult,” said Elliot, a member of the centre right, the rival faction.“At first David Clarke was godfather. It was made clear to me that later, Anthony Roberts [the former planning minister], the Tudehopes and the Perrottets were in charge.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd when it came to the former premier, Dominic Perrottet and his brother Charles, Elliott was scathing.Dominic had “looked him in the eye” at a farewell parade for police commissioner Mick Fuller and promised he could keep the police portfolio, only to move him to transport.Elliott thought it might have had something to do with Nassif’s arrest for cocaine possession at the Star Casino.“At the bottom of the elevator, there were police dogs, and [Nassif] obviously realised that he had cocaine on him, and the police were about to arrest him,” Elliott said.“Now, conveniently, [with me] the police minister and his adversary, he was able to say: ‘This is all a setup from David out there.’6:07Icac: Catholic schools NSW chief denies performing factory reset on phone to wipe evidence – video“Now, I can assure you, Dr Dwyer, If I’d asked theNew South Walespolice court to issue a parking ticket, they would have punched me in the neck,” he said.Elliott said had no doubt that Charles Perrottet was consulted on the reshuffle. “Charles and Dom were joined at the hip,” he said.Charles Perrottet has been named as a person of interest in Icac in relation to allegations concerning illegal donations from Jean Nassif. He is scheduled to give evidence next week. Dominic Perrottet is not under investigation and is not a person of interest.Much of Elliott’s appearance was spent on the demise of the centre-right councillors prior to the 2022 local government elections and their replacement by the Liberal party’s state executive using special powers.“I was so disgusted with Charles because he lied to me about the council, I pretty much wiped him,” he said.‘Used’ by friendsElliott was not the only one who may have relished the opportunity to ladle out a cold serving this week.Eleni Petinos, the former fair trading minister in the Perrottet government,gave evidence on Thursdayabout how she believed she was used by other people in the Liberal party – first to try to get rid of the building commissioner, David Chandler, and later as a scapegoat.View image in fullscreenEleni Petinos at a press conference in 2023.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPChandler – who is not under investigation by Icac and is due to give evidence next week – came within her portfolio.In late July 2022,Petinos was sacked by Perrottet. The reason given at the time was claims of her bullying of staff. Petinos – who is not under investigation by Icac –denied the allegationsat the time but said she was sorry if she unintentionally offended anyone or made them uncomfortable.Petinos’s chief of staff, Cassandra Lawry, who also gave evidence, said Petinos’ communication sometimes “could be better” but denied the allegation of bullying.On Thursday, Petinos told Icac she now believes there was something else at play.The premier had become aware Chandler had penned an incendiary resignation letter that was going to cause embarrassment and attract Icac’s attention. Did he try to deflect attention by sacking the minister?“I thought there was something very strange at play for Dominic to take the action that he did so swiftly, so coldly, and without the opportunity to even put me in front of a camera. That seemed bizarre,” she said.“I was doing my absolute best for him. I felt like, when men are direct, or when men give clear instructions, they’re applauded. They’re considered to be good leaders. They’re bold, they’re visionaries. But when women in leadership positions demonstrate the same traits, we’re aggressive, we’re bullies, we’re too bossy,” she said at Icac.1:27‘Don’t give me that look’: Icac witness reprimanded during corruption investigation – videoShe was particularly hurt that she was gone in two days while another minister, Stuart Ayres, was afforded weeks of support over another controversial issue – the appointment of John Barilaro as a trade representative to New York – before he was required to stand down.The effect on Petinos was profound. Her friends have said she was shattered by the bullying allegations and battled to find her confidence again.In the witness box on Thursday, Petinos was able to name the people she now believes used her in a campaign to get rid of the building commissioner.They included the right power broker, Charles Perrottet, whom she had known from her time in the Young Liberals, and Chris Spence, another political ally who in 2022 was serving as chief of staff to Roberts. Petinos had helped on his campaigns before entering politics.Spence is not a person of interest and is due to give evidence next week.Clearly exacting revenge feels good. After airing his grievances on Friday, Elliott left the Icac offices, smiling broadly. “It feels weird to be the first Liberal who was happy to appear before Icac.”Explore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South Wales politicsNew South WalesLiberal partynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hiker Lily Hooper remembered as someone ‘everyone liked’ – as it happened | Australia news | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Nick Visser
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 02.08 EDTTributes flow for hiker Lily HooperKat WongLily Hooperhas been remembered for her smile, her talent and her toughness as the local community reels in the wake of the teenage hiker’s death.The 18-year-old’s body was recovered from the dense bush of the NSW Southern Highlands overnight, eight days after she was reported missing and the night after it was incorrectly communicated that she had been found alive.Condolences have poured in for her family and her martial arts teacher,Mark Szalajko, paid tribute to Hooper in a post on social media.double quotation markShe was a talented and tough martial artist, but despite that toughness, Lily was such a lovely person. She was one of those people who everyone simply liked.As a martial arts teacher, people walk into and out of our lives every day for many different reasons. Some leave a positive impact on us and on our dojo, and we wish they could have stayed longer. Lily was one of those people.I will really miss her smile, her conversations and the moments we shared on the mat.The Wollondilly Performing Arts centre and Wollondilly Shire library have been lit up in purple in memory of Hooper and on Friday evening, a vigil will be held in Oakdale, where she lived with her family.Guardian reporterIma Caldwellvisited the now-still command post last night – read more below.Lily Hooper’s family was told she’d been found alive. ‘She’s coming home,’ her father said – then tears of joy turned to griefRead moreShareUpdated at03.09 EDT

title: Dutch regulator fines Uber $966m for automating driver suspensions | Uber | The Guardian
description: European regulators have imposed billions in penalties on US technology companies due to privacy, competition and digital market rules
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: European regulators have imposed billions in penalties on US technology companies due to privacy, competition and digital market rules
Content: Uber’s fine by the Dutch Data Protection Authority is the second-largest penalty issued under GDPR.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUber’s fine by the Dutch Data Protection Authority is the second-largest penalty issued under GDPR.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockUberDutch regulator fines Uber $966m for automating driver suspensionsEuropean regulators have imposed billions in penalties on US technology companies due to privacy, competition and digital market rulesReutersFri 21 Aug 2026 16.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 16.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Dutch data protection authority has fined ⁠Uber €825m ($966m) for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequately informing them, according to a 17 August decision.The penalty would be the second-largest issued yet under Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).It is behind only a €1.2bn ($1.4bn) fine ⁠imposed onMetaby Ireland in 2023 for unlawfully transferring European Facebook users’ data to the United States. Meta is appealing.Uber said it would also appeal.“We strongly disagree with this decision and disproportionate fine,” a spokesperson ⁠said, adding that the company takes drivers’ rights seriously and its policies include both human reviews and opportunities for drivers to dispute platform suspensions.The Dutch ​authority confirmed the decision later on Friday.“Uber has committed ‌serious infringements” by deactivating driver accounts without ‌warning or human involvement, the organization’s deputy chair Monique Verdier said in a statement.“From one moment to the next they no longer ‌had any income … A computer should not make decisions on its own that have (such) major consequences.”European regulators have imposed billions of euros in penalties on large US technology companies in recent years under privacy, competition and digital market rules. The EU fined Google €890m ($1.04bn) for anti-competitive actions last month.Meta, Google, Apple and Amazon all face multiple fines, though headline fines are often reduced or reversed after years-long appeals processes. Donald Trump has criticized such fines. In April, a US state department official said they were the “biggest ‌single source of friction” in US-EU economic relations.GDPR rules ban decisions made solely by computer algorithms when they have a significant impact on people’s lives, such as on employment, saying such decisions require meaningful human review and a way to challenge a ​decision.The case against Uber concerns European incidents from 2018 to 2022, stemming initially from a French complaint. It was handled by the Dutch regulator because Uber’s European headquarters are in theNetherlands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber temporarily suspended accounts of some drivers who were suspected of fraud, including when its systems concluded drivers had taken unnecessary detours to inflate fares or accepted trips without intending to complete them.Uber said such suspensions were usually brief, and it did not ⁠permanently deactivate such accounts without human review.Drivers with low customer ratings were sometimes permanently deactivated by ​computer, the Dutch agency said. Uber disputed that, ​saying it had never automated permanent deactivation decisions.The ​company said one reason it considers the fine disproportionate is that only a small number of drivers were affected, ​with 126 having been deactivated ‌in Europe as a ​result of low customer ratings in ​2021.The agency said the fine was calculated as a fraction of Uber’s 2025 annual turnover. Swiss digital-rights group PersonalData.IO – which helped French Uber drivers seek data about the algorithmic decisions affecting their work, eventually leading to the Dutch investigation – said it was pleased with the decision. Founder Paul-Olivier Dehaye said the group is preparing a class action suit against Uber seeking compensation for drivers.Explore more on these topicsUberNetherlandsEuropeMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Gun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports | Germany | The Guardian
description: Germany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinations
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Germany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinations
Content: Germany’s interior minister described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a ‘low-level agent’.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGermany’s interior minister described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a ‘low-level agent’.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesGermanyGun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reportsGermany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinationsDeborah Colein BerlinFri 21 Aug 2026 10.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany is seeking to extradite a suspect fromRomaniaover the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.Two weeks after German authorities found adrone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.“This case demonstrates that ‌we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.View image in fullscreenInterior minister Alexander Dobrindt, who confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation.Photograph: Katharina Kausche/AFP/Getty ImagesThe find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports byDer Spiegelmagazine and an investigative team led bySüddeutsche Zeitung.Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had ‌been detained so far this year.Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.View image in fullscreenThe headquarters of German domestic intelligence in Cologne.Photograph: Patrik Stollarz/AFP/Getty ImagesSinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.Last yearPolish security officials arrested several peopleallegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly posted from Romania.Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalledreports in 2024that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries inEuropethat have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.Explore more on these topicsGermanyRussiaEuropeRomaniaEspionagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Airbus bows to remote working demands after series of strikes | Airbus | The Guardian
description: Aeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a week
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Aeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a week
Content: Workers mark the inauguration of the Airbus A320 aircraft family assembly line in Blagnac, France, in June.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWorkers mark the inauguration of the Airbus A320 aircraft family assembly line in Blagnac, France, in June.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAirbusAirbus bows to remote working demands after series of strikesAeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a weekKalyeena Makortoffand agenciesFri 21 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTFirst published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirbus has bowed to employee demands on remote working, after a series of strikesover its chief executive’s return-to-the office orders.The world’s largest aeroplane maker is said to have watered down plans to restrict remote working to one day a week from September. At present, staff are able to work remotely for two.It was part of a high-profile campaign by theAirbuschief executive, Guillaume Faury, to get staff back into the office, in an effort to ensure the company could meet record demand and prepare new products after hiring thousands more staff.Faury told employees in June that while home working had been a lifeline during the Covid pandemic, the opposite was now true as Airbus needed them to share their skills in person. “I count on all of you to support this,” he said in a memo, reported by Bloomberg.But disruption caused by a series of strikes, including in Spain,Franceand the UK in recent months, has forced him to backtrack, according to Reuters. Managers have now been told staff can work at home an average of two days a week, in effect curbing the chief executive’s efforts.InSpain, staff have been striking on and off since July, with approximately 40% of the company’s 14,000 local workers taking part in stoppages in recent weeks over issues including remote working, transport, paid leave and salaries.There have also been sporadic protests in France over plans to force white-collar staff into the office four days a week.However, Reuters said Airbus production – which is at the heart of the European defence industry – had not been affected by the strikes.An Airbus spokesperson said: “Our objective remains the same: we aim for increased on-site presence to ensure better collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“However, effective change requires listening to our people. Based on employee feedback, we have decided to implement this transition more gradually.”The spokesperson added: “We are empowering managers to organise hybrid working within their teams in a pragmatic and practical way that maximises collective efficiency and reflects the reality of their working environments. This will be done within the scope of Airbus’s current collective agreements for hybrid working.”Explore more on these topicsAirbusAirline industryWorking from homeWork-life balanceIndustrial actionFranceSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Many males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidance
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Many males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidance
Content: In the year to the end of March, 2,247 Albanians were deported from the UK – accounting for a quarter of enforced returns.Photograph: Benjamin John/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn the year to the end of March, 2,247 Albanians were deported from the UK – accounting for a quarter of enforced returns.Photograph: Benjamin John/AlamyImmigration and asylumHome Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to AlbaniaMany males are returned even if they have been trafficked but Home Office must now consider new legal guidanceUK politics live – latest updatesDiane TaylorFri 21 Aug 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHome Officecould be blocked from deporting many young male trafficking victims to Albania after a major court ruling.Thousands of Albanian males have been identified as potential trafficking victims in the UK in recent years. Many are sent back to their country even if they are potential or confirmed victims of trafficking, as the Home Office contends they will be safe there.The ruling is likely to come as a significant blow to the government, which is trying to increase the number of people it removes.Albanians have been the most common nationality forcibly removed from the UK in the last five years, with 2,247 deported in the 12 months to the end of March, accounting for a quarter of enforced returns, according toUK government figures.Data disclosed in the court case shows that while Albanian females were previously major victims of trafficking, in their case into the UK sex industry, they have been overtaken by males – mainly boys and young men – who are trafficked into the drugs trade, either to distribute illegal drugs or to work as “gardeners” in cannabis farms.In 2022, 4,107 Albanian males were referred to UK services over potential trafficking, in comparison with 502 women. In 2023, the figure was 3,463 males and 588 females.The legal challenge was brought by a 21-year-old victim of trafficking from Albania who was first exploited by an Albanian gang in Belgium when he visited the country with his father at 16. He was sold to another Albanian gang, who brought him to the UK and forced him to work cultivating cannabis plants. He later escaped and was recognised as a victim of trafficking, but was denied asylum because he was told it would be safe for him to return to Albania.A panel of three senior judges in the upper tribunal of the immigration court accepted his asylum claim and found that even though five years had passed since he was first trafficked, he remained at “real risk” from his traffickers and could not safely move back to Albania.The judges issued new country guidance to the government, which must be considered by the Home Office before deciding whether to send male trafficking victims back to Albania.The judgment found that while Albania has made progress on tackling corruption, it continues to be a widespread problem and that there are no dedicated shelters for adult male trafficking victims, while the risk of victims being retrafficked if returned to Albania is significant.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIslington Law Centre, which has particular expertise in representing Albanian trafficking victims, highlighted many concerning practices that gangs subject their victims to. These include deliberately videoing sexual abuse including rape of child trafficking victims and threatening to release the footage on social media; they also show videos of loved ones in Albania to young people to let them know they know who their families are; and the gangs also inflict physical injuries such as broken bones on children and young people.Esme Madill, a solicitor at Islington Law Centre specialising in representing young Albanian trafficking victims, welcomed the judgment: “This measured judgment has been reached by a court which had the benefit of significant and detailed evidence as to the worrying issue of trafficking of boys and young men by organised Albanian criminal networks. The profiles of trafficking survivors and the risks recognised in the judgment accord strongly with what we see in our work with deeply brutalised and traumatised young survivors every week.”Home Office sources said they were considering whether to apply for permission to appeal.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeAlbaniaDrugsDrugs tradeHuman traffickingEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settler attacks shift focus to West Bank areas under direct Palestinian rule | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Report says violence is moving from Israeli-controlled areas to those earmarked for a future Palestinian state
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Report says violence is moving from Israeli-controlled areas to those earmarked for a future Palestinian state
Content: Palestinians inspect the damage to a house set on fire by Israeli settlers in the Hallet al-Fara area of Yatta, in the southern West Bank city of Hebron.Photograph: Wisam Hashlamoun/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPalestinians inspect the damage to a house set on fire by Israeli settlers in the Hallet al-Fara area of Yatta, in the southern West Bank city of Hebron.Photograph: Wisam Hashlamoun/Anadolu/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraeli settler attacks shift focus to West Bank areas under direct Palestinian ruleReport says violence is moving from Israeli-controlled areas to those earmarked for a future Palestinian statePeter BeaumontandQuique Kierszenbaumin JerusalemFri 21 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleViolent Israeli settler attacks in the two areas of the occupiedWest Bankunder direct Palestinian rule have almost doubled since 2025, as settlers pursue a self-proclaimed “great settlement revolution” in the very heart of the territory earmarked for a Palestinian state.According to areport by the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, shared with the Guardian, data shows that almost two-thirds of incidents of settler violence so far in 2026 have taken place in the so-called Areas A and B – placed under Palestinian Authority governance in the 1995 Oslo accords.The report, The Next Frontier, Violence by Israeli Civilians in Areas A and B, describes the “rapid shift” in “violence and pressure exerted by the government, military and settlers on Palestinians … from Area C into Areas B and even A”.View image in fullscreenA graffito reading ‘Greater Israel’ and several Stars of David are painted on Palestinian property in the Jordan valley near the West Bank city of Tubas on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAWhile all three designated administrative areas on the West Bank were intended under the Oslo peace deal to encompass the shape of a future Palestinian state, successive Israeli governments, driven by the settler movement, have pursued a long-term policy of undermining Palestinian claims.In Area C, accounting for 60% of the West Bank, Israel was initially given what was supposed to be temporary responsibility for all civil and security affairs pending a final status agreement for a Palestinian state. This arrangement was exploited for settlement. All government-approved Israeli settlements (regarded as illegal under international law) are located in Area C, as are the main roads and traffic arteries of the West Bank.In Area A, which makes up about 18% of the West Bank and includes the major Palestinian cities, the Palestinian Authority became responsible for civil affairs and internal security. In Area B (22%), which includes the built-up areas in Palestinian rural spaces, the PA became responsible for civil affairs and public order.mapSince 2024, Israel’s settlement movement has explicitly and violently expanded its efforts by establishing new farming “outposts” in areas A and B. Settler leaders have said openly that these are designed to “gain a foothold” in “very strategic” Palestinian locations. As the report says: “Most Palestinian daily life occurs in these areas.”According to the report’s analysis, the percentage of violent West Bank incidents taking place in Area B stands at 55% so far this year, compared with 25% last year, while attacks in Area C declined in the same period from 67% to 37% of the overall figure, indicating a deliberate change in strategy.“As settler and state violence against Palestinian communities in Area C has intensified in recent years, Palestinians have been forcibly pushed into Areas A and B, making these areas increasingly critical for maintaining safety and a semblance of normal everyday life,” said Yesh Din, which has been documenting settler violence for more than two decades.A map posted earlier this summer in the WhatsApp group of the Hilltop Foundation, an organisation that supplies equipment, support and funding for the establishment of Israeli outposts in the West Bank, showed 16 outposts between the major Palestinian cities of Ramallah and Nablus alone. The map was accompanied by text boasting of “the great settlement revolution under way in the Oslo areas” and pledging the foundation’s continuing support for the establishment of outposts in Area B.The Yesh Din report said that “the successful establishment of so many outposts in obvious violation of Israeli law, demonstrates that Israel is deliberately choosing not to effectively address the issue and that the settlers’ openly declared goals align with government policy”.“Senior ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich [who have both called for the cancelling of the Oslo accords] openly speak of their ambition to gain control of Area B and abolish the division created under the Oslo accords.”There is increasing international concern over the escalating pace of settler violence on the West Bank. Sanctions have been placed in the US and Europe on settlers and pro-settler figures, including Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister.Announcing France’s sanctions against Ben-Gvir on Wednesday, the French foreign, minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said what was happening on the West Bank was “ utterly disgraceful and should fill us all with revulsion”.According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, as of 20 July, 18 Palestinians had died during attacks involving settlers, of whom 12 were killed by settlers and three by Israeli forces. Responsibility for the remaining three deaths was disputed, OCHA said.According to the UN agency, there were about 190 attacks a month in the first four months of 2026, putting the West Bank on a trajectory to reach more than 2,000 attacks by the end of this year.Yesh Din concludes: “This Israeli strategy, implemented in part through the expansion of outposts and the settler violence launched from them into new areas, pushes Palestinian residents into the centres of towns and villages and empties surrounding areas of Palestinian presence.“In doing so, it advances Israel toward the realisation of a policy, already reflected in ministers’ public statements, that seeks to annex as much West Bank territory as possible with as few Palestinians as possible living there.“The path to this goal is paved with systematic, organised criminality, backed and supported by state institutions, revealing a clear intent: to make the area Palestinian free, in other words, to carry out ethnic cleansing.”The Israeli military has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Girl, 6, dies three days after Shoreham sea incident that killed parents and sister | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Saja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West Sussex
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Saja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West Sussex
Content: A family lay flowers on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four members of the El-Khawas family died after getting in trouble in the sea.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenA family lay flowers on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four members of the El-Khawas family died after getting in trouble in the sea.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAWest SussexGirl, 6, dies three days after Shoreham sea incident that killed parents and sisterSaja El-Khawas had been in critical condition after being pulled from sea in West SussexHarry CockburnFri 21 Aug 2026 18.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA six-year-old girl has died in hospital three days after being pulled from the sea off Shoreham inWest Sussex, in an incident that also killed her mother, father and sister.Saja El-Khawas died on Friday after the deaths of her sister Sara El-Khawas, 14, and her parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, on Tuesday.Saja had been in hospital in a critical condition since the incident.Police, paramedics, coastguard crews and a lifeboat attended the scene at Shoreham Fort early on Tuesday afternoon after a report of four people in difficulty in the water.In a statement, Sussex police said: “It is understood the family travelled down from their home in London to visit Shoreham, and entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort around 2pm on Tuesday afternoon, before getting into trouble.“The investigation into the incident remains open, but following review of CCTV footage and initial witness accounts, the current hypothesis is that this was a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement.”Her identity and death were confirmed in a legal notice from solicitors acting on behalf of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS foundation trust, as well as the Palestinian Forum in Britain. The Palestinian embassy previously confirmed her father was a British citizen of Palestinian descent.Sussex police said the family’s next of kin “are aware and continue to receive the full support of our officers during this unimaginably difficult time”.Ch Supt James Collis said: “This heartbreaking update is one we all feared in the aftermath of Tuesday’s tragic events.“I cannot imagine the devastation felt by the wider family of Hassan, Zeina, Sara and Saja after this loss. On behalf of everyone at Sussex police, I extend our thoughts and heartfelt condolences.“The impact of this tragedy has been felt across the country, and I know the Shoreham community, emergency responders and all involved will continue to be affected for a long time to come.”“I would like to thank all of the public who have shared their sympathies and kind words, and once again ask for the victims’ family and loved ones to be left to grieve in privacy.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000 | Liberal Democrats | The Guardian
description: David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam
Content: David Campanale in Cheam in 2022. He says he was told a ‘secular party’ was being built with no place for Christians.Photograph: Sutton Liberal democratsView image in fullscreenDavid Campanale in Cheam in 2022. He says he was told a ‘secular party’ was being built with no place for Christians.Photograph: Sutton Liberal democratsLiberal DemocratsDeselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and CheamAletha AduPolitical correspondentFri 21 Aug 2026 15.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow much is a career in politics worth? TheLiberal Democrats, despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000.It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against hisChristianitycost him his political career in a civil case against the party.Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023.The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court.Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”.But in a counter-schedule filed on Friday, the Lib Dems described Campanale’s claim as “grossly inflated and egregious”. Their lawyers say £14,000 should be awarded for injury to feelings, and as a volunteer political party member, Campanale could have been expected to withstand “rigorous political debate and criticism”. They put aggravated damages, past and future loss of earnings, an MP’s pension and the loss of political capital at £0.Campanale says he was mocked and abused over his Christian beliefs and faced an organised campaign to remove him, while some activists refused to campaign for him.In his claim Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022, he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. He also claims he was excluded from election leaflets and told not to campaign in certain wards because activists disagreed with his beliefs.His claim also referred to a phone call in March 2022 in which he said Luke Taylor, his replacement, told him that he had no right to a conscience based on his faith and that a “secular party” was being built with no place for Christians.After Campanale was removed, Taylor won the seat with a majority of 3,801. The seat has since become safer territory for the Lib Dems with recent polls putting them well ahead of the Conservatives.The case has prompted criticism from senior Liberal Democrat figures inside and outside the party. The former leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes have backed calls for an independent inquiry. Farron has urged the party to apologise, saying there had been “manifest discrimination” against Campanale and party figures at all levels of the party failed to intervene.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, warned the position taken by the Liberal Democrats could make it “impossible” for Christians and people with other strong religious beliefs to represent the party.Before admitting the claims, the Lib Dems said in their defence that the party could deselect candidates where the expression of religious beliefs conflicted with its policies or values. The Lib Dems defence also described as a “statement of fact” the claim that the era associated with prominent Christian Liberal Democrats such as Shirley Williams and Charles Kennedy was over.A Lib Dem spokesperson said before their submitted counter-schedule: “This is an ongoing legal case so it would not be appropriate to comment. The Liberal Democrats are home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians. Three Liberal Democrat MPs in neighbouring seats to Sutton and Cheam are practising Christians including party leader Ed Davey.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsChristianityReligionSurreyDiscrimination at worknewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño develops | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave
Content: Network Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenNetwork Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAClimate crisisBritain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño developsExperts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwavePriya BharadiaFri 21 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRailway companies are racing to prepare for another brutal summer next year, as a developing El Niño could see 2027 break more heat-related records.Britain’s railway system has already been under stress from extreme heat this summer, with several operators reducing timetables and train speeds.Two trains derailedwithin 24 hoursduring the UK’s fifth heatwave in August, in what Network Rail said had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.“Traditionally, our railway system hasn’t been designed for hot weather. So that puts our railway system under stress but also our overhead lines as well. That can also cause trouble for the whole [railway] system, not just the ground infrastructure,” said Xueyu Geng, a professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick.The Met Office has said that theEl Niño eventdeveloping over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than 100 years, with the UK forecast to experience increased rainfall and stormy weather this autumn due to the “unprecedented” weather pattern.In 2024,Network Railincreased their projected five-year spending on climate, earthworks and drainage by five times the amount allocated from 2019.“I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate,” Geng said.She warned Britain must begin to factor in higher temperatures as part of the design standards for its railways. “We need to look at how the hot countries are managing their railway systems. For example, in Spain, their rail system is managing between 0C and 45C. Saudi Arabia is 10C to 55C. The track is pre-stressed. We need to manufacture the pre-stress level in order to cope [with extreme heat].”Geng explained that Britain’s railways can typically handle temperatures as low as -10C, and this will need to be maintained. “We might have extreme cold as well. But, in the meantime, we need to look at the upper boundary temperature, and to actually manufacture our rail to cope with both kinds of extreme temperatures.”Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, said the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented. “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, [with Pacific sea temperatures] peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records.”Rail operators need to be prepared in the coming year for both “potentially prolonged periods of hot dry weather and more intense rainfall and storminess,” said William Powrie, professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.“There will need to be a serious look at parts of the network where past decisions have compromised the infrastructure, such as the extensive singling on the Salisbury to Exeter line, and reducing the train speed to account for poor track quality as a result of soil moisture deficit destroys the timetable,” Powrie said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The immediate priority should be to use the warning time we have,” said Ioannis Koliousis, associate professor at the Cranfield School of Management. “Before a potentially wetter and stormier autumn and winter, Network Rail should intensify drainage clearance, culvert inspections, earthwork monitoring and vegetation management, particularly at locations with a known history of weather-related failures.“The most important consideration is that we should now distinguish between maintenance and adaptation. Clearing a drain prepares us for the next storm, [but] redesigning or increasing the capacity of that drainage system prepares us for the next 30 years. We need to be doing both.”A spokesperson for Network Rail said: “Our long-range forecast suggests it will be a warm, wet winter – in line with climate change predictions for Britain – and we are doing all we can to be ready for that. Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world and improving its resilience to more frequent and extreme weather is an ongoing priority.“We are continuing to invest in making the railway more resilient to extreme weather and climate change. This includes a £2.6bn programme of works in track maintenance and renewals, including drainage, earthworks, track and overhead power improvements, as well as monitoring and predictive technologies to identify risks earlier and enable proactive intervention.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisNetwork RailRail industryRail transportTransportTravel & leisureEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: MPs ‘failing to learn lesson’ over freebies after accepting £400,000 of hospitality | Politics | The Guardian
description: MPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awards
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: MPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awards
Content: Lucy Powell, then Labour’s deputy leader and now education secretary, declared tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley.Photograph: Anthony Pham/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLucy Powell, then Labour’s deputy leader and now education secretary, declared tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley.Photograph: Anthony Pham/ShutterstockPoliticsMPs ‘failing to learn lesson’ over freebies after accepting £400,000 of hospitalityMPs receive Harry Styles concert tickets worth £858, Chelsea flower show tickets worth £1,839, and £3,432 of hospitality at Brit awardsRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 21 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMPs have been accused of failing to learn their lesson over freebies after taking almost £400,000 of hospitality to concerts, sport matches and other events this year, with Louise Haigh, Lucy Powell and Wes Streeting among those accepting tickets.Despite the outcry in 2024 over Keir Starmeraccepting football tickets and gifts of clothing, MPs appear to have been declaring hospitality since the start of the year on a greater scale than previously seen.The most recent disclosures include £858 worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group, which was accepted by Powell, the deputy leader and education secretary. And Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, accepted tickets to the Chelsea flower show from Lloyds Banking Group worth £1,839.Haigh also accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivor Novello awards, while Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip, enjoyed Brit Awards hospitality for two worth £3,432, hospitality at Cheltenham festival horse racing from the betting company Flutter worth £350, and tickets to the Grand National valued at £560. All were backbench MPs while accepting the hospitality and have now been elevated to cabinet jobs under Andy Burnham.Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted £1,480 of tickets to the men’s Wimbledon singles final while in her cabinet job, while Ellie Reeves, the attorney general, accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivors while solicitor general.View image in fullscreenJannik Sinner serves against Alexander Zverev in the men’s singles final at Wimbledon. Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted tickets worth £1,480 to the match.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBurnham declared hospitality worth about £6,000 this year – mostly relating to his former role as the mayor of Greater Manchester, such as £3,800 tickets to the Brit Awards in Manchester, but also £500 worth of tickets to Ladies’ Day at the Grand National in Aintree.The acceptance of free hospitality by MPs appeared to fall after mid-2024 when the spotlight fell on Starmer’s string of free tickets to watch Arsenal football games. In March 2025, Rachel Reeves, the then chancellor, said shewould not accept free concert tickets againafter she was criticised for using free tickets to take a family member to see Sabrina Carpenter at the O2 arena. She defended the decision on security grounds but said she would not do it again because she understood “how people feel about it”.At the time, another government minister, Matthew Pennycock, said he had accepted “zero” free concert tickets as he personally did not think it was appropriate. “If I want to go to a concert at the O2, I’ll pay for it. But individual MPs, individual ministers, make their own decisions,” he said.The value of free tickets being accepted by MPs was at about £300,000 a year in 2025, according to the Times last December. But this appears to have increased, with almost £400,000 of complimentary tickets, hospitality and other gifts having been declared between January and July this year – not including foreign trips.Sue Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, suggested MPs should consider whether they should accept free tickets. “Some ministers and MPs appear to have short memories of the freebie-gate scandal that engulfed the first few months of Starmer’s time in No 10,” she said.“Showering MPs and ministers with gifts and hospitality is a tried and tested lobbying tactic by big business and foreign governments. There is no good reason why elected officials should be accepting jaunts and tickets to events that have nothing to do with their parliamentary or constituency business.”View image in fullscreenOlivia Dean performing at the Brit Awards in Manchester in February. Andy Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, accepted tickets to attend worth £3,800.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesDuncan Hames, the director of policy at Transparency International UK, added: “Just because something is permitted it is not necessarily appropriate.“MPs should be clear-eyed about why these invitations are really being offered. Before accepting hospitality, they should stop to consider what the company might be hoping to gain and what the public will make of it.”The scale of the declared hospitality may have gone up partly because ministers have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on theMPs’ register, after Starmer changed the rules around transparency. Previously, some ministers declared the value of their free tickets on the MPs’ register and some only put it on the quarterly ministerial register without showing a value if they could argue it was connected to their government job.Now both registers are updated at least monthly and have to show how much the hospitality or gifts were worth. Ticket prices have also risen, with many consumers complaining about the unaffordable costs of going to events.Under theupdated ministerial code,the last government set out a “well-established and recognised rule that ministers should not accept any gifts, hospitality or service which would, or might reasonably appear to, compromise their judgment or place them under an obligation to people or organisations that might try inappropriately to influence their work in government”.View image in fullscreenKing Charles during his visit to the Chelsea flower show. The shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, took £1,839 of hospitality from Lloyds Banking Group to attend the show.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/ReutersIt points out that ministers have a responsibility to represent the government, and their duties will sometimes require them to attend events where hospitality may be offered, and adds that it is “primarily a matter of judgment for ministers who are personally responsible for deciding how to act” in relation to accepting gifts.The acceptance of free tickets is not limited to Labour. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accepted tickets to Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the AllEnglandClub, while her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, took £1,839 of hospitality from Lloyds Banking Group to visit the Chelsea flower show. The shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith, also took tickets worth £919.50 to go to the Chelsea flower show, and £1,800 of tickets to the Formula One grand prix from Silverstone.Hundreds of backbench MPs were also wined and dined by corporations, including Google and Diageo, the drinks company. Many free tickets were provided by sports hosts and concert promoters, and some of them related to constituency interests, such as Powell, the Manchester Central MP, accepting tickets to Manchester City football matches and the first hosting of the Brit Awards in Manchester.View image in fullscreenConservative party leader,  Kemi Badenoch, enjoyed tickets to Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageAfter cabinet ministers who accepted hospitality were asked why they took free tickets and whether they would do so again while in office, a Labour party spokesperson said: “After Labour entered office, the ministerial code was strengthened to include new transparency requirements and clear principles governing the acceptance of gifts and hospitality. All declarations have been made in line with ministerial and parliamentary rules.”A Conservative source said: “All hospitality was properly declared in line with the rules. Transparency matters and we would expect the same standards and scrutiny to be applied consistently to politicians of all parties.”A PRS for Music spokesperson said: “PRS for Music advocates to policymakers on behalf of our songwriter, composer and music publisher members to protect the rights of creators and promote thevital contribution of the music industry to the UK economy.“Our public affairs initiatives create opportunities for stakeholders to engage directly with creators, experience how our industry works, see first‑hand the challenges they face, such as the impact of AI and post‑Brexit EU touring barriers, and understand the real world implications of policy decisions on music creators’ livelihoods.”Explore more on these topicsPoliticsParty fundingEnglandLobbyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour stalling on Jackdaw and Rosebank because ‘heart’s not really in it’, says Badenoch – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: Conservative leader says it is essential decision on oil and gas fields made as soon as possible, despite widespread concerns about climate impact
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: Conservative leader says it is essential decision on oil and gas fields made as soon as possible, despite widespread concerns about climate impact
Content: 09.52 EDTIt is “absolutely essential” a decision is made on the Rosebank and Jackdaw oilfields as soon as possible, Conservative leaderKemi Badenochhas said.Consultations for both developments have closed in recent weeks, with ministers now set to make a decision on their future in what is seen as a key environmental test for prime ministerAndy Burnham.While 3,500 construction jobs could be created, and 880 for the life of the fields, environmental activists have raised concerns about the climate impact. Speaking during a visit to a farm in East Lothian on Friday, Badenoch said the government’s “heart’s not really in it”.When asked if the decision should be made as soon as possible, she said:double quotation markIt’s absolutely essential. If this decision had been made earlier in the summer, we could have had gas from Jackdaw in people’s homes by this winter, by Christmas.All of the gas that’s drilled in the North Sea is used in this country and Labour has been kicking this decision into the long grass because their heart’s not really in it.They don’t know how to actually make energy cheaper, they don’t know how to get genuine tax revenue, and all they’re doing is increasing taxes, destroying businesses.A commonsense approach is to make sure that we drill our own oil and gas in the North Sea, get the tax revenue from that instead of importing oil and gas from countries that drill it in a very dirty way, which is actually increasing carbon emissions.Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch, climbs aboard a combine harvester during a visit to Balgone Barns Farm, on Balgone Estate in North Berwick.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAShare

title: Trump threatens $5bn lawsuit over liberal national guard policy report  | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: A report released by thinktank Cap argues the deployment of the national guard failed to have a measurable impact on crime, despite costing billions
Author: George Chidi
Headline: A report released by thinktank Cap argues the deployment of the national guard failed to have a measurable impact on crime, despite costing billions
