This would go beyond the vetting of AI hacking abilities that the White House is now pursuing. It would look at a range of risks and dig deep into company practices. It should be less like filling out a questionnaire and more like a nuclear safety inspector who has deep, frequent access to the company.If an AI slowdown is needed, auditing would also reassure each company that their competitors are playing by the rules.Second, they could actively participate in the organizations already built for this purpose of coordinating across the industry, such as theFrontier Model Forum, and move quickly to establish complementary ones.Elon Muskrecently saidthat AI companies should meet periodically to share notes on safety – as if this was an unheard-of concept. He or his staff could join existing conversations along these lines tomorrow if SpaceX joined the Frontier Model Forum, which has already worked through the complex antitrust hurdles involved in safety information sharing. Other cross-industry institutions will be needed for other purposes, and do not require government action to get founded and funded.Third, they could invest in the technologies we need to make AI guardrails global.Critics of the idea of an AI slowdown correctly point out that American companies couldn’t slow down for very long without China catching up. Butneither the US nor Chinawants to lose control over AI, and each country takes AI more and more seriously by the day, so cooperation can’t yet be ruled out either. A key question is whether we prepare in advance. In order for the US to be highly confident that China couldn’t violate an AI agreement, and vice versa, we’ll need sophisticated verification technologies like those developed during the cold war for nuclear arms control.Fortunately, there is a growing ecosystem of researchers and engineers developingthoseverytechnologies: tools that can prove a set of chips is only running existing AI systems rather than training new ones, that those chips are in a certain physical location, or that the system that got tested is the same one being deployed at scale. AI companies could accelerate the development of this critical type of technology today through funding and participation in pilot projects, but to my knowledge, they haven’t yet done so.Fourth, they could proactively push – and certainly should not kill – legislation that leads to stronger incentives for safety, security, and external oversight.How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreYou can’t complain about an irresponsibleAI race while fighting commonsense guardrails. Less than a year ago, some of thesame companieswho are asking for regulation now were pushing to overturn most state AI laws. We still have no real legislation on frontier AI on the books at a federal level, and the first AI auditing requirement at the state level won’t kick in until 2028.There are promising bipartisan proposals in Congress right now, such as the Frontier Act from the US representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, which would require developers of advanced AI systems to create a risk management framework, report dangerous incidents, and subject themselves to independent audits. These and other commonsense proposals, such asprotecting AI whistleblowerswho disclose safety incidents directly to the government, deserve vigorous support.I agree with the signatories, and am glad that after many years of being ignored or downplayed, the risks of unbridled AI competition are widely recognized. The US government should be doing its part to address this, and swiftly. But making AI go well is a shared responsibility. Companies that lag behind their peers on safety, don’t invite external audits of their systems, or call for brakes while doing little to build them won’t be able to blame the AI race when something goes wrong.Miles Brundage is an AI policy researcher who leads theAI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute(Averi). He previously worked at OpenAI as head of policy research and senior adviser for AGI ReadinessExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicChinaElon MuskComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: I am often asked how young boys could be rapists. For many adolescent men, the answer is entitlement | Chanel Contos | The Guardian
description: Violent pornography and algorithmic feeds are teaching young people to prioritise their own sexual gratification. As the problem evolves, so too must our solutions
Author: Chanel Contos
Headline: Violent pornography and algorithmic feeds are teaching young people to prioritise their own sexual gratification. As the problem evolves, so too must our solutions
Content: ‘In Australia and the US, adolescent boys have now overtaken adult men as the most likely perpetrators of sexual violence against an under-18-year-old,’ writes Chanel Contos.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In Australia and the US, adolescent boys have now overtaken adult men as the most likely perpetrators of sexual violence against an under-18-year-old,’ writes Chanel Contos.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesOpinionI am often asked how young boys could be rapists. For many adolescent men, the answer is entitlementChanel ContosViolent pornography and algorithmic feeds are teaching young people to prioritise their own sexual gratification. As the problem evolves, so too must our solutionsFri 21 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTShareThis week, the Australian public has borne witness to another devastating string of sexual assault allegations. While the alleged perpetrators vary in age – some are as young as 13 – they have something in common.They are immersed in elite institutions like private all-boys’ secondary schools – places that can socialise entitlement, exceptionalism and impunity in those within them. Of course, to the extent charges have been or are laid in these cases, those accused must be entitled to the presumption of innocence.My thoughts are with the girls and women who have alleged these crimes, and I wish them the best in the criminal process ahead, which we know is often traumatic for victims.In Australia and the US, adolescent boys have now overtaken adult men as the most likely perpetrators of sexual violence against an under-18-year-old. The Australian child maltreatment study found that 18.2% of Australians aged 16 to 24 have experienced sexual abuse by an adolescent before age 18, while a comparative 12% have experienced sexual abuse by an adult.This research solidified what was intuitive to us at Teach Us Consent when we called for, and then published, 6,700 testimonies alleging peer-on-peer sexual assault in teenage years.Across the year, my team has heard from multiple criminal lawyers who all describe a stark drop in the age of defendants and complainants in the courtroom, alongside a rise in violent sexual behaviours including strangulation, anal tearing and other forms of physical harm in youth.These are all behaviours that children are repeatedly exposed to if they access mainstream pornography – unfortunately still the main form of sex education in Australia.Pornographic sexual scripts that romanticise coercion, eroticise violence and depict male domination as the desirable default are victimising both boys and girls as they attempt to navigate their adolescent sexualities in a minefield of distorted desires, body expectations and gendered sexual scripts that reinforce power imbalances.I believe this is increasing entitlement for instant sexual gratification and to women’s bodies.Almost weekly, Teach Us Consent is approached for comment regarding another case of a teen allegedly engaging in a disturbing act of sexual violence. We know that the vast majority of rape cases never get reported, much less make the mainstream media. If we printed every act of gender-based violence that occurred in this country each day, the newspaper would run out of pages.I’m often asked: how can nice, sweet boys be rapists?Most rapists hold misogynistic views, condone violence, endorse rape myths and associate strongly with the masculine role. However, given how many people in our society have raped, it is not useful to understand rapists as a homogenous group.Based on forensic research, the general theme of classification systems of identification are: if the rape committed was motivated by sexual or non-­sexual desires; and then, if non-­sexual, if it was anger, hate or a need for power and control.Finally, there is the question of if the rape was impulsive or planned.Research has categorised offenders into four types. I believe the fourth, the “opportunist rapist,” is better described as the “entitled opportunist” because it is that entitlement that often underpins the motivation.These rapists have high social competence and their offences are predatory acts that are unplanned and show little self-impulse control.Little anger is exhibited and minimal violence, which means their method of rape is usually sexual coercion (tricking, pressuring or forcing someone into a sexual act in a non-­physical way), or using drugs or alcohol so the victim cannot consent or is unable to withdraw consent.Their motivating factor does not come from a place of malice or sadism, but the prioritisation of their own immediate sexual gratification.These types of rapists are often confident, powerful and opportunistic in other parts of their lives – all socially admired values in men.This type of rapist may very well be perceived as a “nice” person, and they are often not aware of the fact that they have sexually assaulted someone until they learn about consent – if they ever do.Importantly, the “entitled opportunist” often perpetrates for the first time when they are a teen, and – unlike the other three types of rapists – is unlikely to reoffend if held accountable for their actions.In question time two days ago, Anthony Albanese was asked by the independent MP Zali Steggall what additional plans his government had to address the worsening scourge of gender-based violence. In his response, the prime minister noted the stark and distressing increase in youth-on-youth perpetrated sexual violence.This awareness and recognition is welcome, because as the problem evolves, so too must our solutions.In addition to the variety of reforms recommended by gender-based violence and child sexual assault prevention experts, this must include addressing predatory social media algorithms, ideally through a robust digital duty of care that prevents tech-induced and facilitated harm before it occurs.At Teach Us Consent, we believe the option to turn off your recommendation algorithm and return to a chronological following-only feed could be one step in addressing this issue.Additionally, young people deserve to understand the factors at play in pornography so they can comprehend that this form of increasingly violent and degrading adult entertainment is not a script for sex to be mimicked.Alternative mechanisms of justice outside the criminal system must be imagined for survivors and perpetrators, because evidence shows us that effective responses that truly restore can prevent further harm – and because the criminal system is no place for children, who are perpetrating these crimes at higher rates than ever.Chanel Contos is the founder of Teach Us Consent and the author ofConsent Laid BareExplore more on these topicsOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way | Attieh Fard | The Guardian
description: I had few resources as a candidate but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better, says lawyer and byelection candidate Attieh Fard
Author: Attieh Fard
Headline: I had few resources as a candidate but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better, says lawyer and byelection candidate Attieh Fard
Content: A Reform UK campaign bus in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, on 4 August 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenA Reform UK campaign bus in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, on 4 August 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionClacton byelection August 2026Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same wayAttieh FardI had few resources as a candidate, but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much betterFri 21 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 09.22 EDTShareIn the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. Itshowed Nigel Farageamong his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.He was referring to the33 other candidateswho had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt ofan undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whomI was one.I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime hasmassacred thousandsof innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago thathe met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassyin London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about£250,000 of taxpayers’ money.Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UKleft the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard,but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, butNigel FarageMP has some serious work to do in Clacton.Attieh Fard is a lawyer who was an independent candidate in the Clacton parliamentary byelectionExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageImmigration and asylumReform UKUK bill of rightsHuman Rights ActHuman rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Women’s football shouldn’t have to copy a men’s game that isn’t working – just look at Ted Lasso | Karen Dobres | The Guardian
description: The rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinct, says author Karen Dobres
Author: Karen Dobres
Headline: The rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinct, says author Karen Dobres
Content: Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in season 4 of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAView image in fullscreenBrendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in season 4 of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAOpinionWomen's footballWomen’s football shouldn’t have to copy a men’s game that isn’t working – just look at Ted LassoKaren DobresThe rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinctKaren Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club BoardFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareThe fourth season of the critically acclaimed football drama Ted Lassohas taken a surprising twist. The show’s writers have decided to have their hero coach AFC Richmond’s women’s team, testing whether Ted’s “Lasso way” can work in a very different footballing environment. We’re only three episodes in, but I’ve already found myself wondering if the series will showcase what makes the women’s game distinct, or just treat it as the same sport with different characters.The early signs are promising: we’ve already seen the issue of substandard facilities, initial disinterest from the club’s fanbase and the flak that Coach Chilton gets for exhibiting the same qualities lauded in the men’s coach, Roy Kent.Watching the show, I found myself thinking about real-life football and asking whether, in growing the women’s game, we can avoid reproducing systems and structures present in its male counterpart.The classicist Mary Beard says in her book, Women & Power, “You cannot easily fit women into a structure that is already coded as male; you have to change the structure.” She was writing about women in public life, but her words could be easily applied to football, which remains stubbornly male-dominated.The typical men’s football clubis loss-makingand more than half of fans feel thathigh ticket costs have made the game less enjoyable. Why copy that?I discovered this reality when I (then an avowed football-disliker) visited Lewes FC in 2017, as this small club in East Sussex became the first in the world to equalise resources and facilities between its men’s and women’s teams. ItsEquality FCcampaign generated headlines around the world, and predictable criticism. Detractors said that the women’s squad didn’t attract the same crowds as the men’s, so why should they get the same resources?I went to watch Lewes FC Women for the first time, because, as a feminist and local, I was drawn by its pioneering closure of football’s gender resource gap. In a safe, joyful, inclusive environment, I experienced an “a-ha moment”. Yes, this is sport, I thought, but it is also a social and political act of defiance and change.Watching these women take up space, compete and play with such physical freedom made me feel like more than just a spectator at a game: I was watching women breaking free from patriarchy.This was something I wanted to champion and I went on to manage Lewes’s Equality FC campaign. I knew that the solidarity I felt, and the festival-like culture I experienced could resonate with other women whom football had not yet made welcome.The women’s game has a markedly different history to the men’s. In 1920, there were around 150 women’s teams and theyfrequently drew bigger crowds than men’s clubs, until theFA banned them from playing for 50 years. The women’s game has developed a rich culture of community, accessibility and inclusion – preciselybecauseit had to survive outside the traditional structures of football.This culture is now colliding with the fast-track “professionalisation” of women’s football, accelerated by big Premier League clubs subsidising their women’s teams. The women’s game is being rushed into copying and pasting the same structures as the men’s. Worse still, the financial chasm opening up at the top of the game –between the big four teams of WSL1 and all other women’s teams– is causing some owners to reasonably conclude that the cost of becoming competitive in women’s football isescalating fasterthan the revenues they can generate. In turn this leads toa fragile football pyramid.View image in fullscreenForest Green Rovers have scrapped their women’s team for the 2026/7 season.Photograph: Phil Mingo/PPAUK/ShutterstockBack in June, Durham, the only independent second-tier women’s club, werejust daysfrom being wound up (though they happily secured last-minute investment). This summer, nearly all of Plymouth Argyle’s women’s squadfound out via emailthat they were going to be let go after the club decided that the venture was “unsustainable”. Forest Green Rovers have scrappedtheir women’s team for all of this seasonandSouthamptonhave alsocut their women’s team’s budget.A female-centric future for the game hinges on players and fans no longer being treated as “small men”. That means reimagining facilities, medical support, childcare, sports science, kit, training and match-day experiences around female bodies and lives, rather than retrofitting a male model. This is happening, but sporadically. Despite money at the very top, the experience of most women’s teams is characterised bychronic underfunding.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis isn’t about handouts, but a wider distribution of revenues from TV money and league sponsorships would enable development of the women’s game across a much wider base. Increased FA Cup prize money, shared more evenly to smaller clubs, would be – literally – a gamechanger.Women’s football offers distinct audiences and values that should be highly attractive to sponsors. Think match-day experiences combining sport with music, food, art and community that would attract people who don’t see football as “for them”.That is the approach I hope Ted Lasso will ultimately showcase. By switching to women’s football, the series can help raise the game’s profile more than any individual club ever could.Women’s football, sidelined and kept humble for so long, may finally get some of the respect it deserves, on, and consequently off, screen. This game can change communities, it can change people’s lives, it can change the world.But ultimately women’s football needs its own identity and ecosystem. And that requires radical thinking.Karen Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club BoardExplore more on these topicsWomen's footballOpinionTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: I put myself in the prime minister’s shoes – and learned some uncomfortable lessons | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: On the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrust, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: On the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrust, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Screenshots from the political survival game No 10: Full Confidence.Composite: Sleepy Boy StudiosView image in fullscreenScreenshots from the political survival game No 10: Full Confidence.Composite: Sleepy Boy StudiosOpinionPoliticsI put myself in the prime minister’s shoes – and learned some uncomfortable lessonsZoe WilliamsOn the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrustFri 21 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTShareNo 10: Full Confidenceis the gameall the lobby journalists and backbenchers are playing on their phones. Westminster hasn’t been so united by an app since the early 2010s, when everyone was trying to figure out whatDavid Cameron saw in Angry Birds.The game is quite engrossing: you are the prime minister, taking office, and your name is Yusuf Dunmore. Popularity starts high in all the important areas – cabinet, backbenchers, the media, the public. But from there, every decision you are called upon to make, from nominating a chancellor to your answers at PMQs, confronts you with an invidious choice between one crisis and another.I was ready to resign in my third week – still technically the honeymoon period. The bad faith was all too overwhelming: an opposition that howled blue murder over things it didn’t even disagree with; a press that misconstrued for fun; a public with the aggregated emotional stability of a three-year-old who hadn’t had a nap. Marshalling all that while maintaining your own probity, when you had only intended to be 15%honest in the first place, seemed like more than any decent person could stand. None of this is to cast any shade on the game itself, which is very fun.It’s always a useful corrective to put yourself in a prime minister’s shoes. Ten years ago, Peter Bull, a psychologist at York University, analysed the ways in which politicians avoid giving direct answers, and submitted that, at the time, Theresa May was our most evasive prime minister yet – in one interview, she answered a question straight only14% of the time.Bull was empathetic. Prime ministers have to protect their positive face (avoid making themselves look bad) at the same time as their negative face (avoid committing to anything, so they keep their freedom of action). The smart move in the immediate term is to say nothing of substance at all, but in the long term, that fosters an almost nihilistic alienation in the electorate. If you can’t trust someone to communicate something when they speak, what can you trust them with?It’s only when you consider things from the politician’s perspective that you recognise we’re in a dynamic system of mutual distrust that spores and intensifies from one prime minister to the next: they’re evasive because they don’t trust our reactions; we lose trust because we can’t believe or make sense of their words. They then become ever more evasive, or alternatively, start to commit themselves wildly – to opinions, policies, values – in a bid for electoral popularity, which they then renege on.It’s obvious, looking back, that May was simply the most evasive PMso far; you would definitely go to her for a straight answer before you’d go to Boris Johnson. Keir Starmer’s defenders always liked to point out, when his approval ratings tanked, that this wasn’t personal; this was politics – in the years since Brexit, every prime minister has faced severe unpopularity scores. We were meant to draw the conclusion that it wasn’t him, it was us, so we should just knuckle down and be governed; but the more devastating implication was that every time trust in a leader wanes, that lingers as a legacy for the next. In some recent cases, that was the prime minister’s only legacy (though, fair play to Liz Truss, mymortgage is also still incredibly high).What a depressing thought, so let’s get back to your phone. The first decision to make as prime minister is who your chancellor should be, and never has theBrazilian philosopher Roberto Ungerbeen more elegantly distilled: we think political ideas are realistic only to the extent that they match what we can already see, he argued. Your choice is between Reginald Forthwright, who the public loves and the markets hate, and Harriet Voss, ex-investment banker, who the markets love and the public has never heard of.Forthwright’s actual economic policy, though, is a 3% flat tax on everything, and Voss has no policies at all. This reflects a truth even harsher than the mutual-suspicion doom loop, which is that we have absolutely lost the ability to conceive of the economic governance of the state, except in terms of the bond markets. Those who kowtow to them are realistic; those who don’t are living in a dream world, and the markets themselves are simultaneously omnipotent and labile – they don’t even know what they’re going to like until they see something they don’t – yet we must all, for the purposes of being grownups, surrender to them.What pushed me over the edge as a new prime minister, though, was my “first howler” – in a press conference, I accidentally gave an answer that was the opposition’s policy, not my own. A gif had been made of my ensuing confusion before the event was over. In the 45 seconds I had to decide what to do next, I dwelt (unwisely, given the time constraints) on how the mistake would have come about. Either I was lukewarm about my policies and was only in the job because I thought I’d be good at it(Cameron-style). Or I was under so much pressure that my mouth was making noises without any input from my brain (could be May, Sunak, even Truss). Or perhaps I would literally just say anything to get out of a spot (a la Starmer).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter a few hours of playing, though, I was sure of one thing: the new normal that is reflected in this game – that was co-created by us, the unforgiving voters – is prime ministers without a communicable sense of self and purpose. Recovery will, likewise, be a group effort, but will have to start at the top.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionAppsMobile gamesTheresa MayDavid CameronGamesLiz TrusscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Illustration: Jason White/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jason White/The GuardianOpinionCyclingI’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not meSimon JenkinsThe essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rulesFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareIplead guilty. I have loved and used the streets ofLondonall my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic.When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders ofebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyoneto moveout of the way.I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineerHans Mondermanboldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out foreach other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials.His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable successacross northern Europe, with accidents falling. In 2023,45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school.As a lifelong cyclist I admit to finding a certain exhilaration in riding a bike. I avoid main thoroughfares but like snaking through streets crammed with traffic, finding shortcuts through alleys and mews. But the essence of cycling is to keep moving. Hence I have to admit to sometimes doing what many London cyclists do at red lights. That is, look carefully, follow Monderman and “share” any unoccupied road space ahead by riding on.Traffic lights can now be rendered sensitive to queues waiting at them, and change sooner to green to allow buses through. Earlier this year, a policy director for the bike hire company Lime said he wantedlights to give priority to cyclists“to improve rider behaviour and encourage more people to cycle”. This makes sense. For the time being, at pedestrian crossings, cyclists should probably just get off at a red light and cross on foot.Investment in London’s cycle network is enabling more people to travel by bike, with the strategic cycle networknow 352km long, up from 90km in 2016. It is impressivethat this network was created by the same London planning authority that, 50 years ago, thought the answer to traffic planning was to build a giganticMotorway Box.Certainly cycling in any city is risky. The only truly safe speed is zero. But allcyclists will have their own “risk thresholds” – and the risk is largely up to them.The Highway Code’s “rules” for cyclistsare near hilarious. They boil down to two words: take care.My argument is less true when applied toebikes, I admit. These clearly do not work in shared space, whatever Monderman might have said. Electric Santander and Lime bikes may have transformed journey times: except for the simplest train ride, they can be the fastest means of travel across town. But this comes at a price.Ebikeslitter public streets with tips of abandoned machines; convenience is the mother of shambles. It cannot go on and technology must ensure bikes are properly parked.Ebikes now come in all shapes and speeds. It is astonishing that the sleek Freesky Alaska, with its 250W engine, can be treated as if it was just another manualpedal bike. To my mind, it is blatantly a motorbike. When a delivery driver on one careers past me in Hyde Park, I wonder if I took a wrong turning. These machines must be put on the roadway where they belong.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLondon used to be unique among great cities in being an enjoyable place to drive. It is no longer that. The bicycle has replaced that pleasure with a new freedom – but like all freedoms, it is one that craves intelligent regulation.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsCyclingOpinionCity transportEbikesTransportLondonRoad safetycommentShareReuse this content

title: Mike D: ‘After Yauch died I couldn’t make music. I’d open a computer file and just feel sadness’ | Beastie Boys | The Guardian
description: As part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his past
Author: Alastair Shuttleworth
Headline: As part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his past
Content: All joking aside … Mike D.Photograph: Dan LoweView image in fullscreenAll joking aside … Mike D.Photograph: Dan LoweBeastie BoysInterviewMike D: ‘After Yauch died I couldn’t make music. I’d open a computer file and just feel sadness’Alastair ShuttleworthAs part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his pastFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s funny how far a joke will get you,” Michael Diamond grins. This time 40 years ago, the New York rapper known as Mike D was working with schoolfriends Adam “MCA” Yauch and Adam “Ad-Rock” Horovitz on Licensed to Ill, their 1986 debut album as theBeastie Boys.The “joke” in question is that record’s cartoonish send-up of frat-bro culture, set to fusions of hard rock riffs and hip-hop beats. As for how far it got them: destinations included global stardom, a page in the history books with rap’s first US chart-topping album, and the crosshairs of British tabloids as they roused a generation to “fight for your right to party”.The Beastie Boys would evolve into one of the most musically and socially progressive acts of their generation, with a run of boundary-pushing albums touching on politics and spirituality until they disbanded in 2012 after Yauch’s death from cancer. Diamond has since focused his creative energies on producing records for Soft Play and the Hives, while his sons, Skyler and Davis, took up performing as musicians themselves with the indie pop duo Very Nice Person.double quotation markWhen you’re 19, you’re just spewing out whatever, like: ‘This is going to be hilarious’Sitting in the lounge of his London hotel, happily munching cereal between questions, the wiry, thoughtful 60-year-old seems content in this quieter chapter of his career. But after jamming with his sons reignited his passion for writing, he is returning to the mic with his dizzyingly creative debut solo album Thank You.The Beastie Boys formed in New York City in 1981; all three members hailed from artsy, middle-class backgrounds – Diamond’s father was an art dealer, and his mother an interior decorator.The group quickly decided “we had to have our own personas that were distinct and separate”, and took inspiration from teen comedies such as 1979’s Meatballs. The results were the beer-crushing, school-hating louts heard on Licensed to Ill. “When you’re 19,” Diamond says, “you’re just spewing out whatever, like: ‘This is going to be hilarious.’ You haven’t faced a majorreactionyet.”In the UK, they faced the strongest reaction of all. With an album strewn with sexist and homophobic jokes, shows featuring a giant inflatable penis and go-go dancers in cages, and tabloids circulating (instantly denied) rumours about them mocking sick children at Montreux pop festival, their 1987 UK tour stirred a Sex Pistols-style moral panic. MPs issued calls to ban them from performing.“Get Lost Beasties” ran one headline in the Mirror.Their Liverpool show was cut short after just 12 minutes and ended in a riot. “Britain was this lightbulb moment of: ‘Wait, what we say does actually impact people,’” Diamond says, calling the experience “terrifying, humbling, alienating and surreal”.They nearly split that year largely due to the fallout. The joke wasn’t funny any more; they also left their record label Def Jam after a dispute over royalties, then Horovitz moved to Los Angeles. But the group were creatively reinvigorated by Horovitz’s new west coast friends, the Dust Brothers, who were masters of digital sampling.“It was like our dream come true. We could have an old blues guitarist with a funk drumbeat and a jazz trumpet,” he says. “We could create these endless possibilities, this musical collage.” That collage was made into their second album, 1989’s Paul’s Boutique,a left turn that received a muted critical reception but has since been hailed as an experimental masterpiece.View image in fullscreenKings of the ill … Mike D (middle) with Adam Yauch and Adam Horovitz of the Beastie Boys, pictured in 1987.Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/GettyEven more striking is how the trio who once delivered punchlines such as “You like men and we like beers” (Hold It Now, Hit It) became beacons of positive social messaging. As mainstream rap largely grew more toxic through the 1990s, the band went the other way and apologised for past lyrics, declaring “the disrespect to women has got to be through”, (Sure Shot); “homophobics ain’t all right” (Alive); and “love can conquer hate in every situation” (Bodhisattva Vow).“In the same way we felt shame after some of the reaction to Licensed to Ill, we felt this nice, enriched feeling,” he says of the later albums. “I don’t want to get too ambitious here, as we are just a rap group, but maybe it changed how some people thought a little bit.” But across their albums, comedy and music remained partners. “They’re both things humanity desperately needs.”Diamond’s new record is also experimental and socially conscious. There’s plenty of his old band’s fun-loving eclecticism, with nods to industrial music, psych and dream-pop, while the lyrics take in self-reflection – the need, he says, to “look under the hood, check inside”. But this time the backdrop of laughter was replaced by grief. “After Yauch died, I couldn’t make music for quite a while. I’d open a computer file, and I’d just feel sadness.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markPart of ageing is this thing of your own mortality. You can push it away or acknowledge it and feel what you’re feelingHis return to rapping emerged from free-wheeling home-studio jams with his sons, whose brand of vivid indie pop is stamped all over Thank You. “When we first started playing, everybody just picked up something we’d basically never played before,” Diamond says. He began to loosen up, scribbling ideas in notebooks as they came to him, and dipping back into them during sessions. “When I started actually being open to writing lyrics that were more genuinely working around how I was feeling, it started to feel good,” he says. “It was this liberating thing.”Reflections on mortality loom large in Thank You; in It’s Time, he raps about “all these things that I want to get done”. For Diamond, Yauch’s death stirred up unresolved feelings. “In the New York we grew up in, there was a high mortality rate. We grew up in a club scene that was filled with drugs. Aids was brand new, and gay figures we knew from clubs started to drop dead. My dad died when I was 15. There was all this emotion I’d never dealt with,” he says. “Part of ageing is this thing of your own mortality. You can push it away and ignore it, or acknowledge it and feel what you’re feeling.”Rap-rock beasts and drive-by eggings: Beastie Boys’ 20 greatest tracks – ranked!Read moreAn acquaintance of his sons, who was getting rich from cryptocurrency at 19, inspired Thank You’s most overtly political track, Crypto. “I was just taken aback to see that’s the reality of the world we’re in,” Diamond says of its reflections on greed and capitalism. “You just get sucked so quickly into this vacuum.” I ask how his own experiences around that age may have shaped his attitudes on greed, given the Beastie Boys’ financial disputes with their label. “It was a great lesson that everything comes with a price.”Rather than money, Diamond feels “time is the most valuable commodity”, and returning to making and releasing his own music is time well spent. “I’m the most whole version of myself when I’m creatively completely engulfed and engaged.” There’s another note of contentment when he reflects on hip-hop generally, which the Beasties helped propel into the mainstream. He praises two artists who released their debut albums just as the Beastie Boys ended: Death Grips (“a real influence” on much current music) and Tyler, the Creator. “When I first saw Odd Future come out, I felt kind of happy inside – it felt like a continuation of an energy we brought.”Thank You’s closing title track is an impressionistic look at his early years, filled with fleeting images of partying with his friends at 16 (“We were just kids freaking out,” he sings). It strikes me as a possible parting tribute to the Beasties, but Diamond explains it’s universal. “It’s for everyone. This combination of your social group, your passion, coming of age, and music all stirred up together.” The title of the album, meanwhile, was inspired by a visit to a Buddhist monastery (the religion practised by his old friend Yauch) which prompted him to reflect on “who I get to make music with, who I’ve made music with”. A smile spreads across his face: “I’m so grateful for all of this.”Thank You by Mike D is out on 28 August.Explore more on these topicsBeastie BoysHip-hopPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: When TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any more | Television | The Guardian
description: They were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted by
Author: Sirin Kale
Headline: They were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted by
Content: Ironically, it’s all too ugly … America’s Next Top Model.Photograph: Hyungwon Ryoo/CBS Broadcasting Inc.View image in fullscreenIronically, it’s all too ugly … America’s Next Top Model.Photograph: Hyungwon Ryoo/CBS Broadcasting Inc.TelevisionWhen TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any moreThey were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted bySirin Kale,Stuart Heritage,Alexi Duggins,Rachel Aroesti,Isabelle Aron,Chitra Ramaswamy,Phil Harrison,George Francis Lee,Michael Hogan,Leah Harper,Ann LeeandJack SealeFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerica’s Next Top ModelWhen I think of the summer holidays when I was a teenager, I think of watching America’s Next Top Model for hours on end, critiquing each contestant with my sister. The makeover episode was always my favourite: girls sobbing as their hair was cropped short, or even shaved off. At the time, Tyra Banks seemed like a big sister, giving the contestants the tough love they’d need to succeed in a ferociously competitive industry. Now I feel differently. I hadn’t watched America’s Next Top Model since I was young, but like many, I recently watched Netflix’s excellentseries, Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model. It was the strangest sensation, rewatching episodes I hadn’t seen in more than two decades. At times I felt almost teleported back. How could I not find these scenes of models collapsing with hunger utterly abhorrent? I wondered what influence watching a show that celebrated eating disorders had on my own brain. I think it had an impact. I think the residual taint of it is still there. I can’t watch America’s Next Top Model any more, nor do I want to. Ironically, it’s all too ugly.Sirin KaleThe ApprenticeView image in fullscreen‘No show has a worse legacy’ … Alan Sugar in The Apprentice.Photograph: Talkback/BBCTruly, has any show in the history of television had a worse legacy thanThe Apprentice? The main culprit is obviously the American original, for the way it legitimised Donald Trump, but the British version doesn’t exactly get away scot-free. In terms of values, it preaches the sort of idiocy that should have been torched after the financial crisis; competitive selfishness and relentless greed at all costs. It has also churned nimrod after nimrod out into the media landscape. Plus, it isn’t fun to sit through. Why are people still applying for this mess? Why are any of us still watching? I can’t believe I used to enjoy this show.Stuart HeritageGood OmensView image in fullscreen‘It used to be my happy place. Now, not so much’ … Michael Sheen and David Tennant in Good Omens.Photograph: Chris Raphael/Amazon PrimeThere are few less complicated joys for me than the writing of Terry Pratchett. In my early teens, I fell for it hard – until that point, I didn’t know books could be that silly, or surprisingly profound, while also featuring a magical orangutan. I spent years diving back into it whenever I needed something to make me smile. So when Prime Video’s adaptation of Pratchett and Neil Gaiman’sGood Omenscame out, I was overjoyed. After years of ropey TV adaptations that failed to channel the way Pratchett’s writing balanced goofiness with seismic moments of drama, they’d finally got it right. David Tennant and Michael Sheen’s sparkling chemistry! Gaiman keeping things true to the book! Special effects that didn’t suck! For years, it was TV that I treasured. Until, that is, Gaiman became embroiled in sexual assault allegations, which he denies. I haven’t even seen the finale. This used to be TV that took me to my happy place. Now, not so much.Alexi DugginsThe OfficeView image in fullscreenDeeply disconcerting … Ricky Gervais as David Brent in The Office.Photograph: BBCFirst things first: I still considerThe Officeto be a masterpiece. As a satire of reality TV, as a character study, as a gimlet-eyed portrait of turn-of-the-millennium Britain, it remains unmatched. And that’s precisely why it’s so difficult to enjoy a quarter of a century later: it recreates the relentless sexist banter of the era with the same nauseating accuracy it brings to everything else. The wink-wink misogyny might seem quaint compared to today’s manosphere, but to revisit the show in 2026 is to be reminded of a time when tedious yet still threatening jokes about women were part of the rhythm of everyday life. The Office was always uncomfortable – it’s pure cringe comedy – but now it feels deeply disconcerting. That’s not necessarily a bad thing: the best art never ages into a cosily banal comfort blanket. Even so, one rewatch should cure most cases of Y2K nostalgia.Rachel AroestiMarried at First SightView image in fullscreenHugely troubling … Brook in Married at First Sight: Australia.Photograph: Geoff Magee Photography/Nine/Seven.One StudiosLooking for some light relief during lockdown in 2020, I started watching Married atFirst Sight Australia. The premise of the reality TV show is this: couples are matched by a panel of experts and meet for the first time at the altar. After they tie the knot, they go on a honeymoon, then move in together. Throughout the “experiment”, as it’s referred to, the group meet every week for dinner and a “commitment ceremony”, where each couple talk through how it’s going with the experts and decide if they want to stay or go. From sparks flying between couples to dramatic arguments at dinner, it makes for compelling reality TV. But earlier this year, a BBC Panoramainvestigationinto Mafs UK revealed that there have been allegations of rape and sexual assault on the show, hearing hugely troubling accounts from three women. Meanwhile, female participants on Mafs Australia havespoken outabout the vetting process, asking why men with past allegations of domestic violence and abuse have been allowed to take part. It’s another example of safeguarding failures in reality TV, and knowing what’s gone on behind the scenes, there’s no way I’d watch it now.Isabelle AronThis LifeView image in fullscreen‘Never again!’ … Daniela Nardini as Anna, Amita Dhiri as Milly, Andrew Lincoln as Egg, Jack Davenport as Miles and Ramon Tikaram as Ferdy in This Life.Photograph: BBCI was 17 whenThis Lifesauntered on to our screens, all miniskirts, Marlboro Lights and wild shagging. A deeply foolish age, I should have reminded myself, when I also believed in cargo pants and New Labour. God knows why I thought Amy Jenkins’s landmark series would have aged well when the 1990s so bracingly have not. Still, I poured myself a (metaphorical) pint of Stella and geared up for a nostalgic rewatch. Would I still fancy Egg? And want to be Anna? (No, and God yes, I’m only human.) I managed about three episodes before I nearly died of casual sexism, homophobia and boredom. Never again.Chitra RamaswamyI’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!View image in fullscreenA new kettle of witchetty grubs … Nigel Farage on I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here!Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockTo be clear, it was only ever the guiltiest of pleasures. But for many years, I foundI’m a Celebritymindlessly enjoyable as a vicarious adventure holiday and a schadenfreude-laden Z-lister hazing ritual. Ant and Dec’s gentle but pointed teasing of the participants was inclusive: it felt as if we were all in on the joke. Everything changed in 2023, when Nigel Farage signed up. Suddenly, the joke was on us. Mainstream political figures were tiresomely tolerable. Farage, though, seemed a different kettle of witchetty grubs: a poisonous figure, trading on the electorate’s worst instincts and being allowed to massage his image in primetime. Clearly, I wasn’t going to watch that – and I never have again. Fortunately, The Celebrity Traitors has arrived now, offering a far more palatable version of challenge-based famous-people foolishness.Phil Harrisonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Great British Bake OffView image in fullscreenRuined like a cake left out in the rain … Sue Perkins and Mel Giedroyc on The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Des Willie/BBC/Love ProductionsBake Offwas ruined for me like a cake left out in the rain when the rights to the show were dramatically bought from the BBC by Channel 4. After seven ad-less series on the BBC, negotiations over production costs saw the baking competition jump three doors down. In an act of solidarity, the show’s presenters Mel Giedroyc and Sue Perkins – along with its resident cake expert Mary Berry – decided not to follow the hit show. Bread baron Paul Hollywood, however, stayed, and a new cast of talent have endured his stoicism and personal brand of handshakes since. Not me, though. The betrayal soured my taste for village fete chumminess. The cutthroat affair was incongruous with the show’s image of wholesome Britain. It taught me that sometimes, under the layers of zingy fruit and flaky pastry, there’s a soggy bottom waiting.George Francis LeeEntourageView image in fullscreen‘Toxic masculinity – the TV show’ … Adrian Grenier, Jerry Ferrara, Kevin Connolly, Jeremy Piven and Kevin Dillon in Entourage.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyThe male Sex and the City™ was kind of fun for a while back there in the 00s butEntouragehas aged appallingly. Based on executive producer Mark Wahlberg’s life, it followed a movie star and his posse of hangers-on as they navigated Hollywood. This mainly involved chasing women around LA while fetishising cars and money. Potty-mouthed agent Ari Gold (Jeremy Piven) was a workplace bully whose treatment of his assistant Lloyd (Rex Lee) was racist and homophobic. Over eight seasons and a flopfilmsequel, it went from insider satire to douche-bro fantasy. I saw it pithily described online as “toxic masculinity – the TV show”. Creator Doug Ellin has accused HBO of burying the show due to “righteous PC culture”. Let’s not hug it out, actually.Michael HoganEuphoriaView image in fullscreenFetish slop … Zendaya as Rue in Euphoria.Photograph: HBOI’ve felt torn over watching the final season ofEuphoria. On the one hand, I was up for Rue’s spiritual awakening and Maddy’s career as a perma-eye-rolling talent agent assistant – plus who wouldn’t want to watch Sydney Sweeney and Jacob Elordi get hitched? But I’m not the only one left disappointed by Rue’s evolution into a horny drug mule, Cassie’s cam-girl aspirations and the fact that Kat (Barbie Ferreira) was entirely MIA. It wasn’t the life I’d dreamed of for my favourite debauched TV teens – and the online discourse calling out Euphoria for its male-gaze misogyny and descent into “fetish slop” didn’t make watching any more fun. Did I enjoy Jules’s turn as a sugar baby? Sadly, no.Leah HarperCouplingView image in fullscreen‘Like watching a sitcom written by Nuts magazine’ … Gina Bellman, Kate Isitt, Richard Coyle, Ben Miles, Jack Davenport and Sarah Alexander in Coupling.Photograph: Bbc/AllstarI first watchedCouplingwhen it aired in 2000, I thought it was a riotous comedy that was bitingly honest about dating, sex and relationships. During a rewatch recently, I couldn’t get past the vacuous characterisation of many of the women – among the group of friends we have Jane, a manipulative stalker, and Sally, whose main focus in life is not getting wrinkles. What I remembered as edgy humour was in fact puerile “jokes” branding women who refuse to be dumped as “unflushables” and about how getting your mate’s porn collection when he dies is a bonus. Then there’s the episode where Patrick is revealed to have a cupboard full of sex tapes after recording his exes without their consent. It was like watching a sitcom written by Nuts magazine, and every bit as sexist and unfunny as that sounds.Ann LeeHouse of CardsView image in fullscreenUnwatchable now … Kevin Spacey in House of Cards.Photograph: Netflix/Sportsphoto/AllstarHouse of Cardsdidn’t work when it tried to continue without Kevin Spacey as scheming politician Frank Underwood. But with Spacey now cast out, the earlier seasons are unwatchable too. That we liked Frank when we really shouldn’t have, because he was honest with us in his asides to camera – and because, dammit, he was good at lying and killing, and some of his victims deserved it – was a unique thrill, a forbidden suspension of our moral codes. The allegations about Spacey’s personal conduct make it impossible to keep that self-deception going.Jack SealeExplore more on these topicsTelevisionReality TVDramaTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You’re Killing Me review – did an AI monkey write this terrible Brooke Shields crime caper? | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second season
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second season
Content: Lower your expectations … Brooke Shields in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVView image in fullscreenLower your expectations … Brooke Shields in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewYou’re Killing Me review – did an AI monkey write this terrible Brooke Shields crime caper?I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second seasonLucy ManganFri 21 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLook, we all want Brooke Shields to be in gainful employment. We all want her to have a fabulous third act to her career. God knows, the child model turned star of prurient fever dreams Pretty Baby and The Blue Lagoon (and the “Nothing comes between me and my Calvins” jeans ad campaign when she was 15) has earned it. Plus, she did a fine turn in Friends and a number of us remember Suddenly Susan very fondly.But she’s terrible in the terrible new thing she’s in, which is a six-part comedy drama called You’re Killing Me. Shields plays successful cosy mystery novelist Allison Chandler, who lives in the picturesque town of Founder’s Cove, Maine. It’s Murder, She Wrote vibes all right, but please lower your expectations.Allison’s publishers are beginning to make noises about the need to attract a younger demographic to her books. Allison – who is less a character than a loose assemblage of simple responses to stimulants, though things improve slightly after the pilot – is outraged. She is also incredibly rude to young true crime podcaster Andi (Amalia Williamson), who comes to her book signing, because she knows Andi has called her work “outdated and inaccurate”. But when her sleazebag pal Nash Gilbert (Matthew MacFadzean) suggests that her latest book maybe isn’t her best work, she executes her reflection-response instead. Could the times actually be a-changing and leaving her behind? If only there was a young person around to ask and maybe learn from, however antagonistic she might be.View image in fullscreenSomeone to learn from? … You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVAlas, before Nash can guide her further on this voyage of self-discovery, he has plummeted to his death from a balcony. An apparent suicide – or is it? Soon, whichever AI monkey is in charge of storyboarding has contrived to bring Andi and Allison together to investigate what they believe to be murder. Soon the police, led by new county detective Coppy McCopface – sorry, I mean Jack Kerrigan (Tom Cavanagh) – agree. Plot is added (a blackmail setup, a naive stepdaughter, impromptu gift shop closures become pivotal, people are flung into car boots when the monkey realises nothing as happened for a while). Murder suspects duly emerge, are given a grilling by Allison and/or Andi, establish their alibis and then are banished to the wings until it is time for one of them to re-emerge and drop himself in it.Repeat with one new murder a week (adulterated EpiPen at a wedding, electrocution in a hot tub, and so on) set against the background of Andi and Allison learning to live, laugh, love and write a book together. It’s not the publishing deal you get that matters, of course – it’s the intergenerational bickering you are scripted along the way.There needs to be a moratorium on boomers/gen Xers watching in horror as young ’uns give their lengthy coffee orders to baristas. And on the latter explaining basic mobile phone functions to them. And on the former reacting like Victorian dowagers when they hear a word like “chatbot” or “Zoom”. I don’t know what the average age of the writers on You’re Killing Me is, but someone needs to tell them that Allison/Shields is 61, not 106. She would know what cancelling someone means and that it is not done by an annoyed woman shouting “I cancel you!” at another. Come on.View image in fullscreenShe’s 61, not 106 … You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVThe whole thing is thin, lazy and so disappointing. It could have been fine – maybe even good. The setup has perfectly legitimate dramedy potential, with each of the two main characters having what the other lacks in terms of skills, experience and attitude. With a little effort, a little genuine wit, intergenerational stuff can be fun, funny and occasionally even illuminating. Someone somewhere should have thought to try it. Shields can do comedy, but here is thrown back on shrillness and interminably hamming it up to try to make things stick. Williamson is clearly capable of much more, too, but Andi is written mostly as an arrogant brat and there is nowhere really to take her.All that said – and I could say more – it has just enough charm (and honestly, if I could work out how, I would bottle it, sell it and retire to a picturesque cove of my own) and enough goodwill attached to Shields that I greet the news that it has been commissioned for a second series with hope rather than despair. I want it to work. I want it to improve, like it did – slightly – between pilot and subsequent episodes, and to become the Gilmore Girls-inflected, Murder, She Wrote homage it once flickeringly promised to be. But they do say that it’s the hope, at least as often as poisoned EpiPens, that kills you.You’re Killing Me aired on U&Drama and is available on U and on Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionTV crime dramaTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I could have put a deposit on a house or do this crazy experiment’: the British musician playing 365 gigs this year | Music | The Guardian
description: Isaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music scene
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: Isaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music scene
Content: ‘No busking!’ … Isaac Neilson performing in Barnsley.Illustration: Luke BrennanView image in fullscreen‘No busking!’ … Isaac Neilson performing in Barnsley.Illustration: Luke BrennanMusic‘I could have put a deposit on a house or do this crazy experiment’: the British musician playing 365 gigs this yearIsaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music sceneDavid RenshawFri 21 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a lively pub in Oxford this week, Isaac Neilson picked up his guitar and performed live for the 231st day in a row.The singer-songwriter’s performance at the Old Bookbinders is part of a marathon effort to play a gig every day this year. The challenge has seen him put nearly 20,000 miles on the clock of his Peugeot 208 and cost him the best part of his life savings. “I was in a position where I could maybe put a deposit on a house or I could do this crazy experiment,” says Neilson, 26. “I chose to go all in on the music.”Neilson plays punchy indie rock (albeit acoustically on these dates), and describes the mission as “insanely ballsy, borderline insane” – but the kind of big play he feels he needs to break into an industry where “nepotism and other invisible barriers” shut out many independent and working-class artists.Over a drink before his show, Neilson says he is determined to make it as a solo artist while also highlighting the UK’s grassroots music scene and testing the “old industry myth that if you work really hard then you can get somewhere”.Isaac Neilson: No Affection – videoSo far, he has performed in more than 60 UK towns and cities including 28 gigs in his native Derby. He performed for more than 500 people supporting Cast in Barnsley and, unsurprisingly, completely empty rooms during the World Cup. He thinks he has gone through “two major mental breakdowns and six minor ones” but says his voice has “never been better”.Often performing more than once a day, he is on course to log more than 400 performances by the end of 2026, an undertaking that takes a daily average of three hours on the road. He is often accompanied by his girlfriend, Ashlea, who manages his social media, while a manager came on board after learning about his goal.Neilson has been booking gigs through relationships with promoters, and by scouring Facebook and Instagram for venues with stage time. He has set just two rules. He must perform every single day, and “no busking”. A promoter in Georgia in the US has promised to fly him out should he maintain his streak until September. “Christmas Day is going to be difficult but I have a plan,” he says.Neilson describes himself as “frugal” and knows what he is doing makes little financial sense. He went into the year with just over £30,000 in savings and expects to end it with about £3,000. He estimates it is costing him about £400 a week to keep going, with fuel as his biggest expense. Friends’ sofas and long drives home help save on accommodation costs.View image in fullscreen‘Virality is overrated’ … at the Old Bookbinders Ale House in Oxford this month.Photograph: Nina Sebastiane/Yin Yang MediaBreaking new artists is an increasingly difficult proposition in a music industry where executives value social media followers and streaming numbers over untapped talent at open mic nights.There was outrage last month when the longstanding BBC Introducing stage at Reading and Leeds festivals was axed. Organiser Festival Republic promised to offer a “much wider pool of emerging talent”, with performances from the children of David Beckham and Liam Gallagher.Neilson is proud of his “anti-algorithmic, anti-AI approach”, though he is also pleased that his streaming figures and follower numbers – both between 3,000 and 4,000 – have increased this year. “Virality is overrated,” he says. “People are yearning for community and looking for a connection. Numbers on a screen don’t represent the impact you can make in the world if you actually go out and meet people. My marketing budget is the time I spend in a room with you.”Neilson’s mission wouldn’t be possible without the pubs, clubs and small venues in which he has performed, sites also facing their own challenges. Recently publishedfigures by the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA)suggest British pubs are in trouble. A total of 161, or two a day, closed in the first quarter of 2026 amid spiralling costs.“Hospitality is an experience economy now,” says Bruno King of the Temple pub in Doncaster, where Neilson performed in May. “You have to offer something different and we have live music three times a week. It’s one of the most popular aspects of our venue. People really do appreciate being able to support grassroots musicians.”‘This keeps the dream alive’: the bands sleeping at venues to make touring workRead moreConversely, last year the number of grassroots music venues in the UKshowed the lowest rate of annual decline since 2018, suggesting that the sector is stabilising five years on from the pandemic. Andy Burnham’s recent announcement thatpubs, clubs and live music venues will receive a 20% cutto their business rates bills next year was further welcome news.Live Trust CEO Jon Collins says the positive figures are “testimony to the commitment and passion of the people who are running the venues” but warns that challenges are still there. “It’s more expensive than ever to put shows on. Customers are still facing cost of living challenges while promoters having a bad night can lose a couple of thousand pounds.”Collins praises Neilson’s commitment and shares his belief that new talent can still be discovered on stage. “Nobody arrives fully formed on [Glastonbury’s] Pyramid stage,” he says. “You learn your trade, you find your voice and you build your audience from those earliest gigs onwards.”In Oxford, Neilson earns big cheers from a packed room of early evening drinkers, most of whom he manages to add to his ever-growing mailing list. After he steps off stage he is relaxed about where his undertaking will take him. “Regardless of the outcome of this year, I can die knowing I threw everything at it,” he says. And with that he is off to his next gig.Neilson plays Frome (21 August), Cwmbran (22 August), Bristol (23 August) and Mexborough (24 August), among others.
