title: David Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needs | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?
Content: Red Guardian – perhaps not an authority on interdimensional metaphysics?Photograph: MarvelView image in fullscreenRed Guardian – perhaps not an authority on interdimensional metaphysics?Photograph: MarvelWeek in geekMoviesDavid Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needsBen ChildThe actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 20.12 EDTShareNobody knows exactly what solemn blood oaths Marvel uses to prevent spoilers. But we do know that Andrew Garfield spent most of the run-up to 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home – in which he would eventually turn up as one of two secret Spideys –behaving as if Kevin Feige was standing behind him, holding up a giant card saying: YOU HAVE NEVER MET TOBEY MAGUIRE. So we can imagine it’s pretty full on. Why, then, has Avengers: Doomsday star David Harbour this weekapparently blurted out the biggest Marvel secretsince Ben Kingsley’s Mandarin in Iron Man 3?Invited by Variety magazine to offer up a line from Doomsday “completely out of context”, Harbour thought for a moment, adopted the Russian accent of his Red Guardian character andcame out with: “You … are Tony Stark.” Which is quite a thing to say about a film whose entire marketing campaign so far has depended on us accepting that Iron Man remains dead, and that the actor who used to play him, Robert Downey Jr, is playing Victor von Doom instead.So what’s going on? The simplest and most likely explanation is that Harbour is trolling us, that Stark is not in the movie at all, and we’re all just fools. The new trailer for Doomsday, premiered last weekend at Disney’s D23 event in Anaheim, leans heavily into the prevailing wisdom that the film’s villain will be the tyrannical, unstoppable baddie of spurious eastern European extraction that Stan Lee and Jack Kirby dreamed up in 1962.We even get to hear more of Doom’s heavily accented voice, and there is no suggestion that it belongs to anyone but Downey Jr beneath the mask. The footage talks repeatedly about “Victor”, hints at the supervillain’s tragic history and seems determined to establish him as a fully fledged character in his own right. IfMarvelis planning a rug-pull here, it is certainly doing an impressively thorough job.Not that this has stopped anyone.Some fans have already noticed that one closeup of the masked villain in the new footage appears to show a pair of blue eyes, rather than Downey Jr’s brown ones. Others noticed that the costume Marvel displayed at D23, on mannequins, was subtly different from the version shown at San Diego Comic-Con in July. From this slender collection of ocular and tailoring evidence has emerged the theory that there may actually be two incarnations of the character: Downey Jr’s version, perhaps initially presented as an ally; and a nastier variant who eventually replaces or kills him.Naturally, because Cillian Murphy has blue eyes and has spent years being fancast as Victor von Doom, the internet has decided that the second man behind the mask must therefore be Cillian Murphy. If it’s correct, this may be the first big Hollywood casting decision achieved entirely through collective wishful thinking – at least since Marvel rewarded years of online fancasting by briefly turning John Krasinski into a variant Reed Richards in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.View image in fullscreenCollective wish fulfilment … Cillian Murphy.Photograph: Mark Sagliocco/Bafta/Rex/ShutterstockThe irony is that Harbour’s line sounds plausible because Marvel has spent the past two years – ever since Downey Jr was unveiled beneath Doom’s mask at San Diego Comic-Con –slyly hinting that if you watch the next two Avengers films, you may just find out what the hell is going on. Now it has to actually make good on that promise, even though this is a universe in which umpteen superheroes (and enough filmgoers to rack up the best part of $3bn at the global box office) watched Stark save all existence by snapping his fingers and expiring in front of them in Avengers: Endgame.Avengers: Endgame review – unconquerable brilliance takes Marvel to new heightsRead morePerhaps Harbour’s line is genuine, and it is only our interpretation of it that is wrong. Red Guardian is hardly the MCU’s leading authority on interdimensional metaphysics: confronted by a man with Stark’s face, “You are Tony Stark” would be a perfectly reasonable thing for Alexei to say even if the answer is simply: “No, actually, I’m Victor von Doom.” This would allow Marvel to acknowledge the elephant in the room without turning its new villain into Iron Man gone bad, and still leave Downey Jr free to be exactly who the studio keeps insisting he is.Either way, the genuinely strange possibility now seems to be that Downey Jr’s return really does have absolutely nothing to do with Tony Stark. And yet, you do not bring back the actor who spent 11 years as the face of the MCU, put another metal mask over that same face and then expect audiences to regard the resemblance as an administrative coincidence. Harbour may have leaked the biggest secret in Doomsday, or he may simply have made up the most obvious line imaginable for a laugh.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekAvengers: DoomsdayRobert Downey JrMarvelSuperhero moviescommentShareReuse this content

title: Who Killed Marilyn? review – dismal attempt to solve mystery of Monroe with Pixie Lott | Theatre | The Guardian
description: An account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond cliche
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: An account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond cliche
Content: Tragic icon … Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at the Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenTragic icon … Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at the Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewWho Killed Marilyn? review – dismal attempt to solve mystery of Monroe with Pixie LottEmerald theatre, LondonAn account of the superstar’s life revisits her relationships and considers some conspiracy theories but never gets beyond clicheArifa AkbarFri 21 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been 600 books written aboutMarilyn Monroesince she died in 1962. So we are told by Monroe (Pixie Lott) herself in Sharleen Cooper Cohen’s play. The star’s body was discovered by her housekeeper, and her death at the age of 36 has spawned as many conspiracy theories as Elvis Presley’s. Was it an overdose, or a contract killing by the Kennedy family because she had kompromat on them? Did the mafia have something to do with it? Was an enema administered on the night she died? These are some of the questions that have been asked by Monroe obsessives.You imagine this drama is setting itself up for something beyond the slew of familiar theories. But there is little to gain from this trot through Monroe’s life, narrated in cliches.Lott has the signature blond hair, red lipstick and white pedal-pushers (she almost but not quite resembles the Marilyn of The Seven Year Itch scenes in a halter-neck dress). Monroe tells us that her husbands only ever saw the famed icon rather than the woman beneath. Ironically, this is what she remains here, due to a thuddingly on-the-nose script that spells out Monroe’s woes and pathologies. There are brief glimpses into her marriages with baseball player Joe DiMaggio (Henry Proffit) and playwright Arthur Miller (Ben Dilloway), and encounters with JFK (Mars Sams) and Bobby Kennedy (Paul Kane). There is no exploration of her first and potentially more illuminating marriage.View image in fullscreenBasic ‘tortured starlet’ psychology … Ryan Ellsworth (left) and Pixie Lott in Who Killed Marilyn? at Emerald theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithUnder the direction of Philip Wm McKinley, Lott struts on to a stage with a bed at its centre – both her place of death and an overused motif for the life of a sex symbol. She keeps strutting on and off, striking Marilyn-esque poses, without giving any true sense of the woman beneath the iconic exterior. The other performances are also underwhelming, with the men in her life played with a wooden uniformity and no uncanny resemblances. A sex scene with JFK ends with his backache and appears like accidental farce. The whiff of drama school end-of-year show persists.Abigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a CinzanoRead moreIt pays little attention to Norma Jeane – the person she was before she created Marilyn. There are fleeting references to her family history of mental instability, her early life in an orphanage, her experience in a psychiatric unit. These are drive-by glances in a play that prefers to centre Monroe’s sex life, in the most hackneyed of ways.Her unravelling at the end conveniently takes place with her psychiatrist (Ryan Ellsworth) in situ so she can expound on her pain and her breakthrough when she realises she has been trying to fill a “bottomless pit” within her. It is basic tortured-starlet psychology, which does little to develop the complexities of her inner world.There is an answer to the titular question at the end but the bigger mystery of who Monroe was remains entirely untouched.AtEmerald theatre, London, until 29 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMarilyn MonroePixie LottreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: As his new film Bitter Christmas is released the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himself
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As his new film Bitter Christmas is released the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himself
Content: ‘The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us’ …. Pedro Almodóvar.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us’ …. Pedro Almodóvar.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movieRyan GilbeyAs his new film Bitter Christmas is released, the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himselfFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlack sunglasses indoors and a tufty cloud of cotton-wool hair: it can only bePedro Almodóvar, bourgeois arthouse darling nonpareil and master of everything from screwball romps (Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown) to clammy thrillers (Live Flesh, The Skin I Live In) – and sumptuous melodramas such as his 24th film, Bitter Christmas, a cautionary tale about the perils of autofiction.We are sitting in the library of a London hotel and Almodóvar is dressed in a thin black windcheater, grey trousers and white trainers; add a whistle on a string and he could pass for a PE teacher. The 76-year-old director may have won more than 60 awards including two Oscars, five Baftas and six Goyas but when the shades come off today, he looks momentarily sorry for himself. He has been deaf in one ear since childhood, he tells me, and now the other one is giving up the ghost. In addition, a nasty stye has turned his left eye a gluey purple. Might he have picked it up while swimming? “I do swim almost every day because I have a pool,” he sighs. Never can those words have sounded so sorrowful.Then again, mixing contradictory flavours is part of what he does. There is the blank, blase approach to extreme material (murder, paedophilia, telekinesis) in his 1984 comedy What Have I Done to Deserve This? Or the climax of Matador, his kinky 1986 thriller, in which the race to prevent a double murder is paused while the characters gawp at a solar eclipse. A rape scene becomes comic in Kika, from 1993, and another rape is euphemised as a silent movie pastiche in 2002’s Oscar-winning Talk to Her.The peculiarities of Bitter Christmas begin but do not end with its release date: whoever heard of a film with a festive title opening during a summer heatwave? Almodóvar agrees: “It is weird.” Though we both know his ardent base would swarm to see whatever he did. Even when he was making cheap, guerrilla-style Super-8 shorts, he has always known the love of a good fan. Afterthe end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975, Almodóvar picked up thousands of underground followers in Madrid and Barcelona. They contributed more than $3,000 toward the budget of his 1980 debut, Pepi, Luci, Bom and the Other Girls on the Heap. Possibly the only thing he could do today to shrink his audience would be to ditch the eye-popping palette and make a film in black and white. “The colours are very important,” he says, as if anyone needed reminding.Part of the new movie already existed as a short story called Bitter Christmas, written in 2003 and published 20 years later inAlmodóvar’s collection The Last Dream. The story concerns a cult film director plagued, as Almodóvar really was at the time, by panic attacks and paralysing migraines. In the movie, Bárbara Lennie plays the stricken director, Elsa, who starts planning a new feature after years spent making commercials. “When I wrote Elsa’s little universe, I immediately got the idea that someone, a film-maker, was writing the story of Elsa that we were seeing,” he explains. That someone is Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia). Almodóvar, then, has directed a film about a director writing a film about a director writing a film.Keeping track of what is happening on screen becomes a case of mind over meta. Why should we care about Elsa’s story, though, when it is merely the product of Raúl’s imagination? “I hope that when the audience discovers that the film-within-a-film is going to change, that this change will surprise and excite them. But you’re right, it’s very risky. I think it is the riskiest film I’ve ever made. I took a whole bunch of risks, even knowing that some might not land. It requires you to pay complete attention, and it does seem to me that film audiences are increasingly getting lazy.”No prizes for guessing where he places the blame. Bitter Christmas sneaks in a jab at Netflix when someone suggests Raúl should take his new project there: “Don’t reduce me to making a TV movie!” he scoffs. Almodóvar made his own views plain in 2017 when he was president of the Cannes film festival jury. Two Netflix titles (Okja and The Meyerowitz Stories) were in competition that year even though they were never going to be exhibited theatrically in France; Almodóvar, who regarded the situation as a case of the US trampling all over European traditions,announced that he could not foresee awardsbeing “given to a film that is then not seen on the big screen”. So it proved.View image in fullscreenVictoria Luengo as Patricia in Bitter Christmas.Photograph: PRHis passionate defence of “the hypnosis of the large screen” was countered, however, by one of his jurors, Will Smith, who stood up for Netflix. The star’s name alone causes an almighty eye-roll today from Almodóvar, stye or no stye. “Will Smith was saying very silly things. The American press said things against me and in favour of him. And then, after years, they discovered how Will Smith is.” He mimes a slap, referring to the star’sattack on Chris Rock at the 2022 Academy Awards ceremony. Almodóvar, whose film Parallel Mothers was nominated for two Oscars that year,had a ringside view of the assault; his snowy dot of a head can clearly be seen in images of the incident. He later described the acceptance speech given by Smith after winning the best actor Oscar as resembling “that of a cult leader”.Reminded of this now, he says he thinks Smith still sounds like he is in a cult. “In our jury discussions at Cannes, everything he said sounded like that. He also showed me in all our discussions that he had very bad taste as a person. It was not a good experience being jury president. I didn’t want to do it but my brother [his producer Agustín Almodóvar] and [Cannes festival director] Thierry Frémaux insisted so much that I had to.”Back toNetflix. Have the streamers won the war? “They’re very close to winning,” he says gravely. “All the elements to do with releasing a film theatrically are disappearing. The film art, the posters, which we can then look back on and want to collect. Even the elements that seem banal, such as the fashion that the stars wear to a premiere.” He falls silent, then adds forlornly: “The excitement.”His principled stand in 2017 remains a lesson in defending home turf from bullies. “You can take this attitude to the political sphere. The European Union should be a shield for the crazy stuff Trump is coming up with in the US. He has created this lawless world, and we in the EU can demonstrate to him that if there’s something he wants to do, he needs to respect European laws. Trump is very angry at the EU and especially at Spain because our president has been brave and vocal in his opposition to his actions toward Ukraine and in his alliance with Israel.”Bitter Christmas is, however, less engaged with global issues than with the interior landscape of the artist, as so many of Almodóvar’s films have been. Insularity is to be expected from a director who admitted in The Last Dream that “writing about myself [is] pretty much the only thing I do”, and Bitter Christmas both addresses auto-fiction and represents an example of it. Raúl, whose loyal assistant, Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón), turns on him after discovering he has plundered her life in his screenplay, is, Almodóvar tells me, “a form of alter ego. At least 80% of Raúl’s dialogue is something I could say.”View image in fullscreen‘Cinema is what motivates me and moves me to live.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAn obsessive, perfectionist director himself, Almodóvar has written proxy figures before, most recently inPain and Glory from 2019, where the auteur played by Antonio Banderas admits that life without film-making is meaningless. But as long ago asThe Law of Desire, the torrid 1987 masterpiece, which he described in 1995 in the book Almodóvar on Almodóvar as “the key film in my life and career”, he was already alert to the threat posed by creative types like himself: that movie ends with the defenestration of a typewriter, which then bursts implausibly but spectacularly into flames.I ask whether he concurs with the poet Czesław Miłosz, who said: “When a writer is born into a family, the family is finished.” Almodóvar offers a minor tweak: “Not finished. But they’re going to have a lot of problems. It is pain that inspires me, not happiness. The writer by nature is selfish, which makes us dangerous to the people around us. It’s not very nice but this is what it is. That’s why I painted Raúl as almost the villain of the film.” Almodóvar claims to have only ever pilfered responsibly. “When I’ve been inspired by someone from my life, I’ve changed many elements to make them unrecognisable.”That isn’t quite true. He took the facts of a friend’s traumatic encounter with Eta terrorists, made them Shias instead, and played the episode for giggles in Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown. The friend was aghast. “Oh yeah,” he says, remembering now. “She got very mad when she saw the film. At that time, I didn’t get it because I saw it as a homage: I’d turned something dark that happened in her life into comedy.”View image in fullscreenAntonio Banderas in Pain and Glory, 2019.Photograph: Manolo Pavón/APThoughts of the damage a writer can do lead to the subject of the late Alice Munro. In 2016, Almodóvar adapted three stories from Munro’s collection Runaway into his film Julieta; one of those stories, Silence, describes a woman who severs contact with her mother, as Munro’s daughter had done. It onlyemerged posthumously in 2024that Munro had stayed married to her second husband after learning he had sexually abused her daughter years earlier.“What’s overwhelming is that she wrote that story after everything that had happened,” the director says. “I try not to judge but I find that incredible. The whole family were silent, too, which is very dirty, and as dark as the position of the mother. If I knew what had happened there, my adaptation would have been completely different.” Would he still have made Julieta, then, even if the terrible facts had emerged in time? “Yes, but the story is much better with the stepfather, the mother doing nothing, the daughter escaping the family.” I don’t doubt his horror at Munro’s behaviour. There is a faint chill, though, in hearing the screenwriter within him express frustration that a vital piece of the narrative puzzle was hidden from view.When it came to writing the scene in Bitter Christmas in which Mónica accuses Raúl of “vampiring” her, Almodóvar found the experience of self-criticism liberating. “All the things she says to him, I could easily say to myself. It’s refreshing and fun to be so nasty about yourself.” That might be because his own critics have been so thin on the ground. What they lack in number, however, they make up for in rigour. In 1993, film-maker Alex Cox pointed out that Almodóvar’s actors speak “the ‘official’ Spanish with the lisped ‘s’”, indicating “a certain societal correctness … which is naturally divisive and detrimental to the culture”. When Volver, a gumbo of ghosts, murder and mother-daughter devotion, was released in 2006,critic Peter Matthews saw onlythe “smooth, velvety craftsmanship” of a “failed iconoclast”. After Parallel Mothers,Leo Robson arguedthat, far from being rebellious, the director’s work has consistently parroted “orthodox and to some degree official Spanish attitudes”.The auto-critique in Bitter Christmas is nowhere near as harsh as all that. Almodóvar may see Raúl, his alter ego, as something of a villain, but he has also described himself as a “victim” of his own passion for cinema. Whether villain or victim, what price has he paid? “Sometimes I’ve suffered during shoots for various reasons,” he recalls. “You can encounter problems that you can’t even fathom. There have been a lot of painful moments but that is the price. One must never complain because it’s part of the adventure.”Almodóvar shows no evidence of slowing down, deafness and styes be damned. This October in Spain, he will even publish his first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. Before we part, though, I remind him that he is now the same age that his hero Luis Buñuel was when he madehis swansong, That Obscure Object of Desire, a film which ends, as The Law of Desire later would, with an explosion. How does it feel to be at that point? “Unlike Buñuel at that time, I am still completely full of desire to keep making films. Cinema is what motivates me and moves me to live. Buñuel was pressured by his producer when what he really wanted was to rest in Mexico.” A flash of defiance. “And I don’t ever want to rest.”Bitter Christmas is in UK and Irish cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmPedro AlmodóvarComedy filmsDrama filmsSpainNetflixComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alice Roberts: ‘By the time I’d finished Richard Dawkins I’d left faith behind’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and Toad
Author: Alice Roberts
Headline: The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and Toad
Content: ‘I love the way Darwin takes his readers on a journey’ … Alice Roberts.Photograph: Dave StevensView image in fullscreen‘I love the way Darwin takes his readers on a journey’ … Alice Roberts.Photograph: Dave StevensThe books of my lifeBooksAlice Roberts: ‘By the time I’d finished Richard Dawkins I’d left faith behind’The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and ToadAlice RobertsFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryThe first books I remember were from The Village with Three Cornersseries Sheila K McCullagh. I loved the – literally – colourful characters, like Johnny Yellow Hat. I was reading with my Grandma, in her garden perhaps, sitting on a small patio, surrounded by bright begonias and busy lizzies.My favourite book growing upArnold Lobel’s wonderful Frog and Toad stories. Toad would get himself tied up in knots, trying to find a button or fly a kite, but Frog was always there – a constant, caring and funny friend. I enjoyed reading these stories to my own children when they were young, and we still sometimes go back and revisit them. They’re so full of humour, heart and simple humanism.The book that changed me as a teenagerAt that time I loved Alan Garner, Susan Cooper and Rosemary Sutcliff. But the book I remember having a really profound effect on me was Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene. I was passionate about biology, and the gene’s-eye view turned it upside down and suddenly evolution made sense. I went on to voraciously read all of Stephen Jay Gould’s essays on evolutionary biology. Those two authors really inspired me.The writer who changed my mindWhen I picked up Dawkins’s The Blind Watchmaker,I was already beginning to seriously doubt the Anglican faith I’d been brought up in. By the time I finished it, I knew I’d left that faith behind. Biological diversity could be entirely explained through natural processes; there was no need for – and no evidence of – a divine creator. I became a humanist, although I didn’t know the word for it back then.The book that made me want to be a writerI never set out to be a writer. I wrote my first book as a handout to go with the first television series I wrote and presented on my own – Don’t Die Young on BBC Two. As a university academic, I wanted there to be something more to go with the programmes. I’d written papers of course, but nothing for a general readership, and I loved doing that. In my writing, whether that’s books or scripts for television and live shows, I always go back to Gould’s advice and example. He was adamant that it was possible to communicate complex ideas without “dumbing down” – you just need enough steps, and to strip away unnecessary jargon.The bookI came back toOne I keep coming back to – and this isn’t surprising for any biologist – is Darwin’s On the Origin of Species by Natural Selection. It’s so full of wonderful details and insights – and I love the way he takes his readers on a journey, from the known and familiar, to the novel and strange.The book I discovered later in lifeGeorge Eliot’s Middlemarch – I only really sat down to read it five years ago. I never got on with the Brontë sisters or Jane Austen at school, and in my head, I’d put Eliot away on the same shelf labelled “novels that were boring and banal but got away with it because they were early examples of the genre and so there wasn’t much competition”! It was Andrew Copson, chief executive of Humanists UK, who finally persuaded me to read Middlemarch and I was blown away by it – the complexity of the characters and the way it challenges your prejudices. It is a masterpiece.The book I am currently readingFor work I’m dipping into Fritz Graf’s Roman Festivals in the Greek East and Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price’s two volume series on the Religions of Rome. For pleasure, I have recently finished Val McDermid’s fabulous Queen Macbeth, and Karen Hao’s fascinating and troubling Empire of AI. I’m also listening to Otto English’s brilliant Notoriousaudiobook. And I am enjoying reading Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem to my teenage son – who still enjoys a bedtime story!My comfort readThe Little Book of Humanism– a book I helped to compile, full of wonderful, everyday humanist wisdom.The Goddess Queen by Alice Roberts is published on 1 September by Gallery UK. title: Salty Brine: How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show) review – one of today’s most powerful stage voices | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description:
Summerhall, Edinburgh
Intertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brew
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Summerhall, EdinburghIntertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brew
Content: Overbrimming … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOverbrimming … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSalty Brine: How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show) review – one of today’s most powerful stage voicesSummerhall, EdinburghIntertwining his diaries with Anne Frank’s gives Brine a tough job, but his passionate performance and force of will combine in a heady brewBrian LoganFri 21 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a hell of a swing to make a show paralleling your first love with Anne Frank’s – the more so for that show about her to end on an uplift. But Salty Brine is nothing if not the man for a big swing. This most overbrimming of cabaret artists is in town with hisLiving Record Collectionproject, which makes shows inspired by, and featuring, the songs from beloved rock and pop albums. This one takes Neutral Milk Hotel’s In the Aeroplane Over the Sea as the launchpad for an inquiry into religious traditions, the origins of the world, the migration of souls – and the adolescent passions of Frank and Brine.Is it in poor taste, I wondered, to co-opt the horrifying story of this murdered teenager for aesthetic effect? In Brine’s defence, the album in question itself riffs dreamlike on Frank’s story, fashioning from it something deeply moving – and the same could be said, for my money, of How Strange It Is.View image in fullscreenDeeply moving … Salty Brine in How Strange It Is (The Neutral Milk Hotel Show)Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianCombining extracts from his diary and from Frank’s, Brine vividly evokes the headlong nature of youthful passion, impossible to restrain even in the most constrained circumstances. Where does all that energy go when a life – not just Frank’s but that of her sweetheart, Peter – stops? With paper aeroplanes, a PowerPoint about reincarnation and one of the most powerful voices on the stage today, Brine hurls Jeff Mangum’s lyrics at the problem to see what sticks.Badgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarnRead moreNot everything does. Brine has a tougher job here than withthe Smiths’andAnnie Lennox’swork (to cite two recent examples) making the lyrics serve the beats of his story or the points he is trying to make. That’s sometimes frustrating – and elsewhere, not all of his connection-making resonates. But the material with which he is conjuring (life and death, what love and life add up to, and what we leave behind) is so emotionally potent, and the force of will applied to the undertaking so irresistible, that he makes the synthesis soar. Rhapsodic source material, passionate performance, cosmic sense-making: it’s a heady brew late night on the fringe, and an intoxicating one.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 7-19 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreCabaretAnne FrankreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Badgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarn | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Playwright and performer Malaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Playwright and performer Malaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer
Content: A message about the allure of storytelling … Malaika Kegode in Badgers.Photograph: Paul BlakemoreView image in fullscreenA message about the allure of storytelling … Malaika Kegode in Badgers.Photograph: Paul BlakemoreEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBadgers review – the audience investigates in this true-crime podcast yarnTraverse theatre, EdinburghMalaika Kegode delivers a supernatural story about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singerMark FisherFri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlaywright and performerMalaika Kegodetops and tails this show for Theatre Royal Plymouth with a message about the allure of storytelling. In a festival city bursting at the seams with stories, it is an unnecessary observation. A more important question is about which stories we choose to tell, which resonate and which pass us by. Why, for example, did Kegode want to write a story – and it is a story rather than a play – about the strange disappearance of a maudlin folk singer?She focuses on the subsequent investigation by Meles Costas, an under-qualified true-crime podcaster, living in the shadow of a high-achieving and terminally ill mother. And she laces her story with gothic fairytale imagery: folk songs with dark-magic properties, human-to-animal transmutation and a hint of witchcraft.Four Walls and a Roof review – fascinating tale of Brecht, the red scare and today’s émigrésRead moreAll intriguing stuff, but if Badgers has a greater purpose than telling a story for its own sake, Kegode does not make it evident. Fortunately, she tells it well. Casting the audience in the role of Meles (whose name is the Latin for badger), she describes a podcast interview with Bridget Brock, the missing man’s landlady, and juxtaposes it with the supernatural: did singer Ben vanish in 2015 because he had turned into a badger and was it because he had been cursed after stealing Bridget’s song?With a badger stripe hair-do, Kegode leads us with charm and precision into the haunting corners of Jenny Davies’s production, with texture added by her longtime collaborators,Jakabol, whose excellent score is played live by Beth Roberts and Joe Williams, tucked away in a sound booth. All good stuff for a dark and stormy night, but unless you are concerned about the ethics of true crime, not particularly urgent.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 August;Theatre Royal Plymouth, 2–5 September;Bristol Old Vic, 8–12 SeptemberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTrue crime (Podcasts)FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Daily Mail accused of stalking woman mistaken as White Stripes drummer Meg White | The White Stripes | The Guardian
description: The tabloid boasted in a now-deleted article that they found White and promised to reveal her ‘secret new life’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The tabloid boasted in a now-deleted article that they found White and promised to reveal her ‘secret new life’
Content: American rock duo The White Stripes, which consisted of Jack White and his ex-wife, Meg White.Photograph: Tim Roney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmerican rock duo The White Stripes, which consisted of Jack White and his ex-wife, Meg White.Photograph: Tim Roney/Getty ImagesThe White StripesDaily Mail accused of stalking woman mistaken as White Stripes drummer Meg WhiteThe tabloid boasted in a now-deleted article that they found White and  promised to reveal her ‘secret new life’Sean CraigFri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Daily Mail newspaper secretly tailed and photographed a woman in Detroit and then published an article and photographs falsely accusing her of being formerThe White Stripesdrummer Meg White, even after she told the newspaper it had mistaken her identity, multiple sources have told the Guardian.The rightwing British tabloid quietly removed the article and photographs, first published on 6 August, from its website last week. The Mail did not issue a correction or editor’s note explaining the removal.Hailed for her inspired use of raw power and space, White wasnamedone of the 100 greatest drummers of all time by Rolling Stone in 2016. Since The White Stripes disbanded in 2011, she has lived as a private citizen in the band’s Michigan home city, eschewing all media appearances and public events.When the highly acclaimed garage rock duo wasinductedinto the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame last year, she declined to attend and instead sent a message of gratitude via former bandmate Jack White.The Mail’s story, written by senior reporter Joe Hutchison, boasted that the paper had found the “reclusive female music megastar” and promised to reveal her “secret new life”, including what it claimed were the first public images of White in 17 years.Instead, the Guardian has been told that the paper followed and photographed a completely different person who is a friend of White’s. The Mail published more than a dozen pictures taken of the unsuspecting woman getting out of a vehicle and socializing with two others outside a restaurant.“Neither Meg nor the friend that was pictured had any idea they were being stalked and, if they had, they for sure would not have voluntarily chosen to be featured in anything having to do with theDaily Mail,” said a music label executive who was involved in multiple White Stripes releases, and who is close friends with both White and the friend that was photographed.Speaking to the Guardian on the condition of anonymity, they confirmed that the woman the Mail photographed and White were not interested in speaking to the press. “I can also assure you that Meg is well and is living the private life she chooses and deserves inDetroit,” they added.According to its own reporting, when the Mail finally approached and accused the woman of being White, she laughed and told the paper it was mistaken.Hutchison wrote that, despite this, the paper concluded she was White because she politely replied “thank you” after the Mail complimented The White Stripes’ music.“That tells the reader and the journalist exactly nothing,” said Dan Axelrod, the chair of the ethics committee at the Society of Professional Journalists, whose code of ethics is one of the most widely cited in the industry. “The person being photographed could’ve been toying with the reporter or may not have heard the question properly and was saying ‘thanks’ to be politely dismissive.”The paper offered no justification for its attempt to pursue and surreptitiously photograph someone who has lived out of the spotlight for 15 years.“What’s so disheartening is the great lengths they took to try and hunt her down and how reckless and cruel it was to post images of another woman all over the internet,” wrote singer-songwriter Karen Elson, the ex-spouse of Jack White, in a since-deleted social media post seen by the Guardian.Elson also stated the woman is a friend of Meg White, adding she is someone “who we also love tremendously”.A third person, a member of a Detroit-area band that knows White and the woman in the pictures, also confirmed the Mail’s error to the Guardian.The Mail, which wasbannedas a source by moderators on Wikipedia because of its reputation for “flat-out fabrication”, is well known for its voyeuristic celebrity coverage. “We take great pride in the quality of our journalism,” the paper states on its website. The paper’s editorial code states “a significant inaccuracy, misleading statement or distortion must be corrected, promptly and with due prominence.”“Tabloids like this tend to view celebrity status as permission to do whatever in terms of violating privacy under the guise of ‘they are public figures so they have to expect this and/or even are asking for it,’” said Erin Meyers, a professor of communication at metro Detroit’s Oakland University who studies media coverage of celebrity.“The fact that a private citizen got caught up in all of this should merit at the very least a correction, if not a full apology,” she added. “But I don’t think that fits in with their bulldog sort of approach to reporting, so instead they just bury it.”The Daily Mail and Hutchison did not reply to multiple requests for comment.The Dacre dynasty: how Britain’s rightwing press was radicalisedRead moreAxelrod said that, while “celebrity and gossip reporting gets stereotyped as inherently unethical, frivolous, and even inhumane,” tabloid reporting “can be ethical and substantive – just look at how just look at how the National Enquirer exposed John Edwards’ extramarital affair”.But the Mail, he observed, “followed none of the most basic principles of journalism”, and the woman it followed “didn’t deserve to be chased around by the Daily Mail, ogled, photographed, and chronicled like a circus bear”.“The SPJ Code of Ethics reminds journalists to ‘realize that private people have a greater right to control information about themselves than public figures’ and to ‘weigh the consequences of publishing or broadcasting personal information’,” he added. “With the power to reach and convince millions of people of facts, the Daily Mail can still be a unique tabloid that entertains and informs without sacrificing accuracy or being inhumane to those it covers.”Representatives for White did not reply to requests for comment.Explore more on these topicsThe White StripesDaily Mail & General TrustDetroitDaily MailNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Odyssey becomes highest grossing R-rated film of all time | Movies | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine
Content: The Odyssey has been R-rated – meaning anyone under 17 must be accompanied by an adult – for ‘violence and some language’.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Odyssey has been R-rated – meaning anyone under 17 must be accompanied by an adult – for ‘violence and some language’.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesThe Odyssey becomes highest grossing R-rated film of all timeChristopher Nolan’s epic has achieved $1.35bn at the global box office, overtaking 2024’s Deadpool & WolverineAndrew PulverFri 21 Aug 2026 06.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has overtaken Deadpool & Wolverine to become the highest grossing R-rated film of all time.According to figures compiled by the Numbers, Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s epic poem has achieved $1.35bn (£990m) at the worldwide box office, compared withthe Ryan Reynolds/Hugh Jackman superhero movie, which stands at $1.34bn (£980m) since its release in 2024.A R-rating as designated by the Motion Picture Association requires anyone under 17 to be accompanied by an adult, and is normally seen as a brake on box office expectations. In its citation, the MPA said The Odyssey was given an R-rating “for violence and some language”.In the UK, The Odyssey has beenrated 15for “strong violence”, while in Australia it has anM-ratingfor “mature themes, violence and coarse language”.Other R-rated features to do well include Nolan’s previous film Oppenheimer, which benefited from the “Barbenheimer” craze to amass $983m worldwide, the Joaquin Phoenix-starring Joker ($1.1bn), and the two standalone Deadpool movies ($782m and $786m respectively).View image in fullscreenHugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, which stands at $1.34bn at the worldwide box office.Photograph: Jay MaidmentAt the North American box office alone, Deadpool & Wolverine remains ahead, having taken $637m against The Odyssey’s $516m. Interest in Nolan’s film, however, is high in other areas of the world: the UK and Ireland’s total of $92.7m is the second highest, followed by France on $69.3m and Italy on $55.6m. China has also contributed a significant amount to The Odyssey’s coffers, with a reported $36.3m.Starring Matt Damon as Odysseus, Tom Holland as Telemachus and Anne Hathaway as Penelope,the film is already the most successful of Nolan’s career, having surpassed his previous highest grossing film, 2012’s The Dark Knight Rises, which has earned $1.082bn (£805.7m) globally.However, The Odyssey’s figures could well rise significantly as it is currently in the middle of a box office battle with Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has alreadytaken more than $2bn worldwide, becoming the second fastest film to do so (after Avengers: Endgame in 2019).Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyFilm industryDeadpool & WolverineChristopher NolannewsShareReuse this content

title: See the Light: Tracey Emin and Steve McQueen illuminate Durham gallery’s revival | Museums | The Guardian
description: Art of international significance planned for £17m redevelopment of museum whose closure sparked uproar
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Art of international significance planned for £17m redevelopment of museum whose closure sparked uproar
Content: The Light, a new contemporary gallery opening in Durham.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Light, a new contemporary gallery opening in Durham.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianMuseumsSee the Light: Tracey Emin and Steve McQueen illuminate Durham gallery’s revivalArt of international significance planned for £17m redevelopment of museum whose closure sparked uproarMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorks by Tracey Emin, Steve McQueen and Olafur Eliasson have gone on display at a new contemporary art gallery and museum in north-east England which aims to show works of international significance.The Lightis a £17mredevelopment of a museum in Durhamthat closed 10 years ago to local uproar.Then it was the Durham Light Infantry Museum andArtGallery. Today it is just the Light, which opens to the public on Saturday with galleries on one floor telling military stories in a human and modern way, while upstairs is 500 sq metres of space for contemporary art.View image in fullscreenThe Light, Durham.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThe opening is part of a bigger cultural story of getting arts and culture to places in England that have felt overlooked and forgotten.The Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art opened in Gateshead in 2002 and Mima – the venue for this year’s Turner prize – opened in Middlesbrough in 2007. They were followed by the likes ofFirstsitein Colchester and the Hepworth in Wakefield. But the opening of new, publicly funded regional galleries had largely dried up, until now.Tony Guillan, who joined as artistic director three months ago, said his story played into that narrative. “I grew up on Tyneside but then left, as many people do, at the age of 18.” He worked in London at organisations including Tate and the Southbank Centre. “I always thought it would be nice to come back but there has been a dearth of opportunity.View image in fullscreenArtistic director Tony Guillan grew up on Tyneside, worked in London, and has returned to the north-east.Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian“Why do you have to leave and move so far away if you want to have a certain type of career? I think perhaps more than any country in Europe we’re so centralised in London, it feels like it has far too many industries, not least the creative and cultural industries.”The development of the Light has been a long, slow process and it opens in a county where, since Labour was virtually wiped out in the 2024 local election, Reform is running the show politically.The Light is funded by Durham county council, but there is little sign in the opening exhibition that the curators are looking over their shoulders in terms of the art they are displaying. It includes works that address themes including immigration.View image in fullscreenStuart Haygarth’s Shadey Family on show in The Light is composed of 62 vintage glass lampshades.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianArt will always have a contentious side, Guillan said. “It’s our role to create the space for dialogue. We’ve recently showed all the politicians and our corporate leadership around. They love what we’re doing. They love the ambition. They are really ambitious. So I’m very confident we’re going to have the kind of space to explore what we want to.”The curators said they wanted to show contemporary art of national and international significance. The inaugural exhibition features artists including the US artist Dan Flavin, famous for his use of fluorescent light tubes, and the Cuban-born US conceptual artist Félix González-Torres, who died in 1996, aged 38. His piece, his first use of lightbulbs, was made after the death of his partner Ross Laycock from an Aids-related illness and is about their unending love.View image in fullscreenDan Flavin’s Untitled, 1987.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianNatasha Howes, who curated the opening show, said she had worked hard to include a good number of women and global majority artists because too many exhibitions were still dominated by white men.“Last year I was looking at a festival in Spain and I think there were 30 artists and no women. I just thought: ‘How is that allowed to happen?’”The Light opens on Saturday 22 August.Explore more on these topicsMuseumsExhibitionsNorth of EnglandHeritageArtCounty DurhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Brooke Shields stars in a silly murder-mystery comedy  | Television | The Guardian
description: A novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: They’re on the case …  Andi (Amalia Williamson) and, right, Allie (Brooke Shields) in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVView image in fullscreenThey’re on the case …  Andi (Amalia Williamson) and, right, Allie (Brooke Shields) in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Brooke Shields stars in a silly murder-mystery comedyA novelist and a podcaster are an unlikely crime-solving team in You’re Killing Me. Plus: get ready to cry over a robot. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellFri 21 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaAllie (Brooke Shields) is a bestselling “menopausal mystery” novelist; Andi (Amalia Williamson) is an aspiring true-crime podcaster. When they meet at a writing convention, it’s a boomer and gen Z culture clash. But then a murder takes place and the two team up to solve the case … Light, rompy crime drama fun.Hollie RichardsonMiles Davis: A Celebration at the Proms8pm, BBC FourCatch it on the radio or sit down and witness jazz trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire in action, as he joins conductor Miho Hazama and the BBC Concert Orchestra to celebrate the legacy of Miles Davis. It’s a night of music from Porgy and Bess, Sketches of Spain and more.HRBergerac9pm, BBC TwoJim Bergerac (Damien Molony) starts the tense season finale of the crime drama reboot at rock bottom, mentally dishevelled and facing the loss of his daughter at the hands of a vengeful criminal who thinks Bergerac fitted him up years ago. An at-gunpoint warehouse showdown beckons, as does a test of loyalty for Bergerac’s colleagues.Jack SealeStation Eleven9pm, Sky AtlanticIf you missed this pandemic drama the first time round, it’s well worth catching up. In these final two episodes, Jeevan (Himesh Patel) gets a crash course in obstetric medicine, there’s an emotional performance of Hamlet, and revelations abound about Miranda (Danielle Deadwyler), creator of the Station Eleven comic.Hannah J DaviesAnn Droid9.30pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenAn emotional ending … Sue (Sue Johnston) and Linda (Diane Morgan) in Ann Droid.Photograph: BBC/Boffola Pictures/Gary MoyesTissues at the ready for an emotional ending to a sitcom that has been both side-splittingly funny and deeply poignant. Sue (Sue Johnston) is saddened when her son says they no longer need carer robot Linda (Diane Morgan). But what happens to Linda when she’s sent back? Let’s just say, fingers crossed for a second season.HRGrimsburg10.45pm, Sky OneThis adult animation starring Jon Hamm as a small-town detective isn’t as sharp as the likes of BoJack Horseman, tending towards the scattergun chaos of Family Guy. Still, there are moments of brilliance in this triple bill, starting with an episode guest-starring Amy Sedaris as a troubled former child star.HJDFilm choiceLes Yeux Sans Visage(Georges Franju, 1960),12.50am, Talking Pictures TVView image in fullscreenEerie … Édith Scob (left) and Alida Valli in Les Yeux Sans Visage.Photograph: Cinetext/The Criterion Collection/AllstarGeorges Franju’s arresting 1960 horror is as interested in dreamlike images as jump-scare moments of terror – and in Édith Scob’s Christiane has a monster with the pathos of Frankenstein’s creature. Disfigured after a car accident, she sports a lifelike but eerie facial mask and drifts around her country house like a pale white ghost. Meanwhile, her surgeon father, Dr Génessier (Pierre Brasseur), and his assistant Louise (Alida Valli) abduct young women to supply full-face skin grafts for her. It’s occasionally grisly but mostly unsettling.Simon WardellLive sportPremier League football:Arsenal v Coventry6.30pm, Sky Sports Main Event.
