title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest
Author: John Self
Headline: The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest
Content: A sense of the ridiculous and the serious … Pirkko Saisio.Photograph: Pirjo HonkasaloView image in fullscreenA sense of the ridiculous and the serious … Pirkko Saisio.Photograph: Pirjo HonkasaloTranslated fiction roundupFictionReviewThe best recent translated fiction – review roundupThe Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra KamiyaJohn SelfFri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Red Book of Farewellsby Pirkko Saisio, translated by Mia Spangenberg, PenguinClassics (£14.99)Following Lowest Common Denominator and Backlight, this book completes Finnish author Saisio’s autofictional trilogy. It covers her young adulthood in the 1970s, where she comes out as lesbian (“The electricity doesn’t go out. The Richter scale remains still”) and falls in love. One of her lovers, Havva, is a communist who’s engaged to a man; she relies on his rich parents for funding, but pees in their private pool as a protest. Later, Saisio is voted vice-president of a political drama company, as “she has the skills to bring about the revolution, specifically via theatre” – despite half-baked productions such as the “napalm opera” Vietnam-a-Go-Go. As that suggests, this is a story with a sense of both the ridiculous and the serious. Told in clear prose, it playfully shifts between third and first person as Saisio recounts her memories then analyses them. This enchanting series deserves to become a modern classic.Short Circuitby Wolf Haas, translated by Jamie Bulloch (HarperVia, £20)“We think [time] goes in one direction. But really you need to think of it as a loop”. This, well, loopy novel opens with jigsaw aficionado and “merciless hair-splitter” Franz Escher getting an electrician in to fix his power – then accidentally killing him. As Franz waits for the ambulance, he reads a novel about Elio, a man who helped put his own mafia family behind bars. Elio, who’s now on witness protection, kills time by reading a novel about … Franz Escher. The two stories pursue one another, accelerating until they collide, incorporating courtship by car alarm, rival funeral orators and multiple identities for many characters. Oh, and what if the electrician Franz killed turns out to be Elio? Short Circuit,recallingthe slipstream fiction ofChristopher Priestand the light-touch experimentations of David Mitchell, is an entertaining literary hall-of-mirrors.Cosmosby Lucia Odoom, translated by Hunter Simpson (Daunt, £10.99)“Lately my leap feels more and more like a fall,” writes Cosmos, a young Ghanaian man who has migrated to Copenhagen, where he contends with Denmark’s “worrying lack of smells” and collects recyclable bottles to earn money. Later he gets a job modelling, and lets the agency believe he’s an asylum seeker so they’ll feel sorry for him. He falls in love with Elizabeth: when she describes something as a guilty pleasure, “I asked her what a guilty pleasure was”. The past presses in: when Elizabeth takes him to the seaside, he recalls the vomit-streaked boat journey to Europe. All this is told in WhatsApp messages to Cosmos’s family back home – even the sex scenes. It’s a story of the challenges and hopes of a migrant’s life, made charming by the funny narrative voice and Cosmos’s optimism: he can see a plane and imagine being a crow, “flying high above the world, high above everything that no one owns”.The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra Kamiya, translated by Daniel Hahn (Pushkin, £12.99)In this collection of stories from a Japanese-Argentinian writer, people rarely say what they mean. The dark secret beneath a woman’s meticulous breakfast preparations is hinted at through imagery: a flower, “open like a yelling mouth”. A story where a family attempts to cope when their son leaves by not talking about him (“I learned to differentiate between many different types of silence”) reads like an epic in miniature. There is black comedy – a woman asks her maid to help her read the letters on an optician’s chart – as well as intense psychological drama, in the tale of a soldier who is told to “dig here until further orders” and keeps going, and going, and going. Kamiya’s collection is remarkable in its variety but united by its laconic, sometimes elliptical style. These are teasing, satisfying stories to be savoured slowly.Explore more on these topicsFictionTranslated fiction roundupFiction in translationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A History of Paper review – Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming sing a fragile romance | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Oliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receipts
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Oliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receipts
Content: Airy and joyful … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenAiry and joyful … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewA History of Paper review – Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming sing a fragile romancePitlochry Festival theatreOliver Emanuel’s musical love story between tenement neighbours is told via origami gifts and restaurant receiptsMark FisherFri 21 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started as a BBC radio drama in 2016, and was reworked asa small-scale musicaltwo years ago. Now, A History of Paper gets the mainstage treatment with two bona fide stars in the leads. The good news is that little is overblown about the production. Stars or not, Shirley Henderson and Alan Cumming only bring a greater degree of subtlety to this fragile work.Written by the late playwrightOliver Emanueland composer Gareth Williams, it recounts an everyday romance through the medium of paper: the postcard messages, the origami gifts, the Pizza Express receipts, the shopping lists and the confetti. A cardboard box full of such detritus is a neat way to encapsulate both the grand emotions and the ephemera that sustain a love affair. Henderson and Cumming carry it with due lightness.View image in fullscreenA touch overbearing … A History of Paper.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanDirected by Dundee Rep’s Andrew Panton, they are the tenement neighbours who go from ratty and rattled to curious and flirtatious. Where Cumming has a puppyish enthusiasm – bounding out of a morose heartbreak soundtracked by Radiohead – Henderson is variously obstinate, contrary and funny.Hers is a fascinatingly unpredictable performance, not least when bending the rhythms of Williams’s songs: talk-singing one minute, soaring to melodic heights the next. Her duets with Cumming under Gavin Whitworth’s musical direction are things of beauty. Dressed down in jeans, cardigans and unbuttoned sleeves, the actors’ presence is airy and joyful. They pace around as if yet to decide where they will go next.On a set by Ana Inés Jabares-Pita, half rugged Fife coast, half Ground Zero and a touch overbearing, this is also a 9/11 play. Emanuel took its theme from the paper that cascaded like snow from the twin towers after they were struck. For all the narrative neatness, the play piggybacks on that event in a way that feels manipulative. No love story, however tender or calamitous, could equal the tragedy of that day.Otherwise, though, the emotions are true and, as Panton uses the bigger scale to his advantage, with Henderson stalking the auditorium and papery interventions from above, it makes for a short, sweet and touching chamber piece.AtPitlochry Festival theatreuntil 12 September. Then atDundee Rep, 16–19 September.Explore more on these topicsTheatreAlan CummingDundee RepPitlochry Festival theatreShirley HendersonMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the righteous jangle and snaking melodies of Jawdropped and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater tradition
Author: Huw Baines
Headline: The LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater tradition
Content: Sun-bleached cool … Jawdropped.Photograph: Julien SageView image in fullscreenSun-bleached cool … Jawdropped.Photograph: Julien SageAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the righteous jangle and snaking melodies of Jawdropped and the week’s best new tracksThe LA-based powerpop project’s triumphant debut is a celebration of low-stakes creativity in the slacker-skater traditionHuw BainesandLaura SnapesFri 21 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromLos AngelesRecommended if you likethe Lemonheads, Sugar, the MuffsUp nextSecret to Spare released 18 SeptemberMaybe it’s to do with getting older, maybe it’s to do with the broad-spectrum grimness of it all, but the thrill of low-stakes creativity, of making something for the joy of making it rather than in the hope ofmaking it, feels particularly vital at the moment. And, if the sun-bleached cool of Jawdropped’s music is anything to go by, starting a powerpop project in your 30s will light up this pleasure centre like a dive bar pinball machine.The US quartet are all on their second, third or fourth go-around with this band thing, having spent years skating through LA’s DIY scenes before forming in 2024. Their chemistry and compositional smarts became immediately apparent on the following year’sJust FantasyEP, where co-vocalists Kyra Morling and Roman Zangari tumbled into slacker harmony over blown-out distortion and plaid-swaddled acoustic guitars.Leaning into the idea of small wins on your own terms, their debut album Secret to Spare offers a collection of stories about keeping your head above water, its luminous hooks casting the plate-spinning of day jobs, house shows and routine disappointments in a triumphant light. The Line has the righteous jangle of peak Lemonheads on a string, whileMonday’s snaking melodies are amped up by gnarly power chord scuzz in the Bob Mould tradition. The singleSplit Liphits bittersweet paydirt with a lilting chorus that doubles as another dose of reality: “Sign us all to a major label / It doesn’t always work out.” It doesn’t. But perhaps that’s OK.Huw BainesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenShygirl.Photograph: Jessica MadavoShygirl – AlyseHere’s a stunning new side to the south Londoner: imagine Bat for Lashes’ crystal-ball balladry dragged feet-first into a cybergoth club and blown up to the scope of Madonna’s William Orbit era. A thrill!Fontaines DC –Marianne“I can help you disappear,” Grian Chatten offers in a dangerously alluring chorus and a song full of cinematic gloom that more than fulfils the Irish heroes’ promise of absolution.Wild Pink – Still Coming DownIf, apparently like many of alt rock’s leading lights right now, you can’t hear Jason Molina’s influence enough, you won’t complain at hearing another gorgeously grizzled slab of Americana in his image.Actress – WithendingThe beautifully intricate synth refrain at the heart of this track undulates as beguilingly as kelp in the ocean deep, dragged deeper by insistent kick drum and haunted by vocal sprites.Heavens to Betsy – Ain’t Never Goin’ Back“I ain’t never goin’ back,” a teenaged Corin Tucker – future of Sleater-Kinney – sings in this unearthed Modern Lovers-ish demo fromthe newly reunited riot grrrl legends, slinging an arrow into the future.Lover1k – On My OwnSome might call it trash, but anyone addicted to the genre of club music best described as “withering woman sounds deathly unimpressed by you over crude beats” … it’s your lucky day.Teenage Fanclub – There Was YouFear not, trash-haters, we’re back on solid ground with Norman Blake and this gently baroque, beautifully wistful tribute to those people that always offer a port in a storm (much like the Fannies always do).Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gaia Wilmer Large Ensemble: Parabólico review – gorgeous reinvention of Gilberto Gil’s grooves | Music | The Guardian
description: Saxophonist and composer Wilmer brilliantly transforms Gil tunes, changing tempos and adding breathy melodies, flourishes of horns or undulating rhythms to luscious effect
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Saxophonist and composer Wilmer brilliantly transforms Gil tunes, changing tempos and adding breathy melodies, flourishes of horns or undulating rhythms to luscious effect
Content: Radical reinventions … Gaia Wilmer.Photograph: Dani GurgelView image in fullscreenRadical reinventions … Gaia Wilmer.Photograph: Dani GurgelGlobal album of the monthMusicReviewGaia Wilmer Large Ensemble: Parabólico review – gorgeous reinvention of Gilberto Gil’s grooves(Sunnyside)Saxophonist and composer Wilmer brilliantly transforms Gil tunes, changing tempos and adding breathy melodies, flourishes of horns or undulating rhythms to luscious effectAmmar KaliaFri 21 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past three years, Brazilian saxophonist and composer Gaia Wilmer has reimagined the catalogues of her country’s virtuosos so radically that it’s become a signature art. Folia: The Music of Egberto Gismonti transformed his finger-picked melodics into an almost prog-influenced cacophony; Trem das Cores, celebrating tropicália pioneer Caetano Veloso, found the eerie tenderness in his lilting melodies. Now returning with the first part of a three-volume homage to singer Gilberto Gil, Wilmer and her 20-piece ensemble produce luscious new works from their deconstructions.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Parabólico: Reflections on Gilberto Gil, Volume I.Photograph: Sunnyside RecordsFor listeners familiar with Gil’s music, hardly any of Wilmer’s arrangements are recognisable from the originals. Her Overture transforms the 25 seconds of strummed guitars and group vocals that open Gil’s 1985 album Dia Dorim Noite Neon into a slowly unfurling four minutes of breathy trumpet melody and twinkling piano accents. Oriente replaces Gil’s wavering, emotive vocal harmony from the 1972 original with flourishes of horn fanfares and jazz swing that bolsters singer Mônica Salmaso’s lightly tripping bossa nova vocalisations. Eu Vim da Bahia even slows one of Gil’s best-known tunes to experimental flute-heavy ambience, transmuting his sprightly melody through the brassy weight of a big-band horn section.Rather than searching for similarities between Wilmer’s arrangements and Gil’s work, the beauty of Parabólico is Wilmer’s ability to reinvent and expand this music while retaining elements of its soul. Aqui e Agora enhances Gil’s trance-like mood with an undulating bass motif that anchors a keening saxophone solo, while Parabolicamará reframes his lively groove through beautifully delicate opening improvisations from pianist Vitor Gonçalves. Instead of covering work that has already been bested by Gil himself, Wilmer’s Ship of Theseus-style project celebrates the remarkable depth that remains to be explored and renewed in these decades-old works.Also out this monthLatin ensembleOrquesta Akokán’s latest albumAmérica! (Daptone) is a heady blend of salsa, cha cha, boogaloo and jazz swing, perfect for playing on sweltering summer days. Singers Miriam Elhajli and Carolina Oliveros are a highlight, soaring through the lithe melodies on No Me Voy and Hace Tiempo. Jordanian-Palestinian singerDana Salahreleases her new album Bent Bladna (Empire), pairing her delicate Arabic vocals with everything from bassy hip-hop swagger to dancehall and dabke rhythms on standout tune Wedding Riddim. Dub producer Adrian Sherwood’s album with Ghanaian singerKing Ayisoba,Pure Confusion (On-U Sound), finds the bass-weight in his two-string kologo lute playing and carves out reverb-laden space for raw vocals that reach an apex on the yearning screams of Leeda-Mampanga.Explore more on these topicsMusicGlobal album of the monthJazzreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stella Lefty: Long Way Home review – Boston singer’s debut is bland, boilerplate and beyond banal | Music | The Guardian
description: The breakout 24-year-old country star’s debut is stunningly unremarkable, offering little in the way of artistic identity or her peers’ originality
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The breakout 24-year-old country star’s debut is stunningly unremarkable, offering little in the way of artistic identity or her peers’ originality
Content: Hard to tell what her USP is … Stella Lefty.Photograph: Jack BalabanView image in fullscreenHard to tell what her USP is … Stella Lefty.Photograph: Jack BalabanMusicReviewStella Lefty: Long Way Home review – Boston singer’s debut is bland, boilerplate and beyond banal(Atlantic Outpost)The breakout 24-year-old country star’s debut is stunningly unremarkable, offering little in the way of artistic identity or her peers’ originalityLaura SnapesFri 21 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnyone railing against nepo babies taking over culture has already lost: the rage they engender is as key to the publicity plan as their ready-made profile. But once in a while, you meet one so egregious that it’s hard not to want to flip a table. The breakout 24-year-old country star Stella Lefty is the daughter of a multibillionaire Groupon co-founder. Given her stunningly unremarkable songwriting, you wonder whether that might explain a few things.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Long Way Home.Photograph: Jack BalabanAfter gaining notice for posting clips of her music, Lefty wanted to work as a songwriter-for-hire until music execs insisted she was anartist. It’s hard to tell what her USP is: her huge hit Boston sounded so much like Noah Kahan’s Stick Season that she had to add a retrospective credit. Her writing has none of his introspection or regional specifics, nor the wry country literacy of close competitor Ella Langley. In Lefty’s songs, she’s often catching some guy’s eye at the bar. Maybe they get together but then she runs, because she always does – but maybe this time, she doesn’t? She knows it’s good when he’s nice to her, or they look good in photos. Props: whiskey, neon lights, bar stools. It’s relatable, right? Right??The sound of Long Way Home is just as indistinct and trope-ridden. Lefty’s putatively “authentic” and grating vocal rasp just highlights the Cali-raised singer’s fake southern accent. There are the songs that evoke drunk gal pals hollerin’ and hootin’ at a dusty bar, the cute banjo-cluckin’ ones, a few heavier numbers. It’s wallpaper for made-for-Netflix movies, beach bars and GRWM videos. All in all, she’s a fine inheritor of the knockdown family business.Explore more on these topicsMusicCountryPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 review – once more unto the mercenary breach | Games | The Guardian
description: This second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releases
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releases
Content: Inhuman hustle … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiView image in fullscreenInhuman hustle … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiGamesReviewMetal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 review – once more unto the mercenary breachPC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5, Xbox Series X/S; KonamiThis second collection remasters another three titles from the illustrious stealth espionage series, but their world has changed little since the original releasesDiego Nicolás ArgüelloFri 21 Aug 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘War has changed,” claims Old Snake in Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. Back in 2008, the team at Kojima Productions waxed poetic about people recruited to fight in proxy wars they have no political or ideological stake in. As these mercenaries follow their orders, traders get rich out of the so-called war economy. The more disastrous the conflict in a specific area, the higher the bidding price.I expected my time with Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 to be nostalgic and, in good old MGS fashion, abundant with fictional events that sound eerily familiar to our current reality. Twenty minutes in, I was having an existential crisis.The package bundles remastered renditions of stealth games Ghost Babel and Peace Walker and the aforementioned Guns of the Patriots. It’s an intriguing selection, spanning a Game Boy Colour reimagination, a PlayStation Portable prequel, and the culmination of the mainline series respectively. Despite being substantially distinct in isolation, all three entries focus on perpetuating acts of cruelty in order to collect a paycheque.View image in fullscreenWar hasn’t changed … Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2.Photograph: KonamiOld Snake willingly takes part in the war economy, every downed soldier dropping their weapon with a satisfyingclink. When picked up, each gun is automatically sold to a black market trader for points, which can be exchanged for bigger, deadlier materiel. An enemy squad stepping on a landmine is no different from unlocking a shiny loot box.Conflict is welcomed as long as it’s profitable. It puts food on the table for the group of mercenaries you lead in Peace Walker and the private military companies in Guns of the Patriots – it has also been the fuel of real-lifeprediction markets. The members of the fictional private military companies are IDed and monitored in real-time by an AI program, while in real lifevideo game datais used to train AI that can be used by the military, with game companiesfacing boycottsfor their alleged involvement in war and genocide.In 2026, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 is whiplash disguised as a trip down memory lane. As a collection, it’s an odd time capsule. Ghost Babel is almost a de-make, following in the footsteps of the original MSX entries while adapting modern mechanics and conventions, from sound detection to overly long cutscenes. Peace Walker, meanwhile, retains the roots of the current live service era – you can play both the main missions and side objectives with up to three other players online – without the predatory microtransactions and battle passes of today.Lastly, while all three games embody nostalgia, Guns of the Patriots is the epitome. Mentions of familiar characters prompt you to repeatedly press a button to get rapid-fire flashbacks to their previous appearances. There’s no shortage of reunions and nods to the entire series, with a fair degree of fan service mixed in. In an era ofremakes, unnecessary sequels and constant recycling of protagonists, it’s satisfying to revisit an entry that dared to put a nail in the coffin without hesitation.All three games now look better and are more easily accessible. The experiences are, for the most part, just as you remember them. As far as remasters go, you’ll feel right at home. At their core, the message is as eternal as ever: war, and its surrounding economy, hasn’t changed. The only noticeable difference is the inflation rate.Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 will be released on 27 August; £44.99Explore more on these topicsGamesMetal Gear Solid VPCPlayStation 5Nintendo SwitchNintendo Switch 2Xbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpse | Games | The Guardian
description: Free from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first game
Author: Bex April May
Headline: Free from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first game
Content: ‘The weakest of the weak’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50View image in fullscreen‘The weakest of the weak’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50Summer games previewsGamesStupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpseFree from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first gameBex April MayFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLove is blind. In Stupid Never Dies, it is also frozen solid and technically dead as Davy, the weakest zombie in monster society, discovers Julia’s body in a shopping centre and falls in love at first sight. He wants to bring her back to life and take her on a date. Unfortunately, that means defeating the King of Monsters (KOM) and accidentally saving humanity along the way.This is the gloriously ridiculous setup for this forthcoming action RPG from GPTrack50, a new studio founded by former Capcom producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi. Its world looks much like ours, except that monsters have always been part of everyday life: whereas we might find a bear in the mountains or a stray dog in the woods, residents here encounter werewolves and zombies.View image in fullscreenEveryday monsters … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50That uneasy normality ends when KOM crushes civilisation and leaves only 2% of humanity alive. Davy begins even lower down the social ladder.Zombies, says Kobayashi, are “the weakest of the weak”. But eating a mysterious egg gives this particularly unimpressive corpse the power to fight back.Because Davy is already dead, combat throws out the usual need for self-preservation. Forget defence: guarding and dodging are pushed aside in favour of “attacking, attacking, attacking”. Kobayashi describes it as a game made “by the action game lover, for the action gamer”.View image in fullscreen‘Funky zombie action’ … Stupid Never Dies.Photograph: GPTrack50Its two main systems make full use of Davy’s unreliable body. He can consume defeated monsters, steal their skills and transform into creatures including a werewolf, vampire or harpy. The “body hack” mechanic goes further, allowing players to replace his head, arms and legs with equipment. Attach a sword to an arm and Davy gains sword attacks; fit a gun and he starts shooting. Being undead has never looked so practical.Kobayashi calls the result “funky zombie action”, a phrase coined to give the development team a shared idea of the game’s tone: fast, colourful and darkly funny. It also captures the freedom Kobayashi found after years working on some of the world’s most famous franchises, includingResident EvilandDevil May Cry.Large franchises bring large audiences and expectations. A new studio making a new IP had neither. As Kobayashi says, “We don’t have a fan yet.” That has allowed its team of around 30 developers, many recruited from companies including Capcom, Konami and Square Enix, to use stranger jokes and sharper humour than they ever could when working on those older series.The studio itself began almost as scrappily as Davy. In its early months, GPTrack50 had programmers and designers but no artists, so the team bought outside assets to build a rough white-box prototype. Around 20 external companies eventually joined the three-year production, drawn, Kobayashi says, by the chance to create something completely from scratch. He hopes players finish thinking: “This is the experience that I was looking for. This is a new thing.”Underneath the monster-eating and gun-limbs is a simple underdog story: Davy rises from the bottom of monster society to challenge its king, but he is not driven by glory. Saving the remaining humans is almost incidental, as Kobayashi explains: “He wants to go out for a date [with] this frozen girl.”Romance isn’t dead; it just needs defrosting.Stupid Never Dies is available onPCand PS5 from 21 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAction gamesZombiesPCPlayStation 5featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tuscany may be beautiful, but do they sell sticks of rock?’: readers’ favourite UK holidays | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: Your best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secret
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: Your best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secret
Content: The beach at Hengistbury Head in Dorset.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe beach at Hengistbury Head in Dorset.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty Images/iStockphotoReaders' travel tipsUnited Kingdom holidays‘Tuscany may be beautiful, but do they sell sticks of rock?’: readers’ favourite UK holidaysYour best UK breaks include an island off Mull, a rail journey along the County Antrim coast and Dorset’s best-kept secretTell us about your favouriteunder-the-radar European city– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 21 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDorset’s take on the MediterraneanMudeford feels like one of England’s best-kept secrets, the sort of place visitors from abroad might never imagine exists here. Golden sand and sparkling water give it an almost Mediterranean feel, while Hengistbury Head adds beautiful coastal walks and wide-open views. Our perfect day is simple: arrive early, wander along the headland, let the children play on the beach, then stop at one of the relaxed cafes for lunch or an ice-cream. My tip is to take thelittle ferryacross the harbour – it turns an already lovely day out into a proper seaside adventure.Priti SingerLancashire’s Forest of BowlandView image in fullscreenThe Forest of Bowland has miles of moorland and valleys to explore.Photograph: Jon Sparks/AlamyThe Forest of Bowland covers a staggering 312 square miles of moorland, forests and valleys, dotted with the occasional village. It may be one of the best places for peace and quiet in England, and is also aDark Skiesarea. It’s perfect for walkers and cyclists. I visitedGisburn forest(where I only met two other people during a five-hour hike); Barley village, which attracts lots of walkers who climb Pendle Hill; and, for spectacular scenery, a trip through the Trough of Bowland is a must. For town life, I’d recommend Skipton, a 35-minute drive away, which has it all with a castle, canal and plentiful shops and restaurants. It’s also the southern gateway to the Yorkshire Dales.CatProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Crabbing and clean beaches in SuffolkView image in fullscreenWalberswick’s rowing-boat ferry.Photograph: Terry Mathews/AlamyWalberswick is popular with walkers and birders, and young families who come here to relax and go swimming on the clean beach or crabbing in the creek. A brilliant way to arrive at the town is on therowing-boat ferry(March to November) across the River Blyth from Southwold. It’s been in the same family for five generations. We had great seafood at heritage pubs like theAnchorand theBell. Across the water, there’s a lot of wonderful fish shops and the famousHarbour Inn.David Innes-WilkinIn search of the Lundy Bunny, DevonView image in fullscreenLundy offers a treasure trail of 27 letterboxes suitable for all ages.Photograph: Philip Bishop/AlamyLundy, off the north Devon coast, offers a hidden adventure for all ages by following the treasure trail of27 Lundy letterboxesspread over the island. Some are wooden boxes, some metal, but they are all hidden. There’s a set of clues to follow, and stamps collected including the elusive Lundy Bunny. My two preteen boys and I loved our exploration of this remote granite island, binoculars and compass in hand, identifying letterboxes, birds and wildlife during our magical trip there.Carol GodsmarkA spectacular rail trip in County AntrimView image in fullscreenWest Strand, Portrush.Photograph: Wirestock/Getty ImagesNo trip I’ve made as an adult has matched the buzz of my annual childhood day trip from Derry to Portrush. The Troubles were at their peak but Portrush was still largely unscathed and had a totally different atmosphere to Derry. The journey was completed by train from Coleraine, and what a train journey it is. The train hogs the coast the whole way and we would be beside ourselves when the big dipper of Barry’s Amusements came into view. We would spend the morning on the beach, fish and chips for lunch and a few hours in Barry’s before heading home. Tuscany may be beautiful but do they sell sticks of rock?Eve KearneyAn arty town in ShropshireView image in fullscreenThe House on Crutches museum in Bishop’s Castle.Photograph: Mike Hayward/AlamyFoxholes campsitesits on a hill above the arty west Shropshire town of Bishop’s Castle. The views across the Shropshire hills are splendid, and a 10-minute walk through fields leads you past a stone Buddha into the town stretched along a medieval high street. Visit theHouse on Crutches museumto get a feel for Shropshire rural life history, and be sure to check out its two brilliant pubs: theThree Tunsis probably Britain’s oldest licensed brewery, having started in 1642, while theSix Bellsprovides an unpretentious family-friendly welcome. For us, though, the highlight was theChai Shopand its charismatic owner Tahira. She serves delicious Indian snacks like bhajis and dal as well as traditional Indian sweets.Matt Luntskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCamping in south WalesView image in fullscreenView of Pen y Fan.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyWe’re by no means an experienced camping family, but we pitched up onRhydywernen Farmnear Brecon after the last August bank holiday and were able to feed goats that were as happy and hoppy as it gets. Before falling asleep to the whisper of a nearby stream and mini-waterfalls, we spent time stargazing as there was no light pollution – it felt we were somehow closer to the stars. A cool stream helped soothe us after a day of hiking on Pen y Fan, the tallest peak in Britain south of Cadair Idris in Eryri (Snowdonia). We had only just bought a tent that summer and then we fell in love with Wales, so we keep coming back for more.IzabelaNorthumberland’s atmospheric border townView image in fullscreenThe trio of bridges in Berwick-upon-Tweed.Photograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyBerwick-upon-Tweedis one of those places that feels more dramatic than its size suggests. I have visited twice, and I loved simply walking around, camera in hand. Its slightly strange sense of being a border town seems to permeate everything. Stand beside the River Tweed and you can see three bridges together: the old Berwick Bridge, the elegant Royal Tweed Bridge and the great Victorian railway viaduct of the Royal Border Bridge. Add theElizabethan walls, the North Sea and castle ruins, and Berwick feels perpetually poised between countries, centuries and land and sea. It makes a wonderfully atmospheric short break.Susanna CallaghanThe natural wonders of the WirralView image in fullscreenThe Roman Boathouse at Birkenhead Park.Photograph: Alan Novelli/AlamyThe Wirral and its country park, south-west of Liverpool, is a brilliant under-the-radar place for a UK summer holiday, full of walks and beaches.Birkenhead Parkis 57 hectares (140 acres) of meadows, fields, gardens, woodland, lakes and structures – we had picnics and family treasure hunts last summer. Opened in 1847, it inspired the 19th-century US landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted in his design of New York’s Central Park, so close your eyes and imagine you are in the Big Apple! Since 1995, it has been listed as a Grade I landscape by English Heritage. With its paths, fossil-hunting areas, bike trails and dramatic sunsets,Wirral country parkhelped us entertain our teenagers. Thurstaston beach and Port Sunlight village are great options too.NicolettaWinning tip: Caribbean vibes on the Isle of Mull, Inner HebridesView image in fullscreenDavid Balfour’s Bay.Photograph: Lynne Sutherland/AlamyDavid Balfour’s Bayis a remote and breathtaking sandy bay with clear turquoise waters and pristine white sands in a stunning setting – the tidal island of Erraid, just off south-west Mull. The play of bright sunshine on crystal clear water and waves is dazzling – it’s a literally brilliant place to visit. Throw in a few palm trees and, on a clear day, you could imagine you were in Barbados – and the sea temperature can reach a pleasant 18C in August and September. To reach the bay, walk from lovely Knockvologan beach at low tide. This scenic walk can be extended to explore the north side of Erraid, where there are magnificent views of the Sound of Iona. Just be careful of tides so you don’t get caught there – a swim back is invigorating – as I found out after an overlong afternoon snooze when some lapping waves woke me up.PeterView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysReaders' travel tipsFamily holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Cafe Cùil’s Buckfast bloody Maìri – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: The favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punch
Content: Cafe Cùil's Buckfast bloody Maìri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenCafe Cùil's Buckfast bloody Maìri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Cafe Cùil’s Buckfast bloody Maìri – recipeThe favourite spicy brunch cocktail gets a Scottish twist, complete with Buckfast and a slice of pickle for punchClare CoghillFri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is our take on the ultimate brunch cocktail, though of course we had to give it a Gaelic stamp of some kind, so have added a shot of Buckfast and renamed it Maìri. If you’re not familiar,Buckfastis a sweet tonic wine, apparently known for its “healing” properties, made in Devon by Benedictine monks, but that has been adopted by the Scots as our own.Buckfast bloody MaìriServes11 tsp capers, drained and very finely chopped1pickled gherkin, drained and very finely chopped1 tsp celery salt, or sea salt1 tbsp sriracha1 tbsp soy sauce1 tsp wholegrain mustard75ml tomato juice1 tsp sea salt1 tsp paprika50mlgin– we useRaasay25ml Buckfast tonic wineTo garnish1 lemon slice2 green olives1 slice pickleFirst, make the spicy tomato mix. Put the capers, gherkins, celery salt, sriracha, soy sauce and mustard in a small bowl, stir thoroughly, then add the tomato juice.Mix the sea salt and paprika on a small plate. Wet the rim of a tall glass, then roll it around in the salt and paprika mix, to coat.Fill the glass with ice, pour in the gin and Buckfast, then top with the tomato mix. Stir well with a long spoon, top with the lemon slice, olives and pickle, and serve.Clare Coghill, chef-owner,Café Cùil, Isle of SkyeExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodBritish food and drinkTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Blondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetness
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Blondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetness
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwiches.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotIce-cream and sorbetBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwichesBlondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetnessBenjamina EbuehiFri 21 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIce-cream sandwiches have really grown on me. I used to find them a bit tricky to eat; far too many of them had outer shells so hard they would crack a tooth, while the rest would turn to mush after a few minutes out of the freezer. Finding the balance between something that has enough structural integrity to hold a good wedge of ice-cream but still soft enough to bite once frozen isn’t all that easy, but blondies make a very good option.Rosemary and cherry blondie ice-cream sandwichesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appI love infusing blondies with fresh herbs to cut through some of the sweetness and add more depth. These would be great with tarragon or thyme, but today I’ve gone with rosemary for a piney, aromatic twist.Prep5 minCook1 hrChill/freeze12 hr+Makes8150g salted butter,plus extra for greasing2 fresh rosemary sprigs180g light brown sugar1 large egg1½ tbspwhole milk130g plain flour¼ tsp salt¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda1 litre vanilla ice-creamFor the cherries150gcherries30g caster sugarSqueeze of lemon juiceHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line a 23cm x 33cm baking tin.Put the butter and rosemary in a small pan and heat gently to melt. Continue cooking until the butter gets foamy and fragrant, and the milk solids turn brown. Pour everything into a bowl, remove and discard the rosemary, and cool to room temperature.Put the sugar in a large bowl and stir in the melted butter. Whisk in the egg until smooth, followed by the milk. Sift in the flour, salt and bicarb, and stir until smooth.Pour the batter into the prepared tin, spreading out evenly; it will be quite thin. Bake for 16-22 minutes, until the blondie looks set with crisp edges but is still a little soft in the middle. Let it cool completely in the tin, then chill in the fridge to firm up – at least six hours, but ideally overnight.Stone and slice the cherries in half, then add to a pan with the sugar and lemon juice and bring to the boil. Cook for a few minutes until the cherries are softened and syrupy; set aside to cool completely.Scoop the ice-cream into a large bowl, let it soften a little, then loosely fold in the cherries – try not to overmix. Cut the blondie in half widthways and scoop the ice-cream on to one half, taking it all the way to the edges. Carefully place the second blondie half on top, then wrap in clingfilm and freeze overnight, until firm.Unwrap and trim the edges to get neat sides, then slice into bars. Serve straight away or wrap individually in baking paper and pop back in the freezer.Explore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe sweet spotFoodDessertHerbs and spicesBiscuitsBakingrecipesShareReuse this content
